name: Abu Simbel: the temples Ramesses carved into a mountain
note: Orientation: two rock-cut temples c. 1264-1244 BC, 280 km south of Aswan, 40 km from Sudan; propaganda to Nubia (gold, trade route); rediscovered by Burckhardt 1813 (sand to the chins), opened by Belzoni 1817; moved 1964-68; the plan of the visit (facade, hall, sanctuary, then the small temple), light in the morning; the Sun Festival on 22 Oct is five days after this visit.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1264-1244 BC
summary: Two temples cut into a Nubian cliff by Ramesses II, buried by sand for centuries, then sawn apart and rebuilt on higher ground in the 1960s.
look: You are on the west shore of Lake Nasser, with two temple fronts cut into the hill and facing east over the water. With the lake behind you, the Great Temple of Ramesses II and its four seated giants is on the left; the Small Temple of Hathor and Nefertari, with six standing figures, is about 100 m to the right. Both hills are artificial: concrete domes dressed with rock, built when the temples were moved in 1964-68.
story:
Ramesses II had both temples carved into a sandstone cliff above the Nile from about 1264 BC, and the work took around 20 years. This was Nubia, about 230 km south-west of Aswan as the crow flies and some 40 km from today's Sudanese border: the land that gave Egypt its gold. The Great Temple honours the state gods and Ramesses himself as a god; the Small Temple honours Hathor and his chief wife Nefertari. Anyone sailing north on the river met them first.

Then the desert moved in. By the 6th century BC sand already reached the colossi's knees. In March 1813 the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt climbed down to the small temple, turned south, and saw one giant head sticking out of a dune. In 1816 the French ex-consul Drovetti left 300 piastres with the local sheikh to pay for digging; the money came back untouched, because nobody saw the use of small metal discs. Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman from Padua, persuaded them, and on 1 August 1817, after 22 days of shovelling, his party broke in. The first through the gap was the slimmest of them, Giovanni Finati, who found the air as hot and damp as a Turkish bath.

In September 1822 drawings of the cartouches here reached Jean-François Champollion in Paris; the first he read was the name Ramesses, a key moment in the decipherment of hieroglyphs. Six years later he crawled in himself, nearly naked, into 52 degrees of heat.

A good order for today: the Great Temple facade, its halls and sanctuary, then the Small Temple, then a look at the rescue. The facades face sunrise, so morning light is kindest. The Sun Festival, when the light reaches the sanctuary, falls on 22 October, five days after your visit.
details: Great Temple, second colossus from the left: its head and torso lie at its feet, probably felled by an earthquake soon after completion.
Above the Great Temple door: the falcon-headed sun god in his niche, the first figure Belzoni freed from the sand.
Small Temple, to the right: Queen Nefertari stands as tall as the king, a rare honour in Egyptian art.
The colossi's legs: graffiti from Greek mercenaries of about 593 BC and from 19th-century travellers.
The hill behind the facades: not a real mountain but rock fill over concrete domes from the 1960s rescue.
fun_fact: When Drovetti paid the local sheikh 300 piastres to dig out the door, the coins came back unspent: nobody in the village saw any use for them. Belzoni first had to convince the workmen that money was worth having.
narration: You are standing on the shore of Lake Nasser, looking at two temples cut into a cliff about 3,200 years ago. On the left is the Great Temple of Ramesses the Second, with its four seated giants. On the right, about 100 metres away, is the Small Temple, made for the goddess Hathor and for his wife Nefertari. Ramesses began the work around 1264 BC, and it took about 20 years. This was Nubia, the land of gold, and the temples were a message to anyone sailing on the river: Egypt is in charge here. Then the desert moved in. Sand buried the Great Temple until only one head stuck out. A Swiss traveller, Johann Burckhardt, spotted it in 1813. In 1817 Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman, dug for 22 days to open a gap at the door. The thinnest man in the team crawled through first, into air as hot as a Turkish bath. A few years later, drawings of the royal names carved here helped Champollion crack hieroglyphs. In the 1960s a new dam was about to drown everything, so the temples were sawn into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground. Even the hill they sit in is man-made. Now look at the second giant from the left. His head and chest lie on the ground at his feet, exactly where they fell long ago.

name: Facade of the Great Temple: the four colossi
note: Four 20 m seated Ramesses II with the double crown; the second from the left lost its head and torso in an earthquake soon after completion (left as found during the move); family members at the knees (Nefertari, Tuya, Bintanath, Nebettawy, Amun-her-khepeshef...); the niche with falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty holding user and Maat = a rebus of the king's throne name User-Maat-Ra; 22 baboons greeting the sun on the cornice; the Greek mercenary graffiti on the leg (Psamtik II, 593 BC, earliest Greek inscriptions).
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1264-1244 BC
summary: Four 20-metre Ramesses sit in a row, one headless since antiquity, with his family at his knees and Greek soldiers' graffiti on his legs.
look: The facade is about 33 m high and 38 m wide, cut from the cliff and facing east to the sunrise. Four seated colossi of Ramesses II, each about 20 m tall, wear the double crown; the second from the left lost its head and torso, which lie at its feet. Small statues of his mother, wives and children stand between and beside the legs, none higher than his knees. Over the door the falcon-headed sun god stands in a niche, and a row of baboons runs along the top.
story:
All four giants are Ramesses, enthroned, hands on knees, staring across the river. Around his legs stands his family: his mother Mut-Tuya, his chief wife Nefertari, his eldest sons Amun-her-khepeshef and Ramesses, and daughters including Bintanath, Nebettawy, Meritamen and Isetnofret. Not one of them reaches above his knee. That is the point.

Look up at the niche over the door. The falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty, crowned with a sun disc, holds a staff topped by an animal head, the hieroglyph user, 'strong', and a small figure of Maat, goddess of truth. Read together: User-Maat-Ra, the throne name of Ramesses II. On either side the king offers to the god, so Ramesses is in effect worshipping his own name. The Greeks later heard that name as Ozymandias. Along the cornice, 22 baboons raise their paws to the rising sun, as baboons in the wild chatter at dawn.

The second colossus from the left broke, probably in an earthquake not long after it was finished. During the 1960s move the engineers chose not to restore it: the fallen head and torso were set back at its feet in the positions where they had been found.

The legs carry the oldest visitors' book in Nubia. Around 593 BC Pharaoh Psamtik II sent an army deep into Kush, and his Greek and Carian mercenaries scratched their names on the left leg of the colossus just south of the door. The Greek text says they came with King Psammetichus to Elephantine and sailed on beyond Kerkis 'as far as the river permits'. It is signed by Archon son of Amoibichos and Pelekos son of Eudamos, and is among the oldest Greek writing that can be dated so closely. In December 1845 Isabella Romer, the first European woman known to visit, cut her name into the throne of the southern colossus.
details: Second colossus from the left: the fallen head and torso at its feet, put back exactly as found during the 1960s move.
Above the door: falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty holding the user staff and a small Maat, a rebus of the king's name User-Maat-Ra.
Very top of the facade: the row of 22 baboons with raised paws, greeting the sunrise.
Left leg of the broken colossus: Greek mercenary graffiti of about 593 BC, among Carian and much later scratches.
Between and beside the legs: Nefertari and the queen mother Tuya, small figures that barely reach the king's knee.
fun_fact: The Greek soldiers who signed this leg around 593 BC were tourists of a sort, and so was every Victorian who added a name later. Please let the tradition end with them.
narration: In front of you sit four giants, each about 20 metres tall, and every one of them is Ramesses the Second. He wears the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt and stares east, over the water, at the sunrise. Around his legs stand his family: his mother Tuya, his queen Nefertari, his sons and daughters. Not one of them reaches higher than his knee. That was the message. Look up above the door. The falcon-headed sun god stands in a niche, holding a staff with an animal head in one hand and the little goddess of truth, Maat, in the other. Put them together and they spell User Maat Ra, the throne name of Ramesses. The Greeks later turned that name into Ozymandias. Along the very top, a row of baboons lift their paws to greet the rising sun. Now find the second giant from the left. He lost his head and chest, probably in an earthquake soon after the work was done. In the 1960s the engineers left him broken and put the pieces back at his feet, as they were found. Around 593 BC, Greek soldiers serving Pharaoh Psamtik scratched a message on his left leg, signed by Archon, son of Amoibichos, and Pelekos, son of Eudamos. It is some of the oldest closely dated Greek writing anywhere. Look for the small Greek letters on that leg.

name: The Hittite marriage stela and the peace treaty
note: Stela at the south end of the terrace recording the marriage in year 34 to a Hittite princess (renamed Maathorneferure), daughter of Hattusili III, sealing the world's first surviving peace treaty (year 21, after Kadesh); a copy of the treaty hangs at the UN; the Hittite king shown bringing her.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, year 34 (c. 1245 BC)
summary: A stela that turns a hard-won diplomatic marriage into a tale of Hittite surrender, the happy ending of the oldest surviving peace treaty.
look: The stela is cut into the rock face at the south end of the terrace, to the left of the four colossi as you face them. It is a tall, round-topped panel: a scene at the top, with the enthroned king receiving the Hittite ruler and his daughter, and a long, weathered hieroglyphic text below. Low side light brings the figures out best.
story:
In 1274 BC Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria and nearly lost. The war dragged on for about 15 more years until, around 1259 BC, in the 21st year of his reign, he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It is the oldest surviving peace treaty and the only one from the ancient Near East known from both sides: the Egyptian text is carved at Karnak and the Ramesseum, the Hittite one survives on clay tablets from Hattusa in Turkey. A copy hangs at the United Nations in New York.

The wedding came 13 years later. The letters survive, and they are very human: Ramesses complains about delays; Queen Puduhepa answers that her daughter needs a proper dowry, which takes time to gather. In autumn 1246 BC the princess left Hattusa with gold, silver, bronze, cattle and slaves, and reached Pi-Ramesses that winter. She became a Great Royal Wife with a new name, Maathorneferure, 'she who sees Horus, the beauty of Ra'.

This stela tells it the Egyptian way. Hattusili comes in person, bringing his goods as tribute and his eldest daughter as a gift, and Ramesses' prayer to the god Seth calms the winter weather for her journey. In reality the Hittite king never came. Same event, two press releases.
details: Top of the stela: Ramesses enthroned, with the Hittite king and his daughter approaching him.
The long text below: the wedding told as a Hittite submission, with Seth calming the winter weather.
Compare with the Kadesh reliefs inside the hall: the war first, then the peace that followed it.
On the 22nd at Karnak: the Egyptian text of the treaty is carved on an outer wall south of the Great Hypostyle Hall.
fun_fact: The treaty was originally engraved on silver tablets, one for each king. Both are lost; we read it today from temple walls in Luxor and clay tablets dug up in Turkey in 1906.
narration: On the rock face here, at the south end of the terrace, is a carved stela about a royal wedding. In 1274 BC Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh and nearly lost. The war ground on for about 15 more years. Then, around 1259 BC, he and the Hittite king Hattusili signed a treaty: the oldest peace treaty that survives. A copy hangs today at the United Nations. Thirteen years later came the marriage that sealed it. The letters between the two courts survive, and they are very human. Ramesses complains about delays. The Hittite queen replies that her daughter needs a proper dowry, and that takes time. The princess finally came to Egypt with gold, silver, cattle and soldiers, and got a new Egyptian name, Maathorneferure. Now read the stela's version. Here the Hittite king comes in person, bringing his treasure and his eldest daughter as tribute, and Ramesses prays to the god Seth to calm the winter weather for them. He never came. Look at the scene at the top, where the Hittite king and his daughter approach the enthroned pharaoh.

name: The Great Hypostyle Hall: Osiride pillars and the Battle of Kadesh
note: Eight 10 m Osiride statues of the king (white crown south, double crown north); the ceiling with vultures of Nekhbet; north wall: the Battle of Kadesh (1274 BC) in comic-strip form (camp, spies beaten, the chariot charge, the king alone, the Orontes, counting hands); south wall: Syrian, Libyan and Nubian campaigns; the side storerooms; the second hall with Ramesses and Nefertari before the barque.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II; Battle of Kadesh 1274 BC
summary: Eight giant Ramesses as Osiris hold up the roof while the walls tell, comic-strip style, the battle he nearly lost at Kadesh.
look: Inside the door is a hall about 18 m long and 17 m wide, cut from solid rock. Eight pillars, four on each side, carry standing statues of Ramesses as Osiris with arms crossed: those on the left (south) wear the white crown of Upper Egypt, those on the right (north) the double crown. The whole right-hand wall is the Battle of Kadesh; the left-hand wall shows other wars. Beyond is a smaller hall with four pillars.
story:
The pillar statues show the king as Osiris, god of the dead and of renewal, holding crook and flail. Above the central aisle the vultures of the goddess Nekhbet spread their wings. Small side rooms opening off the hall were storerooms for temple equipment. In the second hall Ramesses and Nefertari stand before the sacred boat of the god.

The north wall is the star. In May 1274 BC, in year 5 of his reign, Ramesses marched into Syria with four divisions named after gods: Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth. Near Kadesh on the river Orontes, two nomads told him the Hittite army was far away at Aleppo. They were Hittite plants. Ramesses pitched camp. Then two enemy scouts were caught and beaten until they talked: King Muwatalli II and his allies were hiding just behind the city. Hittite chariots smashed into the Egyptian army and broke into the camp. Ramesses charged with his bodyguard and held on until reinforcements arrived from the coast.

With 5,000 to 6,000 chariots in all, it was probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and the first battle whose tactics we can follow. It ended in a stalemate: the Hittites kept Kadesh and pushed the border south. Ramesses came home and carved a victory on his temples, with himself alone against thousands, the hero of his own poem.

The south wall shows the more routine business of empire: the king storming a Syrian fortress and campaigning against Libyans and Nubians. You will meet the Kadesh story again at the Ramesseum on the 21st and on the outer wall of Karnak on the 22nd.
details: Left (south) row of Osiride pillars: the tall white crown; right (north) row: the double crown.
North (right) wall: the Egyptian camp, drawn as a rectangle of shields with horses and chariots resting inside.
Same wall: the two Hittite scouts being beaten with sticks, the moment the king learns the truth.
Same wall, higher up: the king in his chariot shooting arrows, and the Orontes looping round the walled city of Kadesh.
Central aisle ceiling: the outspread wings of Nekhbet's vultures.
fun_fact: Ramesses had this battle carved on several of his temples as a great victory, yet the Hittites kept Kadesh and the war dragged on for years. It may be the most expensive spin campaign in the ancient world.
narration: You are inside the first hall, cut straight out of the rock. Eight statues of Ramesses as Osiris hold up the roof, arms crossed over their chests. On your left they wear the tall white crown of the south, on your right the double crown. Above the middle aisle, vultures spread their wings across the ceiling. Now turn to the right-hand wall. This is the Battle of Kadesh, told like a comic strip. In 1274 BC, Ramesses marched into Syria with four divisions named after gods: Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth. Near the city of Kadesh, two nomads told him the Hittite army was far away. They were Hittite spies. He made camp. Then his men caught two enemy scouts and beat the truth out of them: the Hittites were hiding right behind the city. Too late. Hittite chariots smashed into the army and broke into the camp. Ramesses charged with his bodyguard and held on until reinforcements arrived. It was probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and in the end it was a draw. The Hittites kept Kadesh. Ramesses went home and carved a triumph on his temples. Look for the camp, drawn as a rectangle of shields with horses inside, and the two scouts being beaten with sticks.

name: The sanctuary and the sun alignment (22 Feb and 22 Oct)
note: 65 m deep; the four seated statues: Ptah (Memphis), Amun-Ra (Thebes), the deified Ramesses, Ra-Horakhty (Heliopolis); twice a year the rising sun travels down the axis and lights three of them while Ptah, god of the underworld, stays in shadow; dates shifted by a day after the 1968 relocation (now 22 Feb/22 Oct, originally 21st, possibly birthday and coronation); the festival crowd on those days.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II
summary: At the back of the mountain four gods sit in the dark; twice a year the sunrise reaches three of them and leaves the fourth in shadow.
look: The sanctuary is a small room at the very back, on a straight line from the door, about 60 m into the rock. Four seated statues carved from the living rock sit against the back wall: from left to right Ptah, Amun-Ra, the deified Ramesses and Ra-Horakhty. They are worn, so look for shapes rather than faces. The stone block in front of them is the stand for the god's sacred boat.
story:
This is the temple's heart. The great state gods sit here together: Ptah of Memphis, Amun-Ra of Thebes and Ra-Horakhty, the rising sun of Heliopolis. Between them, as an equal, sits Ramesses himself. A living king placing himself in his own holy of holies was bold even by pharaoh standards.

The temple's axis points at the sunrise. Around 22 February and 22 October the first rays run the whole length of the temple, through both halls, and light the back wall. Amun-Ra, Ramesses and Ra-Horakhty are lit; Ptah, a god often linked with the underworld, stays in shadow. Amelia Edwards, the Victorian traveller who later founded the Egypt Exploration Fund, watched the beam and was convinced it was a calculated effect.

Two stories often come with the dates. One says they were Ramesses' birthday and coronation day: there is no direct evidence for that. The other says the 1960s move shifted the dates by a day. In fact the engineers watched the light reach the statues in the original temple on 22 February 1966, before it was cut, and set out the rebuilt temple to repeat it, to a tolerance of a few millimetres. Over 3,000 years the slow wobble of the Earth's axis has probably shifted the effect more than the move did.

On festival mornings thousands of people queue in the dark to see it. You are here five days before the October date, which means fewer elbows.
details: Far left: Ptah, the one god the sun never reaches.
Second from the right: Ramesses himself, seated as an equal among the gods.
Far right: falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty, the same rising-sun god who stands over the front door.
The block in front of the statues: the stand where the god's sacred boat rested.
Turn round: the dark rooms, the bright doorway and the lake beyond sit on one straight line.
fun_fact: When they rebuilt the temple 65 metres higher, the engineers set its orientation to within about 5 millimetres, so that the sun would still find the same three gods.
narration: You have reached the sanctuary, the deepest room of the temple, about 60 metres inside the rock. Four figures sit against the back wall. From left to right: Ptah, the creator god of Memphis. Amun Ra, king of the gods, from Thebes. Then Ramesses himself, sitting with the gods as one of them. And on the right, the falcon-headed sun god, Ra Horakhty. The faces are worn, so look for the shapes. Now the famous trick. The temple is aimed at the sunrise. Around the 22nd of February and the 22nd of October, the first rays run the whole length of the temple, through both halls, and light up this back wall. Amun, Ramesses and the sun god shine. Ptah, a god often linked with the underworld, stays in shadow. You may hear that these dates were the king's birthday and coronation. There is no evidence for that. You may also hear that the 1960s move shifted the dates by a day. In fact the engineers watched the light reach these statues on 22 February 1966, before they cut the temple apart, and aimed the rebuilt one to repeat it. The festival this year is on the 22nd, five days from now, with thousands of people queueing in the dark. Turn around now and look back: the dark halls, the bright doorway and the lake beyond sit on one straight line.

name: The Small Temple of Hathor and Nefertari
note: Dedicated to Hathor and to Nefertari 'for whom the sun shines'; facade with six 10 m standing colossi, four of the king and two of the queen, the queen the same height as the king (almost unique); Hathor-headed pillars inside; Nefertari crowned by Isis and Hathor; the king smiting before the queen; the cow Hathor emerging from the rock in the sanctuary; compare with Nefertari's tomb QV66 on 21 Oct.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II
summary: A temple for a queen: on its facade Nefertari stands as tall as Ramesses, an honour almost no other Egyptian queen received.
look: About 100 m north of the Great Temple, the facade holds six standing statues a little over 10 m tall, set between deep buttresses: on each side of the door a statue of Nefertari between two of Ramesses. She wears Hathor's cow horns, sun disc and tall plumes; small figures of their children stand at the knees. Inside is a hall of six pillars with Hathor-faced capitals, a cross-room, and a small sanctuary with the cow of Hathor in the back wall.
story:
Nefertari was Ramesses' first Great Royal Wife, and this temple belongs to her and to the goddess Hathor. It is only the second Egyptian temple we know of dedicated to a queen, after Akhenaten's temple for Nefertiti. In Egyptian art size means rank, and queens normally stand knee-high beside their husbands, as they do next door. Here she is the same height as the king. The dedication calls her, in a well-known translation, the one for whom the sun shines.

Inside, the six pillars carry Hathor's face with cow's ears, shaped like the handle of the sistrum, the rattle her priestesses shook. On the walls Nefertari offers flowers and plays the sistrum; in one scene the goddesses Isis and Hathor crown her; in another Ramesses smites an enemy before the gods while the queen stands behind him. In the sanctuary niche Hathor appears as a cow stepping out of the mountain, the 'Mistress of the temple'.

Nefertari fades from the record not long after the temples were inaugurated, around year 24 of the reign, and she may not have lived to see much of their life. On the 21st you can visit her tomb, Q V 66 in the Valley of the Queens, where she appears again, painted, playing board games and meeting the gods.
details: Facade: Nefertari, the middle figure on each side, as tall as the king, with Hathor's horns, sun disc and plumes.
At the knees of the giants: small figures of their sons and daughters, arranged symmetrically.
Hall pillars: the face of Hathor with cow's ears at the top, like the handle of a sistrum rattle.
Inner walls: Nefertari between Isis and Hathor, who place a crown on her head.
Sanctuary back wall: the cow of Hathor stepping out of the rock.
fun_fact: Nefertari's name means 'beautiful companion'. Ramesses had several Great Royal Wives over his long reign, but she is the one who got a temple of her own.
narration: This is the Small Temple, made for the goddess Hathor and for Nefertari, the first chief wife of Ramesses. Count the six figures on the facade, each a little over 10 metres tall. Four are Ramesses. Two, the middle figure on each side, are Nefertari, dressed as Hathor with cow horns, a sun disc and two tall feathers. Here is the remarkable thing: she is exactly as tall as the king. In Egyptian art, size means rank, and queens normally stand knee-high beside their husbands, like the little ones next door. This is only the second temple we know of dedicated to a queen. Its inscription calls her the one for whom the sun shines. Inside, the pillars carry the face of Hathor with cow's ears, shaped like the rattle her priestesses shook. On the walls Nefertari offers flowers and shakes her own rattle, and two goddesses, Isis and Hathor, place a crown on her head. At the back, Hathor appears as a cow stepping out of the mountain. Nefertari fades from the record soon after these temples were finished. On the 21st you can see her tomb in the Valley of the Queens, Q V 66, still bright with colour. Before you go in, look at the small figures at the giants' knees: their children, standing guard.

name: The rescue: cutting a mountain into 1,036 blocks
note: 1964-68, UNESCO campaign, $40 million (about $300 million today), Swedish VBB engineering; the temples sawn into blocks of up to 30 tons by hand-saws to keep cuts thin, lifted 65 m higher and 200 m back, reassembled inside concrete domes (visible from the back door of the hill); the artificial mountain; the rejected alternatives (lifting on jacks, underwater viewing); the gift temples to Spain (Debod), USA (Dendur), Netherlands (Taffeh), Italy (Ellesyia) in thanks; birth of the World Heritage idea.
period: Rescue 1964-1968
summary: In the 1960s engineers sawed both temples into 1,036 blocks, lifted them 65 metres up the hill and rebuilt them inside a man-made mountain.
look: Everything here was rebuilt. The cliff around the facades is a skin of rock over two concrete domes; the Great Temple's dome spans 55 m. Look closely at the facades, walls and ceilings and you can find the thin straight joints where the blocks were cut and fitted back together. With your back to the temples, the original site lies about 65 m lower and some 200 m out, under the lake.
story:
The Aswan High Dam would raise the water at Abu Simbel by up to 60 m. In 1959 Egypt asked UNESCO for help, and in March 1960 UNESCO launched its appeal to save the monuments of Nubia. The French Egyptologist Christiane Desroches Noblecourt and the Egyptian culture minister Tharwat Okasha drove it; Jacqueline Kennedy lobbied her husband for American money.

The proposals were wild: a dam around the temples, leaving them underwater for visitors to view, or an Italian plan to jack up the whole Great Temple, about 250,000 tons, in one piece. In 1963 Egypt chose the Swedish firm VBB's cheaper plan: cut the temples apart.

First a cofferdam held back the rising river and 31,000 tons of sand were dumped against the facades to protect them. Workers removed about 300,000 tons of rock from above. Then they sawed: interior blocks were limited to 20 tons, facade blocks to 30, and cuts were kept to about 6 mm. In all 1,036 blocks were numbered, lifted and stored. The Great Temple was rebuilt 65 m higher and about 200 m inland, aimed at the sunrise to within about 5 mm, roofed with a concrete dome and covered with an artificial hill. It was inaugurated on 22 September 1968, 18 months early, at a cost of about 42 million dollars, half paid by Egypt.

Egypt thanked the donors with four temples: Debod went to Madrid, Dendur to the Metropolitan Museum in New York, Taffeh to Leiden and Ellesyia to Turin. The campaign also led to the 1972 World Heritage Convention: the idea that some places belong to everyone.
details: Facade and inner walls: thin straight joint lines crossing the carving, where the saw cuts were made.
The broken colossus: its fallen head and torso were put back on the ground exactly where they lay before the move.
The hill: rock fill heaped over concrete domes, a mountain made in the 1960s.
Look out at the lake: the original site is under the water, about 65 m below the present terrace.
If a door into the dome behind the temple is open, peek in: it is the concrete shell that carries the hill.
fun_fact: Before cutting began, workers buried the facades under 31,000 tons of sand to protect them. After 150 years of digging it out, the temple was buried again on purpose.
narration: Everything around you was moved here between 1964 and 1968. The cliff is man-made: a skin of rock over two huge concrete domes. In the 1950s Egypt decided to build the High Dam at Aswan. Its lake would rise up to 60 metres here and drown both temples. So in 1960 UNESCO launched a worldwide appeal. The ideas were wild. A dam around the temples. Leaving them underwater for visitors to view. Jacking up the entire Great Temple, a quarter of a million tons, in one piece. In the end Egypt chose the cheaper plan, from a Swedish firm: cut the temples into blocks and rebuild them higher up. First, workers buried the facades under sand again to protect them. Then they cleared the rock above and began to saw, keeping the cuts to about 6 millimetres. Blocks weighed up to 30 tons. In all there were 1,036 of them, each numbered, lifted and stored. The Great Temple was rebuilt 65 metres higher and about 200 metres back from the water, and aimed at the sunrise to within a few millimetres. The rescue cost about 42 million dollars. Egypt thanked the donor countries with temples: one stands today in Madrid, another in New York. Now look closely at the facade for thin straight lines crossing the stone. Those are the saw cuts.

name: Lake Nasser and drowned Nubia
note: 500 km reservoir created by the High Dam (1964-70), 1/3 in Sudan; 100,000+ Nubians relocated to Kom Ombo (Egypt) and Khashm el-Girba (Sudan), villages, palm groves and 45 temples lost or moved; crocodiles back in the lake; the Toshka project; the Nubian memory that the Nubian Museum (19 Oct) explains; the drive north along it on the 18th.
period: Created 1960-1970
summary: The lake in front of you is a drowned country: some 480 km of Nubian villages, palm groves and monuments lie beneath it.
look: Turn your back to the temples and you face Lake Nasser, the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam. It is about 479 km long and up to 16 km wide; you are near its southern end, with Sudan only about 40 km away. Under the water in front of you lies the old Nile valley, including the spot where the temples stood until 1964.
story:
The High Dam was built between 1960 and 1970 and inaugurated in 1971. It ended the yearly flood that had shaped Egyptian life for millennia, gave the country water all year round and, at first, up to half its electricity. Behind it rose a lake of 5,250 square km, most of it in Egypt; the Sudanese call their southern part Lake Nubia.

The price was Nubia. Tens of thousands of Nubians, by many estimates around 100,000 people in Egypt and Sudan together, left their villages for good. In Egypt most were resettled on new land around Kom Ombo, which you pass on the 20th; in Sudan many went to Khashm el-Girba, far to the east. Houses, palm groves, graves and the river bank itself disappeared. Twenty-two monuments were moved in the UNESCO campaign; others, like the fortress of Buhen, are still underwater.

The lake has a life of its own now: 52 species of fish, fishing camps and Nile crocodiles. When the water is high it spills west into the desert and has created the Toshka lakes. The Nubian Museum in Aswan, on the 19th, tells the human side of this story.
details: Out on the water: the original temple site, about 65 m below the terrace and some 200 m out.
The shoreline: bare rock to the water's edge; the old green strip of the valley is all underwater.
Fishing boats, if you see any: tilapia and Nile perch are the main catch.
On the 19th: the Nubian Museum in Aswan tells the story of the lost villages.
fun_fact: At high water the lake overflows westward into the Sahara through a spillway and has made the Toshka lakes: new lakes in the middle of the desert.
narration: Turn your back to the temples and look at the water. This is Lake Nasser, the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam, and it is about 480 kilometres long. Before the 1960s there was no lake here. There was the Nile, a thin green strip of palm groves, fields and Nubian villages, and these temples sat on its bank, 65 metres below where you stand. The dam was built between 1960 and 1970. It ended the yearly flood, gave Egypt water all year round, and at first produced up to half of the country's electricity. The price was Nubia. Tens of thousands of Nubians, by many estimates around 100,000 people in Egypt and Sudan, had to leave their homes. In Egypt most were resettled near Kom Ombo, which you will pass on the 20th. Some monuments were saved and moved. Others, like the fortress of Buhen, are still down there. The lake now holds 52 kinds of fish, and Nile crocodiles. Look out across the water and picture the old valley floor far below: houses, graves and fields, all still there in the dark.

name: Why here? Ramesses and the gold of Nubia
note: Nubia (Wawat and Kush) as Egypt's gold mine ('nub' = gold, folk etymology), source of soldiers, ivory, ebony, incense; the Viceroy of Kush; Ramesses' seven Nubian temples (Beit el-Wali, Gerf Hussein, Wadi es-Sebua, Derr, Abu Simbel...) as statements of control; the deified king worshipped alongside the state gods; the temple seen from the river by traders coming north.
period: New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC; Ramesses II 1279-1213 BC
summary: Abu Simbel stands not in Egypt's heartland but in Nubia, the land of gold, and that is exactly why Ramesses put his biggest faces here.
look: Look at the Great Temple facade the way an ancient boatman did: from the river, coming north from deeper Africa. The four colossi face east over the water, the first great image of Egyptian power a traveller met. South of you lies Sudan, the old land of Kush.
story:
Nubia is the Nile valley south of Aswan, broken by rocky cataracts. Egyptians called the northern part Wawat and the southern part Kush, and the whole region Ta-Seti, 'the land of the bow', for its archers. It sent north gold above all, plus ivory, ebony, incense, animal skins and soldiers. The Egyptian word for gold was nub, and many link the name Nubia to it, though that is not certain.

Around 1500 BC Thutmose I crushed the Nubian kingdom of Kerma, and for about four centuries Egypt ruled the region through a governor with the title King's Son of Kush, the viceroy. Ramesses II filled Nubia with temples, at least seven: Beit el-Wali, Gerf Hussein, Wadi es-Sebua, Derr, the two at Abu Simbel and more. In several of them the living king is worshipped as a god beside Amun, Ra and Ptah, as you saw in the sanctuary.

They were statements of control. A trader bringing gold north passed a mountain with the king's face on it four times. Nobody needed to read to get the message. The tables turned later: in the 8th century BC kings from Kush conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty.
details: The facade: the colossi face east across the water, where traders and gold boats once passed.
Sanctuary: Ramesses seated as a god among Amun, Ra and Ptah, the theology behind these Nubian temples.
Hall, south wall: the king's campaigns, including against Nubians, the force behind the message.
On the 19th: the Nubian Museum in Aswan tells the same centuries from the Nubian side.
fun_fact: Foreign kings constantly begged Pharaoh for gold. In the Amarna letters a Babylonian king even complained that a shipment shrank badly when melted down, and much of that gold came from Nubia.
narration: Why carve the biggest statues of your reign here, so far south? Because this was Nubia, and Nubia meant gold. The Nile south of Aswan ran through a narrow land the Egyptians called Kush and Wawat, or simply the land of the bow, for its famous archers. From here came gold, ivory, ebony, incense, animal skins and soldiers. Around 1500 BC Pharaoh Thutmose the First crushed the Nubian kingdom of Kerma, and for about four centuries Egypt ruled the region through a governor called the King's Son of Kush. Ramesses the Second covered it with temples, at least seven of them, and in several he is worshipped as a god. Think of this facade as a billboard on the river. A trader sailing north with a cargo of gold would come round the bend and see the king's face four times, each 20 metres high, staring down at him. Nobody needed to read hieroglyphs to get the message. Centuries later the tables turned, and kings from Kush conquered Egypt itself. Look at the colossi now and imagine seeing them from a small boat on the water below.

name: Aswan: Egypt's southern gate
note: Orientation: ancient Swenett/Syene, the border town at the First Cataract, granite quarries, trade with Nubia (ivory = Elephantine), Eratosthenes measured the Earth using Syene's noon sun; what the two days hold: felucca, Botanical Garden, Philae, Nubian Museum, Unfinished Obelisk; the souq; the slower Nubian pace; Agatha Christie at the Old Cataract.
period: Swenett, Greek Syene: Egypt's frontier town from about 3000 BC to today
summary: Egypt began here: the frontier town at the First Cataract, where Nubian gold and ivory came in, and a Greek used the noon sun to measure the Earth.
look: Stand on the Corniche on the east bank and face west. The river, about 650 metres wide just upstream, is broken by granite islands: the long one in front is Elephantine, the ancient town, with Kitchener's Island and its gardens behind it. On the west bank a cliff riddled with tomb doorways rises under a small domed shrine, and further south, on a hill, stands the pink mausoleum of the Aga Khan. Upstream to the south, out of sight, lie the old dam, the High Dam and Philae.
story:
The Egyptians called this town Swenett; the Greeks called it Syene. Egyptians oriented themselves facing south, towards the source of the Nile, so for them the country did not end here, it began here. Just upstream lay the First Cataract, a maze of boulders and rapids that made a natural border. Under every dynasty Swenett was a garrison town, and every boat passing north or south paid tolls. Through it came the riches of Nubia: gold, ebony, incense and ivory. The island opposite was called Abu, 'elephant'.

The hills here gave Egypt its finest hard stone. Red granite from Aswan went into obelisks, colossal statues, shrines and sarcophagi the length of the country, and an abandoned obelisk still lies in its quarry on the edge of town.

Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, the scholar who ran the Library of Alexandria, used a report about Syene: at noon on midsummer's day the sun stood almost straight overhead, shining down a deep well. Comparing that with the shadow cast at Alexandria on the same day, and the distance between the two cities, he calculated the circumference of the Earth. (Strictly, Syene is not exactly on the tropic: on the solstice a staff still cast a tiny shadow, about one four-hundredth of its length.)

By 1900 Aswan was a winter resort for Europeans, and since the dams it has also been the heart of Egyptian Nubia. Your two days here hold a felucca on the river, the Botanical Garden, Philae, the Nubian Museum, the Unfinished Obelisk and the souq. The pace is slower than Cairo's. Enjoy it.
details: From the Corniche: the long island opposite is Elephantine; its rounded grey boulders may be what gave it the name 'elephant'.
On the west-bank cliff, the small dome on the summit: Qubbet el-Hawa, the Dome of the Wind, above the Tombs of the Nobles.
On the hill further south-west, the pink Fatimid-style mausoleum of the Aga Khan.
In the souq: heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers, Aswan's signature crop, sold for karkade.
At the south end of the Corniche, on its granite rock, the terracotta-coloured Old Cataract Hotel.
fun_fact: Geologists' word 'syenite' comes from Syene, the Greek name for Aswan; the irony is that Aswan's famous stone is, technically, a granite.
narration:
You are standing at the southern gate of ancient Egypt. In front of you the Nile is wide and scattered with granite islands, and just upstream, to your left, lay the First Cataract, a barrier of boulders and rapids.

The Egyptians called this town Swenett, and the Greeks called it Syene. Egyptians faced south, towards the source of the Nile, so for them the country did not end here. It began here. Every passing boat paid customs. Through this gate came the riches of Nubia: gold, ebony, incense and ivory. The long island in front of you is Elephantine, and its Egyptian name simply meant elephant.

Aswan also gave Egypt its finest hard stone. Red granite from these hills went into obelisks, colossal statues and royal sarcophagi all down the Nile.

Now a Greek story. Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, the scholar who ran the Library of Alexandria, heard that at noon on midsummer's day the sun at Syene shone almost straight down a well. In Alexandria, at that moment, a stick still cast a shadow. From that angle and the distance between the two cities, he worked out the size of the whole Earth.

Over the next two days you will sail a felucca, visit Isis at Philae, and meet Nubia in its museum. Before you go, look across to the far bank: the small dome on top of the cliff marks the Tombs of the Nobles.

name: Felucca on the Nile and the First Cataract
note: The lateen-rigged felucca and how it tacks; what you pass: Elephantine, Kitchener's Island, the Aga Khan mausoleum, the dunes of the west bank, Sehel island with 250 rock inscriptions (Famine Stela); the First Cataract as the ancient border ('where the Nile is born' in myth, Khnum's cavern); the Nilometers; negotiating the ride.
period: A living tradition; the cataract tamed by the dams of 1902 and 1970
summary: A wooden boat with one huge sail and no engine, on the rocky stretch of river that marked Egypt's southern border for most of its history.
look: A felucca is an open wooden boat under one big triangular lateen sail, hung from a long sloping yard; it usually takes about ten passengers with a crew of two or three. Sit low and keep your head clear when the captain swings the yard. A typical loop goes round Elephantine and Kitchener's Island, along the west bank under the Tombs of the Nobles and the Aga Khan's hill, and back past the Old Cataract Hotel. The dark, rounded boulders all around are the visible edge of the old cataract zone.
story:
The felucca works with the two forces that shaped Egyptian life. The current flows north; the prevailing wind blows from the north. So for thousands of years boats drifted downstream with the mast lowered and sailed upstream under canvas. When your captain swings the yard across and the boat zigzags, he is tacking, climbing into the wind one diagonal at a time.

The First Cataract was not a waterfall. The word comes from Greek for 'flowing down', but this was a stretch of shallow water broken by granite boulders and rocky islets. For most of Egyptian history it was the southern frontier: cargo between Egypt and Nubia was unloaded and reloaded at Syene and Philae. Since the first Aswan dam of 1902 the old cataract has been drowned under the water behind it.

Myth gathered here. The Egyptians believed the flood rose from caverns beneath the cataract, guarded by the ram god Khnum. Herodotus was told in Egypt that the springs of the Nile lay between two hills near Syene and Elephantine and were bottomless; he suspected his informant was joking. On Sehel Island, upstream, expedition leaders cut hundreds of inscriptions into the rocks, including the Famine Stela, a Ptolemaic text claiming that King Djoser ended seven years of famine by honouring Khnum.

Agree the price, the route and the time before you board; the price is usually per boat per hour. With no wind it will be slow, and that is part of the charm. A small tip for the boy who sings or helps with the sail is welcome.
details: Watch the captain tack: he swings the long yard across the mast and the boat zigzags into the wind.
On the west bank, rows of doorways cut in the cliff: the Tombs of the Nobles under the Dome of the Wind.
The smooth grey-black boulders around Elephantine, polished by the river; some really do look like bathing elephants.
On the hill to the south-west, the Aga Khan's pink mausoleum; below it, his white villa by the water.
Sehel Island and its inscriptions lie further upstream; short rides rarely reach it, so ask if you want to go.
fun_fact: In hieroglyphs, 'to travel south' is written with a boat under full sail and 'to travel north' with a boat whose mast is down: the wind blows upriver, the current flows down.
narration:
You are on a felucca, a wooden Nile boat with one great triangular sail on a long sloping yard. There is no engine, so listen: water on the hull, the creak of rope, maybe a captain humming.

This boat works with two forces the ancient Egyptians built their world around. The current flows north, and the wind mostly blows from the north. So for thousands of years boats drifted downstream with the mast down and sailed upstream with the sail up. In hieroglyphs, the word for travelling south is a boat under sail, and travelling north is a boat with no sail at all. When your captain swings the yard across and the boat zigzags, he is tacking, climbing into the wind one diagonal at a time.

Just upstream lay the First Cataract. Not a waterfall, but a maze of granite boulders and rapids. For most of history it was Egypt's southern border, and cargo had to be unloaded and carried around it. The Egyptians believed the flood itself rose from caverns beneath these rocks, guarded by the ram god Khnum. The Greek historian Herodotus was told that the Nile's springs lay here, bottomless, between two hills, and he suspected his informant was joking.

Since the first dam in 1902 the rapids have been tamed. Look now at the boulders around you: smooth, dark and rounded, like elephants bathing.

name: Kitchener's Island: the Aswan Botanical Garden
note: Short. Given to Lord Kitchener after the 1898 Sudan campaign; he imported palms and exotic trees from India and the Far East; now a research station; royal palms avenue, sausage trees, hoopoes and sunbirds; walk the length and take the felucca from the far end.
period: British era, early 20th century; a government research garden since
summary: A whole island turned into a garden by Lord Kitchener: royal palms, trees from India and busy birds, in the middle of the Nile.
look: The island is about 750 metres long and less than half a kilometre wide; feluccas land at the south-eastern end. A main avenue runs up its spine under tall royal palms, with side paths through beds and groves. Walk the length and have your boat collect you at the far end.
story:
The island is named after Horatio Herbert Kitchener, the British general who reconquered Sudan in 1898 and later governed Egypt as Britain's Consul-General from 1911 to 1914. Accounts differ on when the island came to him; Wikipedia ties the gift to his consul years. What is clear is what he did with it. With help from the Ministry of Irrigation he turned 750 metres of Nile island into a garden of exotic trees, many brought from India, laid out with walkways for strolling.

After Kitchener the island passed to the Egyptian government and became a research station, the Botanical Research Institute. The collection he began has been tended ever since: royal palms with smooth grey trunks, sabal palms, and subtropical trees from Asia and Africa.

Today it is where Aswan families come for weekend picnics and where hot travellers come for shade. The birds are part of the show: hoopoes probing the lawns, and tiny iridescent sunbirds working the flowering shrubs.
details: The royal palm avenue along the island's spine: smooth grey trunks so regular they look poured from concrete.
On the lawns, early or late in the day: hoopoes, cinnamon-coloured with a punk crest and a long curved bill.
In flowering shrubs: tiny metallic sunbirds sipping nectar like hummingbirds.
Any tree hung with long, heavy, sausage-shaped fruit is an African sausage tree; do not linger under it in a breeze.
From the island's west edge, look across at the golden dunes of the desert bank.
fun_fact: Kitchener's face became the most famous recruiting poster in British history in 1914, yet his gentlest legacy is this garden of palms.
narration:
This whole island is a garden, and it began as one man's project. It is known as Kitchener's Island, after Lord Kitchener, the British general who took Sudan in 1898 and later governed Egypt as Britain's Consul General. With help from the Ministry of Irrigation he turned 750 metres of Nile island into a park of exotic trees, many brought from India, with shaded walks for strolling.

Later it became a government research station, and his collection has been tended ever since. Look up at the royal palms along the main avenue: smooth grey trunks so regular they look poured from concrete.

Today Aswan families come here for weekend picnics, and so do the birds. Walk the full length of the island and ask your boat to pick you up at the far end. On the way, watch the lawns for hoopoes, cinnamon-coloured birds with a punk crest and a long curved bill, and the flowering shrubs for tiny sunbirds flashing green and purple.

name: Elephantine Island: the ancient town
note: Abu 'elephant/ivory' town, border fortress from the Old Kingdom; the German-Swiss excavations; temples of Khnum, Satet and Anuket (the cataract triad); the Nilometer; the Aswan Museum; the two Nubian villages (Siou and Koti) with painted houses; the Movenpick tower; Harkhuf's expeditions started here.
period: Border fortress from about 3000 BC; town into the Roman period
summary: Ivory Island: Egypt's border fortress for 3,000 years, with temple ruins, a Nilometer, a Jewish garrison's papyri and Nubian villages.
look: Elephantine is about 1.6 km long and 450 m wide at its widest. The southern end, around the Aswan Museum, is the ruin field of ancient Abu: mounds of mud-brick houses, the temples of Khnum and Satet, and the Nilometer stairs down to the river. The middle of the island holds Nubian villages with painted houses; a hotel tower stands at the northern end.
story:
The Egyptians called the island Abu, 'elephant', perhaps because ivory was traded here, perhaps because the rounded grey boulders on its banks look like elephants bathing. The Greeks translated the name as Elephantine. A fort stood here by about 3000 BC, under the First Dynasty, and for most of Egyptian history this was the frontier: customs post, garrison, and the base from which caravan leaders like Harkhuf set out south. Its governors were buried in the cliff opposite, at Qubbet el-Hawa.

Its temples served the gods of the cataract: Khnum the ram, Satet, protector of the border, and Anuket of the rapids. Satet's shrine began around 3000 BC as a niche between boulders and was rebuilt on the same spot for some 3,000 years.

Since 1969 the German Archaeological Institute, with Swiss colleagues, has taken the town apart layer by layer. Finds range from a mummified sacred ram of Khnum, now in the island's museum, to the Aramaic papyri of a 5th-century BC Jewish garrison. Temples of Thutmose III and Amenhotep III stood nearly intact until 1822, when they were demolished during Muhammad Ali's campaign to conquer Sudan.
details: South of the museum: low mud-brick walls of houses from many centuries, stacked like a layer cake.
The partly rebuilt temple of Satet, over the spot where her cult began between boulders.
At the southern tip: the platform and gateway of the Khnum temple.
Near the museum, the Nilometer stairs running down to the water.
In the villages: doorways and walls painted in blue, ochre and white.
fun_fact: Elephantine has produced documents in hieratic, demotic, Aramaic, Greek, Latin and Coptic: a postbag from one border town spanning many centuries.
narration:
This island was Egypt's southern frontier post for about 3,000 years. Its ancient name was Abu, which means elephant. Maybe because ivory changed hands here, maybe because of the smooth grey boulders on its banks that look like elephants bathing. The Greeks translated the name: Elephantine.

A fort stood here by about 3000 BC. Boats paid customs, soldiers watched the south, and caravan leaders set off from here into Africa.

The town honoured the gods of the cataract: Khnum the ram, who released the flood, Satet, guardian of the border, and Anuket of the rapids. Satet's first shrine was a niche between boulders around 3000 BC, and her temple was rebuilt on the same spot again and again for 3,000 years.

Since 1969 German and Swiss archaeologists have been peeling this mound apart, layer by layer. That is what the low brick walls around you are: houses stacked on houses. Look for the rebuilt temple of Satet, then walk down towards the river to find the Nilometer stairs.

name: Temple of Khnum and the shrine of Heqaib on Elephantine
note: Short. The ram-headed Khnum who formed humans on his potter's wheel and controlled the inundation from the cataract; the Ptolemaic gate; the Satet temple rebuilt layer by layer back to a 3000 BC shrine between boulders (reconstructed by the Swiss); the sanctuary of the deified official Heqaib with Middle Kingdom statues.
period: Site used from the Old Kingdom; temple rebuilt in Dynasty 30 and the Ptolemaic period
summary: The house of Khnum, the potter who shaped people and released the flood, next to the shrine of a local governor who became a saint.
look: At the southern tip of Elephantine the Khnum temple survives mostly as a raised platform, column bases and a granite gateway. Among the town ruins nearby are the walled sanctuary of Heqaib and the partly rebuilt temple of Satet.
story:
Khnum, the ram-headed god of the cataract, was said to control the Nile flood from caves beneath this island and to shape every child on his potter's wheel. His temple here is recorded as early as the Third Dynasty and was rebuilt from scratch in the 30th Dynasty, just before Alexander's conquest; little stands today beyond the platform and gateway.

More personal is the sanctuary of Heqaib, a Sixth Dynasty governor of Elephantine who was worshipped after his death as a local saint. In the Middle Kingdom, later governors such as Sarenput I added shrines and statues beside his, so the little sanctuary kept growing for generations.
details: The raised platform of the Khnum temple at the island's southern tip, with its granite gateway.
The Satet temple, partly rebuilt by the excavators, near the boulders where her cult began.
The Heqaib sanctuary: a walled court lined with shrines added by Middle Kingdom governors.
From the tip of the island, look across the water to the Old Cataract Hotel.
fun_fact: Heqaib is a rare case of an ordinary official becoming a god: centuries after his death, governors still queued to place their statues next to his.
narration:
These ruins at the island's southern tip were the house of Khnum, the ram-headed god of the cataract. Egyptians said he kept the Nile flood in caverns under this island and let it out each summer. He was also a potter, shaping every child on his wheel before birth. His temple here goes back at least to the Third Dynasty, and it was rebuilt from scratch in the 30th Dynasty, just before Alexander the Great arrived.

Nearby is a more personal shrine. Heqaib was a local governor of the Sixth Dynasty, and after his death people worshipped him as a saint. Later governors set up their own statues beside his. Look for the walled court of his sanctuary among the ruins of the town.

name: The Nilometers of Elephantine
note: Two Nilometers: the Khnum temple one (staircase with 90 steps, Roman and 19th-century scales in Greek, Arabic and Egyptian cubits) and the Satet one; the flood level set the year's taxes (Strabo); 16 cubits = ideal; the first was the southernmost, giving Egypt first warning; the river no longer floods since 1970.
period: Pharaonic origins; last rebuilt in Roman times; used into the 19th century
summary: A staircase into the Nile that doubled as a tax calculator: the higher the flood climbed these steps, the more Egypt paid.
look: Elephantine has two Nilometers. The famous one is a stone corridor with a staircase descending to the river, associated with the temple of Satet; its walls carry scales in Arabic, Roman and hieroglyphic numerals. The second, probably older, is a rectangular basin at the island's southern tip near the Khnum temple, opposite the Old Cataract Hotel.
story:
Between July and November the Nile used to spill over its banks and spread black silt over the fields. Too little flood meant famine; too much washed villages away. A Nilometer told the authorities exactly where the year stood, and because Elephantine was Egypt's southern border, this was the first place the rising water could be measured.

The reading was also a tax bill. A good flood meant a good harvest, so the state expected more. Access was restricted to priests and officials: a reading was power. The Greek geographer Strabo described a Nilometer here, though nobody can be sure which of the two he meant. After the Arab conquest, the general Amr ibn al-As reported to the caliph that 16 cubits gave an abundant harvest and 18 brought disaster.

The corridor Nilometer was last rebuilt in Roman times and was still in use in the 19th century; deep marks cut at the water's edge go back to the 17th Dynasty. Since the High Dam was completed in 1970 the river no longer floods at all.
details: Walk down the corridor stairs and read the wall scales: Arabic, Roman and older numerals side by side.
At the bottom, by the water, older marks cut deep into the rock.
The square basin near the Khnum temple at the island's tip: the second, probably older, Nilometer.
From the stairs, look across the water to the Old Cataract Hotel on the east bank.
fun_fact: In Cairo, the right to read the Roda Nilometer was handed to a scholar in 861 and stayed with his descendants for more than three centuries.
narration:
You are at the Nilometer of Elephantine, a staircase running down into the Nile like a ruler laid on its side. Before the dams, the river flooded every summer, spreading black silt over the fields. Too low a flood meant hunger. Too high, and villages washed away. Priests came down these steps to read exactly how high the water stood.

Elephantine was the southern border, so the rising flood could be measured here first.

The reading was also a tax bill. A high flood meant a rich harvest, so the state demanded more. After the Arab conquest, the general Amr ibn al As told the caliph that 16 cubits gave an abundant harvest, and 18 meant disaster. The Greek geographer Strabo described a Nilometer here, though no one knows which of the island's two he meant.

This corridor was last rebuilt in Roman times and still used in the 19th century. Since the High Dam was finished in 1970, the river no longer floods. Look at the walls now: you can find scales in Arabic, Roman and older numerals side by side.

name: The Aswan Museum on Elephantine
note: Short. In the 1898 villa of Sir William Willcocks, designer of the old dam; finds from Elephantine (mummified ram of Khnum, Middle Kingdom statues from Heqaib); the annexe with the German team's finds; often quiet.
period: Founded 1912; finds from prehistory to the Roman period
summary: A quiet villa museum on Elephantine full of the island's own finds, starring a mummified sacred ram of Khnum.
look: The museum stands at the southern end of Elephantine beside the ruins of ancient Abu. The old building is a villa in a garden; a newer annexe just to the north, added in the early 1990s, shows what the German excavations found on the island: pottery, tools, weapons, statues and mummies.
story:
The British Egyptologist Cecil Firth set up the museum in 1912, at first to hold finds from Nubia gathered as the old dam's reservoir rose. The villa is often said to have been built for Sir William Willcocks, the engineer of the first Aswan dam.

Since 1969 the German Archaeological Institute has excavated the island, and the annexe displays its finds: everyday objects from the frontier town, Middle Kingdom statues of officials, and mummies of the ram, the sacred animal of Khnum. It is usually quiet, cool and unhurried.
details: The mummified ram: the living animal of Khnum, embalmed and buried with honour on the island.
Statues of Middle Kingdom officials; several came from the sanctuary of the deified governor Heqaib.
In the annexe: pots, tools and weapons from the town, arranged by period.
The garden between the buildings, and the path down to the Nilometer.
fun_fact: Rams were mummified on Elephantine because each was a living image of Khnum; this museum is one of the few places you can meet one face to face.
narration:
This small museum on Elephantine tells the island's own story. It was set up in 1912 by the British Egyptologist Cecil Firth, in a villa often said to have been built for Sir William Willcocks, the engineer of the first Aswan dam. The newer annexe nearby shows what German archaeologists have found on the island since 1969: pottery, tools, weapons and statues from 3,000 years of frontier life.

The star is a mummified ram. Rams were the living animal of Khnum, the god of the cataract, and his sacred rams were embalmed and buried here with honour. Find the ram first, then look for the Middle Kingdom officials in stone, with their calm, watchful faces.

name: The Elephantine papyri: a Jewish garrison and its temple
note: 5th century BC Aramaic archive of a Jewish mercenary community serving the Persians, with its own temple to YHW, marriage contracts, a letter about Passover, and the temple's destruction in 410 BC by Khnum's priests; one of the earliest Jewish archives; the lady Mibtahiah's property deeds.
period: Persian period, 5th century BC
summary: A Jewish garrison's letters and contracts from 2,400 years ago: marriages, divorces, a festival letter, and a temple burned by its neighbours.
look: There is little to see on the ground. The Aramaic papyri came from houses at the northern edge of the town mound, an 'Aramaic quarter' found in 1907, and the originals are scattered across museums in Berlin, Brooklyn, Cairo, London, Munich and Paris. Stand among the town ruins and picture the neighbourhood where they were written.
story:
In the 5th century BC Egypt was part of the Persian empire, and Elephantine's garrison included Judean soldiers and their families. They wrote in Aramaic, the empire's office language, and the dry soil kept their papers: loans, house sales, marriage and divorce contracts, the freeing of slaves. The archive of a woman named Mibtahiah follows her property and marriages across decades.

The community had its own temple to Yahweh, which stood near the temple of Khnum. In 410 BC it was destroyed, the documents say at the instigation of Khnum's priests, and letters survive asking the Persian governor Bagoas for help to rebuild it. A letter of 419 BC gives instructions for the Festival of Unleavened Bread.
details: The northern edge of the ruin mound: the Aramaic papyri came from houses on this side.
Look south towards the Khnum temple: the two temples were close neighbours.
One theory for the conflict: Khnum was a ram god, and the Passover sacrifice of lambs may have offended his priests.
The largest collection of Elephantine documents is in Berlin, not here.
fun_fact: Belzoni and Drovetti were buying papyri from this archive in the 1810s, but nobody realised they came from Elephantine until almost a century later.
narration:
Somewhere in these town ruins, about 2,400 years ago, Jewish soldiers and their families lived and wrote letters. In the 5th century BC Egypt was part of the Persian empire, and this border fort had a Judean garrison. They wrote in Aramaic, and the dry soil kept their papyri: loans, house sales, marriage and divorce contracts. One woman, Mibtahiah, left a whole family archive.

They even had their own temple to Yahweh, close to the temple of the ram god Khnum. In 410 BC it was destroyed, the letters say at the urging of Khnum's priests, and the community wrote to the Persian governor for help. Look south towards the Khnum temple: the neighbours were that close.

name: Philae: the Temple of Isis on Agilkia
note: Orientation: 'Pearl of Egypt', mostly Ptolemaic and Roman (c. 380 BC to 300 AD), centre of Isis worship for Egyptians and Nubians (the Blemmyes), the last functioning pagan temple (closed by Justinian 535-537 AD), moved 1972-80 from drowning Philae island to Agilkia, reshaped to match; the boat ride, the route through the temple, where the Nile used to lap; sound and light.
period: Late Period to Roman, about 380 BC to AD 300; closed about AD 537
summary: The island of Isis: the last place the old gods were worshipped, and a temple moved stone by stone to save it from the Nile.
look: Boats land at the southern tip of Agilkia island by the Kiosk of Nectanebo, the oldest building. From there a long forecourt between two colonnades leads north to the first pylon; behind it are the birth house, the second pylon, the hypostyle hall and the sanctuary of Isis. Trajan's Kiosk stands on the east shore near the small temple of Hathor, and the Gate of Hadrian on the west side of the main temple. Allow at least two hours.
story:
The original island of Philae was small, about 380 metres by 120, just above the cataract. Its oldest certain temple, a kiosk of Psamtik II in the 6th century BC, gives the first evidence of Isis worship here. Nectanebo I added a temple around 370 BC, but more than two-thirds of what survives was built by the Ptolemies, the Macedonian Greek kings of Egypt, and Roman emperors kept adding to it up to Caracalla.

Isis was the wife of Osiris and the mother of Horus, the great magician who brought her murdered husband back to life. Philae became her greatest sanctuary, overtaking Elephantine. Pilgrims came from Egypt and Nubia and, in Ptolemaic times, from Anatolia, Crete and mainland Greece, and many scratched their names into the walls. Next door, the island of Bigeh was believed to hold the tomb of Osiris.

Philae outlived the old religion elsewhere. Nubian peoples kept worshipping here under treaty, and the last known hieroglyphic inscription (AD 394) and the last demotic one (452) were carved on this island. According to Procopius, Justinian had the temple closed in 537.

In modern times the island was nearly lost. The first Aswan dam (1902) left it flooded for much of the year, and the High Dam threatened it permanently. Between 1977 and 1980 the whole complex was dismantled and rebuilt here on Agilkia, reshaped to match Philae's outline. A Greek footnote: an obelisk from Philae, carried to England by William Bankes, helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs, because it repeated Cleopatra's name in Greek and Egyptian.
details: From the landing, look north up the forecourt to the twin towers of the first pylon.
Greek and Latin graffiti left by ancient pilgrims, scratched on many walls and doorways.
Coptic crosses cut over pagan reliefs: the temple's second life as a church.
On the east shore, Trajan's Kiosk: the island's ancient front door from the river.
From the west side, look across to Bigeh island, the sacred tomb of Osiris.
fun_fact: In 2014 the European Space Agency named its comet lander Philae, after the obelisk that helped crack hieroglyphs; its target landing site was called Agilkia.
narration:
Welcome to Philae, the island of Isis. Strictly speaking, this is not Philae at all. The island under your feet is Agilkia, and every temple on it was moved here, block by block, in the 1970s, from an island about 500 metres away that now lies under the water.

The goddess here is Isis: wife of Osiris, mother of Horus, the great magician who brought her murdered husband back to life. A shrine to her stood on Philae by the 6th century BC, but almost everything you see was built later. First came Nectanebo the First, of the last native dynasty, then the Ptolemies, the Macedonian Greek kings of Egypt, and finally Roman emperors adding the finishing touches.

Pilgrims came from all over Egypt, from Nubia in the south, and even from Crete and mainland Greece, and many scratched their names into the walls. Nubians kept coming long after Rome turned Christian. That is why Philae holds the very last hieroglyphic inscription ever carved, in AD 394. The emperor Justinian finally had the temple closed around AD 537.

Your route: the long colonnaded forecourt, the great first pylon, the birth house, the hypostyle and the dark sanctuary of Isis, then out to Hadrian's Gate and Trajan's Kiosk by the water. Start by looking north up the forecourt to the twin towers of the first pylon.

name: Kiosk of Nectanebo and the colonnades
note: Where you land: the oldest structure (Nectanebo I, c. 370 BC) with Hathor-head columns; the long trapezoidal forecourt with two colonnades, the west one with 32 columns no two capitals alike and windows onto the (old) river; the east unfinished; the small temple of Arensnuphis (Nubian god).
period: Kiosk: Nectanebo I, 380-362 BC; colonnades Ptolemaic and Roman
summary: Where every visitor lands: the oldest building on the island, Hathor faces on the columns, and a forecourt where no two capitals match.
look: At the southern landing stands the Kiosk of Nectanebo I, a small hall of columns with Hathor-faced capitals, linked by screen walls. North of it the forecourt opens between two colonnades: the long west one, with windows that once looked out onto the river, and the shorter east one, left unfinished. Off the east side is the small temple of Arensnuphis. At the far end rises the first pylon.
story:
The kiosk is the oldest thing standing on Philae. Nectanebo I, founder of the 30th Dynasty, the last native Egyptian line, built it around 370 BC as the vestibule of an earlier temple of Isis. When the Ptolemies built the great temple further north, the kiosk stayed at the island's southern tip as the porch where pilgrims came up from the river. Its capitals carry the cow-eared face of Hathor.

The Ptolemies and Romans then laid out the long forecourt, which narrows towards the pylon because it follows the shape of the old island. The west colonnade is the showpiece: walk it and compare the capitals, palm, papyrus and lotus combined differently each time. Its windows once opened straight onto the Nile. The east colonnade was never finished, and some capitals are still roughed-out blocks.

The small temple of Arensnuphis, a Nubian god, received additions from the Nubian king Arqamani in the late 3rd century BC, a sign of how close Philae stood to Nubia. Not long after, Ptolemy V had Arqamani's cartouches erased.
details: On the kiosk columns: Hathor's face with cow ears, beneath a little shrine-shaped top.
West colonnade: walk slowly and compare the capitals; palm, papyrus and lotus never repeat the same way.
The west windows: on old Philae the Nile lapped right below them.
East colonnade: unfinished capitals, still blocky, show the stages of carving.
The small Arensnuphis temple off the east side: a Nubian god in an Egyptian temple.
fun_fact: The Nubian king Arqamani built here in the late 200s BC; a few years later Ptolemy V had his name chiselled out of the walls.
narration:
You have just landed where pilgrims always landed, at the southern tip of the island. The little pavilion of columns is the oldest building on Philae. Nectanebo the First, founder of the last native Egyptian dynasty, built it around 370 BC as the porch of an earlier temple of Isis. Look at the column tops: the face of Hathor, goddess of music and joy, with her cow ears.

Now turn north. The long forecourt in front of you was laid out by the Ptolemies and the Romans, and it narrows towards the great pylon because it follows the shape of the old island. Walk up the colonnade on your left, the west side, and compare the capitals. Palm fronds, papyrus and lotus, combined differently every time. Its windows once opened straight onto the Nile.

The colonnade on the right was never finished: some capitals are still rough blocks. Near it stands a small temple to Arensnuphis, a Nubian god, which a Nubian king helped to build. Find one roughed-out capital on the east side, then compare it with a finished one on the west.

name: The first pylon and the mammisi (birth house)
note: 18 m pylon with Ptolemy XII Neos Dionysos (Cleopatra's father) smiting enemies before Isis, Horus and Hathor; the French 1799 inscription of Desaix's expedition; the gate of Ptolemy II; inside the court, the mammisi celebrating the birth of Horus to Isis in the marshes, Hathor capitals, the king shown as Horus the child; the Ptolemaic political message.
period: Ptolemaic; pylon reliefs of Ptolemy XII, 80-51 BC
summary: Cleopatra's father smiting enemies before Isis, Napoleon's soldiers signing in, and the house where the goddess gave birth to Horus.
look: The first pylon is two towers about 18 metres high with a gateway between them, guarded by two granite lions. On the front, the king grasps a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his club before Isis, Horus and Hathor. Inside the gateway passage is a French inscription of 1799. Through the gate, the mammisi (birth house) runs along the left, west side of the court, its columns topped with Hathor faces.
story:
A pylon was the horizon in stone: two mountains with the sun rising between them, the gateway into the god's house. The smiting king on this one is Ptolemy XII Neos Dionysos, nicknamed Auletes, 'the flute-player', father of Cleopatra VII. In life he was driven out by his own Alexandrians and restored with Roman help; on the wall he crushes the world. Temple reliefs were not news, they were eternity. An older gateway of Nectanebo I is built into the pylon, and in front of it stood a pair of obelisks; one was carried off to England by William Bankes in the 19th century.

The pylon is also a visitors' book. Greek inscriptions on the towers are cut through by later Egyptian figures. Three Romans left their names here in the summer of 116 BC, the oldest known Latin inscriptions in Egypt. Inside the gateway a French text records that in 1799 General Desaix's division of Napoleon's army pursued the Mamluks beyond the cataracts.

The mammisi celebrated the birth of Horus. Isis hid in the papyrus marshes to bear and nurse her son, safe from his murderous uncle Seth. Because every king was Horus, the reliefs cast the king as the divine child: the Macedonian Ptolemies presenting themselves as true sons of Isis. The Nubian king Arqamani also contributed to the building.
details: On the pylon front: the giant smiting king, Ptolemy XII, before Isis, Horus and Hathor.
The two granite lions at the foot of the gateway.
Inside the main gateway: the neat French inscription left by Napoleon's expedition in 1799.
In the court, on the left: the mammisi, with Hathor-faced capitals on its columns.
On the mammisi walls, look for Isis with the infant Horus among papyrus.
fun_fact: Ptolemy XII's Greek nickname, Auletes, means the flute-player: the conqueror on this pylon was remembered in Alexandria for his music.
narration:
In front of you is the first pylon of the temple of Isis: two massive towers, about 18 metres high, with the gate between them. To an Egyptian, a pylon was the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them.

Look at the big figures on the front. The king grabs a cluster of enemies by the hair and raises his club, while Isis, Horus and Hathor look on. That king is Ptolemy the Twelfth, Cleopatra's father, nicknamed Auletes, the flute player. In real life his own people in Alexandria drove him out, and Rome had to put him back on the throne. On this wall he conquers the world. Temple walls were not news, they were eternity.

Walk into the gateway and look for a neat inscription in French. It records that in 1799 the division of General Desaix, of Napoleon's army, chased the Mamluks beyond the cataracts. Visitors have been signing this temple for over 2,000 years, including three Romans in 116 BC, the oldest Latin writing known in Egypt.

Through the gate, on your left, is the mammisi, the birth house. Here Isis gives birth to Horus, hidden in the papyrus marshes from his murderous uncle Seth. And who appears as the divine baby? The king himself. A Greek dynasty was telling Egyptians: we are the children of Isis. Look on its walls for the goddess with her infant among the papyrus.

name: Second pylon, hypostyle hall and the sanctuary of Isis
note: Second pylon with the granite outcrop built into it (Ptolemy VI stela); hypostyle with ten columns still showing colour; Coptic crosses and an altar from the church conversion (Bishop Theodore 6th c.); the three vestibules and the sanctuary with the pedestal for Isis' barque (Ptolemy III); the stairs to the Osiris rooms on the roof (Osiris' resurrection reliefs) if open.
period: Ptolemaic, 3rd-2nd century BC; a church from the 6th century AD
summary: Colour still on the columns, Coptic crosses cut over the gods, and the dark room where Isis lived for some 800 years.
look: The second pylon stands at the north end of the court; at its base a natural granite outcrop was left in place and smoothed into a stela of Ptolemy VI. Through it, the hypostyle hall has ten columns with painted floral capitals, crosses carved on the walls and a Christian altar. Beyond are three small vestibules and, at the back, the windowless sanctuary with a granite pedestal for the sacred boat of Isis. Stairs lead to the Osiris chapels on the roof, usually closed.
story:
The builders of the second pylon met a lump of bedrock granite and, instead of removing it, dressed it into a stela recording a grant of land by Ptolemy VI. Behind the pylon the hypostyle hall is the temple's roofed forest: each step inward was darker, lower and holier. Its capitals keep much of their green, blue and red.

After the temple was closed in the 6th century, this hall became a church of St Stephen, and inscriptions credit Bishop Theodore with the conversion. Christians carved crosses into the walls and chiselled away the faces of the old gods, though figures of Horus are often oddly spared.
