The sanctuary is small and windowless. Here the statue of Isis stood in its shrine. Every morning a priest broke the seal on the shrine, woke the goddess, washed, dressed and fed her, then sealed her in again. The granite pedestal in the middle carried her portable barque, the boat in which she travelled in procession; it is usually attributed to Ptolemy III and Queen Berenice.

On the roof, if open, small chapels show the death and resurrection of Osiris: his body laid out, and Isis restoring him to life.
details: At the base of the second pylon: the natural granite outcrop smoothed into a stela of Ptolemy VI.
Hypostyle capitals: look up for original green, blue and red paint.
Coptic crosses cut into the walls and doorways, and gods with hacked-out faces.
In the sanctuary: the granite pedestal that carried the barque of Isis.
The stair to the roof and the Osiris chapels, if the guards have it open.
fun_fact: Christians defacing the reliefs often left Horus untouched; one suggestion is that the falcon-headed son of a divine mother seemed too close to their own story.
narration:
You are passing from the court into the heart of the temple. Before you go in, look down at the base of the second pylon. The builders hit a lump of natural granite and, instead of removing it, they smoothed it into a stela, recording a gift of land by King Ptolemy the Sixth.

Inside is the hypostyle hall, a roofed forest of columns. Look up. The capitals, flowers and palm leaves still carry their green, blue and red after more than 2,000 years. The dimness is deliberate: each step deeper into an Egyptian temple is darker, lower and holier.

Now look for crosses. In the 6th century, after the temple closed, Bishop Theodore turned this hall into a church of Saint Stephen. Christians carved crosses into the walls and chiselled away the faces of the old gods, though Horus is often oddly spared. A Christian altar survives from those days.

Go through the three small rooms beyond and you reach the sanctuary. It is tiny, with no windows. Here stood the statue of Isis in her shrine. Every morning a priest broke the seal, woke the goddess, washed, dressed and fed her, then sealed her in again. The granite pedestal in the middle once carried her sacred boat for processions. Stand still in the dark for a moment, and look at that pedestal.

name: Gate of Hadrian and the last hieroglyphic inscription (394 AD)
note: West of the temple: the gateway where the relief shows Hapi in the cavern under Bigeh island pouring the Nile from two jars (the mythical source), and the dead Osiris carried by a crocodile; here, on 24 August 394 AD, the priest Esmet-Akhom carved the last dated hieroglyphic inscription, and in 452 AD the last demotic; the script then went unread for 1,400 years until Champollion. The Abaton of Bigeh across the water, Osiris' tomb, where no bird sang.
period: Roman, Hadrian (AD 117-138); last hieroglyphic inscription AD 394
summary: The doorway where the Nile is born from a cave, and where in AD 394 a priest carved the last hieroglyphs anyone has found.
look: West of the main temple, near the second pylon, a gateway stands in a wall: the Gate of Hadrian. On its inner wall a relief shows the Nile god Hapi crouching in a cave beneath piled rocks, ringed by a snake, pouring water from two jars; nearby a crocodile carries the body of Osiris. The last hieroglyphic inscription is a small graffito beside a figure of the Nubian god Mandulis on this gate; it is easy to miss, so ask a guard or guide. The large rocky island nearby is Bigeh.
story:
Hadrian's gateway opened towards Bigeh, the sacred island the Greeks called the Abaton, 'the place not to be entered', where Osiris was believed to lie buried. Only priests crossed over, and the island was to be kept quiet: no music, no shouting, no fishing or hunting near the god's tomb. Ancient writers repeated that no bird flew over it and no fish came near its shores.

The relief of Hapi is theology's map of the Nile. Egyptians knew the river came from far to the south, yet they placed its mythical source right here, in a cavern under the cataract, from which the flood was poured out each year.

On 24 August 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest called Esmet-Akhom, son of a second priest of Isis, carved a figure of Mandulis on this gate with a short hieroglyphic text and a longer note in demotic: he made the figure for all time, he says, because the god had been kind to him. It is the last dated hieroglyphic inscription known. The last demotic inscription followed on Philae in 452.

After that, the temples closed and the scribes died out. For some 1,400 years nobody could read a single sign, despite many attempts, until Jean-Francois Champollion cracked the system in 1822 with the help of the Rosetta Stone and of an obelisk from this very island.
details: On the gate's inner wall: Hapi in his cave under the rocks, ringed by a snake, pouring the Nile from two jars.
Nearby, a crocodile swimming with the body of Osiris on its back.
The small, rather crude figure of Mandulis in a tall plumed crown, with the AD 394 graffito: ask a guard to point it out.
Look across the water to Bigeh island, the Abaton, Osiris's tomb.
fun_fact: The last person known to have written hieroglyphs signed off with a dedication to a Nubian god, not an Egyptian one.
narration:
You are at the Gate of Hadrian, a Roman doorway on the west side of the temple. It faced the next island, Bigeh, which the Greeks called the Abaton, the place no one may enter. Egyptians believed Osiris lay buried there. Only priests crossed over, and the island was meant to stay silent: no music, no shouting, no fishing.

Look at the relief on the inner wall. Under a pile of rocks, inside a cave ringed by a snake, the Nile god Hapi crouches and pours water from two jars. This is the source of the Nile as theology placed it: right here, under the cataract. Nearby, a crocodile carries the dead body of Osiris across the water.

Now the moment this gate is famous for. On the 24th of August, AD 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest called Esmet Akhom carved a figure of the Nubian god Mandulis here, with a few lines in hieroglyphs. They are the last dated hieroglyphs anyone has found. A last note in demotic script followed on Philae in 452. Then the knowledge died. For about 1,400 years nobody could read a single sign, until Champollion cracked the code in 1822.

Look for the small, rather crude figure of Mandulis in his tall plumed crown. Those few scratches are the final words of a script that had lasted more than 3,000 years.

name: Trajan's Kiosk, 'the Pharaoh's Bed'
note: 14 columns with composite capitals carrying unfinished screen walls, roofless (wooden roof lost); Trajan shown offering to Isis and Osiris inside; probably the ceremonial river entrance where the barque landed; the 19th-century painters' favourite (David Roberts); look how the capitals were never finished.
period: Roman, probably begun under Augustus; decorated under Trajan (AD 98-117)
summary: Fourteen columns by the water, a wooden roof long gone, and the postcard of Philae: Isis's grand river entrance, never finished.
look: On the east shore stands a rectangular pavilion about 15 by 20 metres and nearly 16 metres high: fourteen columns, four on each end and five on each side, joined by screen walls, with doorways in the east and west facades. It is open to the sky. Inside, on the screen walls, Trajan burns incense before Isis and Osiris.
story:
Archaeologists call it a hypaethral temple, from the Greek for 'under the sky'. It was the island's main entrance from the river, and probably sheltered the sacred barque of Isis when it landed on the east bank. The name comes from the reliefs inside showing the emperor Trajan as pharaoh, burning incense to Isis and Osiris, but most of the structure may be older, possibly from the reign of Augustus.

It was never finished. Each column carries a different, lavish composite capital, topped by a plain block over 2 metres high that was meant to be carved into a figure of the dwarf god Bes, as in the birth houses at Philae, Armant and Dendera. The carving never happened.

The roof was wood. Sockets in the stone architraves show where three timber trusses, each about 12.5 metres long, carried a gently vaulted roof: an unusual marriage of wood and stone in an Egyptian temple.

Locals call it Pharaoh's Bed. In the 1830s the Scottish painter David Roberts drew it under that name, and travellers have been sketching it ever since.
details: Above each capital, a tall plain block: it was meant to become a carved figure of Bes.
Compare the capitals: each is a different composite of plant forms.
Along the top of the architraves, look for the sockets that held the wooden roof trusses.
On the inner screen walls: Trajan as pharaoh burning incense before Isis and Osiris.
Stand at the water's edge and look back: this is the postcard view.
fun_fact: During the decades when the old dam flooded Philae, boats could glide right between the columns of this kiosk.
narration:
This is Trajan's Kiosk, the building on every postcard of Philae. Locals call it Pharaoh's Bed. It stands on the east shore, and that is the point: this was the island's grand entrance from the river, where the sacred boat of Isis came and went in procession.

Count the columns: fourteen, four along each end and five down each side, joined by low screen walls. It is nearly 16 metres high, and it has no roof. It did once. Look along the tops of the stone beams and you can find the sockets for big timber trusses that carried a gently curved wooden roof. Wood and stone together like that is rare in an Egyptian temple. Archaeologists use a Greek word for a temple like this, hypaethral, open to the sky.

It is named after the Roman emperor Trajan, because inside he appears as a pharaoh, burning incense before Isis and Osiris. But most of it may be older, from the time of Augustus. And it was never finished. Each capital is topped by a tall stone block that was meant to be carved into the dwarf god Bes. The sculptors never came back.

In the 1830s the Scottish painter David Roberts drew it as the Bed of Pharaoh. Now look up at those plain blocks above the capitals: that is where Bes was supposed to be.

name: Temple of Hathor with the musicians and Bes
note: Short. Small Ptolemaic temple east of the main one: reliefs of Bes playing the harp and tambourine, monkeys playing the lute, flute players: Hathor as goddess of music and joy; the Nubian festivals.
period: Ptolemaic and Roman
summary: A small temple where the gods play music: Bes on harp and tambourine, a monkey on the lute, all for Hathor, goddess of joy.
look: East of the main temple, a few steps from Trajan's Kiosk, stands the small temple of Hathor: a front hall of columns and a ruined inner part. The reliefs worth finding are on the columns and screen walls of the front hall: musicians, dancers and offerings of drink.
story:
Hathor was the goddess of love, music, dancing and drunkenness, and on Philae she had a small temple of her own beside Isis. Its front hall is a party in stone. The dwarf god Bes, protector of homes and of childbirth, plays the harp and beats a tambourine; a monkey plays the lute; other figures play pipes and offer wine.

The theme comes from a myth. Hathor once stormed off to the south in fury as a lioness, and the gods had to coax her home to Egypt with music, dance and drink. Philae, on the southern border, was a natural place to welcome her back.
details: Bes, short, bearded and bandy-legged, playing a harp.
Bes again with a tambourine: Hathor's festivals were loud.
A monkey playing the lute among the musicians.
Figures offering jars of wine: drink was part of Hathor's worship.
fun_fact: One of Hathor's feasts was known as a Festival of Drunkenness: getting merry in her honour was a religious duty.
narration:
This small temple belongs to Hathor, goddess of love, music, dancing and, yes, drinking. Look at the reliefs in the front hall: it is a concert. The dwarf god Bes, bearded and bandy-legged, plays the harp and bangs a tambourine. A monkey plays the lute. Others blow pipes and offer wine.

There is a myth behind the music. Hathor once stormed off to the south as a furious lioness, and the gods had to coax her home with songs, dancing and drink. Philae, on the southern border, was the place to welcome her back. Find Bes with his harp first, then look for the monkey with the lute.

name: From Isis to Christ: the closing of Philae
note: The Blemmyes and Nobatae nomads kept worshipping Isis under treaty (Diocletian allowed them to borrow her statue yearly) long after Christianity won; Justinian's general Narses closed the temple c. 535-537, imprisoned the priests, took the statues to Constantinople; Bishop Theodore turned the hypostyle into St Stephen's church, hacking the faces of gods and carving crosses; the two Coptic churches on the island.
period: AD 298 to the 6th century
summary: Isis outlived the old gods elsewhere by well over a century here, thanks to Nubian peoples and a treaty, until Justinian ordered her temple closed.
look: The Christian layer is everywhere once you look for it: crosses cut into doorways and walls, gods with their faces hacked away, and a Christian altar in the hypostyle hall of the Isis temple, which became a church of St Stephen.
story:
In AD 298 the emperor Diocletian pulled Rome's frontier back to Philae and agreed to pay the Nobades and the Blemmyes, two peoples of the south, a yearly stipend in gold to keep the peace. Both worshipped Isis. So while temples were closing across the Christian empire, Philae stayed open. In 452 a treaty between the Roman commander Maximinus and the Blemmyes and Nobades still guaranteed them access to the cult image of Isis. The last hieroglyphic (394) and demotic (452) inscriptions were carved here.

Christians lived on the island too: by the mid-5th century there were several churches beside the temples. The historian Procopius says the end came under Justinian: his commander Narses destroyed the sanctuaries, put the priests under guard and sent the statues to Constantinople. The closure is dated to 537. Many scholars now argue, with Jitse Dijkstra, that organised worship had faded long before, since the last evidence of an active priesthood dates to the 450s.

Afterwards five temples were turned into churches, the temple of Isis becoming a church of St Stephen. The crosses and hacked faces you see are the scars.
details: In the hypostyle hall: crosses cut over the reliefs, and a Christian altar.
Gods with chiselled-out faces next to figures of Horus left untouched.
Small crosses scratched into door jambs by Christian worshippers.
Greek inscriptions from the church period among the reliefs; ask your guide to point one out.
fun_fact: Isis was still being worshipped here under a Roman treaty in 452, some 60 years after the emperor Theodosius had outlawed pagan sacrifice.
narration:
Look around and you will find crosses carved into these walls, and gods with their faces chiselled away. They tell how Philae became the last stand of the old religion.

In AD 298 the emperor Diocletian pulled Rome's border back to this island and paid two southern peoples, the Nobades and the Blemmyes, a yearly gift of gold to keep the peace. Both worshipped Isis. So while temples were closing all over the Christian empire, Philae stayed open for them. A treaty in 452 still guaranteed them access to the statue of Isis.

Christians lived here too, with several churches beside the temples. The historian Procopius says the end came under the emperor Justinian, around 537. His general Narses tore down the sanctuaries, put the priests under guard and sent the statues to Constantinople. Many scholars now think the old cult had already faded by then.

The temple of Isis became a church of Saint Stephen. Look for a cross cut right across an ancient relief, and notice which faces were hacked. Horus, oddly, is often spared.

name: Moving Philae: coffer dam and 40,000 blocks
note: After the 1902 dam Philae stood half-submerged ten months a year (tourists rowed through the hypostyle); after the High Dam it would have drowned permanently; 1972-80 UNESCO/Italian Condotte-Mazzi: a coffer dam of two rows of steel sheet piles, pumped dry, 40,000 blocks cleaned and numbered, Agilkia island cut down and reshaped to the same outline, 500 m away and 13 m higher.
period: Flooded from 1902; moved to Agilkia 1977-1980
summary: For decades visitors rowed through a half-drowned temple; then engineers drained the river, cut Philae into 40,000 pieces and rebuilt it on another island.
look: Stand at the edge of Agilkia and look out over the water: the original island of Philae lies about 500 metres away under the reservoir between the old dam and the High Dam. Agilkia was cut down and reshaped to copy Philae's outline, so the temples sit in the same relation to each other and to the water as before, but 12.4 metres higher. Look closely at any wall for the fine joints between reassembled blocks.
story:
When the British finished the first Aswan dam in 1902, its reservoir covered Philae for much of the year. The dam was raised again in 1907-1912 and 1929-1934, and the island emerged only when the sluices were open, from July to October. Visitors rowed between the capitals; plants and paint washed away and silt crusted the stone. Proposals to move the temples were rejected in favour of strengthening the foundations.

The High Dam (1960-1970) made it worse: Philae would sit permanently in water that rose and fell between the two dams. By the 1960s up to a third of the buildings were under water all year. UNESCO's Nubian campaign at first left Philae out, but international pressure brought it in, and a plan by Egyptian designers won the competition.

A coffer dam of two rows of steel plates, with a million cubic metres of sand between them, was built around the island and the water pumped out. Every structure was recorded by photogrammetry and cut into about 40,000 numbered blocks weighing 2 to 25 tons. The Egyptian High Dam Company levelled Agilkia and laid the foundations; the Italian firms Condotte and Mazzi Estero dismantled and rebuilt the 95 structures. The operation ran from 1977 to 1980.
details: Fine joints between the blocks: each of about 40,000 pieces went back to its numbered place.
From the island's edge, look towards the old island's site, about 500 metres away under the water.
Notice how the temples still sit right at the water's edge: Agilkia was reshaped to copy Philae.
On some lower walls, look for paler, washed-out reliefs: decades of flooding stripped their paint.
fun_fact: The European Space Agency's comet lander Philae aimed for a landing site named Agilkia in 2014; it bounced and came to rest about a kilometre away.
narration:
Everything around you has been taken apart and put back together. For almost 70 years this temple spent much of each year under water.

When the British finished the first Aswan dam in 1902, its lake rose over Philae. The dam was raised twice more, and the island only came out when the sluices opened in summer. Tourists rowed between the tops of the columns.

Then came the High Dam. Philae would now sit forever in water rising and falling between the two dams, grinding the stone. So in the 1970s engineers built a double wall of steel plates around the island, filled it with sand, and pumped the inside dry. Every building was measured, photographed and cut into about 40,000 numbered blocks, some weighing 25 tons. Meanwhile nearby Agilkia island was cut down to match Philae's outline, about 12 metres higher. Italian firms rebuilt the temples, and the work was finished in 1980.

Look closely at a wall near you and find the fine joints between the blocks. Each one went back exactly where it came from.

name: The Nubian Museum: how to see it
note: Orientation: opened 1997 (Aga Khan Award for Architecture, Mahmoud El-Hakim), built in local sandstone like a Nubian village, to hold what was saved from drowned Nubia; the chronological route: prehistory, A-Group, C-Group, Kerma, New Kingdom Nubia, Kush/Napata (25th Dynasty), Meroe, Christian Nubia, Islamic Nubia, ethnography; the garden with a Nubian house and the cave painting; ~2 hours.
period: Opened 1997; collections from prehistory to the 20th century
summary: Built to hold what was saved when Lake Nasser drowned Nubia: the story of Egypt's southern neighbour in one walk.
look: The building, in local sandstone and granite, steps down a steep slope like a Nubian village, set in a large landscaped garden. Inside, a big main hall holds the largest monuments, and the galleries run in order from prehistory through the Nubian kingdoms, Egyptian rule, the Kushite pharaohs, Meroe, Christian and Islamic Nubia, ending with Nubian village life. Outside, paths lead past a reconstructed Nubian house and other open-air displays. Allow about two hours.
story:
Egypt asked for this museum in 1960, when the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia began. The High Dam's lake was about to cover Lower Nubia, and archaeologists from all over the world raced to excavate and rescue what they could. The finds needed a home, and the Nubians a place for their memory. A trust fund from donor states and the governments of Egypt and Sudan paid for it.

The Egyptian architect Mahmoud El-Hakim designed it, and it opened on 23 November 1997. In 2001 it won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. The site covers about 50,000 square metres, of which 7,000 are building, on three floors with a library and documentation centre. Around 3,000 objects were registered for it, from geology and prehistory through Pharaonic, Roman, Coptic and Islamic times to the history of Aswan.

Why does Nubia deserve a museum of its own? Because it was the corridor between Egypt and the rest of Africa, a source of gold, ivory, ebony and incense, and home to kingdoms that rivalled Egypt and once ruled it. This museum lets you see that story from the Nubian side. It is air-conditioned, which makes it a good midday visit.
details: From the entrance, look at the building itself: stepped sandstone volumes echoing a Nubian village.
In the main hall, the colossal statues: check each label for the site it was rescued from.
Follow the galleries in order; the labels give the period for each case.
In the garden, the reconstructed Nubian house and its painted entrance.
fun_fact: Only about 7,000 of the site's 50,000 square metres are building; the rest is garden, so leave time to wander outside.
narration:
Welcome to the Nubian Museum. It exists because of a flood. When Egypt built the High Dam in the 1960s, the lake behind it was going to drown Lower Nubia, the whole valley between Aswan and the Sudanese border, with its temples, cemeteries and villages. Archaeologists from all over the world rushed to dig and rescue what they could, and Egypt asked UNESCO for a museum to keep it. This is the result, opened in 1997.

Notice the building first. The architect, Mahmoud El Hakim, used local sandstone and granite and stepped it down the slope like a Nubian village. It won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Why Nubia? It was the corridor between Egypt and the rest of Africa. Gold, ivory, ebony and incense all came north through it. The Egyptians called it Ta Seti, the Land of the Bow, after its famous archers. For 3,000 years Egypt and Nubia traded, fought, intermarried and took turns conquering each other.

The galleries run in order: prehistory, the early Nubian cultures, the kingdom of Kerma, Egyptian rule, the Kushite kings who became pharaohs, Meroe, Christian and Islamic Nubia, and finally Nubian village life. Give it about two hours, then walk the garden. Start in the main hall, and look up at the biggest statue there.

name: Nubia in ten minutes: Egypt's rival and twin
note: Ta-Seti 'Land of the Bow'; the corridor between Egypt and Africa; Lower Nubia (Wawat) vs Upper Nubia (Kush); the cycle: Egyptian conquest (Middle Kingdom forts, New Kingdom temples) then Nubian conquest of Egypt (25th Dynasty 'Black Pharaohs' c. 747-656 BC); Napata and Meroe; more pyramids in Sudan than in Egypt; Nubian language and identity today; the two displacements (1902-1964).
period: From prehistory to today
summary: Egypt's southern neighbour, rival, colony and conqueror: the Land of the Bow, whose kings once ruled Egypt and built more pyramids than the pharaohs.
look: No single object here: use this as the key to the museum. On any map of the Nile find the cataracts. Lower Nubia lay between the First and Second Cataracts, now largely under Lake Nasser; Middle and Upper Nubia, the heartland of Kush, lie upstream in Sudan, as far as the meeting of the Blue and White Niles at Khartoum.
story:
Nubia is the Nile valley between the First Cataract and Khartoum. The Egyptians called it Ta-Seti, 'the Land of the Bow', after its archers. Egyptian texts distinguished Wawat, the north, from Kush, the south.

The two peoples were intertwined from the start. Around 3100 BC rulers of the A-Group culture were buried at Qustul with real wealth, until Egypt's First Dynasty apparently destroyed them. From about 2500 BC the kingdom of Kerma grew into a power that controlled the valley from the First to the Fourth Cataract and raided deep into Egypt. Egypt built fortresses against it and, around 1500 BC under Thutmose I, conquered it; for nearly five centuries Egyptian viceroys ran Nubia for its gold and built temples like Abu Simbel.

Then the tables turned. In the 8th century BC the kings of Kush, ruling from Napata, conquered Egypt as the 25th Dynasty, until Assyria drove them out. The kingdom moved its centre south to Meroe and lasted until the 4th century AD. Three Christian kingdoms followed, Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia; Makuria fought off the Arab armies in 652 and kept a treaty with Egypt for some 600 years. From the late Middle Ages Nubia became Muslim.

Nubians live on, with their own languages. Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and the High Dam displaced about 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan.
details: On the museum's maps, find Qustul, Kerma, Napata and Meroe: the four great centres in order.
Look for bows and arrowheads: the archers who gave Ta-Seti its name.
Compare faces: Nubians in Egyptian art are shown with darker skin, short curled hair and distinctive dress.
Watch for objects that mix the two styles: Egyptian gods in Nubian hands, Nubian pottery in Egyptian graves.
fun_fact: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: over 200 at Meroe alone, steeper and narrower than those at Giza.
narration:
Here is Nubia in a few minutes, so the museum makes sense. Nubia is the Nile valley south of Aswan, from the First Cataract to around Khartoum. The Egyptians called it Ta Seti, the Land of the Bow, because Nubian archers were the best they knew.

Think of Egypt and Nubia as two neighbours who never stopped arguing. Around 3100 BC Nubian chiefs at Qustul were buried with real wealth, until Egypt's first kings crushed them. Then the kingdom of Kerma rose in Sudan and grew strong enough to raid deep into Egypt. Egypt answered with fortresses and, around 1500 BC, with conquest: viceroys, gold mines, and temples like Abu Simbel.

Then the tables turned. In the 8th century BC the kings of Kush marched north and ruled all Egypt as pharaohs, the 25th Dynasty, until the Assyrians drove them home. They moved their capital south to Meroe and built more pyramids than Egypt ever did. Later came Christian Nubian kingdoms that fought off the Arab armies and then kept the peace by treaty for 600 years, and finally Islam.

Nubians are still here, with their own languages. In the 1960s about 100,000 of them in Egypt and Sudan lost their homes to the lake behind the High Dam. As you walk the galleries, watch how Egyptian and Nubian styles keep borrowing from each other.

name: Prehistory and the A-Group: Nubia before Egypt
note: Eggshell-thin painted pottery of the A-Group (c. 3800-3100 BC), the Qustul incense burner showing a crowned king before Egypt's First Dynasty (the 'Nubian kingship first?' debate), rock art of cattle and giraffes from the drowned region, the Nabta Playa stone circle (older than Stonehenge) in the Western Desert nearby.
period: A-Group, 4th millennium BC to about 2900 BC
summary: Pottery as thin as eggshell and a royal incense burner that started an argument: was Egypt's kingship born in Nubia?
look: The first galleries cover Nubia before writing: stone tools, images of cattle and wild animals, and A-Group pottery. Look for two kinds: eggshell ware, with walls only millimetres thick, often painted with patterns that resemble basketry, and black-topped red ware, polished red pots with a black rim.
story:
George Reisner named this culture the 'A-Group' in 1907, a label now outdated but still used. Its people lived between the First and Second Cataracts, from Kubaniyya near Aswan to Buhen: semi-nomadic herders, fishers and hunters who began farming late in the 4th millennium BC. They grew rich as middlemen, trading incense, ebony, ivory, carnelian and gold north for Egyptian goods, which ended up in their graves.

Their potters were superb. Eggshell ware has impossibly thin walls. Black-topped red ware was fired red, then the hot rim was dipped in sawdust to starve it of oxygen and turn it black.

In 1960-64, before the lake rose, the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute excavated the royal Cemetery L at Qustul, near Abu Simbel. One grave held nearly 200 vessels. Bruce Williams studied an incense burner from it carved with royal imagery and suggested kingship might have developed in Nubia first. Most scholars disagree: older royal images from Egypt itself suggest the Qustul rulers adopted Egyptian symbols. Around 2900 BC the A-Group disappears, apparently destroyed by Egypt's First Dynasty.
details: Eggshell ware: find the thinnest bowl in the case; its walls are only millimetres thick.
Black-topped red pots: the black rim came from dipping the hot pot in sawdust.
Images of cattle and wild animals: the world of Nubian herders and hunters.
Any object labelled Qustul: the A-Group royal cemetery near Abu Simbel, now under Lake Nasser.
fun_fact: At Nabta Playa in the desert west of Abu Simbel, prehistoric people set up a stone circle that may be one of the world's first astronomical devices, about 2,000 years before Stonehenge.
narration:
These first rooms show Nubia before history, and the star here is pottery. Look for two kinds. Eggshell ware has walls only millimetres thick, so fine it is hard to believe it was made without a wheel. Black-topped red ware was polished red, then its rim was dipped in sawdust while hot, starving it of oxygen and turning it black.

The people who made them have a dull name, the A-Group, given by the archaeologist George Reisner in 1907. They lived between the First and Second Cataracts, herding, fishing and hunting, and they grew rich as middlemen, passing incense, ebony, ivory and gold north to Egypt.

Their chiefs were buried at Qustul, near Abu Simbel. An incense burner from one royal grave carries royal symbols, and one scholar suggested that kingship might have begun here, not in Egypt. Most experts disagree, because older royal images exist in Egypt itself. Around 2900 BC the A-Group vanished, probably crushed by Egypt's first kings. Now find the thinnest bowl in the case.

name: C-Group, Pan-Grave and the Kingdom of Kerma
note: C-Group cattle herders with their decorated bowls and cattle burials; the Medjay desert archers who became Egypt's police; Kerma (c. 2500-1500 BC), first great African kingdom south of Egypt, with its mud-brick Deffufa temple and kings buried with hundreds of sacrificed retainers; the Middle Kingdom fortresses (Buhen, Semna) built against Kerma, now under Lake Nasser; the Hyksos-Kerma alliance against Thebes.
period: C-Group about 2400-1550 BC; Kerma about 2500-1500 BC
summary: Cattle herders, desert archers and the first great kingdom of inner Africa, which once invaded Egypt while the Hyksos held the north.
look: This section mixes several peoples. Look for C-Group bowls with incised geometric patterns and images of cattle; weapons and grave goods of the desert archers; and Kerma pottery, thin polished beakers flaring like tulips, red with a black top.
story:
The C-Group (about 2400-1550 BC) were cattle herders in Lower Nubia. Cattle meant milk, blood, hides and status, and their stone-circle graves had offering chapels with stelae showing cattle and horns. Their neighbours included desert peoples known as the Pan-Grave culture, usually linked with the Medjay, archers whom Egypt hired as scouts and soldiers; in the New Kingdom 'Medjay' came to mean police.

Further south, at Kerma in Sudan, grew the first great kingdom of inner Africa. By its classic phase (1750-1500 BC) Kerma was a city of about 25 hectares with a huge mud-brick temple, the Western Deffufa, which still stands. Its kings were buried under great mounds with large numbers of human sacrifices. At its height Kerma controlled the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract.

Egypt was afraid of it. Middle Kingdom kings built forts at Buhen, Aniba, Kor and elsewhere, now under the lake. Kerma allied itself with the Hyksos, the foreign kings of northern Egypt, and an inscription in the tomb of Sobeknakht at El-Kab records a Kushite invasion deep into Egypt between about 1575 and 1550 BC; statues looted from Egypt were carried to Kerma. Around 1500 BC Thutmose I destroyed it.
details: C-Group bowls: incised geometric patterns, sometimes filled with white.
Images of cattle and horns: the C-Group's wealth walked on four legs.
Kerma beakers: tulip-shaped, red body, black rim, walls thin and polished.
Bows, arrowheads and daggers: the archers of the desert.
fun_fact: The Theban king Kamose caught a messenger in the desert carrying a letter from the Hyksos king to the ruler of Kush, inviting him to attack Egypt from the south and share the spoils.
narration:
This room is about the peoples who filled Nubia after the A-Group, and one of them nearly broke Egypt.

First, the C-Group, cattle herders from about 2400 BC. Cattle were their wealth: milk, blood, hides and status. They decorated graves and pottery with cattle, so look for horned animals scratched into stone and clay.

Next, desert archers known as the Medjay. Egypt hired them as scouts and soldiers, and later the word Medjay simply meant police.

Then the giant: the kingdom of Kerma, far south in Sudan. By 1750 BC Kerma was a real city, with a huge mud-brick temple that still stands. Its kings were buried under great mounds with many sacrificed servants. Egypt built fortresses to watch it. Around 1550 BC, while foreign Hyksos kings held the north of Egypt, Kerma invaded from the south. An Egyptian king even caught a messenger carrying a letter from the Hyksos king to the ruler of Kush, proposing an alliance. Around 1500 BC Egypt struck back and destroyed Kerma. Look for Kerma's tulip-shaped beakers, red with a black rim.

name: New Kingdom Nubia: the viceroys and the temples
note: The colossal Ramesses II statue from Gerf Hussein near the entrance; Nubian princes raised at the Egyptian court (Hekanefer); the tribute scenes (gold rings, panther skins, giraffes); the 'King's Son of Kush' administration; temples of Amada, Derr, Wadi es-Sebua, Dakka, Kalabsha moved from the lake.
period: New Kingdom, about 1550-1070 BC
summary: When Egypt ruled Nubia: a viceroy called the King's Son of Kush, Nubian princes raised at court, and gold by the ring.
look: This section shows Nubia as an Egyptian province: statues and stelae of officials, temple pieces from sites now under Lake Nasser, and objects that blend Egyptian and Nubian styles. The colossal royal statues in the main hall belong to this chapter; check their labels for the sites they were rescued from.
story:
After Thutmose I destroyed Kerma around 1500 BC, Egypt governed Nubia for nearly five centuries. In charge was a viceroy who reported directly to pharaoh, first titled 'King's Son of the Southern Lands' and, from Thutmose IV's reign, 'King's Son of Kush'. Under him were two provinces: Wawat in the north, centred at Aniba, and Kush in the south, centred at Soleb and later Amara West. He had two deputies, scribes, an overseer of cattle and the priests of the Egyptian-built temples.

The prize was gold. The tomb of the viceroy Amenhotep, called Huy, at Thebes shows the tribute being counted and shipped north to the king. Among the Nubians in those scenes is Heqanefer, prince of Miam, who had been brought up at the Egyptian court and was buried in Nubia in an Egyptian-style tomb.

Pharaohs filled Nubia with temples, from Amada and Wadi es-Sebua to Abu Simbel; most were moved in the 1960s. Revolts flared for centuries, and after about 1070 BC, as Egypt weakened, the title King's Son of Kush faded away.
details: The colossal statues in the main hall: read the labels for where they once stood.
Statues or stelae naming a King's Son of Kush, Egypt's viceroy of Nubia.
Gold objects: rings, jewellery or ingots, the reason Egypt wanted Nubia.
Pieces where Egyptian and Nubian styles mix: Nubian faces and dress in Egyptian poses.
fun_fact: The name Nubia may come from nub, the Egyptian word for gold, though no ancient text actually uses it that way.
narration:
This part of the museum covers the centuries when Egypt ruled Nubia. Around 1500 BC Thutmose the First destroyed Kerma, and for nearly 500 years Egyptian control reached deep into Sudan.

The man in charge was a viceroy with a grand title: King's Son of Kush. He reported straight to the pharaoh and ran two provinces, Wawat in the north, roughly the area now under Lake Nasser, and Kush in the south.

What did Egypt want? Gold, above all. Nubia's deserts held the richest mines Egypt knew. In the tomb of one viceroy, Huy, at Thebes, the yearly tribute arrives and is counted for the king. Among the Nubians in those scenes is a prince called Heqanefer, raised at the Egyptian court, who was later buried at home in an Egyptian-style tomb.

Pharaohs also covered Nubia with temples, Abu Simbel among them, and most were moved in the 1960s to escape the lake. Look in this section for a statue or stela naming a King's Son of Kush, and ask yourself whether the face looks Egyptian or Nubian.

name: The Black Pharaohs: Napata and the 25th Dynasty
note: Piye's invasion c. 727 BC recorded on his Victory Stela (horses!), the Kushite pharaohs Shabaka, Shebitku, Taharqa, Tanutamun ruling from Napata and Memphis, the double uraeus, the cap crown, the ram of Amun of Gebel Barkal; Taharqa's buildings at Karnak (kiosk, 22 Oct), the Assyrian invasion that ended them (671-663 BC); the archaising art.
period: 25th Dynasty, 8th-7th century BC; Taharqa 690-664 BC
summary: Kings from Sudan who conquered Egypt, revived its ancient art and temples, and fought Assyria before being driven home.
look: Look for Kushite royal images: kings wearing a close-fitting cap crown with two cobras on the brow instead of one, with broad faces and strong necks. Look too for Amun as a ram, the god of Gebel Barkal, the holy mountain at Napata. Some pieces may be originals and some casts; trust the labels.
story:
After Egypt withdrew from Nubia, a new kingdom grew at Napata, beneath the sacred mountain of Gebel Barkal, where Thutmose III had founded a temple of Amun. Its kings worshipped Amun fervently. King Kashta took over Upper Egypt peacefully, and his daughter Amenirdis became God's Wife of Amun at Thebes.

His son Piye ruled from 744 BC. When Tefnakht of Sais led a coalition of Delta princes south, Piye marched north in his 20th year, arrived at Thebes in time for the Opet festival, took Hermopolis after a five-month siege and captured Memphis. His Victory Stela from Gebel Barkal tells how he made his soldiers purify themselves before battle, and how he was more upset that the horses of Hermopolis had been starved than by the rebellion itself. Then he went home and never returned.

His successors Shabaka, Shebitku, Taharqa and Tanutamun ruled from Memphis and Napata. Taharqa (690-664 BC) enjoyed a great flood and a building boom at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal, and was buried in the largest Nubian pyramid, at Nuri, with over 1,070 shabtis. These kings revived the styles of the Old and Middle Kingdoms on purpose. In 701 BC a Kushite army marched to help Hezekiah of Judah against Sennacherib; the Bible calls Taharqa Tirhakah. Assyria struck back: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 and captured Taharqa's family, and Ashurbanipal's army sacked Thebes in 663. Herodotus, writing in Greek more than two centuries later, remembered an 'Ethiopian' king Sabakos, Shabaka, who put criminals to work building embankments instead of executing them.
details: Two cobras on a king's brow: the sign of a Kushite pharaoh.
The close-fitting cap crown, typical of the Kushite kings.
Amun as a ram, or a ram's head: the god of Gebel Barkal.
Heavy, muscular royal statues that deliberately copy Old Kingdom models.
Taharqa's name in a cartouche; you will see his giant column at Karnak on the 22nd.
fun_fact: When the Assyrians took Memphis, they carried colossal statues of Taharqa home as trophies; pieces of three were found at the entrance of a palace at Nineveh.
narration:
This section is about the kings Greek writers called Ethiopians, often called today the Black Pharaohs: the rulers of Kush, from Napata in Sudan, who governed all of Egypt for most of a century.

They worshipped Amun as fervently as any Theban, and they saw Egypt as a land that had lost its way. In the 720s BC King Piye marched north, timed his visit to Thebes for Amun's great festival, besieged Hermopolis for five months and took Memphis. He ordered his soldiers to purify themselves before battle. And he loved horses: in his victory inscription he is angrier that the horses of Hermopolis were starved during the siege than about the rebellion itself. Then he sailed home and never came back.

His successors stayed. Shabaka, Shebitku, and above all Taharqa, who ruled from 690 to 664 BC and built at Karnak, where you will see his giant column on the 22nd. These kings deliberately revived the art of the pyramid age. Their armies fought Assyria in Palestine, and the Bible remembers Taharqa as Tirhakah.

In the end Assyria won. It took Memphis in 671 BC and sacked Thebes in 663, and the Kushites went home to build pyramids in Sudan. Look for a king with two cobras on his brow instead of one: that is the sign of a Kushite pharaoh.

name: Meroe: iron, queens and an unread script
note: Capital moved south to Meroe c. 300 BC; iron smelting ('the Birmingham of Africa'), the steep narrow pyramids (over 200), the ruling queens (Kandake/Candace, Amanirenas who fought Augustus and buried his bronze head under a doorstep), Meroitic script still undeciphered; the lion god Apedemak; the Ballana post-Meroitic X-Group kings with their silver crowns (some here, some in Cairo).
period: Kingdom of Kush at Meroe, about 590 BC to AD 350
summary: Iron, ruling queens, an alphabet nobody fully understands, and a bronze head of Augustus buried under a temple step.
look: Look for fine painted Meroitic pottery, jewellery, offering tables and stelae carved in Meroitic script, an alphabet of 23 signs in two forms, one hieroglyphic and one cursive. Lion-headed figures represent Apedemak, Meroe's own war god.
story:
After the Assyrians, Kush turned south. King Aspelta possibly moved the capital from Napata to Meroe, between the Fifth and Sixth Cataracts, around 590 BC, and from about 280 BC the royal cemetery moved there too: more than 200 steep pyramids still stand. Meroe sat on iron ore and hardwood for fuel, and its iron industry led the scholar Archibald Sayce to call it 'the Birmingham of Africa', though modern scholars debate the scale.

Queens mattered. The king shared authority with the kandake, the queen mother, and some queens ruled. Meroe kept Egyptian gods such as Amun and Isis beside its own, like the lion-headed Apedemak.

In the 20s BC Meroitic forces raided Roman Egypt and carried off statues from the towns around Aswan. The prefect Petronius retaliated and sacked Napata, and a peace was agreed between Augustus and Queen Amanirenas. One looted bronze head of Augustus was buried under the steps of a temple at Meroe; it is now in the British Museum.

The Meroitic script has 23 letters derived from hieroglyphs. Scholars can read the sounds, but the language itself remains poorly understood.
details: Meroitic script on stelae or offering tables: hieroglyph-like signs or a flowing cursive, 23 letters in all.
Fine Meroitic pottery: thin, painted with plants and animals.
Lion-headed figures: Apedemak, the Meroitic god with no Egyptian twin.
Iron objects, the industry that made Meroe rich.
fun_fact: The Greek New Testament mentions a kandake: in Acts, Philip baptises the treasurer of 'Candace, queen of the Ethiopians', that is, of Meroe.
narration:
This room is Meroe, the last and longest chapter of ancient Kush. After the Assyrians pushed the Kushite pharaohs out of Egypt, the kingdom's centre shifted south to Meroe, far up the Nile in Sudan, and it lasted until the 4th century AD. Its kings and queens were buried there under more than 200 steep, narrow pyramids.

Iron helped make it rich. Queens had real power. The title kandake, queen mother, reached Greek as Candace, and the New Testament mentions the treasurer of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.

One queen, Amanirenas, took on Rome. Meroitic raiders looted statues from the towns around Aswan, Rome hit back, and in the end she made peace with Augustus. A bronze head of Augustus, taken in the raids, was buried under the steps of a temple at Meroe, perhaps so that everyone who went in walked over the emperor. It is now in the British Museum.

Look for writing in Meroitic script, an alphabet of 23 letters borrowed from hieroglyphs. Scholars can sound it out, but most of the words are still not understood.

name: Christian and Islamic Nubia
note: Conversion in the 6th century, kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, Alodia; the Baqt treaty with the Arabs (652 AD, slaves for grain and wine, 600 years of peace); the Faras cathedral frescoes rescued by the Poles (split between Warsaw and Khartoum, a few here), bishops with dark faces and white hands; Old Nubian language; conversion to Islam from the 14th century; the Fatimid-era tombstones from Aswan's cemetery.
period: Christian kingdoms from the 6th century; Islamic Nubia from about the 14th century
summary: Christian Nubian kingdoms that beat back the Arab armies, signed a treaty that lasted 600 years, and wrote their own language in Greek letters.
look: This section shows medieval Nubia: church objects and crosses, boldly painted pottery, inscriptions in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, and Islamic tombstones. The great wall paintings of the cathedral of Faras are mostly in Warsaw and Khartoum; if a painting fragment is on show here, its label will say where it came from.
story:
When Kush collapsed in the 4th century, three kingdoms took its place: Nobatia in the north, Makuria around Dongola, and Alodia in the south. In the 6th century rival missions from Constantinople, one backed by Justinian and one by his wife Theodora, raced to convert them. Probably in the 7th century Makuria absorbed Nobatia and reached as far north as Philae.

In 651-652 an Arab army under Abdallah ibn Saad besieged Dongola and bombarded it with catapults but could not take the citadel; Muslim sources praise the skill of the Nubian archers. The two sides agreed the Baqt: an annual exchange of Nubian slaves for Egyptian wheat and textiles, later expanded to protect travellers on both sides. Makuria was recognised as independent, and the Baqt lasted, with interruptions, for more than six centuries.

From the 9th to the 11th century Makuria flourished: churches covered in murals, fine painted pottery, and documents in Old Nubian, written in a Greek-based alphabet with extra signs, and readable today. The Polish team that excavated the cathedral of Faras in the 1960s rescued its paintings. Pressure from Mamluk Egypt, internal conflict and changing trade brought decline; Muslim kings ruled Dongola briefly in the 1310s and 1320s, and over the following centuries most Nubians became Muslim.
details: Old Nubian writing: letters that look almost Greek, with a few extra signs.
Christian-period pottery painted with bold birds, fish and geometric bands.
Crosses on stone, bronze or pottery from Nubian churches now under the lake.
Islamic tombstones in angular Kufic Arabic script, like those of Aswan's Fatimid cemetery.
fun_fact: Arab writers nicknamed the Nubians 'the pupil smiters', because their archers could hit an enemy in the eye.
narration:
For a thousand years after the pyramids of Meroe, Nubia was Christian. In the 6th century missionaries from Constantinople converted its kingdoms, and the strongest, Makuria, came to rule from Dongola as far north as Philae.

Then came a famous standoff. In 652 an Arab army marched south from newly conquered Egypt and besieged Dongola with catapults. It could not take the citadel. Arab writers nicknamed the Nubian archers the pupil smiters, because they aimed for the eyes. So both sides made a deal called the Baqt: every year Nubian slaves went north and Egyptian wheat and cloth went south. With interruptions, it lasted for more than 600 years.

Makuria flourished. Its cathedral at Faras was covered in paintings, rescued in the 1960s by Polish archaeologists. Nubians wrote their own language, Old Nubian, in a Greek-based alphabet that scholars can still read. From the 14th century the kingdom weakened and Nubia slowly became Muslim. Look for writing that looks almost Greek but not quite: that is likely Old Nubian.

name: Nubian life: houses, jewellery, music and the lost villages
note: The dioramas of a Nubian wedding, the waterwheel (saqiya) and the painted vaulted houses with plates set in the walls; Kenzi vs Fadija Nubians and their languages; the 1964 exodus photographs; the mahogany-coloured henna, the women's gold; the garden's reconstructed house; what the Gharb Soheil village visit shows (and what is staged).
period: Traditional Nubian life; resettlement after the dams, 1902-1964
summary: Painted vaulted houses, waterwheels and wedding songs, and the photographs of the 1960s, when a whole people left their valley to a lake.
look: The last galleries show traditional Nubian life in life-size scenes: a mud-brick house with a decorated facade, a waterwheel, a wedding, crafts and jewellery. Photographs show the old villages before Lake Nasser.
story:
Nubians are not a vanished people: they are Aswan's neighbours. In Egypt the main groups are the Kenzi, who speak Kenzi, and the Fadija, who speak Nobiin, a descendant of the medieval Old Nubian language. Further south in Sudan live the Halfawi, Sukkot, Mahas and Danagla.

Their villages once lined the river between Aswan and the Second Cataract, on a narrow strip of farmland watered by the saqiya, an ox-driven waterwheel lifting pots of water to the fields. Houses were built of mud brick with vaulted or domed roofs and big courtyards, their facades whitewashed and painted with patterns, birds or boats, some with china plates set into the walls. This architecture fascinated the Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy, who later designed the Aga Khan's villa here.

Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and families rebuilt higher up. The High Dam ended that: about 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan were displaced, and in Egypt the Kenzi and Fadija were resettled in 'New Nubia' villages near Kom Ombo, away from the river. For many families the move is still living memory, and today many Nubians live in Aswan, Kom Ombo and Cairo.
details: The house reconstruction: look for the vaulted roof and the painted decoration around the door.
The saqiya: an ox turns a wheel that raises a chain of pots from the river.
Photographs of villages before the lake: compare them with Gharb Soheil today.
Silver and gold jewellery: a bride's wealth worn on her body.
fun_fact: Nubian builders roofed rooms with mud-brick vaults raised without wooden scaffolding, leaning each course against the last, a trick Egyptians already used in the Ramesseum's granaries 3,000 years ago.
narration:
These last rooms bring Nubia up to living memory. The Nubians are not a lost people: they are Aswan's neighbours, and many still speak their own languages, Kenzi and Nobiin, at home.

Look at the house. Nubian homes were built of mud brick, with vaulted or domed roofs raised without wooden scaffolding, a big courtyard, and a facade whitewashed and painted with patterns, birds or boats. Some had china plates set into the walls.

The waterwheel, the saqiya, was turned by oxen, lifting pots of water to the fields along the narrow strip of the valley. Weddings went on for days, with drums, clapping and songs.

Then look at the photographs. Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and families rebuilt higher up. The High Dam finished the job. About 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan had to leave, and in Egypt many were resettled in new villages near Kom Ombo, away from the river. Find a photograph of a village before the lake, and picture it now under water.

name: The Unfinished Obelisk
note: 42 m, 1,168 tons, would have been a third larger than any obelisk ever raised; abandoned when a crack appeared; probably Hatshepsut's (compare her Karnak pair, 22 Oct); shows the whole method: pounding trenches with dolerite balls (you can see the pounder marks), test shafts, the plan to undercut; the Lateran obelisk comparison; the small museum of quarrying; go early, no shade.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, possibly Hatshepsut's reign, about 1479-1458 BC
summary: The biggest obelisk ever attempted, still lying in its quarry: about 42 metres and some 1,090 tonnes, abandoned when the granite cracked.
look: From walkways you look down into an open granite quarry. The obelisk lies on its back, its upper faces and sides cut free, its underside still part of the bedrock. A crack runs across it. Around it are the workers' trenches, their walls scooped into rounded hollows by pounding, and here and there faint ochre lines. There is no shade: come early.
story:
Finished, it would have stood about 41.75 metres tall and weighed nearly 1,090 tonnes, nearly a third larger than any obelisk Egypt ever raised. The largest standing today, the Lateran Obelisk in Rome, originally from Karnak, is 32.2 metres and 455 tonnes. Nobody signed this one, but it is often attributed to Hatshepsut, possibly as a partner to the Lateran obelisk; you will see her surviving obelisk at Karnak on the 22nd.

It shows the whole method. Quarrymen outlined the shape, then pounded the granite away with balls of dolerite, a stone harder than granite, working shoulder to shoulder in trenches around the block. Their marks, and the ochre lines marking the work, are still visible. Reginald Engelbach studied the site in detail in 1922. The next stage would have been to undercut the obelisk, free it from the bedrock, drag it to the river and float it north on the flood.

Then cracks appeared in the granite and the project was abandoned. It is a rare snapshot of a monument caught halfway. In 2005 an unfinished obelisk base and rock carvings were found elsewhere in the Aswan quarries, which are protected as an open-air museum.
details: The crack running across the body of the obelisk: the reason it was abandoned.
The trench walls: rows of rounded scoops left by dolerite pounders.
Faint ochre lines on the stone, where overseers marked the work.
The underside, still part of the bedrock: the cut that was never made.
Look at the pointed end: you can judge the full length from tip to base.
fun_fact: The word obelisk is Greek: obeliskos means 'little spit', a skewer for roasting meat. A cheeky name for a thousand tonnes of granite.
narration:
Below you lies the largest obelisk anyone ever tried to make, and it never left the ground. If it had been finished, it would have stood about 42 metres tall and weighed around 1,090 tonnes, nearly a third bigger than any obelisk the Egyptians ever raised. The largest one still standing today, in Rome, is about 32 metres.

Nobody signed it, but it is often thought to have been ordered by Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled as king, perhaps to pair with a giant obelisk at Karnak.

What makes it precious is that it shows the method. The workers did not cut this with iron tools. They pounded the granite with balls of dolerite, a stone even harder than granite, crouching shoulder to shoulder in trenches around the shape. Look at the trench walls: the rounded scoops are their pounding marks. You can still find faint ochre lines where the work was marked out.

Then cracks appeared in the granite, and the whole project was abandoned, with the underside still attached to the bedrock. Had it worked, they would have cut it free underneath, dragged it to the river, and floated it north on the flood.

Walk round until you can see the crack across the body of the obelisk. Then look again at the scalloped trench walls: every hollow is the work of human arms.

name: The granite quarries: Aswan stone all over Egypt
note: Red and black granite from Aswan in the King's Chamber of the Great Pyramid, Khafre's Valley Temple, every obelisk, the sarcophagi: 900 km downstream by barge in the flood; wedges and fire, dolerite pounders (dolerite is harder than granite), the 'trial-and-error' sides; the Roman quarries and the ancient inscriptions of quarry expeditions; how an obelisk was raised (the sand-pit theory, Chevrier).
period: Worked from the Early Dynastic period to Roman times, and still today
summary: The hard red and black stone of Egypt's grandest monuments, from Khufu's burial chamber to the obelisks of Rome, came out of these hills.
look: Around the Unfinished Obelisk and along the east-bank hills, look for worked granite: flat cut faces, trenches, and rows of rectangular slots where blocks were split with wedges. The stone is a coarse pink-red granite speckled with black, with grey and darker varieties too.
story:
Aswan granite was Egypt's luxury stone: hard, colourful, able to take a mirror polish and almost indestructible. The quarries on both banks supplied colossal statues, obelisks, sarcophagi and monolithic shrines across Egypt, and the pyramid builders used it for their most important rooms: the burial chamber of Khufu's Great Pyramid is built of it, and so are the great blocks of Khafre's Valley Temple. A road was cut beside the quarries from Syene to Philae.

Moving it was the hard part. Blocks were dragged on sledges to the river and loaded onto barges, ideally when the flood was high, then floated north.

Cutting it took patience. In earlier times quarrymen pounded trenches around a block with balls of dolerite, which is harder than granite; in later periods, especially Roman times, they cut a row of slots, drove in wedges and split the stone. How the Egyptians raised obelisks is still debated; one theory has the obelisk hauled up an earth ramp and lowered, base first, into a sand-filled pit as the sand was let out.

The Greek name syenite comes from Syene, and some quarries are still worked today.
details: Rows of rectangular slots along a rock edge: wedge holes for splitting granite.
Rounded scoops in trench walls: the marks of dolerite pounders.
Look closely at the stone: pink feldspar crystals, grey quartz and black flecks.
From the quarry, look at the surrounding hills: the whole ridge is the same granite.
fun_fact: If you went inside the Great Pyramid on the 12th, the King's Chamber you stood in was made of granite from these hills, carried the length of Egypt by river.
narration:
The rock around you is Aswan granite, Egypt's luxury stone. It is hard, it takes a mirror polish, and it almost never wears away. That is why pharaohs wanted it for their most important work: obelisks, colossal statues, sarcophagi, and the burial chamber deep inside Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza, which is built of blocks from these hills.

Getting it there was the hard part. Blocks were dragged on sledges to the river and loaded onto barges, ideally when the flood was high, then floated north the whole length of Egypt.

Look at how it was cut. In early times, quarrymen pounded it with balls of dolerite, an even harder stone, wearing trenches around the block. Later, they cut a row of slots along a line, hammered in wedges and split the rock. Both kinds of marks survive here.

The Greeks named the stone after the town: syenite, from Syene, the Greek name for Aswan. Find a row of neat rectangular slots on a rock edge nearby: that is where someone set out to split a block, perhaps 2,000 years ago.

name: Qubbet el-Hawa: Tombs of the Nobles
note: Old and Middle Kingdom rock tombs of the governors of Elephantine cut into the west bank cliff below a sheikh's dome; the steep staircases; Sarenput II (12th Dyn, best preserved, Osiride statues and the painted niche), Mekhu and Sabni (6th Dyn, father's body recovered from Nubia), Harkhuf; recent Spanish finds (Jaén University) of a 12th Dynasty family; sunset over the river.
period: Old and Middle Kingdom, about 2300-1800 BC; used from Dynasty 4 to the Roman period
summary: The governors of Egypt's frontier, buried in the cliff above the river: explorers, a son who rescued his father's body, and statues in the rock.
look: On the west bank opposite Aswan, rows of rock-cut tomb doorways line terraces below the summit, where a small domed sheikh's tomb gives the site its name, the Dome of the Wind. Steep stairs climb from the landing. Which tombs are open varies, but they usually include Sarenput II and the double tomb of Mekhu and Sabni; Harkhuf's inscribed facade is nearby. Bring water and a torch.
story:
About 100 tombs have been found here, used from the Fourth Dynasty to the Roman period. Most belong to the governors of Elephantine and the expedition leaders they sent south. Their tomb inscriptions record trading voyages and military campaigns, and are some of the earliest travel writing in the world.

The most dramatic is the double tomb of Mekhu and his son Sabni, of the Sixth Dynasty. Mekhu led a royal expedition south and was killed in Nubia. Sabni raised a force, went south, punished those responsible and brought his father's body home for burial.

The best preserved is the tomb of Sarenput II, governor under Amenemhat II and Senusret II in the 12th Dynasty: a pillared hall, then a corridor with niches holding statues of Sarenput in the form of Osiris, and at the end a painted niche with figures of the governor, its colours still fresh.

Digging goes on. The University of Jaen in Spain has worked here since 2008, ten mummified crocodiles were found in 2019, and three new Old Kingdom tombs were announced in 2025.
details: Sarenput II: the corridor niches with statues of Sarenput as Osiris, wrapped like a mummy.
At the back of Sarenput II's tomb: the painted niche, its colours still bright.
Mekhu and Sabni: a double tomb with rough pillars cut from the living rock.
At the top, the sheikh's dome; the view back over Elephantine is one of Aswan's best.
fun_fact: In 2019 archaeologists here found ten mummified crocodiles, up to 3.5 metres long, more than 2,500 years old and preserved without resin.
narration:
You are climbing to the tombs of the men who ran Egypt's southern frontier. About 100 tombs are cut into this cliff, and the little dome on the summit, the tomb of a Muslim holy man, gives the hill its name, Qubbet el Hawa, the Dome of the Wind.

Most belong to governors of Elephantine in the Old and Middle Kingdoms, between about 2300 and 1800 BC. These men led caravans and soldiers into Nubia, and their walls tell of it.

The most moving story belongs to Mekhu and his son Sabni. Mekhu died on an expedition in Nubia. Sabni gathered troops and donkeys, went south, punished those responsible and carried his father's body home to be buried here, beside his own tomb.

The best preserved is the tomb of Sarenput the Second, a governor around 1900 BC. After the pillared hall, a corridor runs into the rock, lined with statues of Sarenput as Osiris, and at the end is a niche painted in colours that still look fresh.

Before you go inside, turn around. Elephantine, the town these men governed, lies right below you.

name: Harkhuf and the dancing pygmy letter
note: 6th Dynasty caravan leader who made four expeditions to Yam (Sudan), came back with 300 donkeys of incense, ebony, ivory; the letter from the 8-year-old king Pepi II carved on his tomb facade begging him to bring the 'dancing dwarf of the god's dances' safely ('check on him ten times a night'); the first travel narrative in history.
period: Old Kingdom, 6th Dynasty, about 2250 BC
summary: An explorer who brought back a dancing pygmy, and a boy-king's excited letter telling him to check on him ten times a night.
look: Harkhuf's tomb is in the Qubbet el-Hawa cliff. Its fame is carved on the outside: 58 lines of text in soft, flaking stone around the entrance, with prayers above the door, his journeys on either side, and the king's letter in a long block on the far right.
story:
A native of Elephantine, he served kings Merenre and Pepi II as governor and overseer of caravans. He led four expeditions to Yam, a land probably south of modern Khartoum, though some place it in the Libyan desert. The first was with his father. He boasts of routes no one had used before, of winning over the ruler of Yam, and of returning with 300 donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, oil, panther skins, ivory and other fine goods.

On the fourth journey he brought back a dancing pygmy and sent word ahead. The reply came from Pepi II, still a child: come north at once; bring the pygmy alive and well; put good men around him on deck so he does not fall in the water; have them sleep around him in his tent; inspect ten times a night. His majesty wanted to see this pygmy more than the gifts of the mines of Sinai and of Punt. Harkhuf was so proud that he had the letter carved on his tomb.

His inscription also lists his virtues: he gave bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and ferried those who had no boat.
details: The long inscription framing the doorway: 58 lines telling Harkhuf's life.
On the far right of the facade: the king's letter, 26 lines of royal excitement.
Above the entrance: prayers for offerings and Harkhuf's titles.
Look south from the terrace: the direction all four of his caravans set off.
fun_fact: Harkhuf's moral code, 'I gave bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked', was carved more than 4,000 years ago and still sounds like a modern charity appeal.
narration:
This tomb belongs to Harkhuf, one of the first explorers in history. He was from Elephantine, and more than 4,200 years ago he led four caravans deep into Africa, to a land called Yam, probably beyond Khartoum. On one trip he came home with 300 donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, ivory and panther skins.

But the best part is a letter. On his fourth journey Harkhuf brought back a dancing pygmy, and sent word to the palace. The reply came from King Pepi the Second, still a child, and it is wonderfully childlike. Come north at once! Bring the pygmy alive and well! When he goes on board, put good men around him so he does not fall in the water. When he sleeps, have men lie around his tent. Check on him ten times a night! My Majesty wants to see this pygmy more than all the treasures of Sinai and Punt.

Harkhuf was so proud of that letter that he had it carved for eternity. Look at the far right of the doorway and find the long block of text: that is the king's letter.

name: Mausoleum of the Aga Khan
note: Short. Fatimid-style pink limestone tomb of Sultan Mohammed Shah, Aga Khan III (died 1957), leader of the Ismaili Shia (a Fatimid link to Cairo), who wintered in Aswan for the climate; his widow the Begum laid a red rose on the tomb daily until her death in 2000; closed to the public, viewed from the river; his villa below.
summary: A Fatimid-style tomb on the desert hill for the leader of the Ismaili Muslims, where a red rose was laid every day.
look: On the west-bank hilltop stands a pink limestone building with a large central dome on an octagonal drum, four small corner domes, crenellated walls and a single arched door on the west side. Below it near the water is the villa where the Aga Khan wintered. The interior has been closed to visitors since 1997; you see it from the river.
story:
Sir Sultan Muhammed Shah, Aga Khan III, was hereditary imam of the Ismaili Shia Muslims and a well-known figure of the 20th century. He wintered in Aswan in a villa designed by Hassan Fathy and asked in his will to be buried near it. He died in 1957, was first buried in Switzerland, and was reburied here on 20 February 1959 before more than 2,000 guests.

His widow, Begum Om Habibeh, commissioned the mausoleum. The Egyptian architect Farid Shafi'e modelled it on Fatimid buildings, above all the 11th-century Juyushi mosque in Cairo. The choice was deliberate: the Fatimid caliphs who founded Cairo were Ismailis. The tomb inside is of Carrara marble.

The Begum began the custom of laying a red rose on the tomb every day. She died in 2000 and is buried beside her husband, and in February 2025 his grandson and successor, Aga Khan IV, was buried here too.
details: From the river: the central dome and the four small corner domes.
The crenellated parapet along the walls, a Fatimid touch.
Below the hill near the water: the villa, designed by Hassan Fathy.
Compare the dome with the Fatimid buildings you saw in Cairo on the 16th.
fun_fact: The design copies the Juyushi mosque on the Muqattam hills in Cairo, built in 1085, so a medieval Cairo silhouette now overlooks the Nubian Nile.
narration:
On the hilltop across the river is the mausoleum of the Aga Khan, the pink building with one large dome and four small ones at the corners.

Aga Khan is the title of the hereditary imam of the Ismaili Muslims, a branch of Shia Islam. The third Aga Khan, Sultan Muhammed Shah, was a famous figure of the 20th century, a statesman and a racehorse owner, and he spent his winters here in Aswan. He died in 1957 and asked to be buried near his villa, the house you can see near the water below.

The tomb was designed to look like a building from Fatimid Cairo. That was no accident. The Fatimid caliphs who founded Cairo more than a thousand years ago were Ismailis, the Aga Khan's spiritual ancestors.

His widow, the Begum, started a custom: every day a red rose was laid on his tomb. She is buried here too, and in 2025 so was his grandson, the fourth Aga Khan. The inside is closed to visitors. Look for the small corner domes, and the crenellated wall along the top.

name: Monastery of St Simeon (Anba Hatre)
note: Short. 7th century fortress-monastery in the desert behind the Aga Khan, abandoned 1321 (Saladin's raids and water); the two-storey church with faded Christ in Majesty, the monks' cells with graffiti, the keep; reached by camel or a 20-minute walk from the river.
period: Coptic, founded about AD 571; abandoned after 1321
summary: A fortified desert monastery for some 300 monks, with a painted Christ in its apse, abandoned for 700 years behind the Aga Khan's hill.
look: From the boat landing below the Aga Khan's mausoleum, a sandy path climbs a dry valley to the monastery, about 650 metres from the river; camels are usually on offer. Inside walls over 6 metres high, the site steps up two rock terraces: the church on the lower one, and on the upper the three-storey keep with the monks' cells, the refectory, kitchen and workshops. Visitors enter by the east gate.
story:
Older Coptic and Arabic sources call it Deir Anba Hadra, after a 4th-century hermit who became bishop of Syene; the name of St Simeon came later and was adopted by travellers and archaeologists. Building began around 571. In the 10th century it was renewed and enlarged to house about 300 largely self-sufficient monks, with a mill, oil and wine presses, a bakery, stables and kilns.

The church was a three-aisled basilica; in its apse are the remains of Christ enthroned between two angels. In the refectory, seven rings of mud brick on the floor served as seats.

Saladin attacked in 1173 and badly damaged it. Bedouin raids and water shortages followed, and in 1321 attackers destroyed it, killed many monks and drove out the rest. It was never rebuilt.
details: The church apse: faded remains of Christ enthroned between two angels.
The keep: three storeys, with the monks' cells opening off the dormitory.
The refectory: seven rings of mud brick on the floor that served as seats.
Near the oil press: a granite millstone carved with three crosses.
From the upper terrace: open desert in every direction, the reason for the high walls.
fun_fact: The monastery's cemetery holds nearly 200 gravestones, most from the 6th to 9th centuries.
narration:
You are inside the walls of a desert monastery that has stood empty for 700 years. Later travellers named it after Saint Simeon, but older sources call it after Anba Hadra, a hermit who became bishop of Aswan in the 4th century. Building began around AD 571, and at its height, in the 10th century, about 300 monks lived here behind walls over 6 metres high, with their own mill, oil press, wine press and bakery.

In 1173 Saladin attacked. Bedouin raids and water shortages followed, and in 1321 it was destroyed and abandoned. Find the church apse: the faded figure of Christ enthroned between two angels is still there.

name: The Aswan High Dam and the old British dam
note: Old dam 1898-1902 (Willcocks, raised twice, drowned Philae each year); High Dam 1960-70 after the 1956 Suez crisis when the US withdrew funding and Nasser turned to the USSR, Soviet engineers, 3.8 km long, 111 m high, 17x the Great Pyramid in material; results: no more floods or famines, electricity, year-round irrigation, but silt trapped (fertiliser now needed, Delta eroding), Nubia drowned, schistosomiasis; the lotus-shaped Soviet-Egyptian friendship monument.
period: Old dam 1898-1902; High Dam 1960-1970
summary: Two dams that ended the Nile flood: harvests and electricity for Egypt, a lake that drowned Nubia, and silt trapped where the fields can't reach it.
look: From the top of the High Dam you see Lake Nasser to the south and the river running towards Aswan to the north. The dam is 3.8 km long, 111 m high, 980 m wide at the base and 40 m at the crest: a mountain of rock and clay, not a concrete wall. At the western end stands the tall lotus-shaped monument to Soviet-Egyptian friendship. The old dam lies 7 km downstream.
story:
The British built the first dam across the Nile at Aswan in 1898-1902, designed by Sir William Willcocks and opened on 10 December 1902. It was raised twice but held too little water to stop the cycle of floods and droughts.

In 1952 the Greek-Egyptian engineer Adrian Daninos proposed a giant dam, and the new government adopted it. The US and Britain offered loans, then withdrew in July 1956; a week later Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, partly to pay for the dam, and the Soviet Union provided credit, engineers and machinery. Construction began on 9 January 1960 and was completed on 21 July 1970; the lake was full by 1976. The Soviet engineer Nikolai Malyshev designed it, and Egyptian contractors, led by Osman Ahmed Osman's Arab Contractors, built it with some 25,000 Egyptian engineers and workers.

The gains are real: floods and droughts no longer decide the harvest, water is stored over several years, fields can carry two crops a year, and the turbines generate electricity. So are the costs: the silt that once fertilised the valley now settles in the lake, farmers depend on fertiliser and the Delta coast is retreating, and about 100,000 Nubians lost their homeland. The reservoir, Lake Nasser, is about 500 km long.
details: Look south: Lake Nasser, about 500 km long, reaching into Sudan.
Look north: the narrower river and, 7 km away, the old British dam.
The lotus tower at the west end: five petals, a monument to Soviet-Egyptian friendship.
Underfoot: no concrete face, just a vast bank of rock and clay.
fun_fact: The first man asked to dam the Nile here, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham around 1011, decided it was impossible and pretended to be mad to escape the caliph's anger; under house arrest he wrote his famous Book of Optics.
narration:
You are standing on the Aswan High Dam. To the south is Lake Nasser, about 500 kilometres long, reaching into Sudan. To the north, the Nile runs on to the sea, and it will never flood again.

It is not a concrete wall. It is a mountain of rock and clay, nearly 4 kilometres long and 111 metres high.

The first dam here was British, finished in 1902, 7 kilometres downstream. The plan for this giant came from a Greek Egyptian engineer, Adrian Daninos. When America and Britain withdrew their offer of loans in 1956, Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, and the Soviet Union stepped in with money and engineers. Construction ran from 1960 to 1970.

The results are mixed. No more famines from low floods, two harvests a year, and electricity from the turbines. But the fertile silt now settles at the bottom of the lake, farmers need fertiliser, the Delta coast is eroding, and about 100,000 Nubians lost their homes. At the west end, look for the tall lotus-shaped tower, the monument to Soviet Egyptian friendship.

name: Kalabsha, Beit el-Wali and the Kiosk of Qertassi (near the dam)
note: Short. Moved by West Germany 1961-63 to an island near the High Dam: Kalabsha, the largest free-standing Nubian temple (Augustus, to the Nubian god Mandulis), Beit el-Wali (Ramesses II, vivid painted Nubian tribute scenes), the Kiosk of Qertassi; usually quiet; optional if time allows.
period: Roman, Augustus, about 30 BC; Beit el-Wali, Ramesses II, 13th century BC
summary: Nubia's largest free-standing temple, moved in 13,000 blocks by West Germany, with a pig ban and a Christian king's boast in Greek.
look: On the rescue site of New Kalabsha beside the High Dam, usually reached by a short boat ride, stand three monuments: the big temple of Mandulis (Kalabsha), 76 metres long, with its pylon facing the water; the small rock-cut temple of Beit el-Wali behind it, built by Ramesses II, with brightly painted scenes; and the Kiosk of Qertassi with Hathor-headed columns.
story:
Mandulis was a Nubian sun god, and his temple was begun under Augustus around 30 BC over an older sanctuary of Amenhotep II, and never finished. It stood about 50 km south of Aswan. After UNESCO's appeal in 1960, West Germany chose to fund and run this rescue itself. The firm Hochtief started dismantling in 1961 from barges while the temple was still partly under water, numbering 13,000 blocks. It was rebuilt here in 1962-63. In thanks, Egypt gave Germany one of its gates, now in Berlin.

Look for two inscriptions: a decree of the Roman governor Aurelius Besarion of AD 250 banning pigs from the temple, and the victory text of Silko, a 5th-century Christian king of the Nobades, written in Greek, with an image of him on horseback in Roman dress.
details: In the temple: the Silko inscription with the king on horseback; ask the guard to show you.
Beit el-Wali: Ramesses II's Nubian campaign and tribute scenes, still brightly coloured.
The Kiosk of Qertassi: Hathor-headed columns at its entrance.
The view across the water to the High Dam.
