fun_fact: Silko called himself, in Greek, 'kinglet of the Nobades and all the Ethiopians': a Nubian king boasting in the language of Homer.
narration:
This is New Kalabsha, a rescue site beside the High Dam. The big temple belongs to Mandulis, a Nubian sun god. It was begun under the emperor Augustus and never finished, and it once stood 50 kilometres south of here. In the early 1960s West Germany paid to save it. Engineers cut it into 13,000 numbered blocks, some lifted from barges while the temple was still under water, and rebuilt it here.

Inside, look for two odd inscriptions: a Roman governor's order of AD 250 banning pigs from the temple, and the boast of Silko, a Christian Nubian king, written in Greek. Then visit little Beit el Wali behind it, with Ramesses the Second's painted Nubian tribute.

name: The Old Cataract Hotel and Agatha Christie
note: Short. Built 1899 by Thomas Cook for wealthy winter visitors; Agatha Christie wrote part of Death on the Nile here (1937), Churchill, Tsar Nicholas II, Princess Diana stayed; the 1978 film used it; the terrace at sunset with minimum spend; the Moorish hall.
period: Opened 1900
summary: Thomas Cook's grand winter hotel, where Agatha Christie stayed and set part of Death on the Nile, with Aswan's most famous sunset terrace.
look: The historic terracotta-coloured palace wing stands on a granite outcrop at the southern end of the Corniche, facing Elephantine; a 1961 tower wing rises behind it. The terrace looks over the river and the boulders. Since May 2026 the hotel has been run by Mandarin Oriental, with the tower wing under renovation. Non-guests usually need a booking and a minimum spend for the terrace.
story:
Thomas Cook built the Cataract Hotel in 1899 for European winter travellers, and it opened on 8 January 1900 with 120 rooms. It did so well that a third storey and a dining room were added in 1902. The guest list reads like a history lesson: Tsar Nicholas II, Winston Churchill, Howard Carter, Margaret Thatcher, Jimmy Carter, Francois Mitterrand, Princess Diana and Agatha Christie, who set part of Death on the Nile here. The 1978 film was shot at the hotel.

It was closed for restoration from 2008 to 2011, and is due to be renamed Mandarin Oriental Old Cataract in 2027.
details: The terrace at sunset: Elephantine's boulders and the feluccas below.
The 1902 dining room with its high dome, if you are allowed a look.
From the river: the terracotta facade on its granite rock.
Look across to Elephantine's southern tip: the Nilometer and the Khnum temple.
fun_fact: In the novel, Poirot's steamer sails upriver from near Aswan to Wadi Halfa; that whole stretch of river now lies under Lake Nasser.
narration:
The grand terracotta building on the rocks is the Old Cataract Hotel. Thomas Cook built it for wealthy European winter visitors, and it opened in January 1900. It was such a success that two years later another storey was added.

Its guest book is a history lesson: Tsar Nicholas the Second, Winston Churchill, Howard Carter, Princess Diana, and Agatha Christie, who set part of Death on the Nile here. The 1978 film was shot here too.

The terrace is the place for sunset. Non-guests usually need a booking and a minimum spend, so ask at the gate. From the terrace, look straight down at the dark boulders of Elephantine: Poirot saw the same view.

name: Aswan souq and the Nubian village of Gharb Soheil
note: Short. Sharia el-Souq: hibiscus (karkadé), dried spices, dom palm fruit, Nubian baskets, galabiyas, less hassle than Cairo; Gharb Soheil: painted houses, the pet crocodiles (tradition of keeping them for luck), henna tattoos, camels; it is touristy but the hospitality is real; sailing back at dusk.
summary: Spices, hibiscus and baskets in the souq, then painted Nubian houses, crocodiles and real hospitality across the river.
look: The souq street runs parallel to the Corniche, one block back from the river, southwards from near the railway station: stalls of spices, dried hibiscus, dates, baskets, scarves and galabiyas. Gharb Soheil is a Nubian village on the west bank upstream of the city, reached by boat; its lanes of painted houses climb from the landing towards the desert.
story:
Aswan's souq is gentler than Cairo's bazaars. Hibiscus is one of the region's signature crops: dried red flowers sold by weight and brewed as karkade, hot or iced. Look also for dom-palm fruit, henna, spices, Nubian baskets and colourful scarves. Bargaining is expected and friendly: smile, offer less, and be ready to walk on.

Gharb Soheil is one of the Nubian villages that still sits on the river. Houses are painted in blues, yellows and pinks, with patterns, birds and boats. A stuffed crocodile over a door is an old Nubian charm against evil, and many households keep live young crocodiles to show visitors. You can drink tea in a family guesthouse, get a henna design or ride a camel.

Parts of the visit are staged for tourists, but the hospitality is real. Nubians in Egypt live mostly around Aswan and in the villages near Kom Ombo where many were resettled in the 1960s. Sailing back at dusk is part of the pleasure.
details: In the souq: heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers; ask to taste the karkade before you buy.
Dom-palm fruit: hard, brown and faintly gingerbread-flavoured, a local snack.
In Gharb Soheil: look up for a stuffed crocodile over a doorway, a charm against evil.
Painted house walls: boats, birds and geometric bands in blue, yellow and white.
Ask before photographing people, especially women and children.
fun_fact: The dom palm is called the gingerbread tree in English; baskets of its fruit were among the food left in Tutankhamun's tomb.
narration:
Two faces of living Aswan: the souq in town, and a Nubian village across the river.

In the souq, look for heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers. Brewed, they make karkade, Aswan's ruby-red drink, served hot or ice cold. Next to them you will find hard brown dom palm fruit, which tastes faintly of gingerbread, as well as henna, spices, baskets and scarves. Bargaining is expected and friendly: smile, offer less, and be ready to walk on. It is far more relaxed than in Cairo.

Gharb Soheil, on the west bank, is a Nubian village with houses painted blue, yellow and pink, decorated with patterns, birds and boats. You may see a stuffed crocodile over a door, an old Nubian charm against evil, and some families keep live young crocodiles to show visitors. You can sit for tea, get a henna design, or ride a camel.

Yes, parts of it are staged for tourists. But the welcome is real. On the boat back at dusk, look at the west bank: the painted houses turn gold, then pink, then dark.

name: Ancient Egypt in ten minutes: the timeline you need
note: Predynastic (to 3100 BC) and Narmer; Early Dynastic; Old Kingdom (pyramids, 2686-2181); First Intermediate; Middle Kingdom (2055-1650, Thebes rises, Senusret); Second Intermediate (Hyksos); New Kingdom (1550-1069: Thutmosids, Amarna, Ramessides, everything in Luxor); Third Intermediate (priest-kings, Libyans, Kushites); Late Period (Saites, Persians); Ptolemies (332-30, Edfu, Philae, Kom Ombo); Romans; Christianity; Islam 641. Give anchor memory tricks and which sites on this trip belong to which era.
period: Predynastic to the Arab conquest, c. 5000 BC - AD 641
summary: Three thousand years of pharaohs fit one simple rhythm: three strong 'Kingdoms', with messy 'Intermediate Periods' in between.
look: This is the mental shelf on which every other entry sits: whenever a label says '18th Dynasty' or 'Ptolemaic', come back here to place it. On this trip, Giza is Old Kingdom, Luxor and Abu Simbel are New Kingdom, and the river temples of Edfu, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae are Greek and Roman. Islamic Cairo begins with the Arab conquest of 641.
story:
Egyptologists still use the list of 30 dynasties drawn up in the 3rd century BC by Manetho, an Egyptian priest writing in Greek for the Ptolemies. Modern historians grouped them into 'Kingdoms', when one king ruled the whole Nile valley, and 'Intermediate Periods', when the country split. Exact dates are still argued over; those below are the conventional ones.

Before about 3100 BC, farming villages along the Nile grew into two rival kingdoms, Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the Delta. Narmer is the first king we know who claimed both. After the Early Dynastic Period (Dynasties 1-2) came the Old Kingdom (Dynasties 3-6, 2686-2181 BC), the pyramid age, ruled from Memphis. A long reign, over-mighty governors and drought brought the First Intermediate Period.

Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt from Thebes around 2055 BC, opening the Middle Kingdom, the classical age of literature. In the Second Intermediate Period the Hyksos, rulers from western Asia, held the Delta until Ahmose drove them out around 1550 BC. That began the New Kingdom (to 1069 BC): Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II, and nearly everything you will see in Luxor.

Then power fragmented: priest-kings in Thebes, Libyan and Nubian pharaohs, an Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC, a Saite revival, two spells of Persian rule. Alexander arrived in 332 BC; the Greek dynasty of his general Ptolemy ended with Cleopatra in 30 BC, and Rome took over. Christianity slowly replaced the old gods, and the Arab conquest of 641 opened the chapter you will meet in Islamic Cairo on the 16th.
details: Memory trick: Old Kingdom = pyramids, Middle Kingdom = literature and worried faces, New Kingdom = Luxor's temples and tombs.
Giza on the 12th is Dynasty 4. Abu Simbel on the 17th is Dynasty 19. Edfu on the 20th is Ptolemaic.
Siwa's oracle temple (13-15 Oct) is Late Period, the place Alexander came to consult Amun in 331 BC.
Dates marked 'c.' on labels are estimates: for the early dynasties they can be off by decades or more.
fun_fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
narration: Think of this as the shelf where every other story sits. Ancient Egyptian history runs for about 3,000 years, and the trick is a simple rhythm: three strong Kingdoms, with messy Intermediate Periods in between. Before about 3100 BC, villages along the Nile grew into two rival kingdoms, south and north. Narmer is the first king we know who claimed both. Then comes the Old Kingdom, from about 2686 to 2181 BC, the age of the pyramids you will walk around at Giza on the 12th. Drought and greedy governors broke it apart. Around 2055 BC a Theban king, Mentuhotep the Second, put Egypt back together and began the Middle Kingdom, the classical age of poems and careworn royal faces. Next, foreign rulers called the Hyksos took the north, until Ahmose expelled them around 1550 BC. That opens the New Kingdom, the age of Hatshepsut, Tutankhamun and Ramesses the Great, and of almost everything you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel. After 1069 BC, power splinters: priest kings, Libyans, Nubians, Persians. Alexander arrives in 332 BC, his general Ptolemy founds a Greek dynasty, and it ends with Cleopatra in 30 BC, when Rome takes over. The river temples of Edfu, Kom Ombo and Philae belong to that last chapter. So keep this in your pocket: pyramids old, Luxor new, river temples Greek.

name: The Old Kingdom: the age of the pyramids
note: Dynasties 3-6 from Memphis: Djoser and Imhotep's Step Pyramid, Sneferu's three pyramids, Giza, the sun temples of the 5th Dynasty, Pyramid Texts of Unas, Pepi II's 90-year reign, the collapse (drought, provincial power); what Old Kingdom art looks like (the sober, muscular, idealised style you see in Khafre, Rahotep, Ka-aper); GEM main galleries relevance.
period: Old Kingdom, Dynasties 3-6, 2686-2181 BC
summary: Five centuries when Egypt's kings were living gods able to raise mountains of stone, ending in drought and famine.
look: You meet the Old Kingdom at Giza on the 12th and in the museums' earliest galleries. Recognise its art by calm, broad-shouldered, muscular figures staring straight ahead, fists clenched, left foot striding forward: Khafre with the falcon behind his head, Rahotep and Nofret, the wooden Ka-aper.
story:
The capital was Memphis, near modern Cairo, and the king was a god on earth who could command the labour of the whole country. Under Djoser, first king of Dynasty 3, his official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Sneferu, founder of Dynasty 4, built at least three pyramids, at Meidum and Dahshur, and moved more stone than any other king, perfecting the true pyramid by trial and error. His son Khufu, grandson Khafre and great-grandson Menkaure built Giza. The workers were not slaves but rotating crews of farmers and skilled specialists, housed and fed in a town beside the plateau.

Dynasty 5 spent less on pyramids and more on sun temples for Ra at Abusir, and sent ships to Punt for incense. Its last king, Unas, was the first to have the Pyramid Texts, Egypt's oldest religious writings, carved inside his burial chamber.

In Dynasty 6, provincial governors made their posts hereditary and grew rich. Pepi II reigned for more than 60 years (later tradition said over 90) and outlived his heirs; then a drought in the 22nd century BC failed the Nile floods. The tomb of the governor Ankhtifi describes famine stalking the land.
details: Old Kingdom statues: broad shoulders, long torso, visible muscles, fists clenched, left foot forward, eyes fixed far away.
Late in Dynasty 6 the style changes: shoulders narrow, muscles soften and eyes grow larger. A quick way to date a statue.
At Giza, the rows of flat-topped mastaba tombs around the pyramids belong to officials buried beside their king.
The king was not yet called 'pharaoh': that word, 'great house', became a title for the king himself only in the New Kingdom.
fun_fact: Sneferu, Khufu's father, moved more stone than his famous son: he needed three attempts, at Meidum and Dahshur, to get the pyramid right.
narration: The Old Kingdom is the age of the pyramids, roughly 2686 to 2181 BC, Dynasties 3 to 6, ruled from Memphis just south of Cairo. Its kings were living gods, and they could summon the whole country to build. It starts with Djoser, whose official Imhotep stacked stone platforms into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Then Sneferu, founder of Dynasty 4, learned by trial and error, building at least three pyramids and moving more stone than any other king. His son Khufu, grandson Khafre and great grandson Menkaure built Giza. The workers were not slaves: they were farmers on rota and skilled crews, fed and housed in a town beside the plateau. Later kings spent their money on sun temples for Ra, and the last king of Dynasty 5, Unas, carved the first Pyramid Texts inside his tomb. Then local governors grew rich, a very long reign left no clear heir, and a drought failed the floods. The age ended in famine. In the museum, spot Old Kingdom statues by their broad shoulders, calm faces and the left foot striding forward.

name: The Middle Kingdom: the classical age
note: Mentuhotep II reunites from Thebes; the 12th Dynasty of Amenemhat and Senusret at Itjtawy; Nubian forts, the Faiyum projects, the careworn royal portraits, the literature classics (Sinuhe, the Eloquent Peasant, Shipwrecked Sailor), block statues, coffin texts, the rise of Amun and Osiris pilgrimage to Abydos; what you see: White Chapel, Mentuhotep's temple, Senusret III head, the Aswan nobles' tombs.
period: Middle Kingdom, Dynasties 11-12 (and early 13), c. 2055-1650 BC
summary: After a century of chaos, kings from Thebes rebuilt Egypt and left its classic literature and its most human royal faces.
look: You meet the Middle Kingdom in faces: Senusret III's heavy-lidded, worried portraits and Mentuhotep II's black-skinned seated king. In Luxor, the White Chapel of Senusret I in Karnak's open-air museum and Mentuhotep's terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari belong to it, and so do the governors' tombs of Sarenput I and II on the hill at Aswan.
story:
Mentuhotep II took the Theban throne in 2055 BC, defeated the rival kings of Herakleopolis and spent years reuniting the country; he reigned 51 years. Amenemhat I, probably the vizier of the last Mentuhotep and not of royal birth, founded Dynasty 12 and moved the capital north to a new city, Itjtawy, 'Seizer of the Two Lands', near el-Lisht. He was probably murdered in a palace plot, the event that opens the Story of Sinuhe.

To avoid such crises, Dynasty 12 kings made their sons co-regents. Senusret I pushed into Nubia and built the White Chapel at Karnak. Senusret III campaigned brutally in Nubia and built massive mud-brick forts at the Second Cataract; Greek writers later remembered him as the conqueror Sesostris. Amenemhat III turned the Faiyum's marshes into farmland. The line ended with Sobekneferu, the first securely attested woman to rule as king.

Later Egyptians treated this as their classical age. Scribes copied its stories for centuries: Sinuhe the courtier in exile, the Eloquent Peasant, the Shipwrecked Sailor. Officials now painted the old royal spells, the Coffin Texts, inside their own coffins, and pilgrims flocked to Osiris at Abydos.
details: Senusret III's portraits: heavy eyelids, hollow cheeks, big ears. Often read as a king feeling the weight of office.
The White Chapel of Senusret I in Karnak's open-air museum (22nd): Middle Kingdom carving at its crispest.
Block statues, a man squatting wrapped in his cloak like a cube, became popular in this period: spot them in any museum.
Mentuhotep II's temple at Deir el-Bahari (21st), beside Hatshepsut's, was the model she copied five centuries later.
fun_fact: The Story of Sinuhe was a school classic: hundreds of years after it was written, apprentice scribes were still copying it onto pottery shards.
narration: The Middle Kingdom is Egypt's classical age, about 2055 to 1650 BC. After the Old Kingdom collapsed, a Theban king, Mentuhotep the Second, fought the rival rulers of the north and put the country back together. He reigned for 51 years. The kings who followed, called Amenemhat and Senusret, moved the capital north and ruled father and son together to avoid civil war. They pushed deep into Nubia, built huge forts at the Second Cataract, and drained the Faiyum for farmland. Greek writers later remembered one of them, Senusret the Third, as the conqueror Sesostris. This is the age of the great stories: Sinuhe, the courtier who fled into exile, and the Shipwrecked Sailor, marooned on an island with a giant talking snake. Scribes copied them for centuries. Look at the royal portraits of this time: heavy eyelids, hollow cheeks, big ears. Senusret the Third looks tired and worried, a king who knows the job is hard. In Luxor on the 22nd, find the White Chapel of Senusret the First at Karnak, as crisp as the day it was carved.

name: The New Kingdom: empire and gold
note: Ahmose expels the Hyksos; the 18th Dynasty (Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III's golden age, Akhenaten, Tut, Horemheb); the 19th (Seti I, Ramesses II, Merenptah); the 20th (Ramesses III, the Sea Peoples, decline, tomb robberies); Thebes and Amun's wealth; chariots and horses, the empire from the Euphrates to the 4th cataract, the Valley of the Kings, the mortuary temples; this is 80% of what the trip shows.
period: New Kingdom, Dynasties 18-20, c. 1550-1069 BC
summary: Five centuries of empire, when Thebes grew rich on gold and tribute and built most of what you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel.
look: Most of the second half of this trip is New Kingdom: Karnak and Luxor temples, the Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut's terraces, Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, Medinet Habu, and Tutankhamun's treasure at the GEM. Recognise it by bright colour, chariots, slender elegant figures, and cartouches of Thutmose, Amenhotep and Ramesses everywhere.
story:
It began with a war of liberation. Theban kings fought the Hyksos who ruled the Delta, and around 1550 BC Ahmose drove them out and chased them into Canaan. The lesson Egypt learned was to keep enemies far away. Thutmose I became the first pharaoh to cross the Euphrates. Hatshepsut ruled as king and sent ships to Punt. Thutmose III fought about 17 campaigns and held an empire from Syria deep into Nubia. Under Amenhotep III, tribute and Nubian gold made Egypt the richest state of its day. His son Akhenaten replaced the gods with the Aten; Tutankhamun restored them, and the general Horemheb erased the whole episode.

Horemheb chose his vizier as heir, and Ramesses I founded Dynasty 19. Seti I and Ramesses II fought the Hittites, famously at Kadesh, where both sides claimed victory; they later signed a peace treaty. Ramesses built from the Delta to Abu Simbel and put his name on older kings' statues too.

In Dynasty 20, Ramesses III beat back the Sea Peoples in his eighth year, but wars drained the treasury. In his 29th year the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded strike when their rations failed, and he died in a harem plot. Eight more kings called Ramesses watched power drift to the High Priests of Amun while robbers emptied the royal tombs.

Throughout, Thebes was the religious capital. Kings were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings, with mortuary temples out on the plain, and poured their spoils into Amun's house at Karnak. In this age 'pharaoh', literally 'great house', became a word for the king himself.
details: Chariots and horses came into use around the Hyksos period; New Kingdom battle walls at Karnak and Abu Simbel are full of them.
Tomb hidden in the valley, temple public on the plain: that split is why the West Bank has both (21st).
Ramesses II often recarved older kings' statues with his own name: look for cartouches cut deeper than the rest.
The royal mummies of this age, Ramesses II among them, are at NMEC in Fustat, not at the GEM.
fun_fact: History's first recorded strike happened here, in Ramesses III's 29th year, when the royal tomb-builders' grain rations failed to arrive.
narration: The New Kingdom, about 1550 to 1069 BC, is the Egypt of empire and gold, and most of what you will see in Luxor and at Abu Simbel. It begins with a war of liberation. Foreign kings called the Hyksos held the north, until a Theban prince, Ahmose, drove them out. Egypt learned to keep its enemies far away. Thutmose the First marched to the Euphrates. Hatshepsut ruled as king and sent ships to the incense land of Punt. Thutmose the Third fought about 17 campaigns and built an empire from Syria to deep inside Nubia. With Nubian gold and Asian tribute, Amenhotep the Third lived like a sun king. His son Akhenaten threw out the old gods for a single sun disc, and Tutankhamun brought them back. Then the Ramesside kings took over. Seti the First and Ramesses the Second fought the Hittites at Kadesh, both sides claimed victory, and they later signed a peace treaty. Ramesses the Third held off the Sea Peoples, but money ran short, and the royal tomb builders went on the first recorded strike when their bread did not arrive. Through it all, Thebes was the holy city. Kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings and poured their spoils into Amun's temple at Karnak. When you see a cartouche on the 21st or 22nd, try to read Thutmose, Amenhotep or Ramesses.

name: After the glory: priest-kings, Libyans, Kushites, Persians
note: Tanis and Thebes split (Psusennes' silver coffin, Pinedjem), Libyan dynasties (Sheshonq's Karnak list), the Kushite 25th (Taharqa), the Assyrian sack of Thebes 663 BC, the Saite renaissance (Psamtik, Amasis: Siwa's oracle temple), Persians (Cambyses, the lost army), the last native kings Nectanebo I-II (Philae's kiosk, Edfu's naos, Sphinx avenue), then Alexander.
period: Third Intermediate and Late Periods, 1069-332 BC
summary: Seven centuries of priest-kings, Libyan chiefs, Nubian pharaohs and Persian emperors: Egypt divided, invaded, and still building.
look: You meet this age in odd corners: the silver coffin of Psusennes from Tanis in the Cairo museums, Taharqa's single standing column in Karnak's first court, Amun's oracle temple at Siwa, and the kiosk of Nectanebo I at Philae. Its art often copies the Old Kingdom on purpose, so check the label before guessing a statue's date.
story:
After Ramesses XI died, Egypt split, politely: kings ruled the north from Tanis in the Delta while the High Priests of Amun governed the south from Thebes, and the two families intermarried. At Tanis in 1939-40 Pierre Montet found intact royal burials, including Psusennes I in a silver coffin.

Around 945 BC Shoshenq I, of Libyan descent, reunited Egypt and raided Palestine, listing the towns on a Karnak gateway. His successors split into rival lines. Around 732 BC Piye of Kush marched north and founded Dynasty 25 of Nubian pharaohs; Taharqa built at Karnak. Assyria invaded and sacked Thebes in 663 BC.

Psamtik I of Sais reunited the country with the help of Greek and Carian mercenaries and ruled 54 years. Saite kings revived Old Kingdom art, and Amasis courted the Greek world. In 525 BC the Persian Cambyses conquered Egypt; Herodotus tells of an army he sent against Siwa that vanished in a sandstorm. Egypt broke free in 404 BC, and Nectanebo I and II, the last native pharaohs, built furiously until Persia returned in 343 BC. In 332 BC the Persian governor handed Egypt to Alexander without a fight.
details: Karnak's first court (22nd): the one tall column still standing belongs to the kiosk of Taharqa, a Nubian pharaoh.
Saite statues copy Old Kingdom style, smooth and idealised: some look 2,000 years older than they are.
Siwa (13-15 Oct): the oracle temple at Aghurmi dates to this age, usually credited to Amasis of Dynasty 26.
Philae (18th): the first building you reach is the kiosk of Nectanebo I, built by the last native dynasty.
Animal mummies boomed in this age: cats, ibises and crocodiles offered by pilgrims fill museum cases.
fun_fact: In the 590s BC, Greek mercenaries marching south for Psamtik II scratched their names on a leg of one of Abu Simbel's colossi: some of the oldest dated Greek graffiti anywhere.
narration: After the New Kingdom, Egypt spent seven centuries divided, invaded and still building. From about 1069 BC, kings ruled the north from Tanis in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes. Then came pharaohs of Libyan descent, like Shoshenq, who raided Palestine and listed the towns he took on a gateway at Karnak. Around 732 BC, Piye of Kush marched north from Nubia and founded a dynasty of Nubian pharaohs. The Assyrians threw them out and sacked Thebes in 663 BC. Psamtik of Sais rebuilt Egypt with Greek mercenaries, and his dynasty copied Old Kingdom art so faithfully that their statues can look 2,000 years older than they are. In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses conquered Egypt, and Herodotus tells how one of his armies vanished in the sand on its way to Siwa. The last Egyptian born pharaohs, the Nectanebos, built at Philae and Karnak until Persia returned. Then, in 332 BC, Alexander walked in. At Karnak, look for the single tall column of the Nubian king Taharqa, alone in the first court.

name: Greeks and Romans as pharaohs
note: Alexander 332 BC, Ptolemy I takes Egypt, 300 years of Greek kings marrying their sisters and building Egyptian temples (Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae, Esna, Dendera) to win priests; Alexandria and the Library; the Rosetta Stone's three scripts; Cleopatra VII, Caesar, Antony, Actium 30 BC; Rome's breadbasket, emperors in pharaonic dress on temple walls, the Fayum portraits, Christianity and the end of the old religion (Philae 537 AD). For a Greek visitor: the Greek layer everywhere.
period: Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, 332 BC - AD 641
summary: For three centuries Macedonian Greeks ruled as pharaohs and built the river temples you will visit, before Rome made Egypt its granary.
look: From the 18th to the 20th you walk through this age: Philae, Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna are all Ptolemaic or Roman. Recognise it by walls crowded with small, rounded, fleshy figures, columns with elaborate floral capitals, and cartouches that spell Greek names like Ptolemaios and Kleopatra sound by sound. The Greek layer is everywhere: Edfu was Apollonopolis, Aswan was Syene, Esna was Latopolis.
story:
Alexander took Egypt from the Persians in 332 BC, was hailed as son of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria and left, never to return alive. After his death in 323 BC his general Ptolemy held Egypt, diverted Alexander's body to be buried there, and in 305 BC made himself king. Every male heir was called Ptolemy; the queens were Cleopatras, Arsinoes and Berenices, and from Ptolemy II they married their siblings, Egyptian-style.

The Ptolemies ran a two-level country. Greeks lived under Greek law, and Alexandria, with its Library and Museum, became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean: Euclid and Eratosthenes worked there. For the Egyptian majority the kings played pharaoh, funding temples to win over the powerful priests. Ptolemy III began Edfu on 23 August 237 BC; the main temple was finished in 212 BC, the whole complex only in 142 BC. The Rosetta Stone of 196 BC is one such priestly decree, honouring Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek.

Cleopatra VII, by Plutarch's account the only one of her line to learn Egyptian, staked everything on Caesar, then Mark Antony. After defeat at Actium she and Antony killed themselves in Alexandria in 30 BC, and Octavian took Egypt as his personal possession. Emperors appear on temple walls dressed as pharaohs, Egypt shipped grain to Rome, and the Fayum mummy portraits show its mixed Greek-Egyptian middle class.

Christianity spread from the 3rd century. The last hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394, Isis's temple there was closed under Justinian around 537, and the Arab conquest of 641 ended the Roman chapter.
details: Cartouches at Edfu and Kom Ombo spell Greek names sound by sound: look for the lion, which stands for L in Ptolemy and Cleopatra.
At Esna and Philae, Roman emperors offer to the gods in a pharaoh's kilt and crown, named in hieroglyphs as 'Caesar'.
Philae (18th): near the Gate of Hadrian is the last known hieroglyphic inscription, dated AD 394.
Ancient tourists left Greek graffiti on many walls; at Philae, Christians later carved crosses into the reliefs.
fun_fact: Eratosthenes of Alexandria measured the Earth's circumference using the sun's angle at Syene, which is Aswan, where you will be on the 18th.
narration: For the last three centuries before Christ, Egypt's pharaohs were Greeks. Alexander the Great took the country from the Persians in 332 BC, visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria, and left. When he died, his general Ptolemy kept Egypt and made himself king. Every one of his male heirs was called Ptolemy, the queens were Cleopatras, Arsinoes and Berenices, and from the second generation they married their own siblings, like Egyptian gods. The Ptolemies lived as Greeks in Alexandria, with its Library and its scholars, but to the Egyptian priests they played pharaoh. They paid for huge new temples in the old style: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae, the places you will walk through from the 18th to the 20th. The last of the line, Cleopatra the Seventh, was said to be the only one who bothered to learn Egyptian. She allied with Julius Caesar, then Mark Antony, lost to Octavian at Actium, and died in 30 BC. Rome took Egypt as its granary, and the emperors had themselves carved on temple walls in pharaoh's kilts. Christianity slowly closed the temples, and the last hieroglyphs were cut at Philae in 394 AD. On any Ptolemaic wall, look inside the cartouche for a lion: it is the letter L, in Ptolemy or Cleopatra.

name: The gods: a family tree in five minutes
note: The Heliopolitan Ennead: Atum/Ra, Shu and Tefnut, Geb and Nut, Osiris, Isis, Seth, Nephthys, and Horus; the Theban triad Amun, Mut, Khonsu; the Memphite Ptah, Sekhmet, Nefertem; how to identify gods by head and crown (Anubis jackal, Thoth ibis, Horus falcon with double crown, Hathor cow horns and disc, Isis throne or horns, Osiris mummy with atef, Amun two tall plumes, Ptah skullcap, Khnum ram with horizontal horns, Sobek crocodile, Sekhmet lioness, Bes dwarf facing front, Taweret hippo); syncretism (Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty).
summary: Egyptian texts name more than 1,400 gods, but about twenty do most of the work, and you can tell them apart by their heads and hats.
look: Gods fill every temple and tomb wall: usually a human body in a kilt or a long dress, with an animal head or a headdress that works like a name badge. Most hold an ankh in one hand and a sceptre in the other. Read the head first, then the crown, then the short column of hieroglyphs above the figure that gives the name.
story:
The Egyptologist James Allen counts more than 1,400 named deities. Most began as local gods, and as towns merged into a kingdom, priests arranged them into families. The most influential was the Ennead, 'the Nine', of Heliopolis, now under north-east Cairo. The creator Atum, identified with the sun god Ra, rose from the dark waters of Nun onto the first mound and produced Shu, air, and Tefnut, moisture. They had Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. Geb and Nut had four children: Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys. Horus, son of Isis and Osiris, completes the family and its great drama.

Other cities had their own systems. Memphis said Ptah created the world by conceiving it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue, and paired him with the lioness Sekhmet and their son Nefertem. Thebes, where you will spend the 21st and 22nd, built its family around Amun, his wife Mut and their son, the moon god Khonsu. Hermopolis had eight primeval gods, the Ogdoad.

Egyptians did not treat these accounts as rivals. Gods could merge, as Amun-Ra or Ra-Horakhty, and borrow each other's crowns, so Isis wears Hathor's horns. The animal head is not a portrait but a statement of character: the falcon soars like the sky, the jackal prowls the cemetery, the lioness is dangerous.
details: Falcon head: Horus, often in the double crown. Falcon head with a sun disc and cobra: Ra or Ra-Horakhty.
Jackal: Anubis. Ibis or baboon: Thoth. Ram with long wavy horns: Khnum. Crocodile: Sobek. Lioness: Sekhmet.
Two tall plumes and blue skin: Amun. Tight skullcap and mummy body: Ptah. Mummy body, white crown with feathers: Osiris.
Cow horns around a sun disc: Hathor, or Isis borrowing them. Small throne on the head: Isis.
Front-facing dwarf with tongue out: Bes. Pregnant hippo standing upright: Taweret.
fun_fact: The hieroglyph for 'god' is not a face but a flag on a pole, like the giant flagstaffs that once stood in the grooves of every temple gateway.
narration: Egyptian texts name more than 1,400 gods, but you only need about twenty, and you can recognise them like playing cards: by the head and the hat. The core family comes from Heliopolis, now under north Cairo. There, the creator Atum, a form of the sun god Ra, rose from the dark waters onto the first mound of earth. He produced Shu, the air, and Tefnut, moisture. They had Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. Geb and Nut had four children: Osiris and Isis, Seth and Nephthys. Seth murdered Osiris, and Horus, son of Isis, avenged him. That family drama is behind half the walls you will see. Other cities had their own teams. In Memphis, Ptah the craftsman created the world by speaking it. In Thebes, where you go on the 21st, the family is Amun, his wife Mut and their son, the moon god Khonsu. Gods could also merge, so Amun and Ra become Amun Ra, king of the gods. Now the cheat sheet. Falcon head: Horus. Jackal: Anubis. Ibis: Thoth. Ram: Khnum. Crocodile: Sobek. Lioness: Sekhmet. Two tall feathers: Amun. Cow horns around a sun disc: Hathor, or Isis borrowing them. Green skin and a mummy body: Osiris. On the next wall you see, name the first god by the head alone.

name: The Osiris myth: murder, resurrection and the first mummy
note: Osiris the good king, Seth's chest trick and the Nile, Byblos and the tamarisk, the 14 pieces (the fish ate the phallus), Isis the kite conceiving Horus, Nephthys and Anubis the first embalming, Horus vs Seth 80 years of contendings, Osiris as king of the dead; why every dead person became 'the Osiris N'; Abydos; the scenes you will see: Isis and Nephthys at the bier (Philae, Dendera), Horus harpooning (Edfu); Plutarch's version.
period: Attested from the Pyramid Texts, c. 2350 BC, to Plutarch, c. AD 100
summary: A murdered king, a widow who would not give up, and a son who fought 80 years for the throne: the story that let every Egyptian hope to live again.
look: You will see this story in pieces everywhere: Isis and Nephthys kneeling as kites at either end of a mummy on its bier, Anubis bending over the body, Horus with his harpoon. At Edfu on the 20th, Horus spears Seth as a tiny hippo on the inner west wall, and Philae's temple of Isis is built on her side of the tale.
story:
No Egyptian text tells the whole story. Egyptians avoided writing out a god's death, since words could make things real. We piece it together from the Pyramid Texts, hymns and healing spells, a bawdy New Kingdom tale called 'The Contendings of Horus and Seth', and, most fully, the Greek writer Plutarch around AD 100.

Osiris ruled Egypt as a good king until his brother Seth killed him. In Plutarch's version Seth and 72 accomplices made a splendid chest to Osiris's exact size and offered it at a banquet to whoever fitted inside. Osiris lay down, the lid was nailed shut and sealed with lead, and the chest was thrown into the Nile. It drifted to Byblos in Lebanon, where a tree grew around it and the king made the trunk a pillar of his palace. Isis found it and brought the body home; Seth, hunting by moonlight, found it again and cut it into 14 pieces. Isis recovered all but the phallus, eaten by fish, and made a replacement.

With Nephthys, Anubis and Thoth, Isis reassembled Osiris: the first mummy. Hovering as a kite, she fanned breath into him and conceived Horus, whom she hid in the Delta marshes. Osiris went on to rule the dead.

Grown up, Horus challenged Seth before the gods. In 'Contendings' the case drags on for 80 years, through boat races, hippo fights and Seth tearing out Horus's eye, until Horus wins. So every king was Horus alive and Osiris dead, and in time every Egyptian could become 'the Osiris' too.
details: Isis and Nephthys at the head and foot of a mummy, often as winged women or kites: the mourning scene on coffins and tomb walls.
Edfu, inner face of the west enclosure wall (20th): Horus harpoons Seth, shrunk to a hippo small enough to be harmless.
The djed pillar, Osiris's backbone, echoes the palace pillar at Byblos that hid his coffin in Plutarch's version.
Isis seated with the baby Horus on her lap: thousands of bronze figurines of the scene fill museum cases.
fun_fact: Because Osiris drowned in the Nile, Egyptians treated anyone who drowned in the river as sacred.
narration: This is the story behind half of what you will see in Egypt: a murder, a widow who would not give up, and a son's revenge. Osiris was a good king. His jealous brother Seth wanted the throne. In the Greek version told by Plutarch, Seth built a beautiful chest to Osiris's exact size and offered it at a banquet to whoever fitted inside. Osiris lay down, the lid slammed shut, and the chest was thrown into the Nile. It floated all the way to Byblos in Lebanon, where a tree grew around it and became a pillar in the king's palace. Isis, his wife and sister, tracked it down and brought him home. Seth found the body again and cut it into 14 pieces. Isis searched the whole country, found every piece but one, which a fish had eaten, and with her sister Nephthys, Anubis and Thoth, wrapped him back together. Osiris became the first mummy. Isis, as a kite, fanned breath into him and conceived their son Horus, then hid the baby in the marshes. Osiris went down to rule the dead. Horus grew up and fought Seth for 80 years, losing an eye and winning the throne. So every king was Horus in life and Osiris in death, and in time every Egyptian hoped to become an Osiris too. Look for Isis and Nephthys kneeling at the two ends of a mummy: that is this story.

name: Amun, the hidden one who became king of the gods
note: Local Theban god of air/hiddenness who rose with Thebes in the Middle Kingdom, merged with Ra as Amun-Ra 'king of the gods' in the New Kingdom; the ram and the goose; the two plumes and blue skin; Karnak his house, Opet his festival, the oracle (Siwa's Ammon for Greeks, Zeus-Ammon), the God's Wives, the High Priests who ended up ruling; Akhenaten's attack and the restoration; the wealth: 1/5 of Egypt's land by Ramesses III.
period: Attested from c. 2350 BC; king of the gods from c. 1550 BC
summary: A minor god whose name means 'the hidden one' rode Thebes' rise to become king of the gods, and his priests ended up ruling half of Egypt.
look: Amun is the man with blue skin and two tall straight plumes on a flat crown, often seated on a throne. His animals are the ram with curled horns, lining Karnak's avenue as sphinxes, and the goose. You will meet him on almost every wall in Luxor on the 21st and 22nd, sometimes with chisel scars where Akhenaten's agents hacked out his figure.
story:
His name, Imen, means something like 'the hidden one'; a Pyramid Text addresses the god 'whose name is unknown'. He first appears in the pyramid of Unas around 2350 BC, one of eight primeval gods of Hermopolis and possibly a god of the wind. Under Dynasty 11 he replaced the war god Montu as patron of Thebes, and Senusret I began his temple at Karnak.

When Theban kings expelled the Hyksos, they credited Amun. Merged with the sun as Amun-Ra, 'king of the gods', he received the spoils of empire, and Karnak became one of the largest religious complexes ever built. At the Opet festival his statue sailed from Karnak to Luxor Temple. Ordinary people prayed to him too: workmen at Deir el-Medina called him the god 'who comes at the voice of the poor'. He absorbed the ram god of Nubia and the fertile Min.

Wealth made his priests dangerous. Akhenaten closed his temples and erased his name; Tutankhamun restored him. By the end of the New Kingdom, Amun's priests held about two thirds of all temple land and 90 percent of the ships, and from 1080 BC High Priests such as Herihor and Pinedjem ruled the south as kings in all but name.

Greeks knew him through his desert oracle at Siwa and called him Zeus Ammon, with ram's horns. In 331 BC the oracle greeted Alexander as Amun's son, and coins struck by his successors show Alexander wearing the horns.
details: Two tall plumes on a flat crown: Amun. The same crown on a stiff ithyphallic figure with a raised flail: Amun-Min.
Karnak's ram-headed sphinxes (22nd) are Amun as a ram, each sheltering a small figure of the king between its paws.
His wife Mut wears a vulture headdress under the double crown; their son Khonsu has a youth's sidelock and a moon disc.
Siwa (13-15 Oct): the oracle temple at Aghurmi is where Alexander put his question to Amun.
fun_fact: Amun lives on in chemistry and geology: ammonia comes from 'sal ammoniac', salt linked to his temple in the Libyan desert, and ammonite fossils are named for his ram's horns.
narration: Amun is the god with blue skin and two tall feathers on his crown, and Luxor is his city. His name means the hidden one. He began as a minor god of air, one of eight primeval gods, until about 2000 BC, when he became the patron of Thebes. Then Thebes won. When Theban princes drove out the Hyksos around 1550 BC, they thanked Amun, merged him with the sun god as Amun Ra, king of the gods, and poured the treasure of an empire into his house at Karnak. Every year his statue sailed in a golden boat from Karnak to Luxor Temple for the Opet festival. He was not only for kings. Workmen in the tomb builders' village prayed to him as the god who comes at the voice of the poor. His wealth made his priests powerful. Akhenaten closed his temples and chiselled out his name. Tutankhamun brought him back. By the end of the New Kingdom, his priests held about two thirds of all temple land, and the High Priests of Amun ruled southern Egypt like kings. The Greeks met him at the oracle of Siwa and called him Zeus Ammon, with ram's horns. When Alexander visited in 331 BC, the oracle greeted him as Amun's son. At Karnak, look at the avenue of ram headed sphinxes: each ram is Amun, guarding a little king between its paws.

name: Ra and the sun's daily journey
note: Ra of Heliopolis, the sun's three forms (Khepri scarab at dawn, Ra at noon, Atum old man at dusk), the day barque and night barque, the 12 hours of night through the Duat fighting Apophis (what the Amduat in the royal tombs shows), the sun's rebirth each morning, the 'son of Ra' title of every king from the 4th Dynasty; Ra-Horakhty of Abu Simbel; the Eye of Ra and the Destruction of Mankind (Hathor/Sekhmet and the red beer).
period: Rising from Dynasty 2; state god from Dynasty 5, c. 2494 BC
summary: Every night the sun died in the west, sailed through the underworld fighting a giant snake, and was reborn at dawn. Royal tombs are maps of that voyage.
look: Ra is the falcon-headed man with a sun disc ringed by a cobra on his head. At dawn he is Khepri, a scarab beetle pushing the sun; at dusk he is Atum, an old man; at night he is a ram-headed figure standing in a boat. You will meet his night voyage on the walls of the Valley of the Kings on the 21st, and Ra-Horakhty in Abu Simbel's sanctuary and above its entrance on the 17th.
story:
His home was Iunu, which the Greeks called Heliopolis, 'sun city', now buried under north-east Cairo. From the 4th Dynasty every king was 'Son of Ra', and 5th Dynasty kings built him sun temples at Abusir. Other gods were drawn into his orbit: Amun-Ra at Thebes, and Ra-Horakhty, 'Ra who is Horus of the Two Horizons', the rising sun.

The sun lived a life every day. At dawn he was Khepri, the scarab, 'he who comes into being'. At noon he was Ra in full strength, crossing the sky in his day barque. At sunset, old as Atum, he passed through the western horizon into the Duat, the underworld, aboard his night barque. Through twelve hours and twelve regions he sailed a hidden river, woke the dead, merged with Osiris and fought Apophis, the chaos serpent, who tried to swallow the boat or freeze it with his stare. Seth stood in the prow and speared him. At dawn the sun was reborn, often from the body of the sky goddess Nut. New Kingdom royal tombs carry this journey on their walls, in texts such as the Amduat, 'what is in the underworld', so the dead king could ride along.

Ra also had a temper. In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, humans plot against the ageing sun god, and he sends his Eye, Hathor, to punish them. She turns into the lioness Sekhmet and starts a massacre. To stop her, Ra floods the land with beer dyed red; she drinks it, thinking it blood, gets drunk and becomes gentle Hathor again. Humanity survived because the gods got a goddess drunk.
details: Sun disc with a cobra on a falcon head: Ra or Ra-Horakhty. Scarab for a head: Khepri. Ram head in a boat: the night sun.
Abu Simbel facade (17th): in the niche over the door, falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty stands between signs spelling Ramesses' throne name.
Royal tombs (21st): find the sun disc in its boat and a long snake nearby, Apophis, often pierced by knives.
A king's second cartouche is introduced by a duck and a sun disc: 'Son of Ra', a title every king used from Dynasty 4.
fun_fact: Egyptians said humans were made from Ra's tears: in Egyptian the words for 'people' and 'tears', remetj and remyt, sounded almost the same.
narration: Ra is the sun, and in Egyptian eyes the sun lived a whole life every day. At dawn he was Khepri, a scarab beetle pushing the new sun over the horizon. At noon he was Ra, a falcon headed man with a blazing disc on his head, sailing across the sky in his day boat. At dusk he was Atum, an old man, stepping down into the west. Then came the dangerous part. For the twelve hours of night the sun sailed a dark river under the earth, the Duat, in a night boat, wearing a ram's head. He visited the dead, joined with Osiris, and every night fought Apophis, a giant serpent of chaos who tried to swallow the boat. Seth, of all gods, stood at the prow and speared him. At dawn the sun was born again. That journey is what the painted walls of the Valley of the Kings are about: the dead king rides in Ra's boat and rises with him. From the age of the pyramids, every pharaoh called himself Son of Ra. Ra also had a temper. When humans plotted against him, he sent his Eye, Hathor, who became the lioness Sekhmet and began to slaughter them. To stop her, Ra poured out beer dyed red. She drank it, thinking it was blood, fell asleep drunk, and woke up gentle. In a royal tomb, look for a long snake cut by knives: that is Apophis, losing again.

name: Osiris: king of the dead
note: Green or black skin (vegetation, Nile silt), mummiform, atef crown with ostrich feathers, crook and flail; judge of the dead in the Hall of Two Truths; the djed pillar as his backbone; Abydos and the Osireion; corn mummies; link to every tomb (Osiris receiving the king) and to the Osiris chapels of Karnak and Philae; why the pharaoh wanted to be him.
period: Worshipped from Dynasty 5, c. 2400 BC, to the 6th century AD
summary: Green-skinned, wrapped like a mummy, holding the crook and flail: Osiris judged the dead, and every Egyptian hoped to become him.
look: Osiris wears mummy wrappings from the chest down, has green or black skin, a tall white crown flanked by two ostrich feathers (the atef), and the crook and flail crossed on his chest. In tombs he sits enthroned at the end of a scene, receiving the dead king or the newly judged. The Osiride pillars at Abu Simbel (17th) and Medinet Habu (21st) show the king in his pose.
story:
His Egyptian name was something like Wesir; the Greeks made it Osiris. He appears in the 5th Dynasty, and soon the formula on tomb doors, 'an offering which the king gives to Anubis', became 'to Osiris'. His titles say what he was: Khentiamentiu, 'Foremost of the Westerners', that is, of the dead, and Wennefer, 'the one who remains perfect'.

Green skin means sprouting plants and black means the Nile's fertile mud, because he was also the power in the yearly flood and the growing grain. In the month of Khoiak priests sowed 'Osiris beds', trays of earth in his shape, and watched him sprout; one was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. At Abydos, where his tomb was said to lie, his death and resurrection were staged as a public drama for centuries.

His backbone was the djed pillar, symbol of stability. As judge he presides in the Hall of Two Truths while the heart is weighed. First only kings became Osiris at death; from the Middle Kingdom ordinary people did too, and their texts call them 'the Osiris So-and-so'. Becoming Osiris meant being dead but restored: the best deal Egyptian religion could offer.
details: Crook and flail crossed on a mummiform chest: Osiris, or a king dressed as him, as on Tutankhamun's coffins at the GEM.
Osiride pillars at Abu Simbel (17th) and Medinet Habu (21st): the king wrapped like Osiris, arms crossed, for eternity.
A green face on a coffin lid shows the dead person as Osiris, reborn like spring plants.
Karnak's small Osiris chapels and the Temple of Opet (22nd) celebrated his rebirth inside Amun's own precinct.
fun_fact: Women became Osiris too: a dead woman's coffin could call her 'the Osiris' followed by her name, a male god's title worn without fuss.
narration: Osiris is the god wrapped like a mummy, with green or black skin, a tall white crown with an ostrich feather on each side, and a crook and flail crossed on his chest. He is the murdered king of the myth, put back together by Isis, who became ruler of the dead. His green skin is new plants, his black skin the fertile mud of the Nile. Egyptians saw him in the flood and in the sprouting grain. Priests even planted Osiris beds, trays of earth in his shape sown with grain, and watched him come back to life. One was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. As judge, he sits on his throne at the end of the hall where the heart of the dead is weighed. His backbone was the djed pillar, the sign of stability. At first only dead kings became Osiris. Later everyone could, and texts call the deceased the Osiris so and so. At Abu Simbel and Medinet Habu, look at the pillars: the king stands wrapped and holding crook and flail, dressed as Osiris for eternity.

name: Isis: great of magic
note: Her name means throne (the headdress), the mother who nursed Horus in the marshes (the model for Madonna and child), the trickster who learned Ra's secret name, the kite mourning Osiris; Philae her last home; her cult spread across the Roman world (Pompeii, London); the tyet knot amulet; how to tell Isis from Hathor (the horns are borrowed).
period: Attested from Dynasty 5, c. 2400 BC; worshipped at Philae until c. AD 537
summary: Horus's mother and the cleverest of the gods, Isis outlived the pharaohs and was worshipped from Philae to Delos, Pompeii and Rome.
look: Isis is a woman with a small throne on her head, the hieroglyph of her name. From the New Kingdom she often wears Hathor's cow horns and sun disc instead, so check the label. She kneels with spread wings at the foot of coffins, nurses the baby Horus on her lap, and is the lady of Philae, whose temple you visit on the 18th or 19th.
story:
Her name, Aset, is written with the throne sign, and some scholars think she began as the throne itself, the 'mother' that made a man a king. She first appears in the 5th Dynasty and grows with the Osiris myth: the wife who searched Egypt for her husband's body, the mourner, the magician who revived him long enough to conceive Horus, and the mother who hid the baby from Seth in the Delta marshes.

She was 'more clever than a million gods'. In one tale she makes a snake from Ra's spittle and earth; it bites him, and she will not cure him until he tells her his secret name. Healing spells cast a sick child as Horus and the healer as Isis. In the New Kingdom she took over much of Hathor's role, horns included.

In the last millennium BC she became Egypt's most popular goddess. Her temple at Philae served Egyptians and Nubians alike and outlasted every other. Greeks made her a protector of sailors and inventor of marriage, and her cult spread around the Mediterranean, with temples on Delos, at Pompeii and in Rome. Images of Isis nursing Horus are often compared with the Virgin and Child, though how far one shaped the other is debated.
details: Throne on the head: Isis. Cow horns with a sun disc: Hathor, unless the label or the scene says Isis.
Winged woman kneeling with arms spread at the foot of a coffin or sarcophagus: Isis protecting the dead.
The tyet, or 'Isis knot', looks like an ankh with drooping arms; amulets of it were often made of red stone.
Philae (18th-19th): Isis's last great temple, with Christian crosses cut into its walls after it was closed.
fun_fact: Late Roman sources say the desert peoples south of Philae were allowed to borrow Isis's statue for their own festivals, one reason her cult there survived so long.
narration: Isis is the goddess with a small throne on her head. That throne is the hieroglyph of her name, and some scholars think she began as the royal throne itself, the mother that turns a man into a king. In the myth, she is the wife who searched all of Egypt for her murdered husband Osiris, put him back together, and conceived their son Horus. Then she hid the baby in the marshes and raised him to take back the throne. She was also the cleverest of the gods. In one story she makes a snake that bites the sun god Ra, and will only cure him if he tells her his secret name. He gives in. Later she borrowed Hathor's cow horns and sun disc, so check the label before you decide which goddess you are looking at. In Greek and Roman times her cult spread across the Mediterranean, to Delos, Pompeii and Rome. Her image nursing Horus may even have shaped pictures of the Madonna and child. At Philae, her last temple, look for crosses carved by Christians on the walls of her house.

name: Horus and Seth: order against chaos
note: Seth, god of desert, storms, foreigners, with the unidentifiable 'Seth animal' head (aardvark? donkey? invented); not simply evil: he defends Ra's barque against Apophis every night and was patron of the Ramessides (Seti means 'man of Seth'); his later demonisation; Horus the falcon as the living king; their contendings as the myth of legitimate succession; the unified 'two faces' statue.
period: From late Predynastic times, c. 3200 BC, to the Roman period
summary: The falcon and the mystery beast: their 80-year feud was Egypt's myth of rightful succession, and Seth was never simply the villain.
look: Horus is the falcon, or a man with a falcon's head, often in the double crown; Edfu (20th) is his temple, guarded by granite falcons. Seth has the head of an animal nobody can identify: curved snout, tall square-tipped ears, stiff forked tail. On throne sides you may see the two of them knotting the plants of south and north around the sign for 'unite'.
story:
The falcon's name probably means 'the one far above'. He was the god of Nekhen in the south, and from the beginning the living king was his earthly form. Seth, lord of the red desert, storms, violence and foreigners, balanced him as lord of the black, fertile land.

In the myth Seth murders Osiris, and Horus, son of Isis, claims the throne. The New Kingdom tale 'The Contendings of Horus and Seth' turns their trial into farce: the case drags on for 80 years because the judge, Ra, favours Seth; they race boats and fight as hippos; Seth tears out Horus's eye and Horus damages Seth's testicles; Isis tricks Seth into condemning himself. Horus wins, as the rightful son must.

Seth was more than a villain. Every night he stood in the prow of Ra's boat and speared the serpent Apophis. The Hyksos made him their chief god, and the Ramesside kings came from his cult centre in the Delta: Seti means 'man of Seth'. Only after Libyan, Nubian, Assyrian and Persian conquests was he demonised as the god of hated foreigners, and his images hacked away. The Greeks equated him with Typhon, the monster that fought Zeus.
details: Seth animal: down-curved snout, square-topped ears, forked tail. Aardvark, donkey and wild dog have been proposed; none fits.
Edfu (20th): granite falcons of Horus flank the pylon entrance; the best one, in the double crown, stands at the hypostyle door.
Throne sides: two gods knotting papyrus and lily around a windpipe sign. Sometimes Nile gods, sometimes Horus and Seth.
Edfu's west wall: Horus harpoons Seth, shrunk to a small hippo so he cannot harm the temple.
fun_fact: Ramesses II set up a stela celebrating 400 years of Seth's cult in the Delta: the god of chaos got an anniversary party.
narration: Horus is the falcon, and Seth is the strange animal with a curved snout, tall square ears and a stiff forked tail that nobody has ever matched to a real beast. Aardvark, donkey and wild dog have all been suggested. Horus was the sky and the king: every living pharaoh was Horus on earth. Seth was the red desert, storms and foreigners. In the myth, Seth murders his brother Osiris, and Horus, the son, claims the throne. A New Kingdom story turns their court case into a comedy: it drags on for 80 years, they race boats, fight as hippos, Seth tears out Horus's eye, and Isis tricks Seth into condemning himself. Horus wins, because the rightful son must. But Seth was not simply evil. Every night he stood at the front of the sun's boat and speared the chaos serpent. The Ramesside kings came from his cult centre, and Seti means man of Seth. Only after foreign invasions was he turned into a devil. At Edfu on the 20th, find the granite falcon at the gate: that is Horus himself.

name: Anubis and Thoth: the embalmer and the scribe
note: Anubis the black jackal (colour of resin and fertile earth, not of jackals), 'he who is upon his mountain', guardian of the necropolis and the mummification tent, who weighs the heart; Thoth the ibis or baboon, moon god, inventor of writing, the gods' scribe and arbiter who records the verdict and healed the Eye of Horus; Hermopolis; Greeks made him Hermes Trismegistus; the baboons greeting the sunrise at Abu Simbel and Luxor obelisk bases.
period: Anubis from Dynasty 1, c. 3000 BC; Thoth from the Old Kingdom; both to the Roman period
summary: One guards the cemetery and wraps the dead; the other invented writing and keeps the gods' minutes. Together they run the judgement of the soul.
look: Anubis is the black jackal lying on a shrine, or a man with a jackal's head bending over a mummy or adjusting the scales. Thoth has the long curved beak of an ibis, often with a moon disc on a crescent, and holds a scribe's palette; he can also appear as a baboon. Both stand at the weighing of the heart in tomb paintings and Book of the Dead papyri.
story:
The jackal god, Egyptian Inpu, appears from the 1st Dynasty. Jackals dug up shallow graves at the desert edge, so Egyptians set a jackal to guard the dead: fight like with like. His black is not the animal's colour but that of the resin-soaked mummy and of fertile Nile mud, meaning rebirth. His titles describe the job: 'He who is upon his mountain', watching the necropolis; 'He who is in the place of embalming'. He embalmed Osiris, priests in jackal masks played him at funerals, and at the judgement he checks the scales. The Greeks merged him with Hermes, guide of souls, as Hermanubis.

Thoth, Djehuty, was the moon, reckoner of time, inventor of writing and scribe of the gods. His animals were the ibis and the baboon, whose chatter at sunrise looked like greeting the sun. He mediated between Horus and Seth, restored Horus's torn eye, gave Isis the words to revive Osiris, and records the verdict on the dead. His city was Hermopolis, whose huge temple porch was still standing in 1826, before it was demolished to fill a sugar factory's foundations. Greeks called him Hermes Trismegistus, 'thrice great', and later alchemists and mystics claimed his secret books.
details: Black jackal lying on a chest or shrine: Anubis guarding the tomb, as on Tutankhamun's Anubis shrine at the GEM.
Ibis head with a moon disc on a crescent, pen and palette in hand: Thoth writing down the verdict.
Abu Simbel facade (17th): along the very top runs a row of baboons raising their hands to the rising sun.
Luxor Temple (22nd): look at the base of the obelisk by the pylon for baboons greeting the sun.
fun_fact: In Plato's Gorgias, Socrates swears 'by the dog, the god of the Egyptians': Anubis made it into Greek philosophy.
narration: Two gods run the judgement of the dead. Anubis is the black jackal, or a man with a jackal's head. Jackals dug up shallow graves at the desert edge, so Egyptians set a jackal to guard the dead: fight like with like. But his black is not the colour of jackals. It is the colour of a mummy soaked in resin, and of the fertile Nile mud, which means rebirth. He embalmed Osiris, the first mummy, and at funerals a priest wearing a jackal mask played his part. At the weighing of the heart, Anubis checks the scales. Thoth is the ibis, or sometimes a baboon. He is the moon, the inventor of writing and the scribe of the gods, and he writes down the verdict. He also healed the torn eye of Horus. The Greeks matched Thoth with Hermes and called him Hermes Trismegistus, thrice great. And Socrates, in Plato, swears by the dog, the god of the Egyptians. At Abu Simbel on the 17th, look up along the top of the facade: a row of baboons raises its hands to greet the rising sun.

name: Hathor: love, music, drunkenness and the cow
note: Horns and sun disc, cow ears on column capitals (Philae, Deir el-Bahari, Abu Simbel small temple), the sistrum and menat rattle, mistress of the west who receives the dead from the mountain, the 'golden one' of love and drunkenness (the festival of drunkenness), nurse of the king (Hatshepsut suckled by the cow), the Seven Hathors who foretell fate, Nefertari as Hathor; her fury as Sekhmet; Dendera; the Greeks' Aphrodite.
period: Prominent from Dynasty 4, c. 2600 BC, to the Roman period
summary: Goddess of love, music, beer and the sky, Hathor could also become a lioness that nearly wiped out humanity. No goddess had more temples.
look: Hathor is a woman with cow horns curving around a sun disc, or a cow, or a calm woman's face with cow's ears on top of a column. Those Hathor capitals are in the Small Temple at Abu Simbel (17th), Hatshepsut's Hathor chapel (21st) and at Philae (18th). She shakes a sistrum rattle or holds a heavy menat necklace, and in the Theban hills she is a cow stepping out of the western mountain to receive the dead.
story:
Her name, Hut-Hor, means 'House of Horus': she was the sky in which the falcon lived, or the womb from which the sun was born each day. Cow goddesses go back to prehistory, but Hathor rose with the pyramid kings of Dynasty 4 to become Ra's wife and the divine mother of the king. Her great temple was at Dendera, north of Luxor, and more temples were dedicated to her than to any other goddess.

She was the 'Golden One' of love, sex, beauty, music, dance, perfume and drunkenness. A text at Edfu says the gods play the sistrum for her 'to dispel her bad temper'. That temper is the other half of her story. As the Eye of Ra she was sent to punish rebellious humans, became the lioness Sekhmet and began a massacre, until Ra flooded the land with red-dyed beer. The Festival of Drunkenness re-enacted her calming, and at the Temple of Mut in Karnak excavators found a 'porch of drunkenness' built by Hatshepsut.

In the Theban necropolis she was 'Mistress of the West', the cow emerging from the mountain, and the sycamore that gave the dead food and water. She nursed kings: at Deir el-Bahari a relief shows Hatshepsut suckled by the Hathor cow. The 'Seven Hathors' appeared at births to announce a child's fate. Ramesses II dedicated the Small Temple at Abu Simbel to her and to Nefertari, who wears her horns and disc. The Greeks equated her with Aphrodite.
details: Abu Simbel Small Temple (17th): pillars topped with Hathor's face and cow ears, and Nefertari wearing her horned crown.
Hatshepsut's temple (21st): in the Hathor chapel, Hathor-faced capitals and the queen suckled by the divine cow.
Philae (18th): the small Hathor temple shows musicians, and Bes dancing and playing for her.
Sistrum: a rattle with Hathor's face on the handle. Menat: a heavy bead necklace with a counterweight, shaken in her rites.
fun_fact: Texts speak of 'Seven Hathors' who turned up at a birth to pronounce the baby's fate, rather like the fairies at Sleeping Beauty's christening.
narration: Hathor is the goddess with cow horns curving around a sun disc, or simply a cow, or a woman's face with cow ears on top of a column. Her name means House of Horus: she was the sky that held the falcon, and the mother of the sun. She was the Golden One, goddess of love, beauty, music, dance, perfume and drunkenness, and more temples were built for her than for any other goddess. Musicians shook rattles called sistra to keep her happy, and one text admits why: to drive away her bad temper. Because Hathor had a dark side. When humans plotted against the sun god Ra, he sent her as his Eye to punish them. She turned into Sekhmet, a lioness, and began to slaughter everyone. To save humanity, Ra flooded the fields with beer dyed red. She drank it, thinking it was blood, got gloriously drunk, and turned back into sweet Hathor. Egyptians celebrated with a Festival of Drunkenness, and Hatshepsut built a porch of drunkenness at Karnak for it. In Thebes she was also Mistress of the West, a cow stepping out of the mountain to welcome the dead. She nursed kings, and the Greeks called her Aphrodite. At Abu Simbel's Small Temple on the 17th, look for the pillars topped with her calm face and cow ears.

name: Ptah and Sekhmet: the craftsman and the lioness
note: Ptah of Memphis who created by thought and speech (the Memphite Theology), patron of craftsmen, mummiform with skullcap and was-djed-ankh sceptre (the god in the dark at Abu Simbel and the 'Egypt' etymology via Hut-ka-Ptah); his wife Sekhmet 'the powerful', lioness of plague and war whose breath is the desert wind, appeased with 730 statues by Amenhotep III and beer at festivals; priests of Sekhmet as doctors; Nefertem the lotus son.
period: Ptah from the Early Dynastic Period; Sekhmet from Dynasty 5; both to the Roman period
summary: The craftsman god who created the world by speaking it, and his wife, a lioness whose breath was the desert wind. Egypt itself is named after his temple.
look: Ptah stands wrapped like a mummy with his hands free, a tight skullcap, a straight beard and a staff combining the was, ankh and djed signs. Sekhmet is a woman with a lioness's head and a sun disc. You meet Ptah in the dark of Abu Simbel's sanctuary (17th) and in his small temple at Karnak, where a black Sekhmet stands alone in a shrine (22nd).
story:
His home was Memphis, the old capital. A text carved on the Shabaka Stone around 700 BC says he created the gods 'through this heart and this tongue', conceiving things and naming them, an idea often compared with 'In the beginning was the Word'. He was patron of craftsmen, architects and sculptors; the sage Imhotep was later called his son, and the tomb-builders of Thebes prayed to 'Ptah who listens to prayers'. His Memphis temple, Hut-ka-Ptah, 'enclosure of the ka of Ptah', became Greek Aigyptos and our 'Egypt'. Greeks matched him with Hephaestus.

Sekhmet, 'the Powerful', was his wife, a daughter of Ra and his Eye at its most violent. She breathed fire, her breath was the hot desert wind, and plagues were her messengers. The same power could heal, and she was invoked against disease. Amenhotep III had around 700 statues of her carved, perhaps more; many now stand in the Precinct of Mut at Karnak and in museums worldwide. Their son was Nefertem, the young god of the lotus, often with a lotus flower on his head.
details: Abu Simbel sanctuary (17th): four seated gods. Ptah, at the left end, is the one the sunbeam never reaches.
Karnak, Temple of Ptah (22nd): Sekhmet stands in a dark shrine lit only by a hole in the roof.
Rows of black granite Sekhmets, seated or standing, come from Amenhotep III; you will meet them in museums and at Mut's precinct.
Ptah's staff stacks three signs: was for power, ankh for life, djed for stability.
Tutankhamun's head rising from a lotus at the GEM shows him as Nefertem, the child god born from the flower.
fun_fact: The word 'Egypt' is Ptah's: his Memphis temple, Hut-ka-Ptah, became the Greek Aigyptos, so every Greek saying 'Aigyptos' is naming a god's house.
narration: Ptah is the god wrapped like a mummy, with a tight skullcap and a straight beard, holding a staff that stacks three signs: power, life and stability. He was the god of Memphis, the old capital, and the patron of craftsmen and sculptors. One text says he created the world by thinking of it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue, a bit like In the beginning was the Word. His temple at Memphis was called Hut ka Ptah, the house of Ptah's spirit. The Greeks heard it as Aigyptos, and that is where the word Egypt comes from. They matched him with their own smith god, Hephaestus. His wife Sekhmet, the Powerful, is a woman with a lioness's head. Her breath was the hot desert wind and plague was her messenger, yet she was also called on to heal the sick. Amenhotep the Third had around 700 statues of her carved to keep her calm. At Abu Simbel's sanctuary on the 17th, look at the god on the far left: that is Ptah, the one the sunbeam never reaches.

name: Local gods you'll meet: Khnum, Sobek, Min, Montu, Satet, Anuket
note: Short. Min of Koptos, the ithyphallic fertility god with the flail and lettuce (Luxor's Opet, Karnak's White Chapel, Medinet Habu's festival); Montu the Theban falcon war god; the cataract triad Khnum, Satet (the antelope-horned archer) and Anuket (gazelle, feather crown) at Aswan; Sobek at Kom Ombo; Meretseger of the peak; Hapi the Nile with pendulous breasts tying the two lands.
summary: A potter, a crocodile, a fertility god with lettuce, a war falcon and two southern goddesses: the local gods of the places on this trip.
look: Khnum has a ram's head with long wavy horizontal horns and often sits at a potter's wheel; Sobek has a crocodile's head. Min stands stiffly with an erect phallus, one arm raised with a flail and two tall plumes on his head; Montu is a falcon with two plumes and a sun disc. Satet wears the white crown with antelope horns, Anuket a tall crown of feathers.
story: Every town had its own god. At Aswan's First Cataract, Khnum the ram controlled the flood and shaped people on a potter's wheel, with the goddesses Satet and Anuket; you will see his temple ruins on Elephantine (18th-19th) and his Roman-period hall at Esna (20th). Sobek the crocodile shares Kom Ombo with Horus. Min of Koptos ruled fertility and harvest; lettuce, whose milky sap suggested semen, was his plant, eaten for potency. Montu was Thebes' war god before Amun. Above the Valley of the Kings, the cobra Meretseger, 'she who loves silence', guarded the peak.
details: Min on Karnak and Luxor walls: stiff figure, erect phallus, raised flail, tall plumes, often with lettuces behind him.
Khnum at his potter's wheel shaping a royal child: in Hatshepsut's birth scenes (21st) and at Luxor Temple (22nd).
Kom Ombo (20th): one half of the twin temple is Sobek's; mummified crocodiles wait in the museum next door.
Esna (20th): Khnum's hymns credit him with shaping gods, people, animals and plants.
fun_fact: Khufu's full name was Khnum-Khufwy, 'Khnum protects me': the builder of the Great Pyramid was named after the potter god.
narration: Every town had its own god, and this trip passes through their homes. At Aswan, Khnum, the ram with long wavy horns, controlled the Nile flood and shaped every child on his potter's wheel, helped by the goddesses Satet and Anuket. At Kom Ombo, Sobek the crocodile shares a double temple with Horus. Min, the stiff god with the raised flail and the very obvious erection, was lord of fertility. His sacred plant was lettuce, eaten for potency. Montu, a falcon, was the war god of Thebes before Amun. At Esna on the 20th, look for Khnum's ram head among the Roman columns.

name: Ma'at, Nut and Geb: truth, sky and earth
note: Ma'at the feather, cosmic order and justice that the king maintains (the tiny figure he offers to the gods on every wall) and against which the heart is weighed; Nut the sky arched over Geb the earth, separated by Shu, swallowing the sun each evening and giving birth at dawn (the ceilings of Ramesses VI, Hatshepsut, Dendera), the mother on coffin lids; Geb's goose; the five epagomenal days when Nut gave birth to Osiris, Horus the Elder, Seth, Isis and Nephthys.
summary: Maat is the order of the universe in the shape of a feather; Nut is the sky arched over her husband Geb, swallowing the sun every evening.
look: Maat is a seated or kneeling woman with one tall ostrich feather on her head; kings constantly offer a tiny figure of her to the gods. Nut is a long, star-covered woman bent over the world on fingertips and toes, painted across tomb ceilings and inside coffin lids. Geb lies beneath her, often green, sometimes with a goose on his head.
story:
The word maat meant the order set in place at creation: truth, justice, balance, the seasons turning and the sun rising. Her opposite was isfet, chaos. Kings claimed to 'live on Maat', put her in their names, and in countless temple scenes offer the gods a tiny squatting figure of her, a way of saying 'I have kept the world in order'. From the 5th Dynasty the vizier who ran justice was called 'Priest of Maat', and at the judgement of the dead the heart was weighed against her feather.

Nut was the sky, daughter of Shu, the air, and Tefnut, moisture. Unusually, the sky was female and the earth, her brother-husband Geb, male. Shu holds them apart. Each evening Nut swallows the sun, which travels through her body during the night and is born from her at dawn. Coffin lids were painted with her on the inside, so the dead lay in the sky's embrace, waiting to rise like the sun.

Plutarch tells how the sun forbade Nut to give birth on any day of the year. Thoth won five extra days by gambling with the moon, and on them she bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Seth, Isis and Nephthys: the five extra days at the end of the Egyptian calendar.
details: Watch for the king holding out a tiny crouching woman with a feather: he is offering Maat herself to the gods.
Tomb of Ramesses VI, KV9 (21st): two huge figures of Nut stretch back to back across the burial-chamber ceiling.
Inside coffin lids in the museums: Nut with outstretched arms or wings, embracing the dead person.
Throne names often contain her: Hatshepsut's Maatkare and Ramesses II's Usermaatre both include the Maat sign.
fun_fact: Egypt made the earth a man and the sky a woman, the reverse of most mythologies, including the Greek pair of Ouranos the sky and Gaia the earth.
narration: Three gods here hold the universe together. Maat is the woman with a single ostrich feather on her head. She is truth, justice and order, everything that keeps the sun rising and the river flooding. Her opposite was chaos. A king's first job was to uphold Maat, and on temple walls you will see him offering the gods a tiny crouching figure of her: proof that he kept the world in order. When you died, your heart was weighed against her feather. Nut is the sky, a long woman covered in stars, arched over the world on her fingertips and toes. Geb, the earth, lies beneath her, and their father Shu, the air, holds them apart. Unusually, the sky here is female and the earth male, the reverse of the Greek Ouranos and Gaia. Every evening Nut swallows the sun, and every dawn she gives birth to it again. That is why she is painted inside coffin lids: the dead lie in her arms, waiting to be reborn. In the tomb of Ramesses the Sixth, look up: Nut's body stretches across the whole ceiling.

name: Bes and Taweret: the household protectors
note: Bes the bandy-legged dwarf with lion mane and tongue out, facing front (unusual), who scared demons from childbirth and bedrooms with music and dance (Philae's Hathor temple, Edfu's mammisi, Deir el-Medina houses, Dendera); Taweret the pregnant hippo with crocodile back and lion paws, protector of mothers; both on beds, headrests and mirrors; the popular religion that lived beside the state cults.
period: Household gods, popular from the Middle Kingdom, c. 2000 BC, to the Roman period
summary: A grimacing dwarf and a pregnant hippo never got grand temples, but they guarded every Egyptian bedroom, birth and baby.
look: Bes is a bandy-legged dwarf with a lion's mane and ears, a feather crown and often his tongue out, and he faces you head-on, which almost no other Egyptian god does. Taweret stands upright: a pregnant hippo with human breasts, lion's paws and a crocodile's back and tail, often leaning on the sa sign of protection. Look for both on furniture, headrests, mirrors and amulets in museum cases, and for Bes dancing at Philae's Hathor temple.
story:
Egypt's great gods lived in temples ordinary people could not enter. At home, people relied on smaller, tougher protectors. Bes, possibly of Nubian origin, killed snakes, scared off demons, watched over children and stood by women in labour. His ugliness was the point: demons fled his face, and his music and dancing drove off evil.
