He appears on beds, headrests, mirror handles, feeding bottles and magic knives, and a painting at Deir el-Medina shows a musician with Bes tattooed on her thigh. Later he guarded the birth houses of Ptolemaic temples, and his cult spread to Phoenicia, Cyprus, Persia and Ibiza.

Taweret, 'the Great One', a polite name for a dangerous creature, was the female hippo, fiercest of mothers. Egyptians hunted male hippos as agents of chaos but honoured the female for defending her young. Hippo-goddess amulets go back to prehistory; from the Middle Kingdom Taweret appears on ivory birth wands and children's cups. Even at Amarna, where Akhenaten banned the old gods, people kept her image at home.

Do not confuse her with Ammit, the crocodile-lion-hippo 'devourer' who waits at the judgement of the dead.
details: Bes faces you directly while almost every other god is in profile: the stare is meant to frighten demons away.
Philae (18th): in the small Hathor temple, Bes plays instruments and dances for the goddess.
Edfu's birth house (20th): little figures of Bes squat on top of the columns above the capitals.
Taweret's crocodile tail runs down her back like a cape: look at her figurines from the side.
fun_fact: The Minoans of Crete borrowed Taweret: the lion-like 'Minoan Genius' carrying jugs on Cretan seals is widely thought to descend from her.
narration: The great gods lived in temples ordinary people could never enter. At home, Egyptians trusted two tougher, friendlier guards. Bes is the bandy-legged dwarf with a lion's mane, a crown of feathers and his tongue sticking out. Unlike almost every other god, he faces you head on, because his job was to stare demons down. He killed snakes, protected children, danced and played music to scare evil away, and stood beside women giving birth. You find him on beds, mirrors, headrests and baby bottles, and one painting shows a musician with Bes tattooed on her thigh. Taweret, whose name means the Great One, is a pregnant hippo standing on her hind legs, with lion's paws and a crocodile's back. Egyptians feared male hippos but admired the females, the fiercest mothers on the river. Even when Akhenaten banned the old gods, people kept Taweret at home. On Crete, the Minoans borrowed her too. At Edfu's birth house on the 20th, look at the tops of the columns: little figures of Bes squat there, grinning.

name: The Aten and the Amarna revolution
note: Amenhotep IV becomes Akhenaten (c. 1353 BC), the sun disc with rays ending in hands offering ankhs, the new capital Akhetaten (Amarna) built in a few years, Nefertiti's equal role, the Great Hymn to the Aten (compared to Psalm 104), the closing of Amun's temples and chiselling of his name, the art style (elongated, intimate family scenes), the Amarna letters diplomatic archive, the collapse after his death, Tut's restoration, Horemheb's erasure; was it monotheism? what you see: talatat wall (Luxor Museum), colossi (Cairo), the Aten on Tut's throne, KV55.
period: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, Amarna Period, c. 1353-1336 BC
summary: For some 17 years a pharaoh shut down Egypt's gods for a single sun disc, built a capital in the desert and changed art. Then it all vanished.
look: The Aten is a plain sun disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding ankhs to the noses of the royal family. Amarna art is easy to spot: long faces, full lips, narrow shoulders, wide hips, and tender family scenes. You will meet it in the Akhenaten colossi in the Cairo museums, on the back of Tutankhamun's golden throne at the GEM (11th) and in the talatat wall at the Luxor Museum (22nd).
story:
Amenhotep IV came to the throne around 1353 BC. The Aten, the 'disc' of the sun, had long been an aspect of Ra and was already honoured under his father, Amenhotep III. The new king went much further. In about his fifth year he became Akhenaten, 'effective spirit of the Aten', and began a capital on virgin ground in Middle Egypt: Akhetaten, 'Horizon of the Aten', today Amarna. Built mostly of whitewashed mud brick, it was largely finished within about four years, and boundary stelae marked its limits.

Aten temples were open to the sky, with no dark sanctuary and no cult statue. Only the king and Nefertiti, shown almost as his equal, could approach the god; everyone else worshipped through them. Amun's temples were closed and his name hacked out across Egypt. Whether this was the first monotheism or the worship of one god without denying the rest is still debated; the Great Hymn to the Aten is often compared with Psalm 104. Art changed overnight: elongated bodies, the king kissing his daughters, sunlight pouring over the family. Clay tablets found at Amarna in 1887, the Amarna letters, preserve the diplomatic mail of Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites and Canaan's rulers.

After Akhenaten's death the experiment collapsed. Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun and the court left Amarna; later kings pulled down the Aten temples and packed their small blocks, talatat, inside Karnak's pylons as fill. That is how thousands survived to be reassembled.
details: Sun disc with long rays ending in hands: the Aten. Only the royal family receives the ankhs held to their noses.
Tutankhamun's golden throne (GEM, 11th): the Aten shines on the young king and queen, a survivor of his Amarna childhood.
Luxor Museum (22nd): the talatat wall rebuilds an Aten temple scene from small blocks recovered inside a Karnak pylon.
Hacked-out and recut Amun figures on Luxor and Karnak walls are scars of this reign and its reversal.
fun_fact: Akhetaten was abandoned so quickly and completely that it is the only ancient Egyptian city whose street plan survives in detail.
narration: For about 17 years, one pharaoh tried to switch off Egypt's gods. Amenhotep the Fourth came to the throne around 1353 BC. Around his fifth year he renamed himself Akhenaten, effective spirit of the Aten, the sun disc, and moved the court to a brand new city on empty desert in Middle Egypt: Akhetaten, Horizon of the Aten, today called Amarna. It was thrown up in mud brick in about four years. The Aten was not a statue. It was sunlight itself, drawn as a disc whose rays end in little hands, holding the sign of life to the noses of the king and his wife Nefertiti. Only they could speak to the god, and everyone else worshipped through them. Amun's temples were closed and his name chiselled out across Egypt. Was it the first monotheism? Scholars still argue. Art changed overnight: long faces, wide hips, the king kissing his daughters in the sun. Then he died, and it all collapsed. His probable son Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun and brought Amun back, and later kings pulled the Aten temples down and stuffed their small stone blocks into the pylons at Karnak. That is why thousands survived. On the back of Tutankhamun's golden throne at the GEM, look for the sun disc with hands, shining on the young king and queen.

name: Hieroglyphs in ten minutes: how the writing works
note: ~700 signs in classic use: sound signs (1, 2, 3 consonants), word signs, and silent determinatives; no vowels (hence 'Amun/Amon/Amen'); read toward the faces of the animals; the uniliteral 'alphabet' worth learning (vulture a, reed i, arm a, quail chick w, foot b, stool p, horned viper f, owl m, water n, mouth r, reed shelter h, twisted flax h, placenta kh, animal belly kh, folded cloth s, pool sh, hill q, basket k, jar stand g, loaf t, tether tj, hand d, cobra dj); hieratic and demotic as cursive forms; Coptic as the last stage; Champollion's 1822 breakthrough via Ptolemy and Cleopatra cartouches.
summary: Hieroglyphs are not picture-writing: most signs stand for sounds. Learn two dozen and you can start reading names off temple walls.
look: Hieroglyphs run in rows or columns, usually right to left, but the signs tell you: people, birds and animals face the beginning of the line, so read towards their faces. Signs on top are read before signs below. On this trip every wall is a text, and the bigger the carving, the more public the message.
story:
Writing appeared in Egypt around 3200 BC, among the earliest in the world and probably invented independently. In the classical Middle Kingdom about 900 signs were in use; Ptolemaic priests multiplied them to more than 5,000.

The system mixes three kinds of sign. Sound signs include 24 'alphabet' signs for single consonants, plus signs for two or three consonants. Word signs show the thing meant: a sun disc for 'sun'. Silent determinatives at the end of a word give its category: a seated man for a person, walking legs for movement, a papyrus roll for an abstract idea. Vowels were not written, which is why books disagree between Amun, Amon and Amen; Egyptologists insert a convenient 'e', so nfr becomes nefer.

For daily use scribes wrote fast cursive forms: hieratic, then from about 650 BC demotic. Coptic, written with Greek letters plus a few demotic signs, is the last stage of the language and still used in Coptic church services.

The last dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394. Greek and Roman writers then imagined the signs as mystical symbols, a belief that blocked decipherment for some 1,400 years. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Building on Thomas Young's work, Jean-François Champollion, who knew Coptic, showed in 1822 that the cartouches of Ptolemy and Cleopatra spelled sounds, and that the script was 'figurative, symbolic and phonetic all at once'.
details: Vulture = a (glottal stop), reed leaf = i, forearm = a (ayin), quail chick = w, foot = b, stool = p, horned viper = f, owl = m.
Water ripple = n, mouth = r, reed shelter = h, twisted flax = h, round placenta = kh, animal belly = kh, folded cloth = s.
Pool = sh, hill slope = q, basket with handle = k, jar stand = g, bread loaf = t, tethering rope = tj, hand = d, cobra = dj.
Which way? Read towards the faces of people, birds and animals, and take the top sign before the one below it.
fun_fact: 'Hieroglyph' is Greek for 'sacred carving', a fair translation of the Egyptians' own name for their script: 'the words of the god'.
narration: Hieroglyphs look like pictures, but most of them are sounds. That was the great discovery of 1822, and it means you can start reading. The system mixes three kinds of sign. Some spell sounds: there are 24 signs for single consonants, like an alphabet, plus signs for two or three consonants together. Some stand for whole words. And some are silent hints at the end of a word, telling you what kind of thing it is: a seated man for a person, walking legs for movement. Vowels were never written, which is why the same god is Amun, Amon or Amen in different books. Now the basics. An owl is m. Water, a zigzag line, is n. A mouth is r. A loaf of bread, a little half circle, is t. A foot is b, a quail chick is w, a horned viper is f, a folded cloth is s, a reed leaf is i, a hand is d. To know which way to read, look at the faces of the birds and people: you read towards them. For everyday writing, scribes used fast handwriting called hieratic and demotic. The last hieroglyphs ever carved are at Philae, dated 394 AD, and you will stand near them on the 18th. And a gift from Egypt to Greece: through the Phoenicians, these signs are distant ancestors of the Greek alphabet. On the next wall, find an owl and say m.

name: Reading a cartouche: spot Ramesses, Tut, Hatshepsut and friends
note: The oval shen rope = eternity, enclosing the two cartouche names of the king's five (Horus, Two Ladies, Golden Horus, prenomen 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt' with sedge and bee, nomen 'Son of Ra' with duck and sun); the cheat sheet of signs: Ramesses = sun disc + Mes (three fox skins) + folded cloth x2 (Ra-mes-su), his prenomen User-maat-Ra Setep-en-Ra (was sceptre, Maat, sun; see Ozymandias); Tutankhamun = Amun + Tut (bread, chick, bread) + ankh; Hatshepsut Maat-ka-Ra (sun, Maat, ka arms); Thutmose III Men-kheper-Ra (sun, scarab, game board), the most common scarab name; Amenhotep III Neb-maat-Ra; Khufu (chick, bread, f viper, chick); Seti (Seth animal replaced by the Osiris knot); Cleopatra and Ptolemy alphabetic: the spelling game to play at every wall.
period: Cartouches used from the end of Dynasty 3, c. 2600 BC, to the Roman emperors
summary: The rope oval around a king's name is a game you can play on every wall: learn six cartouches and Ramesses, Tutankhamun and Hatshepsut will jump out.
look: A cartouche is a stretched oval of rope tied off with a bar at one end, enclosing a royal name; kings usually show two side by side. The first, introduced by a sedge plant and a bee, 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt', holds the throne name; the second, after a duck and a sun disc, 'Son of Ra', holds the birth name. Gods' names inside, like Ra's sun disc or Amun's name, are written first out of respect even when they are read later.
story:
A king had five names; the three outside cartouches (Horus, Two Ladies and Golden Horus names) rarely matter to visitors. The cartouche, Egyptian shenu, is a stretched shen ring, a loop of rope meaning eternity, wrapped protectively around the name. It appears at the end of the 3rd Dynasty and became standard under Sneferu.

The cheat sheet. Ramesses II's birth name, Ra-messu, is the sun disc, a sign like three fox skins tied together (ms), and folded-cloth s signs, usually with 'beloved of Amun'. His throne name, User-maat-Ra, is the sun disc, the goddess Maat with her feather and a jackal-headed staff (user, 'strong'). The Greek historian Diodorus rendered it 'Osymandyas', which became Shelley's Ozymandias.

Tutankhamun: Amun's name (reed leaf, game board, water ripple) on top for honour, then tut (loaf, quail chick, loaf), then the ankh. His throne name Neb-kheperu-Ra is sun, scarab and basket. Thutmose III's Men-kheper-Ra is sun, game board and scarab, stamped on scarab amulets for centuries after his death. Amenhotep III's Neb-maat-Ra is sun, Maat and basket. Hatshepsut's Maat-ka-Ra is sun, Maat and the raised arms of the ka. Khufu is placenta, quail chick, viper, quail chick: Kh-w-f-w.

The Ptolemies spelled Greek names letter by letter, which is how Champollion cracked the code: Ptolemy and Cleopatra share a stool (p), a lion (l) and a looped cord (o).
details: Sedge and bee before a cartouche: 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt', the throne name. Duck and sun: 'Son of Ra', the birth name.
Ramesses II: sun disc, three tied fox skins, folded cloths. Count them at Abu Simbel, Luxor and Karnak.
Tutankhamun: Amun's name on top, then loaf, chick, loaf, then the ankh. Check his coffins and throne at the GEM.
Hatshepsut's Maat-ka-Ra was often chiselled out after her death: look for battered or recut cartouches at her temple.
fun_fact: 'Cartouche' is French soldiers' slang: Napoleon's troops thought the ovals looked like the paper cartridges for their muskets.
narration: Every royal name in Egypt sits inside an oval loop of rope called a cartouche, and reading them is the best game you can play on this trip. The rope is a stretched shen ring, the sign of eternity, wrapped around the name to protect it. The word cartouche comes from Napoleon's soldiers, who thought it looked like a musket cartridge. Kings usually show two cartouches. The first, after a sedge plant and a bee, is the throne name. The second, after a duck and a sun disc meaning Son of Ra, is the birth name. Here is your cheat sheet. Ramesses: a sun disc, then a sign like three fox skins tied together, then folded cloths. His throne name, User maat Ra, has the sun, the goddess Maat with her feather and a jackal headed staff. The Greek historian Diodorus turned it into Osymandyas, Shelley's Ozymandias. Tutankhamun: the name of Amun on top, out of respect, then a loaf, a quail chick, a loaf, and finally the ankh. Thutmose the Third: a sun, a game board and a scarab. Hatshepsut: a sun, the goddess Maat and two raised arms. Gods' names go at the top even when you read them last. The Greek kings spelled their names sound by sound, so Ptolemy and Cleopatra share a stool for p, a lion for l and a loop for o. At Abu Simbel, hunt for the fox skins of Ramesses.

name: Ankh, djed, was, shen, sema-tawy: the symbols on every wall
note: Ankh life (the gods hold it to the king's nose), djed stability (Osiris' backbone), was dominion (the forked sceptre with the Seth-animal head), the triad ankh-djed-was on Ptah's sceptre; shen eternity; sema-tawy the lotus and papyrus knotted around the lungs-and-windpipe sign on thrones (the Two Lands united by Hapi or by Horus and Seth); the tyet knot of Isis; the sa protection sign; the heb festival basin; the neb basket under names (lord); the smiting pose and the bound Nine Bows under the king's feet.
summary: A handful of signs repeat on every wall: life, stability, power, eternity, union. Learn them and the decoration starts to read like a sentence.
look: These signs appear in gods' hands, on thrones, in friezes along the tops and bottoms of walls, and as amulets in every museum case. The ankh is the looped cross; the djed a pillar with four crossbars; the was a long staff with a forked foot and an animal head; the shen a circle of rope sitting on a line.
story:
The ankh means life. The same consonants spelled 'mirror' and 'bouquet', so mirrors were made in its shape. Nobody agrees what object it began as: a sandal strap, a knot, even a bull's vertebra. Gods hold it to the king's nose to give him the breath of life, and chains of ankhs can stand for the water poured over him. Egypt's Christians adopted a looped cross, the crux ansata, and it survives in Coptic art.

The djed pillar means stability and was understood as Osiris's backbone; at festivals the king and priests hauled a djed upright with ropes. The was sceptre, a staff with a forked foot and the head of the Seth animal, means power; Thebes' own name, Waset, is written with it. Ptah's staff combines all three, and friezes repeat them above a basket sign: 'all life, power and stability'.

The shen, a loop of rope tied at the base, is eternity and the origin of the cartouche; falcons and vultures clutch it in their claws. The tyet, the 'Isis knot', means protection. Sema-tawy, 'uniting the Two Lands', is a windpipe-and-lungs sign around which the plant of the south and the papyrus of the north are knotted, by Nile gods or by Horus and Seth, on the sides of royal thrones. Under the king's feet you often find the Nine Bows, Egypt's traditional enemies, or bound prisoners, so he tramples them forever. On temple gateways he smites a bunch of foreigners held by the hair: a pose already on the Narmer Palette, about 5,000 years old.
details: Ankh held to the king's nose: a god giving him the breath of life. Common in Luxor and Abu Simbel reliefs.
Abu Simbel colossi (17th): on the throne sides, two Nile gods knot papyrus and lily around the sema-tawy sign.
Edfu (20th) and Philae (18th) pylons: the king grabs enemies by the hair and raises his mace, the smiting pose.
A flat basket under signs means 'all' or 'lord'; a falcon or vulture with spread wings usually grips a shen ring.
Statue bases and footstools: bows and bound captives under the king's feet, his enemies trampled forever.
fun_fact: When Christians tore down Alexandria's Serapeum in 391, they found ankh-like signs on its stones; pagans said they meant 'life to come', and the Christians claimed them as crosses.
narration: A few signs appear on almost every wall in Egypt, and once you know them, the decoration starts to read like a sentence. The ankh, the cross with a loop on top, means life. Watch the gods hold it to the king's nose: they are giving him the breath of life. The djed, a pillar with four crossbars, means stability, and was thought of as the backbone of Osiris. The was sceptre, a tall staff with a forked foot and an animal's head, means power. Ptah holds all three in one staff, and temple friezes repeat them in rows: all life, power and stability. The shen, a circle of rope tied at the bottom, means eternity. Stretch it long and you get the cartouche around a king's name. The tyet, like an ankh with drooping arms, is the knot of Isis, for protection. On the sides of royal thrones, look for two figures tying a papyrus and a lily around a windpipe and lungs. That is sema tawy, the union of the Two Lands, south and north. On temple gateways the king grabs a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his mace. That pose goes back 5,000 years, to the Narmer Palette. Under his feet there are often bows or bound prisoners, so he tramples his enemies forever. At Abu Simbel on the 17th, look at the side of a colossus's throne: two Nile gods are tying the knot of union.

name: The Eye of Horus and the scarab
note: Wedjat 'the whole one': the eye Seth tore out and Thoth restored, healing and protection, the fractions legend (1/2 to 1/64 summing to 63/64), painted on coffins and boats, the Rx symbol myth; the scarab Khepri 'he who comes into being', the beetle rolling the sun, self-created from dung, millions of amulets with kings' names used like coins or seals (Menkheperre most common), heart scarabs with spell 30B asking the heart not to testify against its owner; winged scarabs on pectorals; the Karnak scarab ritual.
period: Wedjat amulets from the late Old Kingdom, scarabs common from c. 2000 BC, both into Roman times
summary: The eye Seth tore out and Thoth healed, and the dung beetle that rolls the sun: Egypt's two favourite lucky charms, made by the million.
look: The wedjat is a stylised eye with an eyebrow, a line dropping below it and a curl, like the markings on a falcon's cheek. The scarab is a beetle carved in stone or moulded in blue-green faience, its flat underside carrying a name or motto. Museum cases hold hundreds of both, and on Tutankhamun's pectorals at the GEM the scarab often has wings and pushes up a sun.
story:
In the myth Seth tore out Horus's eye, or smashed it to pieces; Thoth, or in another version Hathor with gazelle's milk, restored it. From the New Kingdom it was called the wedjat, 'the whole one'. Horus offered his healed eye to his dead father Osiris, so the eye came to stand for every offering, and its return to wholeness for the waxing moon. It was among the most popular amulets for over 2,000 years; embalmers often laid one over the incision through which the organs were removed. Painted on coffins it let the dead look out, and on boats' bows it let the ship see. A long-popular theory reads the parts of the eye as fractions from 1/2 to 1/64, but it is now challenged, and the claim that the pharmacist's Rx comes from the eye is a modern myth.

The scarab, Egyptian kheper, means 'to come into being'. Egyptians watched the dung beetle roll its ball and saw Khepri rolling the sun into the sky each morning. Scarab amulets became hugely popular around 2000 BC; their flat bases carried names, mottos and designs and worked as seals, and Men-kheper-Ra, Thutmose III's throne name, is the commonest royal name on them. Amenhotep III issued large scarabs like press releases, announcing his marriage to Tiye and his lion hunts. Heart scarabs, large dark stones placed on the mummy, carried Book of the Dead spell 30B, begging the heart not to testify against its owner at the judgement.
details: Middle Kingdom coffins have a pair of eyes painted near the head, so the dead could look out towards the sunrise.
Winged scarabs pushing a sun disc on Tutankhamun's pectorals at the GEM: Khepri bringing the dawn.
Karnak (22nd): Amenhotep III's giant granite scarab stands by the Sacred Lake; visitors walk round it for luck.
Heart scarabs: large, dark green or black stone beetles, the flat base covered in lines of text.
fun_fact: Glass eye beads strung with wedjat amulets from the 13th century BC may be distant ancestors of the blue evil-eye bead, the Greek mati.
narration: These are Egypt's two favourite lucky charms, made by the million. The Eye of Horus is a painted eye with an eyebrow, a line dropping down below it and a curl, like the markings on a falcon's cheek. In the myth, Seth tore out Horus's eye and broke it, and Thoth, the god of wisdom, healed it. Its name, wedjat, means the whole one, the eye made sound again. Horus gave it to his dead father Osiris to bring him back to life, so the eye became a symbol of every offering, and of healing and protection. Embalmers placed one over the cut where they had removed the organs, and Egyptians painted eyes on coffins and on the prows of boats, so they could see where they were going. The scarab is a dung beetle. Egyptians watched it roll a ball of dung and saw the god Khepri rolling the sun up into the sky each morning. His name means coming into being. Scarab amulets were carved with names and used as seals. Amenhotep the Third even sent out large scarabs like press releases, announcing his marriage and his lion hunts. A big stone heart scarab, laid on the mummy, carried a spell begging the heart not to tell tales at the final judgement. At Karnak on the 22nd, find the giant stone scarab by the Sacred Lake. Everyone walks around it for luck.

name: Crowns and regalia: how to tell which Egypt a king rules
note: White hedjet of Upper Egypt (south), red deshret of Lower (north, the Delta), the double pschent; the nemes striped headcloth (Tut's mask, the Sphinx), the khat bag, the blue khepresh 'war crown' (Ramesses in battle), the atef with feathers (Osiris), Amun's twin plumes, Hathor's horns-and-disc worn by queens, the vulture cap of queens; the uraeus cobra (Wadjet) and the vulture (Nekhbet) as the Two Ladies; the false beard (straight for the living king, curled for gods and the dead), crook and flail, the bull's tail, the Sed-festival cloak; Nubian kings' double uraeus.
summary: White for the south, red for the north, both together for all Egypt: a king's crown tells you what he claims and what he is doing.
look: Check the king's head first. A tall white bowling-pin crown is the south; a flat red crown with a tall back spike and a curly wire is the north; one inside the other is the double crown. The striped headcloth is the nemes, the blue helmet dotted with small discs is the khepresh, and the cobra at the brow is the uraeus. You will see them all on Tutankhamun's treasures at the GEM and on every Luxor wall.
story:
The white crown, hedjet, belonged to Upper Egypt, the south; the red crown, deshret, to Lower Egypt, the Delta. Combined they made the double crown, which the Greeks called pschent, from the Egyptian for 'the two powerful ones'. No red or white crown has ever been found, so we know them only from images.

The nemes, a striped linen headcloth gathered into a tail at the back, is the one on Tutankhamun's mask and the Sphinx. The blue crown, khepresh, studded with small discs, is typical of the New Kingdom and often worn in battle scenes. Gods have their own headgear: Osiris's atef, a white crown with feathers; Amun's two tall plumes. Queens wear the vulture cap, wings folded around the head.

At the king's brow rears the uraeus, the cobra goddess Wadjet of the north, said to spit fire at his enemies; on Tutankhamun's mask she rises beside the vulture Nekhbet of the south, together the 'Two Ladies'. Add a false beard, straight and squared for the living king, long, braided and curled at the tip for gods and the dead, the crook and flail, and a bull's tail hanging from the kilt. The Kushite kings of Dynasty 25 wore a close cap with two cobras.
details: Tutankhamun's gold mask (GEM, 11th): nemes headcloth, vulture and cobra side by side at the brow, braided divine beard.
Battle and procession scenes at Abu Simbel and Karnak: look for the blue khepresh with its small gold discs.
Statues' jaws: thin raised lines running up to the ears are the straps that held the false beard on.
Queens and goddesses: vulture cap, often topped with Hathor's horns and disc or two tall plumes, as Nefertari wears at Abu Simbel.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun's mummy wore a beaded linen skullcap decorated with four cobras bearing the name of the Aten, a souvenir of his Amarna childhood.
narration: Before you look at a king's face, look at his hat. It tells you what he claims. The tall white crown, shaped like a bowling pin, is Upper Egypt, the south. The flat red crown with a tall spike at the back and a curly wire in front is Lower Egypt, the north. Put one inside the other and you have the double crown: all of Egypt. No real one has ever been found, so we only know them from pictures. The striped linen headcloth is the nemes, the one on Tutankhamun's gold mask and on the Sphinx. The blue helmet dotted with little discs is the khepresh, often worn in battle scenes. At the brow rises the uraeus, a cobra goddess who spits fire at the king's enemies. On Tutankhamun's mask she has a vulture beside her, the protector of the south. Then the false beard: straight for a living king, curled at the tip for gods and the dead. It was tied on with straps, and even Hatshepsut wore one. On the gold mask at the GEM, find the cobra and the vulture side by side on the forehead.

name: How an Egyptian temple works: the house of the god
note: Not a congregation space but the god's house and a model of creation: enclosure wall as the waters, pylon as the horizon (akhet) with flags, open court, hypostyle as the papyrus marsh with the floor rising and ceiling dropping to the dark sanctuary on the primeval mound where the statue lived in its naos; the daily ritual (awakening, washing, dressing, feeding the statue: the priest as the king's stand-in), the barque processions as the god's outings, the oracle, the sacred lake, the mammisi, the storerooms and the temple as economic machine (Karnak owned 80,000 workers); the mortuary 'temples of millions of years' on the West Bank combining king and Amun; cult vs mortuary; how reliefs were made (sunk vs raised) and painted; the colours' meaning.
period: Old Kingdom to Roman; most standing temples are New Kingdom or Ptolemaic
summary: An Egyptian temple was not a church for worshippers but a house for a god, built as a model of the first morning of creation.
look: You will walk this plan again and again: Philae in Aswan, Kom Ombo and Edfu on the 20th, Karnak and Luxor on the 22nd. Find the main axis and follow it from the pylon gateway, through the open court and the column hall, to the small dark sanctuary at the back. Notice the floor rising and the roof dropping as you go in. Somewhere in the enclosure there is usually a sacred lake, and often a stone stand for the god's boat.
story:
The Egyptians called a temple hwt-netjer, the mansion of the god, and they meant it literally. The god lived in the sanctuary as a statue inside a stone or wooden shrine, the naos. Ordinary people stayed outside: they prayed at the gates, left offerings in outer chapels and met the god only when he came out in procession. The point of the whole operation was maat, the order of the universe. Keep the god fed and content and the sun rises, the Nile floods and chaos stays out. In theory the king was the only priest, which is why he performs every ritual on the walls; in practice priests stood in for him.

The building is a model of creation. The pylon is the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them, with grooves for tall flagpoles. The open court leads into the hypostyle hall, a papyrus marsh in stone. Then the floor climbs and the roof drops toward the sanctuary, the mound that first rose from the waters of chaos. Each dawn a priest broke the clay seal on the shrine, woke the god, washed, anointed, dressed and fed the statue, then sealed it again. The food then went to the priests.

Temples were also economic giants, with farms, herds, workshops and ships, employing tens of thousands. On the West Bank, 'mansions of millions of years' served the dead king and Amun together; many Egyptologists now doubt there was a sharp line between cult temples and mortuary temples. The last temples closed between the 4th and 6th centuries AD.
details: Pylon front: look for the tall vertical grooves where cedar flagpoles stood, and the king smiting enemies on each tower.
Karnak's Hypostyle: open papyrus-flower capitals on the tall central aisle, closed-bud capitals on the lower side aisles.
Raised relief inside, sunk relief outside, where hard sunlight throws the carving into shadow. Compare an outer and an inner wall.
Look up under roofs and architraves for surviving paint: blues, greens and reds last where sun and rain never reached.
A full temple kit: enclosure wall, sacred lake (Karnak), birth house or mammisi (Edfu, Philae), storerooms and priests' houses.
fun_fact: Herodotus says Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies every other day and wore only linen and papyrus sandals; wool was not allowed into temples.
narration: You are standing in a house, not a church. The Egyptians called a temple the mansion of the god, and the god really lived here, as a statue in a stone shrine in the darkest room at the back. Ordinary people stayed outside the gates. Inside, priests acted for the king, who in theory performed every ritual himself. That is why, on almost every wall, you see the pharaoh offering bread, wine or a tiny figure of the goddess Maat to a god. The whole building is a model of the first morning of the world. The great gateway, the pylon, stands for the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them. The forest of columns is a papyrus marsh turned to stone. Walk on and the floor rises while the roof drops, until you reach the sanctuary, the mound that first rose out of the waters of chaos. Every dawn a priest broke the clay seal on the shrine doors, woke the god, washed him, dressed him in fresh linen and served him breakfast. Once the god had eaten in spirit, the priests ate the food. Temples were also landlords, with fields, herds, ships and thousands of workers. Now look along the main axis toward the back: that narrowing line of doorways is the path the god's boat took on festival days.

name: How a royal tomb works: the books on the walls
note: The tomb as the sun's night journey: the entrance corridors with the Litany of Ra (the sun's 75 forms) and the Amduat 'what is in the underworld' (12 hours, the 4th-5th hours in Sokar's desert, the 7th the killing of Apophis, the 12th rebirth), the well shaft, the Book of Gates (12 gates with guardian snakes, the judgement hall, the four races of mankind), the Book of Caverns (punishment of the damned, upside-down), the Book of the Earth (Aker), the astronomical and Nut ceilings (Book of the Day and Night) in the burial chamber, the Opening of the Mouth sequence; the king merges with Ra and Osiris; how to read any tomb in two minutes; where each book is in KV9, KV17, KV34.
period: New Kingdom, c. 1500-1070 BC
summary: A royal tomb is a guidebook to the underworld, painted so the dead king could ride with the sun through twelve hours of night and rise again.
look: You meet these books in the Valley of the Kings on the 21st. The corridors slope down into the mountain like the sun sinking in the west, and the burial chamber is the deepest room. Look for long horizontal bands of figures separated by columns of text, a ram-headed god in a boat, and huge snakes. A dark blue ceiling with yellow stars, or a long arched goddess, means you have reached the sky books.
story:
Royal funerary texts grew over 1,500 years. The Pyramid Texts, carved inside Unas' pyramid around 2400 BC, helped the king climb to the sky. The Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom spread spells to wealthy officials. In the New Kingdom, kings had their own 'books of the netherworld', and the tomb itself became a model of the sun's night journey.

The oldest is the Amduat, 'what is in the underworld'. Fragments appear in tombs of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut, but the first complete copy is in KV34, Thutmose III's tomb. It splits the night into 12 hours, in three bands, with the sun god sailing his boat along the middle band. He has a ram's head: the ram was written with the same sign as ba, the soul. In the 5th hour the boat crosses the sandy realm of Sokar; in the 7th the serpent Apophis is fettered and cut; in the 12th the sun is reborn as the scarab Khepri.

Later books add variety. The Litany of Ra, near tomb entrances, lists 75 forms of the sun. The Book of Gates has 12 gates guarded by serpents, the hall of Osiris' judgement and the four peoples of humankind. The Book of Caverns punishes the sun's enemies. After Amarna, the Books of the Sky put Nut on the ceiling, swallowing the sun at dusk and giving birth to it at dawn; from Ramesses IV two were often painted side by side.

The aim of it all: the king unites with Ra, who travels, and with Osiris, who rests, and rises with the sun every morning.
details: KV34, Thutmose III: the Amduat painted like an unrolled papyrus, with stick-like figures on a beige background.
KV9, Ramesses V and VI: two long Nut figures stretch back to back across the burial chamber ceiling.
KV17, Seti I: the first tomb decorated in every corridor and chamber, with the Litany of Ra near the entrance.
Find the sun god as a ram-headed man standing in a shrine on his boat, often wrapped in the coils of the Mehen serpent.
Upside-down or headless figures in a lower band are the sun's enemies, punished in the Book of Caverns.
fun_fact: The burial chamber of KV34 has rounded corners, shaped like a giant cartouche, so Thutmose III was laid to rest inside his own name.
narration: Think of every royal tomb in the Valley as a map of one night. The Egyptians watched the sun die in the west each evening and come back in the east each morning, and they wanted their king to make the same trip. So the corridors slope down into the mountain like a sunset, and the walls carry guidebooks to the underworld. The oldest is the Amduat, which means what is in the underworld. It splits the night into 12 hours. The sun god sails through them in a boat, with the head of a ram, because the sign for ram also wrote the word for soul. Around the 7th hour the giant serpent Apophis tries to stop the boat and is tied up and cut. In the last hour the sun is reborn as a scarab beetle and rolls out into the dawn. Later kings added more books. The Book of Gates has 12 doors, each guarded by a serpent. The Book of Caverns shows the sun's enemies punished, some of them upside down. On the ceilings you will often find the sky goddess Nut, swallowing the sun at dusk and giving birth to it at dawn. The king joins both great gods: he rides with Ra, and he rests as Osiris. Here is the 2-minute trick for any tomb. Near the door, the king greets the falcon-headed sun. Down the corridors, the night journey. In the deepest room, rebirth. Now find the sun's boat on the wall and see which way it is sailing.

name: The Book of the Dead and the weighing of the heart
note: 'Spells for Going Forth by Day', c. 190 spells on papyrus for private people from the New Kingdom (not a single book), descendant of Pyramid and Coffin Texts; spell 125 the judgement: the Hall of Two Truths, the negative confession before 42 assessors ('I have not stolen, I have not caused tears'), Anubis weighing the heart against Ma'at's feather, Thoth recording, Ammut 'the devourer' (crocodile-lion-hippo) waiting, Horus presenting the justified to Osiris; the Field of Reeds; where to see it painted: Deir el-Medina (TT1, Hathor temple), Nefertari, private coffins in the museums; the Papyrus of Ani (British Museum).
period: New Kingdom to Ptolemaic, c. 1550-50 BC
summary: Not a bible but a pick-and-mix of about 190 spells, bought by anyone who could afford one, to get the dead through the gods' final exam.
look: You will see its pictures on papyri and coffins at the GEM, and painted on tomb walls at Deir el-Medina and in Nefertari's tomb on the 21st. The famous scene is the weighing: a big balance, a heart on one pan, a feather on the other, a jackal-headed god at the scales and a crocodile-headed monster sitting by. Read it like a comic strip: the dead person led in, judged, then presented to Osiris on his throne.
story:
The Egyptian title was 'Spells for Going Forth by Day'; the name Book of the Dead comes from the German Todtenbuch, coined by Karl Richard Lepsius in 1842. It was never a fixed book. About 192 spells are known, but no papyrus contains them all: buyers chose a selection, and cheaper scrolls came ready-made with a gap for the owner's name. The tradition grew out of the royal Pyramid Texts and the Middle Kingdom Coffin Texts, appeared at Thebes around 1700 BC and was used until about 50 BC. Only in the 26th Dynasty did priests put the spells in a standard order.

Spell 125 is the judgement, first known from the time of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. In the Hall of Two Truths the dead address 42 judges, each by name, and deny a list of wrongs: theft, murder, cheating with the scales, making others weep. Then Anubis weighs the heart, seat of memory and conscience, against the feather of Maat. Thoth records the verdict. Ammit, 'devourer of the dead', waits to swallow a heart heavy with wrongdoing: a second death with no return. The justified are led by Horus to Osiris.

Other spells keep the person together. Spell 25 helps you remember your own name, spells 26 to 30 protect the heart and were carved on heart scarabs, and spell 6 wakes the shabtis. The goal was the Field of Reeds, an idealised Egypt of endless harvests. The finest surviving copy, the Papyrus of Ani, was bought at Luxor by Wallis Budge in 1888 and is in the British Museum.
details: The weighing: Anubis checks the balance, Thoth stands by with his scribe's palette, Ammit waits, and the dead person watches.
Along the top of many judgement scenes runs a row of small seated figures: the 42 judges of the Hall of Two Truths.
A human-headed bird near the dead person is the ba, the part of the soul that could fly out of the tomb by day.
Sennedjem's tomb, TT1 at Deir el-Medina (21st): the Field of Reeds, with the couple ploughing and reaping beside canals.
In museum cases, heart scarabs are large, flat-bottomed and often of dark stone, with the heart spell carved underneath.
fun_fact: The heart-scarab spell came with a pedigree: its label claims Prince Hordjedef, a son of Khufu, found it in Menkaure's reign, centuries before any surviving copy.
narration: That big balance you keep seeing is the most famous scene in Egyptian religion: the weighing of the heart. It comes from the Book of the Dead, which was never really one book. The Egyptians called it the Spells for Going Forth by Day, and about 190 spells are known. Families bought a scroll with a selection, sometimes ready-made, with a gap left for the name. Spell 125 is the final exam. The dead person walks into the Hall of Two Truths and faces 42 judges, denying a list of sins: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not made anyone weep. Then comes the test. Anubis, the jackal god, puts the heart on one pan of the scales and the feather of Maat, truth, on the other. The heart held memory and conscience, so it could tell tales. That is why a heart scarab on the mummy's chest carried a spell begging the heart not to testify against its owner. Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, writes down the verdict. Beside the scales crouches Ammit, the devourer, with the head of a crocodile, the front of a lion and the rear of a hippo. If the heart is heavy, she eats it, and that is the second, final death. If it balances, Horus leads the dead to Osiris, and on to the Field of Reeds, a perfect Egypt with endless harvests. In the next judgement scene you find, look at the scales: a pointer standing exactly upright means justified.

name: Mummification: why and how
note: The person as body + ka (life force needing food, the statue as backup body) + ba (bird-soul that travels by day) + akh (transfigured spirit) + name + shadow + heart: the body must survive for them to reunite; natural desert mummies, then natron desiccation (40 days) and 70 total, organs to canopic jars under the four sons of Horus (Imsety liver, Hapy lungs, Duamutef stomach, Qebehsenuef intestines), brain discarded, heart kept, amulets, Opening of the Mouth; Herodotus' account; animal mummies; mummies as medicine and paint (mummy brown) in Europe; unwrapping parties; respect at NMEC.
period: c. 3600 BC to the Roman period
summary: The body was the soul's home address: embalmers spent 70 days drying, filling and wrapping it so the spirit could find its way back.
look: You meet mummies three ways on this trip: Tutankhamun himself, still in his tomb, on the 21st; the small Mummification Museum on the Luxor corniche on the 22nd; and the royal mummies at NMEC in Cairo if you get there. Look for the embalming cut on the left side of the belly, the linen wrappings and amulets, and the jars and tools that came out of and went into the body.
story:
For an Egyptian, a person was made of several parts: the body, the name, the shadow, the heart, the ka or life force, and the ba, a human-headed bird that left the tomb by day. Kept together and fed, they let the dead become an akh, a transfigured spirit. The ba needed a recognisable body to return to; the ka could also live in a statue, a spare body in stone.

The earliest Egyptians were preserved by accident, dried in hot sand, but by about 3600 BC some were already wrapped in linen with resin and plant oils. True evisceration began around the 4th Dynasty, and the classic method peaked in the New Kingdom. The brain was broken up with a rod pushed through the nose and drained; Herodotus thought an iron hook pulled it out. A cut in the left flank removed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, which were dried and placed in four canopic jars. The heart, seat of thought, stayed inside. The body was covered in natron, a natural salt, for about 40 days, then oiled, resined and wrapped in linen with amulets; the whole job took 70 days. Priests then performed the Opening of the Mouth so the mummy could breathe, eat and speak.

Herodotus also lists cheaper options, such as cedar oil injected to dissolve the organs. Over a million animal mummies have been found, many of them cats and ibises. Europeans later ground mummies into medicine and paint pigment, and Victorians unwrapped them for entertainment. In 1903 Thutmose IV became the first mummy to be X-rayed.
details: Embalming cut: on the left side of the abdomen, sometimes covered by a small plate decorated with the Eye of Horus.
Crossed arms on the chest mark many New Kingdom kings; most other mummies lie with arms straight at the sides.
Mummification Museum, Luxor (22nd): natron, resins, embalming tools and animal mummies, from a cat to a crocodile.
Tutankhamun's own mummy still lies in his tomb, KV62, in a glass case: you can see his face on the 21st.
In later mummies, linen, sawdust or mud was packed under the skin to restore a lifelike shape.
fun_fact: For centuries Europeans swallowed powdered mummy as medicine; in 1599 the English writer Richard Hakluyt grumbled that apothecaries made people take it against their will.
narration: Why go to all this trouble? Because for an Egyptian, death split a person into pieces. There was the body, the name and the shadow. There was the ka, the life force, which stayed in the tomb and needed feeding. And there was the ba, a bird with a human head, which flew out by day and had to find its body again at night. If the body rotted, the ba was homeless. So the embalmers worked for 70 days. First they broke up the brain with a rod pushed through the nose and let it drain out. Herodotus thought they pulled it out with an iron hook, but experiments show liquefying works far better. They threw the brain away. Then they cut the left side of the belly and removed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, each dried and stored in its own jar. The heart stayed in, because it held your mind and would be weighed at the judgement. The body was packed and covered with natron, a natural salt from desert lakes, for about 40 days, until it was dry as leather. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with protective amulets tucked between the wrappings. The Egyptians mummified animals too, more than a million of them, many cats and ibises. Europeans later ground mummies into medicine. Next time you see a mummy, look at the left side of the belly for the embalmer's cut, often hidden under a small plate.

name: Canopic jars, shabtis, false doors and other things in tombs
note: Visual glossary for museum cases: canopic jars (lids human, then four sons of Horus), shabtis/ushabtis 'answerers' with hoes and baskets (spell 6), false doors where the ka came to eat (the offering formula hetep-di-nesu: 'an offering which the king gives... a thousand of bread and beer'), offering tables with channels, serdab statue rooms, stelae, headrests, model boats and granaries (Middle Kingdom), soul houses, magic bricks in the four walls, the pesesh-kef knife; how to read an offering formula.
period: Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic
summary: A field guide to tomb equipment: the jars for the organs, the little workers who answered for you, and the door only spirits could use.
look: These fill museum cases at the GEM and turn up in every tomb you visit. Four lidded jars in a set are canopic jars; rows of small mummy-shaped figures holding hoes are shabtis; a flat stone slab carved like a recessed doorway, usually on a west wall, is a false door. Read the text on any of them for the name of the owner.
story:
Canopic jars held the organs removed during mummification. The name is a mistake by early scholars, who linked them to Canopus, helmsman of Menelaus, worshipped in the Delta in the form of a jar. Old Kingdom jars had plain lids; human heads became common later; by the 19th Dynasty the four lids were the sons of Horus. In later periods the organs were wrapped and put back in the body, and dummy jars were buried for form's sake.

Shabtis, later called ushabtis, were servant figures. Their spell, Coffin Text 472 and later Book of the Dead spell 6, promises that if the owner is called to plough, fill the canals or carry sand in the next world, the figure will step up and say 'here I am'. From the 21st Dynasty tombs could hold hundreds, with an overseer holding a whip for every gang of ten; the Kushite king Taharqa had more than a thousand.

The false door, standard in Old Kingdom tombs and usually on the west wall, was the threshold where the ka came out to eat. Before it lay an offering slab, and around it ran the offering formula, hetep-di-nesu, 'an offering which the king gives', asking for a thousand of bread, beer, oxen and fowl for the owner's ka.
details: Canopic lids: human Imsety (liver), baboon Hapy (lungs), jackal Duamutef (stomach), falcon Qebehsenuef (intestines).
Tutankhamun's canopic stoppers show his own face, not animal heads: compare them with later sets.
Shabtis: read down the legs; the spell begins with the owner's name, styled 'the Osiris' plus the name.
Overseer shabtis wear a kilt and hold a whip; there was roughly one for every ten workers.
Offering formula on stelae: look for a sedge plant, a loaf on a mat and a pointed loaf, read hetep-di-nesu.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun took 413 shabtis with him; one popular theory says that is a worker for each day of the year plus overseers to keep them at it.
narration: Here is a quick field guide to the things you will see in every tomb case. First, canopic jars, always in sets of 4. They held the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines. The name is a Greek mix-up: early scholars linked them to Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus, said to be worshipped in the Delta in the form of a jar. From the late New Kingdom the lids show the 4 sons of Horus: a man for the liver, a baboon for the lungs, a jackal for the stomach and a falcon for the intestines. Next, the shabtis, little mummy-shaped figures with hoes. Their spell says that if the dead are called up for farm work in the next world, the shabti will answer: here I am, I will do it. Some people had hundreds, with overseer figures holding whips. Last, the false door: a carved doorway that does not open, usually on the west wall. The spirit stepped through it to eat the food left on the slab in front. Look for the first signs of the offering prayer: a sedge plant, a loaf on a mat and a pointed loaf, meaning an offering which the king gives.

name: Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure: the three Giza kings
note: Sneferu the father who built three pyramids and perfected the shape; Khufu (c. 2589-2566) whom Herodotus painted as a tyrant who prostituted his daughter (propaganda from 2,000 years later), his tiny statue; Djedefre the son who went to Abu Rawash and first used 'son of Ra'; Khafre of the second pyramid and (probably) the Sphinx; Menkaure the 'kindly' one with the smallest pyramid and the finest statues; Shepseskaf who ended pyramids with a mastaba; the Westcar Papyrus magicians' tales told at Khufu's court.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, 26th century BC
summary: Grandfather, son and grandson built the three Giza pyramids within about a century, yet we barely know them as people.
look: You meet them at the GEM on the 11th and on the Giza plateau on the 12th. The biggest pyramid is Khufu's; the one with a cap of smooth casing near its tip is Khafre's, and it looks tallest only because it stands on higher ground; the smallest is Menkaure's. In the museums, look for Khafre enthroned with a falcon behind his head, Menkaure's triads with Hathor, and Khufu's tiny ivory statuette.
story:
Sneferu, almost certainly Khufu's father, built three pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur and turned the stepped shape into a true pyramid by trial and error. Khufu, short for Khnum-khufu, 'Khnum protects me', reigned in the 26th century BC for at least 27 years. Papyri found in 2013 at the Red Sea harbour of Wadi al-Jarf include the logbook of an inspector called Merer, who shipped limestone from Tura to Giza late in Khufu's reign. The king's only complete statue is an ivory figurine found by Flinders Petrie at Abydos in 1903; its head turned up after three weeks of sieving.

Khufu's son Djedefre reigned briefly and built at Abu Rawash. Another son, Khafre, built the second Giza pyramid, 'Khafre is great', and most Egyptologists credit him with the Sphinx. More statues survive of Khafre than of any other Old Kingdom king; Auguste Mariette found several in a pit in his valley temple in 1860. His son Menkaure built the smallest of the three, about 103 metres a side and 65 high, but left the finest sculpture: greywacke triads of the king with Hathor and province gods, and a pair statue with his queen. After him, Shepseskaf chose a mastaba tomb, and Giza's great age was over.

Herodotus, writing some 2,000 years later, portrayed Khufu and Khafre as tyrants who closed the temples and Menkaure as pious. That reflects later legend, not the evidence: Khufu's memory was honoured for centuries, and later storytellers set the magicians' tales of the Westcar Papyrus at his court.
details: Khafre's pyramid keeps a cap of its smooth white casing near the top: once, all three pyramids looked like that.
Menkaure's pyramid: the vertical gash in the north face comes from a failed attempt to demolish it in 1196.
Khafre's diorite statue: Horus the falcon spreads his wings behind the king's head. Find it in the museum.
Menkaure triads: the king between Hathor and a province goddess, who wears her province's emblem on her head.
Khufu's dismantled cedar boats were buried beside his pyramid; the first one is rebuilt at the GEM.
fun_fact: Menkaure's stone sarcophagus survived over 4,000 years inside his pyramid, then sank with the ship carrying it to England in 1838.
narration: Three kings, three generations, one plateau. Khufu came first, in the 26th century BC. His full name was Khnum-khufu, Khnum protects me. His father, almost certainly Sneferu, had built 3 pyramids and found the true pyramid shape by trial and error. Khufu took the lesson and built the biggest of all. Strangely, the only complete statue of him is an ivory figurine smaller than your hand. Flinders Petrie found it headless in 1903, stopped all work and had his men sieve the rubble for 3 weeks until the head turned up. After Khufu came one son, Djedefre, then another, Khafre, who built the second pyramid and, most Egyptologists think, the Sphinx. More statues survive of Khafre than of any other Old Kingdom king. His son Menkaure built the smallest of the three pyramids but left the finest sculpture: the king striding beside the goddess Hathor. 2,000 years later, Herodotus heard that Khufu and Khafre were cruel tyrants and Menkaure was kind. That is later legend, not history. A far better witness has survived: the logbook of Merer, an inspector who shipped limestone blocks along the Nile to Khufu's building site. When you look at the three pyramids, remember that the middle one only looks tallest because it stands on higher rock.

name: Hatshepsut: the woman who was king
note: Daughter of Thutmose I, wife of her half-brother Thutmose II, regent for her stepson Thutmose III, then king c. 1473-1458 BC with full titulary, shown with beard and kilt; Punt, the obelisks, Deir el-Bahari, Senenmut; peaceful prosperous reign; the proscription 20 years after her death (dynastic, not personal, per most scholars); her mummy identified in 2007 by a tooth in a box (KV60), obese, diabetic, cancer from a skin salve?; now at NMEC; the trip's threads: Unfinished Obelisk, Karnak obelisks and Red Chapel, her temple.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1479-1458 BC
summary: A king's daughter and king's wife who made herself king, ruled about 20 prosperous years, and was then chiselled out of history.
look: Her thread runs through the trip: the Unfinished Obelisk in Aswan, her terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari on the 21st, her obelisk and Red Chapel at Karnak on the 22nd. Recognise her by the throne name Maatkare in a cartouche, and by statues of a bearded, kilted king whose inscriptions slip into feminine grammar. Many of her figures and names were hacked out, so a neat chiselled hollow in a relief is often her.
story:
Hatshepsut was the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and Queen Ahmose. She married her half-brother Thutmose II and had a daughter, Neferure. When he died, the heir was Thutmose III, son of a minor wife, still a small child. Hatshepsut acted as regent, and by his year 7 she was king, sharing his count of years but as the senior partner. Her official images gradually lost their femininity: the khat headcloth, uraeus, false beard and kilt. Her temple's divine birth reliefs explain that Amun visited her mother in the guise of Thutmose I and Khnum shaped the child on his wheel.

Her reign, about 1479 to 1458 BC counting the regency, was prosperous and mostly peaceful. In year 9 her ships reached Punt and returned with 31 live myrrh trees. She raised two great obelisks at Karnak, one still standing; the cracked Unfinished Obelisk at Aswan is often linked to her. She built the Red Chapel at Karnak and Djeser-Djeseru, 'holiest of holies', at Deir el-Bahari, helped by officials such as her steward Senenmut.

She vanishes from the record around year 22 of Thutmose III. Late in his reign and under Amenhotep II, her statues were smashed and her name erased. Because this began some 20 years after her death, most scholars see it as securing his son's succession rather than personal revenge. In 2007 a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers by a loose tooth, kept in a box bearing her name, that fitted its jaw. She was overweight and about 50; some experts remain cautious. She is now at NMEC.
details: Her throne name Maatkare: a sun disc, the seated goddess Maat with her feather, and the raised arms of the ka.
Deir el-Bahari (21st): the Punt reliefs on the middle terrace show incense trees carried to the ships in baskets.
Karnak (22nd): her standing obelisk is the second-tallest ancient obelisk still upright; its twin's tip lies by the lake.
Erasures: a neat hollow where a figure was cut out, sometimes recarved as an offering table or another king's name.
Aswan: the Unfinished Obelisk, cracked in the quarry and abandoned, is often linked to her reign.
fun_fact: She is said to have ground charred frankincense from Punt into kohl, so the most powerful person in Egypt wore perfumed eyeliner.
narration: Hatshepsut was the daughter of a king, the wife of a king, and then, unusually, a king herself. Her father was Thutmose the First. She married her half-brother Thutmose the Second, and when he died young, the heir was a small boy, Thutmose the Third, the son of a minor wife. Hatshepsut ruled for him as regent, and within about 7 years she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh. Her official images show a man, with a kilt, a broad chest and a false beard, because that was what a king looked like. Yet the inscriptions often slip into feminine grammar. To justify it all, her temple tells how the god Amun visited her mother disguised as her father, and how Khnum shaped the baby on his potter's wheel. Her reign of about 20 years was peaceful and rich. She sent ships to the land of Punt, which came back with 31 live myrrh trees. She raised giant obelisks at Karnak and built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari. Some 20 years after her death, her statues were smashed and her names cut out. Most scholars now think this was cold dynastic politics, not revenge. In 2007 her mummy was identified thanks to a single tooth that fitted a gap in its jaw. It is now at NMEC in Cairo. Next time you see a neat chiselled hollow where a king's figure should be, ask whether it was her.

name: Thutmose III and Amenhotep III: the conqueror and the sun king
note: Thutmose III: 17 campaigns, the pass at Megiddo chosen against his generals' advice, the Euphrates stela, the Annals at Karnak, the Akh-menu and Botanical Garden, KV34, the greywacke statue; Amenhotep III: 38 years of peace and gold, married Tiye a commoner, the 'Magnificent', Malkata palace, Luxor Temple, the Colossi, 730 Sekhmets, the scarabs announcing his lion hunts and his marriage, obesity and bad teeth in old age, the Aten already rising, father of Akhenaten; the trip's threads everywhere.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1479-1425 and c. 1388-1350 BC
summary: One king built Egypt's empire on campaign; his great-grandson spent its profits on the most lavish golden age Egypt ever knew.
look: Thutmose III's throne name Menkheperre, a sun disc, a scarab and a game board, is the most common name on scarabs, so you will see it in every museum and shop. His Festival Hall and war Annals are at Karnak on the 22nd, and his tomb, KV34, is in the Valley on the 21st. Amenhotep III left you the Colossi of Memnon, Luxor Temple's great colonnade and sun court, and lion-headed Sekhmet statues by the hundred.
story:
Thutmose III was the son of Thutmose II by a minor wife, Iset. Crowned as a child in 1479 BC, he spent about 22 years as junior partner to Hatshepsut, by the end commanding her armies. Sole ruler from about 1458, he died in his 54th year, in 1425 BC. His Annals at Karnak record at least 16 campaigns. At Megiddo he overruled his generals and took the narrow Aruna pass, but his troops stopped to plunder and the city held out seven or eight months. In his 33rd year he hauled boats overland from Byblos, crossed the Euphrates and set up a stela beside his grandfather's. Syrian plants and animals he saw are carved in the 'Botanical Garden' at Karnak. James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt; his tomb, KV34, holds the first complete Amduat.

Amenhotep III, his great-grandson, became king between 6 and 12 and ruled about 38 years. He fought one Nubian campaign and otherwise enjoyed peace and imperial income. He married Tiye, daughter of the courtiers Yuya and Thuya, and publicised the marriage, a lake dug for her and his lion hunts on large scarabs. He also took Mitannian and Babylonian princesses as diplomatic wives. He built the Malkata palace, much of Luxor Temple and the largest mortuary temple of all, now reduced to the Colossi of Memnon. He celebrated three Sed festivals, and in his 30th year called himself 'the dazzling sun disc', a hint of the Aten religion his son would impose.
details: Menkheperre, Thutmose III's throne name: sun disc, scarab and game board. It is the commonest name on scarabs.
Karnak Akh-menu (22nd): the 'Botanical Garden' room shows plants and animals from Syria, some of them fanciful.
Karnak: his Annals surround the granite sanctuary; Megiddo is the first and longest campaign told.
Colossi of Memnon (21st): Greek and Latin verses by Roman-era visitors cover the legs of the northern statue.
Luxor Museum (22nd): Thutmose III in greywacke, a young idealised face, and Amenhotep III with Sobek in calcite.
fun_fact: After an earthquake cracked the northern Colossus of Memnon, it 'sang' at dawn, and Greek visitors decided it was the Trojan hero Memnon greeting his mother Eos.
narration: These two kings bookend the high point of Egypt's empire. Thutmose the Third spent his first 20 years in the shadow of his stepmother Hatshepsut. Once he ruled alone, he never stopped marching. On his first campaign, at Megiddo, his generals begged him to take the safe roads round the mountain. He called them cowards and led the army single file through a narrow pass, horse after horse and man after man, and came out behind the enemy. Then his soldiers stopped to loot the camp, and he had to besiege the city for 7 months. Later he carried boats overland to cross the Euphrates. He fought at least 16 campaigns and had them carved on the walls of Karnak. His great-grandson Amenhotep the Third inherited the profits. He ruled for about 38 years, mostly in peace. He married Tiye, a courtier's daughter, and announced it on large stone scarabs sent around the country, like royal press releases. Other scarabs boast that he shot 102 lions in his first 10 years. He built Luxor Temple's great colonnade, a vast palace across the river, and the mortuary temple whose two giant statues we call the Colossi of Memnon. Late in life he called himself the dazzling sun disc, and his son took that idea much further. Look at any scarab in a shop or museum: a sun, a beetle and a game board spell Menkheperre, Thutmose the Third.

name: Akhenaten and Nefertiti
note: The heretic: Amenhotep IV's year 5 renaming, Akhetaten, the six daughters, the plague?, the end of Nefertiti (died? ruled as Neferneferuaten? the gilded mask made for her?), Smenkhkare, the Berlin bust found 1912 by Borchardt and the dispute, the body in KV55, the DNA 2010 (father of Tut, brother-sister parents), the erasure by Horemheb; his hymn; the art: the GEM/Tahrir colossi and the Luxor Museum talatat wall, the Aten on Tut's throne.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1353-1336 BC
summary: The king who shut the old gods' temples for one sun disc, and the queen whose painted face became the most copied image in Egyptian art.
look: You meet their faces at the GEM on the 11th and the Luxor Museum on the 22nd: long-chinned, full-lipped colossi from Karnak and the talatat wall of small sandstone blocks. Recognise their art by elongated heads, soft bellies and thin limbs, and by the Aten above them, a sun disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding the ankh sign of life. Their names and faces are often hacked out.
story:
Amenhotep IV was a younger son of Amenhotep III and Tiye who became heir when his brother Thutmose died. He took the throne around 1353 BC and at first ruled conventionally, though he soon built temples to the Aten at Karnak from small standard blocks now called talatat. Around his year 5 he renamed himself Akhenaten, 'effective for the Aten', and founded a new capital, Akhetaten, 'horizon of the Aten', at Amarna. Amun's cult was abandoned and his name hacked from monuments. The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the Amarna tomb of the courtier Ay, has often been compared with Psalm 104. Whether this was true monotheism is still argued.

Nefertiti, 'the beautiful one has come', is of unknown origin; Ay may have been her father. She and Akhenaten had six daughters. On early Karnak blocks she appears almost twice as often as the king and even smites enemies, a royal pose. Later she fades from the record. Some scholars identify her with the female king Neferneferuaten who reigned briefly after Akhenaten; others disagree. Her painted bust was found in 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt's German team in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna and is in Berlin; Egypt has asked for it back.

Akhenaten died around 1336 BC. Within a few years the court left Amarna, and later kings called him 'the enemy' or 'that criminal'. DNA studies published in 2010 identified the man buried in KV55 as Tutankhamun's father, possibly Akhenaten, though both the results and the identification are debated.
details: The Aten: a sun disc with rays ending in hands; the hands near the royal faces hold the ankh sign of life.
The Aten's names are written in two cartouches, like a king's: the god was presented as a heavenly king.
GEM colossi from Karnak: long jaw, slit eyes, swelling hips; one figure may show Nefertiti, scholars disagree.
Luxor Museum (22nd): the talatat wall, hundreds of small blocks reassembled from Akhenaten's Karnak temple.
Tutankhamun's golden throne (GEM): the Aten still shines over the young couple, a leftover of Amarna days.
fun_fact: The talatat blocks survive because later kings dumped them as rubble inside Karnak's pylons, where they waited, packed and hidden, for over 3,000 years.
narration: Few couples have changed a country so fast. Akhenaten was born Amenhotep, a younger son of Amenhotep the Third and Queen Tiye, and became king about 1353 BC. Within 5 years he had renamed himself Akhenaten, effective for the Aten, and was building a brand new capital in the desert at Amarna. The Aten was the sun disc itself, drawn with rays that end in little hands, some holding out the sign of life. Amun's temples lost their support, and his name was chiselled off walls across Egypt. Was it the first monotheism? Egyptologists still argue: perhaps it was one god for the royal family, with the king as the only way to reach him. The art changed too: long faces, heavy hips, the family kissing and playing with their daughters. Nefertiti, whose name means the beautiful one has come, was more than a consort. On early temple blocks she appears almost twice as often as her husband, even smiting enemies. She bore 6 daughters, then fades from the record. Some scholars think she ruled briefly as a female king. Her famous painted bust was dug up in 1912 by a German team in a sculptor's workshop and is now in Berlin. After Akhenaten died, his city was abandoned and his successors called him that criminal. Look at the faces: the slanting eyes and drooping chin are the Amarna style, impossible to mistake.

name: Tutankhamun: the boy king, the facts behind the gold
note: Born Tutankhaten c. 1341 BC, son of Akhenaten and a sister (the Younger Lady), king at 9, married half-sister Ankhesenamun, restoration of Amun (Restoration Stela), moved court to Memphis/Thebes, died at 18-19 (leg fracture, malaria, no murder: the 'hole in the skull' was embalmers'), two stillborn daughters in his tomb, succeeded by Ay then Horemheb who erased him: a minor king remembered only because his tomb survived; Ankhesenamun's letter to the Hittite king begging for a prince (the Dakhamunzu affair) and the murdered prince Zannanza.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1332-1323 BC
summary: A minor boy king, erased from the king lists, who became the most famous pharaoh only because his tomb was forgotten and survived nearly intact.
look: He is the man behind the GEM's Tutankhamun galleries on the 11th and the small tomb KV62 on the 21st, where his mummy still lies. His throne name, Nebkheperure, is a sun disc, a scarab, three plural strokes and a basket. His birth name puts the god Amun first in the cartouche, out of respect, and ends with the ankh.
story:
Born around 1342 BC as Tutankhaten, 'living image of the Aten', he was a king's son at Amarna. DNA tests published in 2010 point to the man in KV55 as his father and to the 'Younger Lady' of KV35 as his mother, a full sister of that man; the results and the identifications are still debated. His wet nurse Maia had her own tomb at Saqqara. He became king at 8 or 9 and married Ankhesenpaaten, a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti.

His advisers, probably including Ay and the general Horemheb, steered the reversal. The court left Amarna, the Aten lost his place, Amun returned, and the couple became Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. The Restoration Stela, found at Karnak in 1905, describes temples in ruin and the king renewing cult images and priesthoods. He died at about 19, around 1323 BC. A 2012 study suggested malaria combined with a leg fracture; the bone fragments in his skull, once proof of murder for some, were caused after death. Two stillborn daughters lay in his tomb.

Hittite records tell of an Egyptian queen, called Dakhamunzu, who begged King Suppiluliuma for a son to marry; the prince Zannanza died on the way. She is most often identified with Ankhesenamun. Ay succeeded, then Horemheb, who usurped Tutankhamun's monuments and left the Amarna kings off the lists. A minor reign, forgotten, under rubble: that is why KV62 still held over 5,000 objects when Howard Carter found it in 1922.
details: His cartouche: Amun (reed leaf, game board, water) first out of respect, then Tut (loaf, chick, loaf) and the ankh.
Throne name Nebkheperure: sun disc, scarab, three plural strokes and a basket. It is stamped on many of his objects.
KV62 (21st): the mummy lies in a glass case; the burial chamber shows Ay performing the Opening of the Mouth.
At the GEM, look for his walking sticks: well over 100 were buried with him, and scans suggest a deformed left foot.
The Restoration Stela, found at Karnak in 1905: his decree reopening the temples, with his names later recut by Horemheb.
fun_fact: His tomb's entrance lay under workmen's huts and rubble from the later tomb of Ramesses VI, one reason robbers missed most of it after the first break-ins.
narration: Tutankhamun was a small king with a gigantic afterlife. He was born about 1342 BC as Tutankhaten, living image of the Aten, in the heretic city of Amarna. DNA tests suggest his father was the man buried in K V 55, probably Akhenaten, and his mother a full sister of that man, though not every expert trusts the results. He became king at 8 or 9 and married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. His advisers, not the child, steered the great U-turn: the court left Amarna, the old gods came back, and the royal couple changed their names to Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. He died at about 19. For years people said he was murdered, because of bone fragments in his skull, but scans show the damage happened after death. A broken leg and malaria are the leading suspects now. Two tiny daughters, born too early to live, were buried with him. Then something strange happens. Hittite archives record that an Egyptian queen, very likely his widow, wrote to the Hittite king: my husband is dead, I have no son, send me one of yours. A prince set out and died on the road. Tutankhamun's successors erased his name, so later Egyptians forgot him, and so did the tomb robbers. That is why his tomb survived. Look at his cartouche: the god Amun is written first, out of respect, though you say it last.

name: Seti I and Ramesses II: the Ramesside peak
note: Seti I: restorer after Amarna, the finest relief carving (Abydos, KV17, Karnak hypostyle), the Karnak battle walls; Ramesses II (c. 1279-1213 BC): 66 years, 100 children, Kadesh in year 5 (a draw sold as victory on every wall), the peace treaty with Hatti, the Hittite brides, Pi-Ramesses in the Delta, Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, usurping older statues, the mummy with red hair flown to Paris 1976 with a passport ('occupation: King, deceased'), the Exodus pharaoh question (no evidence either way); the trip's threads: GEM colossus, Luxor pylon, Abu Simbel, Ramesseum, Karnak.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1290-1213 BC
summary: A father who paid for the finest reliefs in Egypt, and a son who put his own name on everything, including other kings' statues.
look: Ramesses II is the face of this trip: the GEM atrium colossus on the 11th, Abu Simbel on the 17th, the Ramesseum on the 21st, Luxor Temple's pylon and Karnak on the 22nd. Spot his throne name Usermaatre Setepenre: a sun disc and the goddess Maat holding a was sceptre. Seti I's work is subtler: delicate raised relief in the north half of Karnak's Hypostyle Hall and in his tomb, while his son's is often deep, bold sunk relief.
story:
Seti I, 'man of Seth', succeeded his father Ramesses I, an elderly vizier and soldier whom Horemheb had named heir. Reigning about 1290 to 1279 BC, Seti restored order after Amarna, campaigned in Canaan, Syria and Libya and briefly took Kadesh; his battle scenes cover the north outer wall of Karnak's Hypostyle Hall. His temple at Abydos and his tomb, KV17, found by Belzoni in 1817 and decorated in every passage, hold some of the finest relief carving in Egypt.

Ramesses II was not born a prince; he was about 11 when his grandfather was named heir. Made prince regent at about 14, he took the throne at about 25 in 1279 BC and ruled 66 years, dying around 90 in 1213 BC. He moved the capital to Pi-Ramesses in the Delta. In year 5, at Kadesh, the Hittite king Muwatalli caught his divided army off guard; Ramesses rallied, reinforcements arrived, and the battle ended in a stalemate that his temples call a triumph. In year 21 he made peace with the Hittites, in a treaty preserved in both Egyptian hieroglyphs and Hittite cuneiform, and later married Hittite princesses.

He celebrated 13 or 14 Sed festivals, fathered more than 100 children and built or usurped on a colossal scale, often recutting older kings' names. His mummy, from the 1881 royal cache, is at NMEC. The Greeks called him Ozymandias, from his throne name Usermaatre. There is no evidence either way that he was the pharaoh of the Exodus.
details: Usermaatre: a sun disc above the goddess Maat holding a was sceptre. Setepenre adds an adze sign, water and another sun.
Karnak Hypostyle (22nd): north half in Seti's delicate raised relief, south half in Ramesses' deeper sunk relief.
Kadesh reliefs: the giant king alone in his chariot firing arrows, and the fortress ringed by the river Orontes.
Usurped statues: freshly cut, extra-deep cartouches on older smooth surfaces, sometimes with a ghost of an earlier name.
Karnak's north outer wall: Seti's campaign scenes, with the forts and wells along the Sinai road each drawn and named.
fun_fact: Shelley's sonnet Ozymandias, with its 'vast and trunkless legs of stone', is usually linked to Ramesses' fallen colossus at the Ramesseum, which you see on the 21st.
narration: You will meet Ramesses the Second more than anyone else on this trip, so meet his father first. Seti the First, whose name means man of Seth, was the son of an army officer who had been handed the throne. He restored order after the Amarna years, fought in Canaan and Syria, and paid for some of the most refined carving in Egypt: his temple at Abydos and his tomb in the Valley, the longest of all. His son Ramesses came to the throne at about 25 and ruled for 66 years. He died around 90, having outlived many of his more than 100 children. In his 5th year, at Kadesh in Syria, he walked into a Hittite ambush. His army was split, he fought his way out, and reinforcements saved the day.
