The result was a draw, but he had it carved as a glorious victory on temple after temple. 16 years later he made peace with the Hittites, in a treaty whose text survives in both sides' versions, and later married a Hittite princess. He also loved to recarve older kings' statues with his own name. The Greeks knew him as Ozymandias, from his throne name Usermaatre. His mummy, now at NMEC, was flown to Paris in 1976 for treatment, and the story goes that he was issued a passport giving his occupation as king, deceased. Look for his cartouche: a sun disc, and the seated goddess with her feather and an animal-headed sceptre.

name: Ramesses III and the end of the Bronze Age
note: The last great pharaoh (c. 1186-1155 BC), imitator of Ramesses II; the Libyan wars and the Sea Peoples' land and sea attack in year 8 repelled at the Delta; the wider collapse of Mycenae, Hatti, Ugarit (drought, earthquakes, migrations, systems collapse: Eric Cline's 1177 BC); economic troubles, the first strike, the harem conspiracy and his cut throat; Medinet Habu as his memorial and KV11; the decline into the tomb-robbery era.
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: When the Bronze Age world collapsed around 1200 BC, Ramesses III held Egypt together, then was murdered in a plot from his own harem.
look: His memorial is Medinet Habu on the West Bank, which you see on the 21st, with the Sea Peoples battles carved on its walls; his tomb is KV11. Recognise him by his throne name Usermaatre Meryamun, a near copy of Ramesses II's, and by the feathered and horned helmets of his enemies in the reliefs.
story:
Ramesses III was the son of Setnakhte, founder of the 20th Dynasty, and only distantly related to Ramesses II, whom he copied down to his throne name. He reigned about 31 years, from around 1186 BC. He repelled Libyan invasions in years 5 and 11, and in year 8 the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, Denyen, Sherden and Tjeker, who came by land and sea. He beat them in Djahy and in the Nile mouths, where archers lined the banks. The Peleset settled in Canaan and are usually identified with the Philistines.

Around him the Late Bronze Age world was breaking up: the Hittite empire, Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces fell between the late 13th and early 12th centuries BC. Drought, earthquakes, migration and failing trade are all blamed; recent work suggests fewer cities burned than once thought.

Egypt survived, poorer. In year 29 the unpaid tomb builders of Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded strike. Then a minor wife, Tiye, plotted to put her son Pentawere on the throne. Trial papyri record 38 death sentences, and a CT scan published in 2012 showed the king's throat cut to the bone. His chosen heir, Ramesses IV, succeeded anyway.
details: Medinet Habu (21st): the sea battle on the outer north wall is often called the oldest picture of a naval battle.
Headgear: Peleset and Denyen wear feathered crowns, Sherden horned helmets; Sherden also served Egypt as guards.
Look for scribes counting the severed hands of dead enemies: the army's grim way of keeping a tally.
KV11 (21st): a side chamber painted with two harpists gave it the name Harpers' Tomb.
fun_fact: During the trial, some of the accused harem women tried to seduce their judges; they were caught, and the judges were punished too.
narration: Ramesses the Third is often called the last great pharaoh. He ruled for about 31 years, from around 1186 BC, and modelled himself on Ramesses the Second, even copying his throne name. His world was falling apart. Around 1200 BC the Hittite empire, the trading city of Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces of Greece all went down. Drought, earthquakes, migrations and broken trade all played a part. In his 8th year a coalition Egypt called the Sea Peoples attacked by land and sea. He beat them in the Nile mouths, with archers lining the banks and grappling hooks to drag the ships in. One group, the Peleset, probably became the Philistines. But the cost was high. In year 29 the royal tomb builders went unpaid and staged the first recorded strike in history. Then a minor queen, Tiye, plotted to put her son on the throne. The trial records survive, and CT scans show the king's throat was cut to the bone. Look at the reliefs for the Sea Peoples' feathered headdresses and horned helmets.

name: Piye and Taharqa: when Nubia ruled Egypt
note: Piye's pious conquest c. 727 BC ('clean yourselves before entering the palace'), his love of horses; Shabaka's Memphite Theology stone; Taharqa (690-664) the builder (Karnak kiosk, Kawa, Gebel Barkal), mentioned in the Bible (Tirhakah) fighting Sennacherib, his Nile-record flood; the Assyrians Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal drive them out, Thebes sacked 663 BC; the Nubian pyramids at Nuri; the double uraeus and the archaising revival of Old Kingdom art.
period: Late Period, 25th Dynasty, c. 744-664 BC
summary: Kings from Napata in today's Sudan conquered Egypt in the name of Amun, ruled it for nearly a century and fought the Assyrians to the end.
look: You meet them in Aswan's Nubian Museum on the 18th or 19th, and at Karnak on the 22nd, where one tall papyrus column in the Great Court is all that stands of Taharqa's kiosk. Recognise a Kushite king by the close-fitting cap crown with two cobras on the brow instead of one, and by faces carved in a deliberately old-fashioned style.
story:
Kush, the kingdom around Napata in today's Sudan, had absorbed Egyptian religion during centuries of New Kingdom rule, and its kings worshipped Amun at Gebel Barkal. Piye, who ruled from about 744 to 714 BC, already controlled Upper Egypt when Tefnakht of Sais led a coalition of Delta rulers south. In his 20th year Piye marched north, celebrated Opet at Thebes, took Hermopolis after a five-month siege, stormed Memphis and received the submission of the Delta kings. His victory stela at Gebel Barkal presents the campaign as a holy war. Then he went home to Napata.

His successors, Shabaka and Shebitku, whose order is debated, ruled Egypt directly. Taharqa, king from 690 to 664 BC, enjoyed a huge Nile flood in his 6th year and built at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal. The Bible calls him Tirhakah, sent against the Assyrian Sennacherib in 701 BC. Taharqa beat the Assyrian Esarhaddon in 674 BC, but in 671 Esarhaddon took Memphis and captured the royal family. Ashurbanipal pressed on, and after Taharqa's death his successor Tantamani's counter-attack ended with the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC. Taharqa lies under the largest pyramid at Nuri. Kushite art deliberately revived Old and Middle Kingdom styles.
details: Double uraeus: two cobras side by side on the brow, probably for the two kingdoms of Kush and Egypt.
Karnak Great Court (22nd): the lone papyrus column standing in the court is all that remains of Taharqa's kiosk.
Kushite royal portraits: round heads, broad cheeks, a close cap crown and often ram-head amulets at the neck.
Archaism: Kushite sculptors copied Old Kingdom models, so a statue can look 2,000 years older than it is.
Aswan's Nubian Museum (18th or 19th) tells their story from the Kushite side; look for the double cobras.
fun_fact: Remains of three colossal statues of Taharqa were found at the gate of the Assyrian palace at Nineveh, most likely carried off as war trophies.
narration: For nearly a century, Egypt was ruled from what is now Sudan. The kings of Kush, at Napata near the holy mountain of Gebel Barkal, worshipped Amun as devoutly as any Theban. When the princes of the Delta squabbled, King Piye marched north, in the 720s BC. He stopped at Thebes for the Opet festival, ordered his soldiers to purify themselves before battle, and took city after city. His victory stela says that at Hermopolis what angered him most was finding the horses starved. Then he sailed home and never came back. His successors stayed. Taharqa, from 690 BC, built at Karnak and across Nubia, and the Bible remembers him as Tirhakah, marching against the Assyrians. In the end the Assyrians won, took Memphis, and in 663 BC sacked Thebes itself. Taharqa was buried under the biggest pyramid at Nuri, with more than 1,000 shabtis. Look for a Kushite king's crown: a tight cap with 2 cobras on the forehead.

name: Alexander, the Ptolemies and Cleopatra
note: Alexander crowned at Memphis 332 BC, founds Alexandria, consults Siwa, buried (eventually) in Alexandria in a tomb never found; Ptolemy I Soter the general, the Library, the Serapis cult; sibling marriages; Ptolemy V's Rosetta Stone decree; the temple builders (III, IV, VI, VIII, XII); Cleopatra VII (69-30 BC), Macedonian Greek who alone learned Egyptian, Caesar and Caesarion, Antony and the Donations, Actium, the asp (or poison); Octavian's Egypt as personal property; the Greek-Egyptian fusion a Greek visitor can see at Edfu and Philae.
period: Macedonian and Ptolemaic, 332-30 BC
summary: For 300 years Greek-speaking kings from Macedon ruled Egypt as pharaohs, and the last of them, Cleopatra, was the first to learn Egyptian.
look: Their temples fill your 20th (Kom Ombo, Edfu, Esna) and Philae in Aswan; Alexander himself waits at Siwa on the 13th-15th and in Luxor Temple's barque shrine on the 22nd. Recognise a Ptolemy by a cartouche spelled out sign by sign, often followed by 'living forever, beloved of Ptah'. Ptolemaic reliefs are crowded and deeply cut, with fleshy, rounded figures quite unlike New Kingdom work.
story:
Alexander reached Egypt late in 332 BC, and the Persian satrap surrendered. He honoured the Apis bull at Memphis, founded Alexandria on the coast and crossed the desert to Siwa, where the oracle of Amun, Zeus-Ammon to the Greeks, hailed him as the god's son. He died in Babylon in 323 BC. His bodyguard Ptolemy, son of Lagos, took Egypt as satrap, intercepted Alexander's body on its way to Macedon and buried it at Memphis, later in Alexandria; the tomb has never been found. Ptolemy called himself king from 305 BC and launched the Library and the Lighthouse.

His descendants ruled until 30 BC. They spoke Greek, lived in Alexandria and, from Ptolemy II and Arsinoe II on, often married their siblings. Crowned by the priests of Ptah at Memphis, they paid for traditional temples to keep the priesthood loyal: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae, Esna and Dendera all carry Ptolemaic cartouches. The Rosetta Stone is a priestly decree of 196 BC honouring Ptolemy V.

Cleopatra VII, born in 69 BC, was the first of her family known to learn Egyptian. Fighting her brother Ptolemy XIII, she allied with Julius Caesar, who arrived in 48 BC, and bore him Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she joined Mark Antony, whom she met at Tarsos in 41 BC; they had three children, and the Donations of Alexandria gave them kingdoms. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC and took Alexandria in 30. Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra died in August, most likely by poison. Egypt passed to Rome, under Octavian's personal control.
details: In a Ptolemy cartouche, the easy signs are a stool for p, a loaf for t, a lion for l and a folded cloth for s.
Edfu (20th): the king offering to Horus is usually a Ptolemy; the temple was built between 237 and 57 BC.
Luxor Temple (22nd): the barque shrine shows Alexander as pharaoh in Egyptian crowns, offering to Amun.
Siwa (13th-15th): the oracle temple at Aghurmi, where Alexander consulted Amun in 331 BC.
Look for Greek letters among the graffiti at Philae and Edfu: your alphabet on Egyptian walls.
fun_fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
narration: For a Greek visitor, this is your chapter of Egyptian history. In late 332 BC Alexander the Great marched into Egypt and the Persian governor gave up without a fight. Alexander honoured the Apis bull at Memphis, founded Alexandria on the coast, and crossed the desert to Siwa, where the oracle of Amun greeted him as the son of the god. 9 years later he was dead in Babylon. His general Ptolemy, son of Lagos, took Egypt, and even hijacked Alexander's body on its way home to Macedon and buried it in Egypt. That tomb has never been found. Ptolemy's family ruled for almost 300 years. They spoke Greek, lived in Alexandria, collected books for the great Library, and often married their own sisters. To keep the Egyptian priests happy, they built temples in the old style: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae, Esna. On their walls a Macedonian king in a pharaoh's kilt offers to Horus. The last of the line, Cleopatra the Seventh, was the first of her family known to speak Egyptian. She allied herself first with Julius Caesar, with whom she had a son, then with Mark Antony. After their defeat at Actium in 31 BC, Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra died soon after, probably by poison rather than the bite of an asp. Egypt became Rome's. Look at any Ptolemy's cartouche: you can spell out the Greek name, sign by sign.

name: Queens and God's Wives: women with power
note: Great Royal Wife and the 'God's Wife of Amun' office: Ahmose-Nefertari (deified at Deir el-Medina with black skin), Hatshepsut, Tiye (diplomatic correspondence in her own name), Nefertari (her letters to the Hittite queen Puduhepa), Tausert as king; in the Third Intermediate Period the God's Wives at Thebes were celibate princesses ruling with the high priests (Shepenwepet, Amenirdis, Nitocris), adopting successors; women's legal rights in Egypt (property, divorce, court) unusual for antiquity; Herodotus' surprise.
period: New Kingdom to Late Period, c. 1550-525 BC
summary: Egypt's queens could be priests, diplomats and even kings, and for two centuries unmarried princesses held power in Thebes as God's Wives of Amun.
look: Queens appear smaller than the king but in their own crowns: the vulture cap, two tall plumes, or cow horns and sun disc. You meet Nefertari at Abu Simbel's small temple on the 17th and in her tomb on the 21st, and Tiye beside her husband in the museums. A God's Wife of Amun wears a close cap with plumes, and her name sits in a cartouche like a king's.
story:
A Great Royal Wife had her own household, titles and ritual roles. Ahmose-Nefertari, wife of Ahmose I, was the first queen to hold the office of God's Wife of Amun at Karnak; after her death she was worshipped at Deir el-Medina, often painted with black skin, the colour of fertile earth and rebirth. Hatshepsut held the same office before becoming king. Tiye, daughter of the courtiers Yuya and Thuya, was written to directly by foreign rulers. Nefertari exchanged letters with the Hittite queen Puduhepa. Tausert ruled as king at the end of the 19th Dynasty.

From Ramesses VI on, the God's Wife was an unmarried king's daughter who adopted her successor. In the 25th and 26th Dynasties these women were the face of royal power in Thebes. Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III, adopted Amenirdis I, daughter of the Kushite king Kashta; in 656 BC Psamtik I made Piye's daughter Shepenupet II adopt his own daughter Nitocris. The office ended when the Persians conquered Egypt in 525 BC.

Ordinary Egyptian women could own and inherit property, make contracts, divorce and go to court. Herodotus was amazed that in Egypt women went to market while men stayed home at the loom.
details: Abu Simbel small temple (17th): Nefertari's standing statues on the facade are as tall as Ramesses' own.
Queens' crowns: the vulture cap with wings over the ears, two tall plumes, and often Hathor's horns and sun disc.
Medinet Habu (21st): the funerary chapels of the God's Wives Amenirdis and Shepenupet stand inside the enclosure, near the gate.
Deir el-Medina (21st): Ahmose-Nefertari, patron of the village, often appears with black skin in tomb paintings.
Nefertari's tomb, QV66 (21st): the queen plays senet and offers to the gods alone, a tomb as fine as any king's.
fun_fact: When Psamtik I reunited Egypt in 656 BC, he took over Thebes partly by adoption papers: the reigning God's Wife had to adopt his daughter Nitocris as her heir.
narration: Egyptian queens were far more than wives. Ahmose-Nefertari, wife of the king who drove out the Hyksos, became the first God's Wife of Amun, a powerful priestly office at Karnak. Later she was worshipped as a goddess by the tomb builders, and painted with black skin, the colour of fertile earth. Queen Tiye, a courtier's daughter, received letters from foreign kings in her own right. Nefertari wrote to the Hittite queen, and Ramesses carved her statues as tall as his own at Abu Simbel. Some women went further: Hatshepsut and later Tausert ruled as kings. Then the God's Wife became something unique. From Dynasty 20 she was a king's daughter who never married, and who adopted the next king's daughter as her heir. For about 200 years these women were the face of royal power in Thebes. Even ordinary women could own land, divorce and go to court, which amazed Herodotus: he wrote that Egyptian women went to market while the men stayed home and wove. Look for a woman's name inside a cartouche: that signals real power.

name: Champollion and the Rosetta Stone
note: Napoleon's 1798 expedition and the savants' Description de l'Egypte; the stone found at Rashid 1799 by Bouchard, taken by the British 1801 (BM), the Ptolemy V decree in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek; Thomas Young's cartouche work; Champollion's 'Je tiens l'affaire!' on 14 September 1822 and fainting; his 1828-29 Egypt journey (he copied at Karnak, Abu Simbel, wept in the Valley of the Kings), death at 41; Egyptology born; the Egyptian claim for return; the Coptic key.
period: Stone 196 BC; decipherment 1822
summary: A broken slab from a French fort and an obsessive young linguist from Figeac unlocked 3,000 years of Egyptian writing in 1822.
look: The real stone is in the British Museum in London; here you will meet copies, and its three scripts all over Egypt. Its top band is hieroglyphs, the middle demotic, the everyday cursive script, the bottom Greek. Every cartouche you spell out on this trip uses the method Champollion worked out from it.
story:
Napoleon's invasion of 1798 brought scholars as well as soldiers; their survey became the Description de l'Egypte. In July 1799 the officer Pierre-Francois Bouchard found the stone reused in Fort Julien near Rashid. It is granodiorite from the Aswan region, about 112 centimetres high and 760 kilograms, a fragment of a larger stela. Its decree, passed by priests at Memphis on 27 March 196 BC, honours Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Under the Capitulation of Alexandria the British took it in 1801; it has been in the British Museum since 1802, and Egyptian scholars have called for its return.

The Greek was translated by 1803. Johan David Akerblad and Thomas Young made progress with demotic, and Young showed that cartouches held royal names spelled phonetically. Champollion, born in Figeac in 1790, had studied Coptic since his teens, convinced it was the last form of Egyptian. In September 1822, after matching the signs in the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, he read native names such as Ramesses and Thutmose and realised that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs and meaning signs. Legend says he burst into his brother's office, cried 'Je tiens l'affaire!', I've got it, and fainted. His Precis of 1824 set out the system; some accused him of not crediting Young.

In 1828 and 1829 he finally toured Egypt and Nubia, reading inscriptions at Karnak, the Valley of the Kings and Abu Simbel. Worn out by the journey, he died in Paris in 1832, aged 41. His Egyptian grammar was published after his death.
details: Rosetta Stone: about 112 centimetres high and 760 kilograms; only the last 14 lines of its hieroglyphic text survive.
Demotic, the middle script, looks like rows of hooks and dashes: everyday handwriting descended from hieroglyphs.
Coptic, still used in Egyptian church services, is Egyptian written in Greek letters plus a few extra signs.
Philae (Aswan): an obelisk taken from there to England gave scholars Cleopatra's cartouche to set beside Ptolemy's.
In a Ptolemy cartouche the recumbent lion stands for L: one of Champollion's first footholds.
fun_fact: For almost two centuries the stone was thought to be black basalt; a 1999 cleaning removed old chalk and wax and revealed grey granodiorite with a pink vein.
narration: Every time you read a royal name on this trip, thank two things: a broken stone and a stubborn young man. In July 1799, French soldiers rebuilding a fort at Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, found a dark slab built into a wall. It carried one decree in 3 scripts: hieroglyphs at the top, demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting, in the middle, and Greek at the bottom. Priests had issued it in 196 BC to honour the young king Ptolemy the Fifth. Since scholars could read Greek, here was a crib. The British took the stone in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum ever since. The race to read it ran for 20 years. The English polymath Thomas Young saw that the ovals held royal names. But Jean-Francois Champollion, from Figeac, had a secret weapon: Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which he spoke to himself and claimed to dream in. Using the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, he matched signs to sounds. Then, in September 1822, he read the names Ramesses and Thutmose and saw that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs with picture signs. Family legend says he ran to his brother shouting I've got it, and fainted. In 1828 and 1829 he finally travelled up the Nile, reading walls no one had read for some 1,400 years. He died at 41. Look at any Ptolemy cartouche: the lion is an L, and that is where it all began.

name: Belzoni, Mariette and the age of plunder and rescue
note: The consuls' race (Salt vs Drovetti) that filled the BM, Louvre and Turin; Belzoni the circus strongman who moved the Younger Memnon, opened Khafre's pyramid, Seti I's tomb and Abu Simbel (1815-19), 'I would cry mummy' crushing them in Qurna; Lepsius' Prussian expedition; Mariette founding the Antiquities Service and the Bulaq museum 1858, the Serapeum, Edfu's clearance, Aida's plot; Maspero and the royal cache; Petrie's scientific method and 'sequence dating'; the partage system and why things are abroad; Egypt's modern restitution campaign.
summary: A circus strongman hauled statues to London, a French clerk founded Egypt's own museum: two faces of the 19th-century scramble for Egypt's past.
look: Belzoni's trail crosses yours: he cleared the sand from Abu Simbel's door (17th), found Seti I's tomb in the Valley (21st) and opened Khafre's pyramid at Giza (12th). Mariette's monument is the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, heir to the museum he founded, and he is buried in its front garden. Much of what you will not see in Egypt is in London, Paris and Turin because of this era.
story:
Under Muhammad Ali, antiquities were a collector's market. The British consul Henry Salt and the French consul Bernardino Drovetti competed for statues and coffins, now in the British Museum, the Louvre and Turin. Giovanni Belzoni, a 2-metre Paduan, had been a strongman in London's circuses. He came to Egypt in 1815 to sell the Pasha a water-raising machine, failed, and went to work for Salt. In 1816 he moved the 7-tonne 'Younger Memnon' bust of Ramesses II from the Ramesseum to the Nile in 17 days with 130 men. In 1817 he cleared Abu Simbel's entrance and found Seti I's tomb; in 1818 he entered Khafre's pyramid.

Auguste Mariette arrived in 1850 to buy manuscripts for the Louvre, spotted a sphinx in the sand at Saqqara and uncovered the Serapeum, the catacomb of the Apis bulls. In 1858 he became Egypt's first conservator of monuments, and in 1863 he opened a museum at Bulaq to keep finds in the country. He cleared Edfu and Dendera, rescued Queen Ahhotep's jewels from the Khedive's hands and sketched the plot of Aida, though he also kept Egyptians out of senior posts. Maspero and Petrie followed. Partage, the splitting of finds with foreign excavators, explains much of what is abroad.
details: Khafre's pyramid (12th): if it is open, look for Belzoni's name painted in big letters in the burial chamber, dated March 1818.
KV17, Seti I's tomb, is still nicknamed Belzoni's tomb; he made casts of its reliefs for a London exhibition in 1820.
Egyptian Museum, Tahrir: Mariette lies in a sarcophagus in the front garden, beside the collection he started.
Abu Simbel (17th): when Belzoni began digging, only the tops of the colossi's heads showed above the sand.
Partage, splitting finds between Egypt and foreign diggers, is why so much is in London, Paris, Turin and Berlin.
fun_fact: Before Egypt, Belzoni performed in London as a strongman billed as the Patagonian Samson.
narration: In the early 1800s, Egypt's antiquities were a free-for-all. The British and French consuls, Henry Salt and Bernardino Drovetti, raced each other to ship statues home, which is why London, Paris and Turin have such collections. Salt's star digger was Giovanni Belzoni from Padua, a 2-metre circus strongman who had come to sell the Pasha a water wheel. In 1816 he dragged the 7-tonne bust of Ramesses the Second from the Ramesseum to the Nile with 130 men. He cleared the sand from Abu Simbel's door, found Seti the First's tomb, and opened Khafre's pyramid. Exploring the mummy pits of Thebes, he admitted sitting on mummies that crumpled under him. A generation later, Auguste Mariette came to buy manuscripts for the Louvre and instead found the Serapeum at Saqqara. He stayed, became Egypt's first director of antiquities in 1858, and opened a museum so finds would stay in the country. He even wrote the story of Verdi's Aida. Inside Khafre's pyramid, look for Belzoni's name, painted in big letters in the burial chamber.

name: Carter, Carnarvon and the curse
note: Carter the draughtsman's son who started tracing at 17, sacked over the Saqqara affair, Carnarvon the racing earl convalescing in Egypt, Davis giving up the valley in 1914 'exhausted', the last season gamble of 1922, the water boy, 'Yes, wonderful things', the ten-year clearance with Burton, Lucas, Mace, the quarrel with the government and the Times exclusive; Carnarvon's death from a mosquito bite in April 1923, the lights of Cairo, the dog Susie, Conan Doyle, Marie Corelli: the curse invented by the press; Carter died in bed in 1939, Lady Evelyn in 1980; the objects Carter 'took'.
period: Discovery 1922; clearance to 1932
summary: An awkward draughtsman, a racing earl and a last-chance season found Tutankhamun; the newspapers then invented the curse.
look: On the 21st you can visit Carter's house near the entrance to the Valley and the tomb itself, KV62; at the GEM on the 11th, everything he catalogued is together for the first time. Harry Burton's black-and-white photographs, widely reproduced, show each piece exactly as Carter found it.
story:
Howard Carter, born in 1874, was the son of an artist and had little formal education. At 17 he went to Egypt to copy tomb scenes at Beni Hasan, then trained under Flinders Petrie at Amarna and recorded Hatshepsut's temple. In 1899 he became Inspector of Monuments for Upper Egypt. After the Saqqara Affair of 1905, when he backed Egyptian guards against French tourists and refused to apologise, he resigned and sold watercolours to survive. In 1907 Gaston Maspero introduced him to George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon, a wealthy collector who wintered in Egypt.

Carnarvon won the Valley of the Kings concession in 1914, after Theodore Davis had declared it exhausted. The war interrupted, and by 1922 Carnarvon was ready to stop; Carter persuaded him to fund one more season. On 4 November 1922 a step appeared under the remains of workmen's huts. On 26 November Carter peered through a hole by candlelight; the remembered reply is 'Yes, wonderful things', though his journal says 'Yes, it is wonderful'. With Harry Burton's photographs, Alfred Lucas's chemistry and Arthur Mace's help, clearing the tomb took until 1932. Carnarvon sold exclusive coverage to The Times, infuriating rival papers.

Carnarvon died in Cairo on 5 April 1923 of blood poisoning. The press supplied a curse, with tales of failing lights and a dog dying at Highclere; Arthur Conan Doyle spoke of 'elementals'. No curse is inscribed in the tomb. Carter died of Hodgkin's disease in London in 1939; after his death, objects from the tomb were found in his collection.
details: Carter's house (21st): near the road into the Valley, with his desk and darkroom; a replica of the tomb stands nearby.
He made the first hole with a chisel his grandmother had given him for his 17th birthday.
Carter numbered every object and group in the tomb; his record cards are still used by researchers.
Carter's gravestone in London quotes the alabaster Wishing Cup, which you can see at the GEM.
Genuine ancient tomb curses are rare, mostly in Old Kingdom private tombs, and none was found in Tutankhamun's.
fun_fact: A 2002 medical study of the Westerners present at the tomb's openings found they lived as long as those who were not; Lady Evelyn, who entered in 1922, died in 1980.
narration: Howard Carter was an artist's son with little schooling, who came to Egypt at 17 to copy tomb paintings. He rose to be an inspector of monuments, then lost the job in 1905 for siding with Egyptian guards against a group of rowdy French tourists and refusing to apologise. For a while he sold watercolours to visitors. His break came through Lord Carnarvon, a racing-mad earl who wintered in Egypt for his health. From 1914 they searched the Valley of the Kings, which another digger had declared exhausted. By 1922 Carnarvon wanted to stop. Carter talked him into one last season. On 4 November, a step was found beneath some old workmen's huts; one version credits a boy bringing water. On 26 November Carter held a candle to a hole in the sealed door. Can you see anything, asked Carnarvon. Yes, wonderful things, Carter is remembered as saying. It took him 10 years to empty the tomb. Then the curse began, though no curse is written anywhere in it. Carnarvon died in Cairo in April 1923, from an infected mosquito bite. Newspapers, angry that he had sold exclusive rights to The Times, filled the gap with tales of lights failing across Cairo and his dog howling in England. Carter, the man who actually opened the coffins, died in his London flat in 1939, aged 64. Look at any of Burton's photographs: every object was recorded before it moved.

name: The Nile flood, the three seasons and the calendar
note: The July-October flood from Ethiopian rains bringing black silt (Kemet 'the black land' vs Deshret the red), the three seasons Akhet (flood), Peret (growing), Shemu (harvest), the 365-day civil calendar of 12 x 30 + 5 days drifting against the heliacal rising of Sirius (Sothis) that marked New Year; Nilometers and taxation; corvée labour during the flood (pyramid building season); Hapi; the flood's end in 1970 with the High Dam; Herodotus' 'gift of the river'.
summary: Egypt's year, its calendar, its taxes and even its name came from one event: the river rising every summer and leaving black mud behind.
look: You are travelling at what was once the height of the flood: in October the old Nile stood at its highest, with the fields under water. Look for the contrast the Egyptians named their land after: the black-green strip of farmland and the red-gold desert, often a single step apart. The stone stairways called Nilometers, at Elephantine and Kom Ombo, measured the rise.
story:
The flood came from the monsoon over the Ethiopian highlands, which swells the Blue Nile and the Atbara between May and August. The rise reached Aswan in early June and kept going into September, often peaking again in October, before falling to its low point the next June. Typical heights were about 14 metres at Aswan and 12 at Luxor. Farmers trapped the water in earth-banked basins for about 45 days, let the silt settle, drained it and sowed. A low flood meant famine, a high one swept villages away. Egyptians called the flood the arrival of Hapi, and myth said it was the tears of Isis for Osiris.

The civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days, grouped into three seasons: Akhet, the inundation, Peret, emergence, and Shemu, harvest or low water. Each month had three 10-day weeks; in the Ramesside period the royal tomb builders seem to have had the last two days of each week off. Five extra days, the epagomenal days, completed the year. With no leap year, the calendar drifted a day every four years against the seasons and against the dawn rising of Sirius, Sopdet to the Egyptians and Sothis to the Greeks, the ideal start of the year. Ptolemy III's Canopus Decree of 238 BC tried to add a leap day; Augustus finally imposed one, creating the Alexandrian calendar that survives as the Coptic calendar.

Nilometers recorded each year's height, which set tax expectations. The annual flood ended in 1970 with the Aswan High Dam.
details: Elephantine Nilometer (Aswan): a stone stairway down to the river, with measuring marks on its walls.
Kom Ombo (20th): the Nilometer is a round stone well with a staircase spiralling down, beside the temple.
Hapi, the flood god: a man with a fat belly and heavy breasts, often tying the plants of north and south together.
Kom Ombo's calendar relief lists festival offerings month by month through the three seasons.
From a boat or car window, watch the sharp line where irrigated green stops and desert starts.
fun_fact: Julius Caesar's calendar reform was advised by a Greek astronomer from Alexandria, Sosigenes, so Egypt's 365-day year is an ancestor of the calendar on your phone.
narration: Imagine Egypt without rain. Every drop of water came down the Nile, and every summer it brought a gift. Monsoon rains fell on the mountains of Ethiopia, the river swelled, and from June the flood crept north past Aswan, peaking around September and October. In an ancient October like this one, the fields around you would be a sheet of brown water. When it drained, it left a layer of black silt so rich that the Egyptians named their country Kemet, the black land, as opposed to Deshret, the red land of the desert. Herodotus called Egypt the gift of the river. The flood shaped time itself. The year had 3 seasons of 4 months: Akhet, the flood, Peret, when the fields emerged and crops grew, and Shemu, the harvest and low water. Each month had 30 days, and 5 extra days at the end were the birthdays of the gods. That made 365 days but no leap year, so the calendar slowly drifted away from the seasons and from the dawn rising of Sirius, the star that in theory opened the year. The Coptic calendar, still used by farmers today, descends from it. Officials measured each flood on stone stairways called Nilometers and set taxes by the result. Since the High Dam was finished in 1970, the flood no longer comes. Look at the edge of the green: you can often stand with one foot in the black land and one in the red.

name: Festivals: Opet, the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Sed
note: The Sed jubilee after 30 years (then every 3) renewing the king's powers with the ritual run between boundary markers and the dual throne (Djoser's court at Saqqara, Amenhotep III at Malkata, the White Chapel); the Opet (Karnak to Luxor); the Beautiful Festival of the Valley when Amun crossed to the West Bank and families picnicked at the tombs of their dead, drinking to meet them (origin of the modern Egyptian cemetery visits); the Min harvest festival (Medinet Habu's second court); the festival of drunkenness of Hathor; the public's role; the festival calendar at Kom Ombo and Esna.
period: Early Dynastic to Ptolemaic
summary: Most of the year the gods stayed hidden; on festival days they came out in golden boats, and the whole city celebrated, prayed and visited its dead.
look: Festival scenes cover the walls you visit on the 21st and 22nd. A model boat with a cabin shrine, carried on poles by priests, is a god on an outing. The Opet procession runs along the walls of Luxor Temple's colonnade, the festival of Min fills a wall of Medinet Habu's second court, and Karnak's White Chapel was built for a king's jubilee.
story:
Festivals were when the gods became visible. Statues travelled in portable barques, model boats with a cabin shrine, carried on priests' shoulders or floated on gilded river barges. Ordinary people could approach, put yes-or-no questions to the god's oracle and share in the food.

The Sed festival, or 'Feast of the Tail', renewed a king after 30 years on the throne and every three or four years after that. He ran a ritual course between boundary markers and was enthroned twice, for Upper and Lower Egypt. Djoser's Sed court at Saqqara and Senusret I's White Chapel at Karnak were built for it. Hatshepsut and Akhenaten held theirs early; Ramesses II held 13 or 14.

Opet, in the second month of the flood season, took Amun, Mut and Khonsu from Karnak to Luxor Temple, where the king was reborn as Amun's son; it lasted 11 days under Thutmose III and 27 by the death of Ramesses III. The Beautiful Festival of the Valley, held at the new moon of the second month of Shemu, carried Amun across to the West Bank temples. Families brought flowers, food and drink to their relatives' tombs, feasting and sleeping beside the dead.
details: Luxor Temple colonnade (22nd): the Opet reliefs show the barques towed upriver, with musicians, dancers and butchers.
The heb-sed sign: a double pavilion with two thrones back to back, for the king's double enthronement.
Medinet Habu second court (21st): the festival of Min, with priests releasing birds to the four directions.
Karnak White Chapel (22nd): built for Senusret I's jubilee; its pillars show the king with the gods, above all Min.
Portable barque: a model boat with a cabin shrine, carried on poles by priests. Wherever you see it, a god is out.
fun_fact: Hathor's Festival of Drunkenness remembered how Ra saved humanity from the raging goddess with beer dyed red, which she drank until she fell asleep.
narration: Most of the year, Egypt's gods lived hidden in dark sanctuaries. On festival days they came out. Priests carried the god's statue in a gilded model boat on poles, and the whole town lined the route. The biggest festival in Thebes was Opet, in the flood season, when Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu travelled from Karnak to Luxor Temple, about 2 kilometres. Under Thutmose the Third it lasted 11 days; under Ramesses the Third, more than 3 weeks. Luxor still carries a boat in procession for its saint, Abu el-Haggag, an echo many see of Opet. The Beautiful Festival of the Valley took Amun across the river to the West Bank temples. Families followed with flowers, food and wine, and feasted at their relatives' tombs, sometimes staying the night. Then there was the Sed festival, the king's jubilee after 30 years, when he ran a ritual course to prove he was still fit to rule. Ramesses the Second held 13 or 14 of them. Look for the boat on poles: wherever it appears, a festival is under way.

name: Daily life: bread, beer, linen, make-up and medicine
note: Bread and beer as wages (the workmen's rations), onions, lentils, fish, fowl, beef for the rich, honey, dates, figs, wine in the Delta, 40 kinds of bread; kohl eye paint (lead, antibacterial), wigs and cones of scented fat, linen (never wool in temples), sandals, jewellery for all classes; mud-brick houses with roofs for sleeping; medicine (Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri, honey on wounds, mouldy bread, the first known pregnancy test with barley); dental wear from sand in bread; games (senet, mehen), music (harp, lute, sistrum), pets (cats, baboons, monkeys), the scribe's status ('be a scribe, it saves you from toil').
summary: Bread with grit in it, beer you could almost chew, eyeliner for everyone: what ordinary Egyptian life tasted, smelled and looked like.
look: You will see daily life in the tombs of the nobles and at Deir el-Medina on the 21st, and in museum cases: model bakeries and breweries, wigs, mirrors, kohl tubes, sandals and board games. In the paintings, look for banquet guests wearing cones on their heads, and long lines of servants carrying loaves, ducks and jars.
story:
Bread and beer were the twin staples, and wages too. Bread was mostly of emmer wheat, pounded, sieved and ground on a saddle quern; by the New Kingdom loaves were slapped onto the inside of cylindrical clay ovens. Grit from the querns wore teeth down badly. Beer was thick, cloudy and nourishing, brewed from lightly baked bread or from malted grain, and still has a cousin in Egyptian bouza. Onions, garlic, leeks, lettuce, lentils, chickpeas, dates and figs filled out the diet; fish and birds were within most people's reach, beef mainly for the rich and for festivals. Geese were force-fed from about 2500 BC.

People wore linen, from simple kilts to fine pleated dresses. Men and women lined their eyes with kohl and wore wigs and jewellery, and banquet guests in paintings wear cones on their heads, perhaps of perfumed fat or wax. Medical papyri such as the Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri cover wounds, fractures and remedies, including honey dressings. People played senet and mehen, made music with harps, lutes, flutes and the rattling sistrum, and kept cats, dogs and monkeys as pets. A scribe ranked above all manual workers, and schoolbooks never let boys forget it.
details: TT52, Nakht (21st): a blind harpist and banquet guests with cones on their heads; TT69, Menna: harvest and field measuring.
TT100, Rekhmire: brick-making, metalwork and bread-making, a whole estate's workshops in one tomb.
Senet: a board of 30 squares in three rows of 10. Tutankhamun took several sets with him.
Kohl pots: little tubes or jars with an applicator stick, in stone, glass or faience, in every museum.
Middle Kingdom models: women grinding grain and men straining beer mash in tiny wooden bakeries and breweries.
fun_fact: Foie gras is Egyptian: tomb reliefs from about 2500 BC already show servants force-feeding geese.
narration: Here is how ordinary Egyptians lived. They ate bread at every meal, made from emmer wheat or barley, ground on stone querns. Grit from the stones got into the flour, and mummies show badly worn teeth. They drank beer every day, thick and cloudy, more like liquid bread, and workmen were paid partly in loaves and jugs of it. Add onions, garlic, lentils, dates and figs; fish and ducks for most people, beef for the rich. They wore linen, and both men and women lined their eyes with kohl. In banquet paintings, guests wear cones on their heads, which may have been scented fat or wax; nobody is quite sure. Doctors wrote textbooks on papyrus and dressed wounds with honey, and one pregnancy test had a woman pass urine on seeds of barley and wheat: if they sprouted, a baby was on the way. Children and adults played senet, a race game you will see among Tutankhamun's treasures. Look for the bread on any offering table: the loaves come in a dozen shapes.

name: Why they drew like that: the rules of Egyptian art
note: Aspective, not perspective: each part shown in its clearest view (face profile, eye frontal, shoulders frontal, legs profile), the left foot forward, the 18-square grid (later 21), hierarchical scale (king big, wife small, enemies tiny), registers and baselines, men red-brown and women yellow, gods' skin colours (green Osiris, blue Amun, black for rebirth, gold for divine flesh), raised relief indoors vs sunk relief for sunlight outdoors, the artist as anonymous craftsman in teams, outline draughtsman and sculptor, the deliberate archaism; why it barely changed in 3,000 years and why Amarna shocked; how a statue 'works' as a ka body (the back pillar, frontality, the eyes).
period: c. 3100 BC to the Roman period
summary: Egyptian artists were not failing at perspective: they drew each body part from its clearest angle, by rules that held for 3,000 years.
look: Every relief on this trip follows the same rules, so learn them once and you can read any wall. A face in profile with a frontal eye, shoulders square to you, hips and legs in profile; the most important figure is the biggest. Scenes run in horizontal strips, each on its own ground line. Standing statues step forward on the left foot and stare straight ahead.
story:
Egyptian had no word for 'art'. Images did a job: to depict something was to make it last, so pictures had to be complete and unmistakable. Each part is shown from its most characteristic angle, which Egyptologists call aspective: a profile head with a frontal eye, frontal shoulders, and hips and legs in profile. Rank decides size, so kings dwarf servants and enemies. Scenes sit in horizontal registers on baselines; people further away are placed higher up or overlapped, not shrunk. Frontality, hierarchy of scale and composite views held from the 1st Dynasty to the Roman period.

Consistency came from method. Draughtsmen snapped a red grid onto the wall; a standing figure measured 18 squares from hairline to soles, and from the 25th and 26th Dynasties a revised 21-square grid was used. A sketch in red was corrected in black, then sculptors cut the relief and painters filled it with mineral colours. Work was done by teams, and most artists are anonymous, though Deir el-Medina's craftsmen left their names on their own tombs.

Colour followed convention: men reddish brown, women paler yellow, gods with golden skin and blue hair, Osiris green or black for growth and fertile silt. Raised relief suited interiors; sunk relief caught the strong sun outside. Statues were homes for the ka: frontal, backed by a pillar, eyes sometimes inlaid with rock crystal. The rules bent under Akhenaten, then returned, and later dynasties deliberately copied Old Kingdom models.
details: KV57, Horemheb (21st): unfinished walls show red grid lines, sketches corrected in black, and carving at every stage.
Hands: on many figures both hands are drawn as left or both as right, because clarity beat anatomy.
Statues: the man steps forward with his left foot; a woman usually stands with her feet together or barely apart.
Compare an outer wall with an inner hall at Karnak or Edfu: sunk relief outside, raised relief inside.
Rahotep and Nofret, in the museum: his reddish skin, her pale skin and their inlaid crystal eyes show the code in 3D.
fun_fact: One Egyptian word used for a sculptor meant 'he who makes alive', because a finished statue could house a living spirit.
narration: Egyptian artists could draw what they saw; they chose not to. A picture was meant to work forever, so every part had to be shown in its clearest view. A face is clearest in profile, but an eye is clearest from the front, so you get a frontal eye in a side face. Shoulders are clearest square on, hips and legs from the side. Egyptologists call this aspective rather than perspective. Size shows rank, not distance: the king towers, his wife may reach his knee, and enemies and servants are tiny. Scenes run in strips, like a comic, each on its own baseline. To keep proportions steady, draughtsmen drew a grid: a standing figure was 18 squares from the hairline to the soles, and from the 7th century BC, 21 squares. A draughtsman sketched in red, a master corrected in black, then sculptors and painters followed, mostly anonymous. Colour had rules too. Men are reddish brown, women pale yellow. Gods have flesh of gold and hair of lapis blue. Osiris can be green or black, the colours of new growth and fertile mud. Indoors they used raised relief; outside, sunk relief, which casts sharp shadows in the Egyptian sun. A statue was a body for the spirit, so it faces straight ahead, backed by a pillar. Only under Akhenaten did the rules bend. Look at the nearest figure: find the frontal eye, the square shoulders and the striding foot.

name: Baksheesh, touts and temple etiquette
note: Practical and friendly: baksheesh as tip/alms/grease with a long history, when it is expected (guards who unlock a chapel or 'show' you something, toilets, photos with locals) and typical small amounts (keep small notes), how to decline a 'guide' or an unwanted 'gift' (la shukran, khalas, keep walking, smile), the camel/horse/felucca negotiation rules (agree total price, per person, including return, before mounting), the 'closed today, come to my shop' line, the papyrus/perfume 'institute' tour stops, photo-permit tickets in museums and tombs, no flash, no touching reliefs (sweat and salt), dress respectfully in mosques (women cover hair, everyone shoulders and knees), shoes off, Friday noon prayers; be firm, be kind, Egyptians are warm and humour works.
summary: Small notes, a smile and a firm 'la, shukran' will carry you through every temple, souq and felucca landing in Egypt.
look: You will meet baksheesh everywhere: the guard who unlocks a side chamber, the toilet attendant, the man who poses with his camel, the boy who 'shows' you the way. Touts gather at site entrances, in souqs and at boat landings. Carry small notes in a separate pocket and decide in advance what you are willing to pay.
story:
Baksheesh comes from the Persian bakhshesh, a gift, and across the Middle East it can mean a tip, alms or a bribe. Travellers have written about it for centuries: Mark Twain, riding through Galilee in 1867, described being mobbed by cries of 'bucksheesh'. In today's Egypt it mostly means a small tip for a small service, and it matters because many wages are low.

Expect to tip toilet attendants, hotel porters, drivers, felucca and boat crews, and site guards who unlock or light something for you. A guard offering to let you into a closed area, or to let you photograph where it is forbidden, is asking you to break the rules, and you can say no. Keep small notes in a separate pocket, and ask your guide or hotel what is normal this year, since prices have been changing fast.

Touts work with polite stories. The temple is closed, but there is a shop; the scarab is a gift, until it is not; the friendly stranger is 'not a guide'. A smile, 'la shukran' and walking on usually ends it; 'khalas', enough, closes the matter. Tour stops at papyrus, perfume and alabaster 'institutes' earn commissions: enjoy the tea, buy only what you want. For camels, horses, carriages and feluccas, agree the total, the number of people, the time and the return trip first, and pay at the end.

Respect the sites: no flash on paintings, no touching reliefs, photo permits where required. In mosques remove shoes, cover shoulders and knees, women cover their hair, and avoid Friday midday prayers.
details: Phrases: la shukran, no thank you; shukran, thank you; khalas, enough; salam aleikum, hello; ma'a salama, goodbye.
Camel, horse or felucca: agree the total price, number of people, duration and return trip before you start; pay at the end.
Photo rules vary by site and change often: check what your ticket covers, and never use flash on paintings.
Shopping stops for papyrus, perfume and alabaster pay guides a commission: drink the tea, buy only what you love.
Mosques: avoid Friday midday prayers; shoes off at the door; scarves or robes are often available at the entrance.
fun_fact: Baksheesh has puzzled visitors for centuries: Mark Twain, riding through Galilee in 1867, said the chorus of 'bucksheesh!' was the worst storm he had ever been in.
narration: Baksheesh is a Persian word that covers a tip, a gift to the poor and a little grease for the wheels, and in Egypt you will meet all three. Wages are low and small tips keep many people going, so treat it as part of the cost of travel, not as an insult. Keep a separate pocket of small notes, 5, 10 and 20 pounds, so you never flash a full wallet. Expect to tip toilet attendants, porters, drivers and boat crews. A guard who unlocks a side room or points his torch at a hidden relief will also expect something. Ask your guide what the going rate is this year, because prices move fast. Touts are the other half of the game. Someone tells you the temple is closed today, but his cousin's shop is open. Someone hands you a scarab as a free gift, then wants paying. Smile, say la shukran, no thank you, and keep walking. Khalas means enough, finished. For camels, horses, carriages and feluccas, agree the total price, per person or for everyone, how long, and whether the ride back is included, all before you climb on. Pay at the end. In mosques, take off your shoes, cover shoulders and knees, and women cover their hair. Do not touch painted walls: skin oil and salt damage the colours. Egyptians are warm and love a joke, so be firm, be kind, and laugh. Right now, check that you have small notes in an easy pocket.

name: Greece and Egypt: Herodotus, Alexandria and the Greek layer
note: For a Greek visitor: Minoan frescoes at Avaris and Keftiu tribute in Rekhmire's tomb; Greek mercenaries of Psamtik I and their graffiti on Abu Simbel's leg (593 BC); Naukratis the Greek trading city; Herodotus' Book II (c. 450 BC), the first guidebook, half right and still quoted; Alexander and the Ptolemies; the Greek names of everything (pyramid, obelisk 'little spit', sphinx, hieroglyph, pharaoh via Hebrew); Plutarch on Isis; the modern Egyptiot community (Alexandria, Cairo) of 250,000 before 1952, Cavafy's Alexandria, the Greek clubs and patisseries that remain; Egyptians' warm response to 'ana min el-Yunan'.
period: c. 1450 BC to today
summary: From Cretan envoys to Cavafy's Alexandria, Greeks have been in Egypt for about 3,500 years, and the words pyramid and obelisk are Greek.
look: The Greek layer is everywhere on this trip: Siwa's oracle of Ammon on the 13th-15th, Greek graffiti at Abu Simbel on the 17th, Philae and the Ptolemaic temples of the 20th, the Colossi of Memnon on the 21st. Look for Greek letters scratched or carved into stone. Read them aloud: you are reading what Greeks wrote there 2,000 to 2,600 years ago.
story:
Contacts are older than Classical Greece. Minoan-style frescoes decorated a palace at Avaris in the Delta, and around 1450 BC the vizier Rekhmire's tomb at Thebes shows Keftiu, usually identified as Cretans, bringing gifts. In the 7th century BC Psamtik I hired Ionian and Carian mercenaries, and Greek traders were based at Naukratis, on the Canopic branch of the Nile. Mercenaries campaigning in Nubia around 591 BC cut Greek graffiti into the colossi at Abu Simbel.

Herodotus of Halicarnassus travelled in Egypt in the mid 5th century BC. Book II of his Histories, the first long description of Egypt by an outsider, mixes sharp observation, priests' tales and errors, and is still quoted, not least for 'the gift of the river'. Alexander arrived in 332 BC, and for three centuries Egypt was ruled from Greek Alexandria; later Plutarch wrote the fullest ancient account of Isis and Osiris. Greek gave the world the names pyramid, obelisk, sphinx and hieroglyph.

In modern times a large Greek community, the Egyptiotes, flourished in Alexandria and Cairo, with schools, newspapers, clubs and pastry shops. The poet Constantine Cavafy was born in Alexandria in 1863. The community shrank sharply after the 1950s, but churches, the Patriarchate of Alexandria and a smaller community remain.
details: Abu Simbel (17th): Greek, Carian and Phoenician graffiti on the legs of the colossi by the door, cut around 591 BC.
Colossi of Memnon (21st): Greek verses by Roman-era visitors, among them the poet Julia Balbilla, on the northern statue.
Rekhmire's tomb, TT100: the Keftiu wear long hair and patterned kilts and carry Aegean-style vessels.
Greek words around you: pyramid, obelisk, sphinx, hieroglyph, papyrus; even Egypt comes from the Greek Aigyptos.
Siwa (13th-15th): the oracle the Greeks knew as Zeus-Ammon, consulted by Alexander in 331 BC.
fun_fact: Herodotus says an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded 1,600 silver talents spent on radishes, onions and garlic for the workers; his interpreter was probably improvising.
narration: As a Greek, you are not a stranger here. Around 1450 BC, men called Keftiu, probably Cretans, were painted bringing gifts in a vizier's tomb at Thebes. In the 600s BC, Egyptian kings hired Greek soldiers, and Greek merchants got their own town in the Delta, Naukratis. Around 591 BC, Greek mercenaries on campaign up the Nile carved their names on the colossi at Abu Simbel, where you can still read them. Herodotus came in the 5th century BC and wrote the first real guidebook to Egypt, half brilliant, half gossip. Then came Alexander, the Ptolemies and Alexandria. Your language named the sights: pyramid probably comes from a Greek word for a wheat cake, obelisk from a little roasting spit, and hieroglyph means sacred carving. In modern times a large Greek community lived in Alexandria and Cairo, and the poet Cavafy was born in Alexandria in 1863. A smaller community remains. Try saying ana min el-Yunan, I am from Greece, and watch the smiles. Look for Greek letters on old stones: you can read them.

name: Islamic Cairo in one day: how the city grew
note: Orientation: Fustat (641), al-Qata'i (Ibn Tulun 870), Fatimid al-Qahira (969, walled city between Bab al-Futuh and Bab Zuwayla), Saladin's Citadel (1176), Mamluk golden age (1250-1517), Ottoman, Muhammad Ali. UNESCO site. The route: Khan el-Khalili, al-Muizz, then Sultan Hassan, Citadel, Abdeen.
period: Islamic era, 641 to the 1870s
summary: Cairo is five capitals in a row: each new dynasty built its own city next to the last, and today you walk through them in order.
look: Today's route runs roughly north to south and then west: Khan el-Khalili and al-Muizz Street inside the old Fatimid walls, then south past Bab Zuwayla to Sultan Hassan and the Citadel on its spur of the Muqattam hills, and finally Abdeen Palace in the 19th-century city. From the Citadel terrace you see most of it at once: minarets and domes over flat roofs, and on a clear day the pyramids on the western horizon.
story:
Cairo was not founded once. It was founded again and again, each new ruler building his own capital beside the old one. The Arab commander Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt in 640 to 641 and, instead of ruling from Greek Alexandria, founded Fustat next to the Roman fortress of Babylon on the Nile. The Abbasids added al-Askar after 750. In 870 Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish officer from Samarra, built al-Qata'i. The Abbasids burned it in 905 but spared his great mosque.

In 969 the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia, conquered Egypt. Their general Jawhar al-Siqilli laid out a walled palace city to the north, and when Caliph al-Mu'izz arrived in 973 it became al-Qahira, 'the Victorious', the source of the word Cairo. It was a royal enclosure closed to ordinary people: two great palaces, the mosque of al-Azhar, and a main street from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla. In 1168 the vizier Shawar set fire to Fustat so that the Crusader king Amalric could not use it.

Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and in 1176 began the Citadel on the hill to the south. The rulers moved up there and the palace city opened to merchants and common Cairenes. Under the Mamluks (1250-1517) Cairo grew into perhaps the largest city in the world outside China, with an estimated 500,000 people under al-Nasir Muhammad, and sultans lined the old main street with mosques, schools and tombs.

The Ottomans made it a provincial capital in 1517. Napoleon's army held it from 1798 to 1801, and Muhammad Ali took power in 1805. His grandson Khedive Ismail built a European-style city to the west and in 1874 moved the government to Abdeen, leaving the old city to itself, which is one reason so much survived. UNESCO listed Historic Cairo as a World Heritage site in 1979.
details: Bab al-Futuh in the north and Bab Zuwayla in the south: the Fatimid gates that bracket the 1 km of al-Muizz Street.
Bayn al-Qasrayn on al-Muizz: the open stretch where the two Fatimid palaces once faced each other.
Below the Citadel: Sultan Hassan (1363) and al-Rifa'i (finished 1912) face each other, built five centuries apart to match.
From the Citadel walls, look west: on a clear day the Giza pyramids show through the haze.
16 October 2026 is a Friday: mosques close to sightseers around the midday prayer. Spend that hour in the bazaar or a museum.
fun_fact: Cairo's name means 'the Victorious'. One old story says the city was named after the planet Mars, al-Qahir, 'the Conqueror', which was rising when the foundations were laid.
narration: You are walking through a city that was founded five times, each new ruler building his own capital next to the last. In 641 the Arab general Amr ibn al-As camped beside a Roman fortress on the Nile and founded Fustat. The Abbasids added a quarter of their own, and in 870 Ahmad ibn Tulun built another, whose great mosque still stands. In 969 the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia, conquered Egypt and walled a palace city further north. They called it al-Qahira, the Victorious, and that is where the word Cairo comes from. For two centuries it was closed to ordinary people. Then Saladin ended the Fatimid line in 1171 and began the Citadel on the hill to the south. The rulers moved up there, and the old palace city filled with merchants, schools and mosques. Under the Mamluk sultans, from 1250 to 1517, Cairo became one of the biggest cities on earth, and most of what you will see today is theirs. The Ottomans came in 1517, Napoleon in 1798, Muhammad Ali in 1805. Then Khedive Ismail built a European city to the west and left the old one alone, which is partly why so much survived. Today's walk follows that story in order: the bazaar and al-Muizz Street, then Sultan Hassan, the Citadel, and finally Ismail's Abdeen Palace. When you reach the Citadel, look west on a clear day: the pyramids sit on the horizon.

name: Fatimids, Ayyubids, Mamluks, Ottomans: a 5-minute cheat sheet
note: Fatimids: Shia caliphs from Tunisia, founded al-Qahira 'the Victorious' 969, al-Azhar. Ayyubids: Saladin (Kurdish), Sunni restoration, Citadel. Mamluks: slave-soldiers who became sultans, defeated Mongols at Ain Jalut 1260, built most of what you see (Qalawun, al-Nasir, Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay, al-Ghuri). Ottomans 1517. Muhammad Ali 1805 and his dynasty to Farouk 1952. How to tell styles apart: striped ablaq, muqarnas, stone domes with carved patterns.
period: Fatimid 969 to the end of the Muhammad Ali dynasty, 1952
summary: Four dynasties built nearly everything you will see today. Learn who they were and you can roughly date a building by its stripes and domes.
look: Nothing single to look at: use this on the street. Striped red-and-white stone, honeycomb carving over doorways and domes of carved stone mean Mamluk. Pencil-thin minarets and big central domes mean Ottoman or Muhammad Ali. Keel-shaped arches and angular Kufic script often mean Fatimid.
story:
The Fatimids (969-1171) were Isma'ili Shia caliphs who claimed descent from Fatima, the Prophet's daughter. They came from Tunisia with an army of Kutama Berbers, founded al-Qahira and al-Azhar, and ruled a sea-to-desert empire from palaces that have vanished. Their Armenian vizier Badr al-Jamali rebuilt the walls and gates in stone between 1087 and 1092.

Saladin, a Kurdish officer sent by the Syrian ruler Nur al-Din, became vizier in 1169 and abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, turning Egypt back to Sunni Islam. His family, the Ayyubids, fought the Crusaders and began the Citadel. Their armies relied on mamluks: boys bought from the steppes, mostly Kipchak Turks, raised as Muslims, trained as cavalry and then freed.

In 1250, in the middle of Louis IX's crusade, the mamluks of the last great Ayyubid sultan seized power. In 1260 Qutuz and Baybars stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut. Historians split the Mamluk Sultanate into a Turkic 'Bahri' period (1250-1382) and a Circassian 'Burji' period (1382-1517). The throne usually passed from one ex-slave to another rather than father to son, often by murder. Yet these soldiers were the great builders of Cairo: Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad, Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay and al-Ghuri. Sultan al-Ghuri died fighting the Ottoman Selim I in 1516, and Egypt fell in 1517.

Under the Ottomans the Mamluk beys crept back to power until Napoleon arrived in 1798. Then Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer born in Kavala, in today's Greece, took over in 1805. His descendants ruled as pashas, khedives and finally kings until Farouk was overthrown in 1952.
details: Ablaq: alternating courses of dark and light stone around Mamluk doorways and windows. Spot it on the next portal you pass.
Muqarnas: honeycomb niches stepping out under a portal hood or a minaret balcony. Mamluk builders loved them.
Carved stone domes with zigzags or interlacing stars: late Mamluk, mostly 1400s and early 1500s.
Pencil-shaped minarets with conical caps: Ottoman taste. The Muhammad Ali mosque on the Citadel has two.
Keel arches and stiff, angular Kufic letters: Fatimid. See al-Azhar's courtyard and the al-Aqmar facade.
fun_fact: Mamluk means 'owned'. Barquq, once sold as a slave boy, was Egypt's strongman by 1381, when his Christian father came to Cairo, converted to Islam and took the name Anas.
narration: Here is today's cast list, so every building makes sense. First the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia who claimed descent from Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet. They conquered Egypt in 969, founded Cairo and al-Azhar, and lived in palaces you can no longer see. Then Saladin, a Kurdish officer, who abolished their caliphate in 1171, brought Egypt back to Sunni Islam, fought the Crusaders and began the Citadel. His family, the Ayyubids, bought boys from the steppes, trained them as soldiers and freed them. These were the mamluks, a word that means owned. In 1250 the mamluks took the throne for themselves, and ten years later they beat the Mongols at Ain Jalut. For the next 267 years the crown passed from one former slave to another, often by murder, yet these men built most of what you will see today: Qalawun, Sultan Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay and al-Ghuri. In 1517 the Ottoman Turks conquered Egypt and hanged the last Mamluk sultan at Bab Zuwayla. Finally Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer born in Kavala, in today's Greece, took power in 1805, and his family ruled until 1952. A quick key for the street: striped stone, honeycomb carving and carved stone domes are Mamluk. Pencil-thin minarets are Ottoman. Look for the stripes on the next doorway you pass.

name: Khan el-Khalili
note: Built 1382 by emir Jaharkas al-Khalili over the Fatimid caliphs' tombs (he threw out the bones); rebuilt by Sultan al-Ghuri c. 1511 (the surviving gates); the lanes by trade (goldsmiths, coppersmiths, spices, perfume); al-Fishawi café (since 1773) and Naguib Mahfouz; bargaining culture; the Muski street; what is real vs made in China.
period: Mamluk, 1380s; gates rebuilt by al-Ghuri, 1511
summary: A Mamluk emir threw out the bones of the Fatimid caliphs to build a merchants' inn here, and Cairo has been shopping on their graves ever since.
look: The bazaar is a maze of lanes between al-Muizz Street on the west, al-Muski Street on the south and the al-Hussein Mosque on the east. The oldest stonework stands on Sikkat al-Badistan, the lane through the middle: Sultan al-Ghuri's two carved stone gates of 1511. The goldsmiths cluster towards al-Muizz, and the busiest souvenir lanes are near al-Hussein Square.
story:
A thousand years ago this was the southern end of the great eastern palace of the Fatimid caliphs, and the site of their mausoleum, the Turbat az-Za'faran, 'the Saffron Tomb'. When Saladin opened the royal city to everyone, merchants poured in. The old main street filled up with shops, so new trading buildings went east, towards al-Azhar and the shrine of al-Hussein.

In the 1380s, during Sultan Barquq's first reign, his Master of the Stables, Jaharkas al-Khalili, demolished the Saffron Tomb to build a big khan: an inn for travelling merchants, with storerooms round a courtyard, lodgings above and shops on the street. He reportedly tipped the bones of the Fatimid family onto the rubbish hills east of the city. His name stuck, first to the building and then to the whole district.

Around 1511 Sultan al-Ghuri pulled down al-Khalili's khan, rebuilt it and laid out a market street with monumental stone gates, perhaps copying the bedestens of rival Ottoman cities. By 1517 there were 21 khans and wikalas here; by 1798, just before Napoleon, about 39. Under the Ottomans this was the Turkish merchants' quarter. Al-Muski Street was cut through in the 19th century, and much of the eastern sector, the most touristy part, was rebuilt for Princess Shawikar in the late 1930s.

Today it sells souvenirs, antiques and jewellery, while workshops in courtyards and upper floors still beat copper and inlay boxes. Bargaining is expected and friendly. Be aware that many of the cheapest trinkets are imported; handmade brass, inlay and silver cost more and look it.
details: Bab al-Badistan and Bab al-Ghuri: al-Ghuri's carved stone gates of 1511 on Sikkat al-Badistan, the oldest structures in the bazaar.
Opposite Bab al-Ghuri: the half-ruined Wikala of Sulayman Agha al-Silahdar, built in 1837 over a Mamluk khan.
Look up and into courtyards: the workshops on upper floors make some of what is sold below. Follow the hammering.
The goldsmiths' lanes towards al-Muizz Street: this is where Cairenes buy wedding gold, sold by weight.
El Fishawi café, in an alley just off al-Hussein Square: mirrors, brass trays and mint tea since the late 1700s.
fun_fact: In the late 1400s this was Cairo's hub of foreign trade, where precious stones and slaves changed hands. The souvenir papyri came about 500 years later.
narration: You are in Khan el-Khalili, and under your feet lie the Fatimid caliphs, or rather they used to. A thousand years ago this was the end of the great eastern palace, and here stood the Saffron Tomb, where the caliphs were buried. In the 1380s an emir called Jaharkas al-Khalili, Master of the Stables to Sultan Barquq, knocked the tomb down to build a khan: an inn for travelling merchants, with storerooms round a courtyard and bedrooms above. The story goes that he threw the royal bones onto the rubbish heaps outside the walls. His name stuck to the whole district. Around 1511 Sultan al-Ghuri rebuilt the area as a grand market with stone gates, and those gates are the oldest things you can still touch here. By Napoleon's time there were about 39 khans and wikalas in this quarter. Today it is half souvenirs, half real Cairo: local families buy wedding gold from the goldsmiths, and craftsmen still hammer copper in workshops upstairs. Bargain with a smile. Start low, take your time, and be ready to walk away; nobody is offended, and a deal should leave both sides happy. Now find the lane called Sikkat al-Badistan and look for al-Ghuri's carved stone gate, Bab al-Badistan.

name: El Fishawi café and Naguib Mahfouz
note: Short. Open 24h since 1773, mirrors and brass; Nobel laureate Mahfouz wrote there; mint tea, sahlab, shisha; expect tissue sellers and oud players; the Mahfouz novels set in these alleys (Midaq Alley, Cairo Trilogy).
period: Ottoman, late 18th century (1773 or 1797; sources differ)
summary: Open round the clock, mirrors on every wall, and once the regular haunt of Naguib Mahfouz, Egypt's Nobel Prize-winning novelist.
look: A narrow alley just off al-Hussein Square, lined with small tables, brass trays and big carved wooden mirror frames on the walls. There are a few small rooms inside, but most people sit in the alley itself and watch the traffic of sellers and musicians.
story:
The café is named after its first owner, and the same family has run it for at least seven generations. Sources date its opening to 1773 or 1797; either way it is one of Egypt's oldest cafés, and it is open 24 hours a day.

In the 20th century writers and intellectuals made it their sitting room. The most famous regular was Naguib Mahfouz (1911-2006), who was born in the Gamaliya quarter a few minutes north of here and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, still the only Egyptian to do so. His Cairo Trilogy follows one family through these streets from the First World War to 1952, and Midaq Alley is set in a lane of this quarter. The chemist Ahmed Zewail, another Egyptian Nobel laureate, was also a customer.
details: The mirrors: big carved wooden frames along the walls, the café's trademark for generations.
Order mint tea or sahlab, a hot milky drink traditionally thickened with orchid-root flour and topped with nuts and coconut.
Tissue sellers, oud players and shoe-shiners will drift past: a smile and 'la, shukran' (no, thank you) is enough.
Mahfouz's Midaq Alley is set in a lane of this same quarter, close to the Khan.
fun_fact: In 1945 Mahfouz, then a civil servant, asked to be transferred to the library in Sultan al-Ghuri's mausoleum, a short walk from here, and used the job to interview people from his childhood neighbourhood.
narration: This narrow alley of brass tables and old mirrors is El Fishawi, one of the oldest cafés in Cairo. It opened in the late 1700s, it is named after its first owner, and the same family has run it for seven generations. It never closes, day or night. In the 20th century it was a meeting place for writers, and the most famous regular was Naguib Mahfouz, who grew up in this quarter and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. His Cairo Trilogy is set in these very lanes. Order a mint tea or a hot sahlab and watch the alley go by. Then look at the walls: those big carved mirror frames are the café's trademark.

name: Al-Azhar Mosque and University
note: Founded 970-972 by the Fatimids as a Shia foundation, became the chief Sunni university after Saladin; five minarets from different centuries (Qaytbay's double-finial, al-Ghuri's); the Fatimid courtyard; students from all over the Muslim world; dress and shoe etiquette; Sheikh al-Azhar's role today.
period: Fatimid, 970-972; additions to the 18th century
summary: Built in 972 to teach Shia Islam, al-Azhar became the most respected seat of Sunni learning in the world: a thousand-year change of heart.
look: Enter by the Barbers' Gate, Bab al-Muzayinin, then walk through a passage between two 14th-century madrasas and under the Gate of Qaytbay (1495) into the white marble courtyard. Ahead is the prayer hall, its first part Fatimid, its back half an 18th-century extension. Turn round to see the minarets of Qaytbay and al-Ghuri side by side above the way you came in. Shoes come off at the entrance; women cover hair, arms and legs (robes are usually provided), men wear long trousers.
story:
Jawhar, the general who founded Cairo, began the mosque on 4 April 970, and the first Friday prayer was held here on 22 June 972, during Ramadan. It was the congregational mosque of the new Fatimid royal city and a base for spreading Isma'ili Shia teaching. Its name, 'the resplendent', probably echoes al-Zahra, a title of Fatima, from whom the caliphs claimed descent, though another theory links it to the palaces. In 988-989 the vizier Ya'qub ibn Killis paid a group of scholars to teach here, the seed of the university.

Then the tide turned. Saladin, a Sunni, took power in 1171. His chief judge banned Friday prayers here, student stipends were cut, and the silver band naming the Fatimid caliphs was stripped from the mihrab. Nearly a century of neglect followed, until the Mamluk sultan Baybars restored the Friday sermon in 1266. Afterwards sultans competed to leave their mark: Qaytbay built a gate and minaret, al-Ghuri a two-headed minaret in 1509, while Barquq and al-Mu'ayyad both built stone minarets that were so faulty they had to be pulled down.

In the 1750s the Ottoman-era grandee Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda nearly doubled the mosque, adding a prayer hall, three gates and lodgings for students, including a hall for blind students. On 21 October 1798 a revolt against Napoleon's army started here, and the French fired on the mosque.

In 1961 the university was made a separate, state-run institution. Al-Azhar is often called the second-oldest continuously running university after al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, and its Grand Imam is the most prominent voice of Sunni Islam in Egypt. Students still come from all over the Muslim world.
details: Bab al-Muzayinin, the Barbers' Gate (1753), now the main entrance, said to be named after the barbers who shaved students' heads.
The courtyard arcades: keel-shaped arches and carved stucco panels from the Fatimid restoration of 1138.
Al-Ghuri's minaret (1509) near the entrance: it ends in two square shafts with twin bulb tops, like a pair of heads.
Beside it, Qaytbay's carved stone minaret with balconies on honeycomb muqarnas, above his gate of 1495.
In the old prayer hall, the original mihrab: the stucco carving in its semi-dome is probably Fatimid.
fun_fact: In 1800 General Kléber, commander of the French army in Egypt, was stabbed to death by an al-Azhar student, Suleiman al-Halabi. The French closed the mosque until August 1801.
narration: In front of you is al-Azhar, the first mosque of Cairo and one of the oldest universities in the world. Work began in April 970, the year after the Fatimids conquered Egypt, and the first Friday prayer was held here in June 972. The Fatimids were Shia, and they built al-Azhar to teach their faith. The name probably means the resplendent one, an echo of Fatima, the Prophet's daughter, from whom the caliphs claimed descent. Then history flipped. Saladin, a Sunni, took power in 1171, stopped Friday prayers here and cut the teachers' pay. For almost a century the mosque was neglected, until the Mamluk sultan Baybars brought it back in 1266. After that every ambitious sultan wanted his own minaret on al-Azhar, which is why the roofline is a museum of styles. Today al-Azhar is the most respected centre of Sunni learning in the world, with students from across the Muslim world. In 1798 a revolt against Napoleon's army started here, and the French fired on the building. Shoes come off at the gate. Once you are in the white marble courtyard, turn back towards the entrance and look up: the minaret with two heads, side by side like twins, was built by Sultan al-Ghuri in 1509.

name: Al-Hussein Mosque
note: Said to hold the head of Hussein, the Prophet's grandson, brought from Ascalon in 1153; Cairo's most beloved shrine, the mawlid crowds; the 1870s Ottoman-Gothic rebuild; non-Muslims may not be admitted inside the shrine; the square's cafés.
period: Shrine founded 1154; rebuilt 1874
summary: Cairo's best-loved shrine is said to hold the head of the Prophet's grandson Hussein, carried here in 1153 to keep it from the Crusaders.
look: The mosque stands on the square across the road from al-Azhar, with Gothic-style pointed windows, slim Ottoman-style minarets and giant mechanical umbrellas that open to shade worshippers in the plaza. On the south side, the lower part of the gate called Bab al-Akhdar is the only Fatimid survivor, with an Ayyubid minaret of 1237 above it. Non-Muslims are usually not admitted, but you can see the outside from the square.
story:
Hussein, son of Ali and Fatima and grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, was killed at Karbala in Iraq in 680. According to Fatimid tradition his head was later buried at Ascalon on the coast of Palestine, where the vizier Badr al-Jamali built a shrine after it was 'rediscovered' in 1091. As the Crusaders advanced, Caliph al-Zafir had the casket dug up and brought to Cairo. It arrived on 2 September 1153 and was buried close to the caliphs' own Saffron Tomb. The shrine was finished in 1154. Damascus and Karbala also claim the head, but for Cairenes there is no doubt.

The building was rebuilt under the Ayyubids in 1237 and burned eleven years later. What you see is mostly Khedive Ismail's reconstruction of 1874, a mix of Gothic Revival and Ottoman styles.
