A side room added in 1893 keeps relics believed to have belonged to the Prophet, including part of a cloak, a staff, a sword and four hairs. The mosque was restored in 1996 and renovated again in 2022.

At the mawlid, the festival of Hussein's birthday, the square fills with Sufi orders, chanting, food stalls and huge crowds from all over Egypt.
details: South side: the lower part of Bab al-Akhdar, the 'Green Gate', is the only piece left of the 1154 Fatimid shrine.
Above that gate, the Ayyubid minaret of 1237 with carved arabesque panels, the oldest minaret here.
The giant steel-and-Teflon umbrellas over the plaza fold open mechanically to shade worshippers, on the Saudi model.
The cafés along the square: a good seat to watch families arrive after Friday prayers.
fun_fact: The relic room holds a lantern-shaped case said to contain four strands of the Prophet's hair, and a Quran on deer skin attributed to Ali himself.
narration: The mosque in front of you is al-Hussein, for many Cairenes the holiest place in the city. Tradition says it holds the head of Hussein, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at Karbala in Iraq in 680. According to the Fatimid story, the head was buried at Ascalon on the coast of Palestine. When the Crusaders closed in, the caliph had it carried to Cairo, where it arrived in September 1153 and was buried beside the tombs of the caliphs themselves. Damascus and Karbala also claim the head, but here nobody doubts it. The building you see is mostly from 1874, when Khedive Ismail rebuilt it with Gothic pointed windows and Ottoman pencil minarets. On Hussein's birthday festival the square fills with Sufi chanting and huge crowds. Non-Muslims are usually not allowed inside, so enjoy it from the square. Walk round to the south side and find the old door called the Green Gate: its lower part is the last piece of the original Fatimid shrine, and the minaret above it dates from 1237.

name: Al-Muizz Street: the Fatimid spine
note: 1 km from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla along the Fatimid Qasaba, 'the greatest concentration of medieval monuments in the Islamic world'; Bayn al-Qasrayn 'between the two palaces' where the Fatimid palaces stood; restored 2008, pedestrian; order of monuments walking south; Mahfouz's Palace Walk; lit at night.
period: Fatimid street laid out 969-970; monuments 11th to 19th centuries
summary: One kilometre between two Fatimid gates, lined with mosques, tombs, schools and fountains from nine centuries: medieval Cairo's main street.
look: The street runs about 1 km north to south inside the old walls, from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla, and busy al-Azhar Street cuts across it near the middle. The northern half holds the grandest buildings, above all Bayn al-Qasrayn, where Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad and Barquq stand shoulder to shoulder on your right as you walk south. South of al-Azhar Street it turns into a crowded market street leading past al-Ghuri to Bab Zuwayla.
story:
Jawhar laid out the street in 969-970 as the spine of the new royal city. Known as the Qasaba, it ran from Bab al-Futuh in the north to Bab Zuwayla in the south and passed between the caliphs' two great palaces, across the open square of Bayn al-Qasrayn, 'between the two palaces'. Under the Fatimids ordinary people were not allowed into the city at all.

After 1171 Saladin moved the court to the Citadel, the palaces were demolished and their sites redeveloped. The Qasaba became the most prestigious address in Cairo: the route of royal processions and the city's main market. Ayyubid and Mamluk rulers lined it with madrasas, mausoleums and mosques, each funded by a waqf, a charitable trust whose shops and rents paid the staff forever. Al-Salih Ayyub's madrasa (1250), Qalawun's complex (1285), al-Nasir Muhammad's madrasa (1303) and Barquq's (1386) all stand on the old palace square. Ottoman officials and Muhammad Ali's family later added charity fountains and houses.

In the 20th century al-Azhar Street sliced the street in two. From 1997 the government restored 34 monuments along it and about 67 nearby, repaved it in its old style, lowered some tall modern buildings and added night lighting. Some find the result a little polished, but it is the easiest place in the Islamic world to walk through so much medieval architecture in one go.

Naguib Mahfouz named the first volume of his Cairo Trilogy after this stretch: Bayn al-Qasrayn, translated as Palace Walk.
details: Bayn al-Qasrayn: Qalawun (1285), al-Nasir Muhammad (1303) and Barquq (1386) side by side on your right as you walk south.
The stretch by Qalawun is still called al-Nahhasin, the coppersmiths' street: listen for hammering in the side shops.
Small kiosks with bronze grilles are sabils, charity fountains; the Katkhuda sabil at the fork is the finest.
Cross al-Azhar Street to reach al-Ghuri's two buildings facing each other, then the twin minarets on Bab Zuwayla.
Come back after dark if you can: the façades are floodlit and the street fills with Cairene families.
fun_fact: You are walking well above the Fatimid street: when Bab Zuwayla was restored, the ground had risen nearly two metres since it was built.
narration: You are on al-Muizz Street, the old main street of Fatimid Cairo, about a kilometre long from the northern gate, Bab al-Futuh, to the southern gate, Bab Zuwayla. When the Fatimids laid it out in 969, it ran between the caliphs' two great palaces, and the stretch in the middle is still called Bayn al-Qasrayn, between the two palaces. Back then ordinary Cairenes were not even allowed inside the walls. After Saladin moved the court up to the Citadel, the palaces were pulled down and this became the most prestigious address in the city. Every sultan who could afford it wanted his tomb and his school here, on the route of the great processions, with rows of shops underneath to pay for the upkeep forever. That is why you can walk past nine centuries of buildings in twenty minutes: Fatimid mosques, Mamluk tombs, Ottoman fountains and merchant houses. From 1997 the street was restored, repaved and lit at night. Naguib Mahfouz named the first novel of his Cairo Trilogy after this stretch: Palace Walk. Walking south, look out on your right for three giant facades in a row: Sultan Qalawun, his son al-Nasir Muhammad, and Sultan Barquq.

name: Bab al-Futuh and Bab al-Nasr, the Fatimid gates
note: Built 1087 by Armenian vizier Badr al-Jamali with three architects from Edessa; Byzantine-style military architecture, rounded (Futuh) vs square (Nasr) towers, machicolations; Napoleon's troops carved their names (Tour Julien); the wall walk between them; the Northern Cemetery beyond.
period: Fatimid, 1087
summary: Two stone gates of 1087, built for an Armenian vizier like a Byzantine fortress, with the names of Napoleon's officers still carved on the towers.
look: Bab al-Futuh, with two rounded towers, closes the north end of al-Muizz Street. A short walk east along the same wall stands Bab al-Nasr, with square towers. Between them runs a stretch of the stone wall, with the minaret of al-Hakim's mosque built into it. Step outside the gates to see them as an attacker would have.
story:
Cairo's first walls of 969 were mud brick. In 1087 the vizier Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian general who had restored order for Caliph al-Mustansir, rebuilt them in stone, starting with Bab al-Futuh, 'the Gate of Conquests', and Bab al-Nasr, 'the Gate of Victory'. Bab Zuwayla in the south followed in 1092. The chronicler al-Maqrizi says three Christian monks from Edessa, today's Urfa in south-east Turkey, designed the gates, and the stonework does look closer to northern Syrian or Byzantine fortifications than to anything Cairo had built before.

Bab al-Futuh is 22 metres high. Its arch carries carved lozenges, and the overhang between the towers rests on brackets shaped as ram's heads: the ram is the sign of Mars, the planet linked to Cairo's name. Bab al-Nasr's square towers are carved with round shields and swords, and a panel over the arch carries the Shia creed naming Ali, the Fatimid signature.

In 1798-1801 Napoleon's army held these walls. The French named each tower after an officer, and you can still read 'Tour Julien' and 'Tour Courbin' carved near the top of Bab al-Nasr. Julien was one of Bonaparte's aides-de-camp.
details: Bab al-Futuh's outer face: two stone brackets above the arch are carved as ram's heads, the sign of Mars.
Bab al-Nasr's towers: carved round shields and swords, and the French names 'Tour Julien' and 'Tour Courbin' up high.
The panel over Bab al-Nasr's arch: the Shia creed with the name Ali, a Fatimid signature in stone.
Between the gates: al-Hakim's northern minaret, wrapped in its square bastion and built into the wall in 1087.
Ask the guardian whether the wall walk between the gates is open; access changes.
fun_fact: Just outside Bab al-Nasr lies Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, the Swiss explorer who found Abu Simbel in 1813. He died in Cairo in 1817 and was buried as 'Sheikh Ibrahim'.
narration: These are the northern gates of Fatimid Cairo, rebuilt in stone in 1087 by the vizier Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian general who had restored order for the caliph. Bab al-Futuh, the Gate of Conquests, has rounded towers. A short walk east along the wall is Bab al-Nasr, the Gate of Victory, with square towers carved with shields and swords. The chronicler al-Maqrizi says three Christian monks from Edessa, in today's Turkey, designed them, and the masonry does look more like a Byzantine fortress than anything Cairo had built before. Seven centuries later Napoleon's soldiers manned these walls, named each tower after an officer, and carved the names into the stone. And just outside Bab al-Nasr lies Burckhardt, the Swiss explorer who found Abu Simbel, which you will see tomorrow. Now look at the outer face of Bab al-Futuh, just above the arch: two stone brackets are carved as ram's heads, the sign of Mars, the planet that may have given Cairo its name.

name: Mosque of al-Hakim
note: Begun 990, finished 1013 by the 'mad caliph' al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah who banned molokheya and women's shoes, vanished on the Muqattam in 1021 (Druze await his return); the odd minaret bastions; used as a prison for Crusaders, Napoleon's fort, a boys' school; rebuilt in marble by the Bohra Ismailis 1980.
period: Fatimid, 990-1013
summary: Finished by the caliph remembered as 'mad', this vast mosque has been a prison, a stable, a fortress and a school before turning white marble in 1980.
look: Just inside Bab al-Futuh, on your left as you walk in, a huge courtyard of 120 by 113 metres, more than twice the size of al-Azhar, is ringed by arcades. Since 1980 nearly everything gleams in white marble and gold trim. The two minarets stand at the front corners inside massive square bastions; the northern one is built into the city wall.
story:
Caliph al-Aziz began the mosque in 990, and his son al-Hakim inaugurated it in Ramadan 1013, spending 40,000 dinars on the building. Al-Hakim (985-1021) is the 'Mad Caliph' of Western books. In 1009 he ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem; he forced Christians and Jews to wear distinguishing marks, and chroniclers say he banned mulukhiyya and ordered women to stay indoors. Some modern historians think his enemies made a monster of him. On the night of 12-13 February 1021 he rode into the Muqattam hills and never came back; only his horse and bloodstained clothes were found. The Druze, whose faith took shape around him, revere him.

In 1010 the minarets were encased in brick bastions. Nobody knows why: one theory is political, another links it to his growing puritanism. Later the mosque decayed. It held Crusader prisoners, was a stable under Saladin, a fort under Napoleon, a museum from 1890 and a boys' school in the 20th century.

In 1980 the Dawoodi Bohras, an Ismaili community from India who see the Fatimids as their imams, rebuilt it in marble. Conservationists objected, but a ruin became a working mosque again.
details: The bastions round the minarets: the original towers of 1003 survive inside; the tops were rebuilt after the 1303 earthquake.
The northern minaret meets Badr al-Jamali's wall of 1087: see it from the wall side by Bab al-Futuh.
Original Fatimid survivals: carved stucco, wooden tie-beams and Kufic inscriptions along the prayer hall arches.
Bohra pilgrims: men in white with gold-trimmed caps, women in brightly coloured two-piece robes.
fun_fact: Chroniclers say al-Hakim banned mulukhiyya, the slimy green leaf stew that is now practically Egypt's national dish. Cairenes forgave him nothing and kept cooking it.
narration: You are in the mosque of al-Hakim, the second great mosque of Fatimid Cairo, twice the size of al-Azhar. It was begun in 990 and finished in 1013 by the caliph al-Hakim, a ruler Western writers call the Mad Caliph. He ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem destroyed, and chroniclers say he banned mulukhiyya stew and ordered women to stay indoors. Some historians now think his enemies exaggerated. In February 1021 he rode out alone into the Muqattam hills at night and never returned. Only his horse and his bloodstained clothes were found, and the Druze still revere him. His mosque fell on hard times: a prison for Crusader captives, a stable, a fort for Napoleon's army, a boys' school. In 1980 the Bohras, an Ismaili community from India, rebuilt it in gleaming white marble. Now look at the front corners: the minarets are wrapped in massive square bastions, added in 1010 for reasons nobody can fully explain.

name: Bayt al-Suhaymi: a Cairene merchant's house
note: 1648 + 1796, Darb al-Asfar; the salamlik/haramlik split, mashrabiya screens (see out, not in, cool the air, jars of water), the courtyard garden, the bath, the marble fountains in the qa'a; how wealthy Ottoman Cairo lived; Mahfouz's Palace Walk house.
period: Ottoman, 1648, enlarged up to the 1790s
summary: The best place in Cairo to see how a rich Ottoman-era family lived: a courtyard garden, screened windows and separate worlds for men and women.
look: Down Darb al-Asfar, a lane running east off al-Muizz just north of al-Aqmar, a plain door leads through a passage that turns a corner into a courtyard garden with trees. Around it rise rooms on several levels behind turned-wood mashrabiya screens. Men were received around the courtyard on the ground floor; the women's rooms are upstairs.
story:
Abd al-Wahab al-Tablawi built the house in 1648 on Darb al-Asfar, then one of the smartest and most expensive lanes in Cairo. A later owner, Hajj Ismail Shalabi, added another wing. In 1796 Sheikh Ahmad al-Suhaymi bought it and absorbed neighbouring houses into it. His family lived here for generations, until they sold it in 1931 to the committee that looked after Cairo's monuments.

The plan is all about privacy and air. The entrance passage bends so that nobody at the street door can see into the courtyard. Downstairs, around the courtyard and in an open loggia, the master entertained his male guests. Upstairs, the women's quarters look down through mashrabiya screens of turned wood: from inside you see everything, from outside the screen looks solid, and the breeze passes through. The grand reception hall has marble floors, a fountain and painted wooden ceilings, and the house even had its own small bath.

The house was restored in 1996 with a grant from the Arab Fund, together with neighbouring houses, and is now a museum of how old Cairo lived.
details: The bent entrance passage: it turns so that no one at the street door could see into the family courtyard.
The maq'ad, an arched loggia upstairs facing the courtyard, where men sat in the breeze.
Upstairs, stand behind a mashrabiya: you see the courtyard clearly, while from below the screen looks solid.
The main reception hall: marble paving, a fountain in the lower centre, and painted wooden ceilings.
Look for the family's private bath, a luxury few Cairo houses had.
fun_fact: Mashrabiya probably comes from the Arabic for 'drinking': porous water jars were set in the screened niches to cool in the breeze.
narration: Welcome to Bayt al-Suhaymi, the house of a wealthy Cairo family, and one of the best places to imagine daily life in the old city. It was built in 1648 by Abd al-Wahab al-Tablawi, enlarged by a later owner, and bought in 1796 by Sheikh Ahmad al-Suhaymi, whose family absorbed the houses next door and lived here until 1931. Notice how you came in: the entrance passage turns a corner, so nobody at the street door could see into the courtyard. The whole house is built around privacy and shade. Downstairs the master received his male guests. Upstairs, the women's rooms look down through screens of turned wood called mashrabiya. You can see out, but nobody can see in, and the breeze passes through. Jars of water were set in the window niches to cool. Go upstairs and try it: stand behind a mashrabiya, look down into the courtyard garden, and imagine watching the guests arrive without ever being seen.

name: Sabil-Kuttab of Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda
note: 1744, where the street forks: a sabil (public fountain, charity water from a cistern) below and a kuttab (Quran school for orphans) above; Iznik-style tiles inside; the type is Cairo's signature charity building; Katkhuda the great Ottoman patron.
period: Ottoman, 1744
summary: Free water downstairs, a boys' school upstairs: Cairo's favourite kind of charity building, placed where the street forks so everyone sees it.
look: A small two-storey building on a triangle of land where al-Muizz splits into two lanes, so three of its sides stand free. Below, each side has a rounded bay on marble columns with a metal grille: this is the sabil, where water was handed out. Above, behind wooden screens under a painted roof, was the kuttab, the Quran school.
story:
Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda (died 1776) was a Mamluk grandee who rose to command the Janissaries, the leading Ottoman army corps in Egypt, and became the greatest builder of 18th-century Cairo. He nearly doubled al-Azhar and rebuilt the dome over Qalawun's tomb. In 1744 he set this sabil-kuttab on the triangle where the street forks, so that it closes the view for anyone walking up from Bayn al-Qasrayn.

A sabil is a charity fountain. A cistern under the floor was filled with Nile water, and an attendant passed it out through the grilles, which have openings wide enough for a cup. Giving water to the thirsty is among the most praised good deeds in Islam, and a sabil kept its founder's name on people's lips. The kuttab upstairs taught local boys, often orphans, to read and recite the Quran. Cairo builders had combined the two since Mamluk times.

The style is Mamluk two centuries after the Mamluks lost power: grey and white stone with marble inlay. Inside the sabil room are Ottoman tiles, one showing the Great Mosque of Mecca, and the entrance inscription quotes the Quran's story of the People of the Cave.
details: The metal grilles of the sabil windows: openings sized so a cup could pass through to the water.
Upstairs: the kuttab's wooden screens and painted roof, where the boys sat and recited.
Inside the sabil room, if open: Ottoman tiles, including a view of the Great Mosque of Mecca.
Over the entrance: verses about the People of the Cave, a theme Katkhuda used on his buildings.
Walk all the way round: three free façades, each with its marble columns.
fun_fact: The People of the Cave in the inscription are the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, young Christians who slept for centuries in a cave near the Greek city: a story told in both the Quran and Greek Christian tradition.
narration: This little building where the street forks is a sabil-kuttab, a charity fountain with a school on top, built in 1744 by Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda, the greatest builder of 18th-century Cairo. He commanded the Janissaries, the leading Ottoman army corps in Egypt, and he also enlarged al-Azhar. Downstairs is the sabil. Under the floor was a cistern filled with Nile water, and an attendant handed out free drinks through the grilles. Giving water to the thirsty is one of the most praised good deeds in Islam, and patrons competed to put a sabil on the busiest corners. Upstairs, behind the wooden screens, was the kuttab, a primary school where local boys, often orphans, learned to read and recite the Quran. Katkhuda chose this spot so that the building closes the view for anyone walking up from the palaces. Walk round it: three sides stand free, and in each window grille you can see openings just big enough to pass a cup through.

name: Al-Aqmar Mosque: the 'moonlit' façade
note: 1125, first Cairo mosque with a decorated stone street façade aligned to the street while the interior turns to Mecca; the shell niche with 'Muhammad' and 'Ali' medallion (Shia Fatimid); the 'bent' plan; tiny and easy to miss.
period: Fatimid, 1125
summary: A small Fatimid mosque of 1125 that solved an old Cairo problem: its façade follows the street while the prayer hall inside turns to Mecca.
look: Easy to miss: a grey stone façade on the east side of al-Muizz, just north of the fork with the Katkhuda fountain. The doorway sits under a niche carved like a scallop shell, with a round pierced medallion in its centre. The left half of the façade is original Fatimid carving; the right half is a 1990s copy of it.
story:
The vizier al-Ma'mun al-Bata'ihi built this neighbourhood mosque in 1125 for Caliph al-Amir, near the north-east corner of the eastern palace. He did not enjoy it long: he was arrested that same year and executed three years later. 'Al-Aqmar' is usually translated 'the moonlit', one of the light names the Fatimids gave their mosques, like al-Azhar, 'the resplendent'.

Its trick was new. A mosque must face Mecca, but the street did not, so the builders aligned the façade with the street and turned the interior, making the walls thicker on one side to absorb the difference. It was also the first mosque with its whole street front covered in carving, an idea every later builder on this street copied. The medallion over the door carries the names Muhammad and Ali, a statement of the Fatimids' Shia legitimacy.

The Mamluk emir Yalbugha al-Salimi restored the mosque in the 1390s and added the minaret, whose upper part fell in 1412. In 1993 the Dawoodi Bohras renovated it and rebuilt the southern half of the façade as a copy of the northern half.
details: The shell hood over the door, ribbed like a real scallop, with a pierced medallion naming Muhammad and Ali.
The cut-off left corner: a small muqarnas niche set at an angle so traffic could turn into the side lane.
At the far left: a carved window grille, read either as a mihrab or as the window where the caliph showed himself.
Compare the halves: the left is Fatimid original; the crisper right half is the 1990s copy.
Under the cornice: fragments of the foundation inscription naming Caliph al-Amir and his vizier.
fun_fact: The angled corner may be Cairo's oldest piece of traffic engineering: carved in 1125 so that people and loaded animals could turn into the alley without scraping the wall.
narration: This small grey facade is al-Aqmar, the Moonlit Mosque, built in 1125 by the vizier al-Mamun al-Bataihi for the Fatimid caliph. The vizier did not enjoy it for long: he was arrested that same year and executed three years later. Al-Aqmar solved a problem every builder on this street would face. A mosque must face Mecca, but the street does not. So the builders made the facade follow the street and turned the prayer hall inside, making the walls thicker on one side to absorb the difference. It is also the first mosque in Cairo with its whole street front carved with decoration. Look at the doorway: above it is a niche carved like a scallop shell, and in its centre a round pierced medallion carries the names Muhammad and Ali, a statement of the Fatimids' Shia faith. Now look at the left corner of the building. It is cut off at an angle, with a small carved niche, so that people and animals could turn into the side lane without bumping into the wall.

name: Complex of Sultan Qalawun: mausoleum, madrasa and hospital
note: 1284-85, built in 13 months with Crusader columns from Acre; the mausoleum is the most lavish Mamluk interior in Cairo (marble, mother-of-pearl, stucco, the dome's inner octagon echoing the Dome of the Rock); the bimaristan hospital treated all free with music therapy and separate wards, operated 600 years; the madrasa; Qalawun founder of a dynasty.
summary: A sultan's tomb, a college and a free hospital built in about a year; the hospital went on treating Cairenes for more than 500 years.
look: On the west side of Bayn al-Qasrayn, a façade about 67 metres long with tall pointed-arch panels, a minaret by the entrance and a striped arch over the door. A long corridor runs inside, with the madrasa on your left and the mausoleum on your right; the hospital lay beyond. The mausoleum is the room not to miss: piers and columns in an octagon under a high dome, walls of marble mosaic and carved stucco, and painted, gilded ceilings.
story:
Qalawun was a mamluk, a Kipchak Turk bought as a slave soldier, who became sultan in 1279 and beat the Mongols at the Second Battle of Homs. His descendants held the throne, with interruptions, for about a century. In 1284 he began his funerary complex on the ruins of the Fatimid Western Palace, and the speed was astonishing: the hospital went up in under six months, and the whole complex took about thirteen.

The speed had a price. The historian al-Maqrizi says the overseer, the emir Sanjar al-Shuja'i, used forced labour, including Mongol prisoners, seized property and evicted residents, and some scholars urged a boycott of the building. The columns of the mausoleum reportedly came from the palace of Qalawun's old master, al-Salih, on Roda Island.

The bimaristan, or hospital, was the heart of the gift. Al-Maqrizi says Qalawun had once fallen ill in Damascus, been treated in Nur al-Din's hospital there, and vowed to build one. Its endowment paid for treatment, medicines, food, clothing and the teaching of medicine. It kept working into the late Ottoman period, more than 500 years, before most of it was demolished in 1910.

The mausoleum holds Qalawun and his son al-Nasir Muhammad. Four piers and four columns form an octagon under the dome, a plan many historians compare with the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. New emirs were invested here, beside the founder's tomb. The dome itself is a 1908 reconstruction, after an earlier Ottoman rebuild by Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda.
details: The façade: tall pointed-arch panels framing windows, which scholars compare to Gothic work of the Crusader period.
Mausoleum: four piers and four columns in an octagon carrying the dome, the plan likened to the Dome of the Rock.
The mausoleum mihrab, often called the most lavish in Cairo: a horseshoe niche framed by marble columns.
The madrasa mihrab, left of the corridor: glass and mother-of-pearl mosaic in deep red, with scrolling vines.
The minaret by the entrance: three storeys, rebuilt by al-Nasir Muhammad after the 1302 earthquake.
fun_fact: The tomb chamber was also a ceremonial stage: new Mamluk emirs were invested here, swearing loyalty beside the founder of the dynasty.
narration: This long facade belongs to the complex of Sultan Qalawun: a mausoleum, a college and, behind them, one of the great hospitals of the Middle Ages. Qalawun was a mamluk, a Turkish slave soldier who became sultan in 1279 and founded a dynasty that held the throne for about a century. He built all this in 1284 and 1285, astonishingly fast: the hospital in less than six months, the whole complex in about thirteen. The speed had a price. A chronicler tells us the overseer used forced labour, including Mongol prisoners, and threw people out of their houses, and some scholars urged a boycott. The hospital, though, was a real gift. Qalawun had once been treated in a hospital in Damascus and vowed to build one himself. Here patients received treatment, medicine, food and clothes, all paid for by the endowment, and it kept working for more than 500 years. Inside, the corridor leads to the mausoleum on your right. Qalawun lies here, and so does his son al-Nasir Muhammad. Look up at the ring of columns and piers carrying the dome: many historians see in it an echo of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem.

name: Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad (with the Gothic portal)
note: 1295-1304; the marble Gothic portal was looted from a Crusader church in Acre (1291) and re-erected here, a trophy; the stucco minaret with North African/Andalusian style; al-Nasir Muhammad's three reigns and Cairo's peak.
period: Mamluk, about 1295-1303
summary: Its marble doorway is a Gothic church portal, carried off from Acre after the last great Crusader city fell in 1291 and set up here as a trophy.
look: Squeezed between Qalawun and Barquq, a narrow façade with a white marble Gothic portal: a pointed arch with triple recesses and slender colonettes. Right above the door rises the minaret, its lowest storey covered in fine carved stucco. Inside, little survives but the stucco mihrab; the dome over the tomb fell in 1870 and was never rebuilt.
story:
The madrasa was begun around 1295 by Sultan al-Adil Kitbugha, who had pushed aside the boy sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. When al-Nasir returned to power he finished it and inaugurated it in 1303. The façade inscription still carries the original foundation date: he simply had his own name put in place of Kitbugha's.

The portal comes from Acre. In 1291 Qalawun's son al-Ashraf Khalil captured the city, the last great Crusader stronghold, and sent the emir Sanjar al-Shuja'i to demolish its walls and churches. The emir had this portal taken down and moved intact to Cairo. Which church it came from is disputed: St Andrew, St Agnes and St John the Baptist have all been proposed. Kitbugha seized it and installed it here, a trophy of the end of the Crusades.

Al-Nasir Muhammad became sultan at nine in 1293, lost the throne twice, and ruled for real from 1310 to 1341, the high point of Mamluk Cairo. He was not buried here: fearing unrest, his emirs buried him secretly in his father's mausoleum next door. This tomb holds his mother and his son Anuk.
details: The apex of the Gothic arch: the word Allah carved into a Christian church portal.
The minaret's lower storey: dense stucco medallions and keel-arched niches, possibly by North African or Andalusian craftsmen.
Inside, the stucco mihrab, the last of its kind in Egypt, close in style to work from Tabriz in Mongol Iran.
Look up in the tomb chamber: the dome fell in 1870, and a plain wooden roof replaced it.
fun_fact: This is one of only three madrasas in Cairo that taught all four schools of Sunni law under one roof.
narration: Look at this doorway carefully, because it is a Gothic church portal. In 1291 the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil captured Acre, the last great Crusader city on the coast of Palestine. One of his emirs demolished its walls and churches and had this marble portal taken down and carried intact to Cairo. Historians still argue which church it came from. A few years later Sultan Kitbugha set it up here, in front of his new madrasa, as a trophy of victory. Kitbugha had pushed aside the boy sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun. But al-Nasir came back, finished the building in 1303, and simply had his own name carved in place of Kitbugha's. During his third reign, which lasted until 1341, Cairo reached its peak. He is not buried here, though: he was laid secretly in his father's tomb next door. Now look up to the top of the pointed arch. Right at its apex, carved into a Christian portal, is the word Allah.

name: Madrasa-Khanqah of Sultan Barquq
note: 1384-86, first Circassian (Burji) Mamluk sultan; the bronze-plated door, porphyry columns, the painted ceiling of the prayer hall; the Sufi khanqah function; Barquq's daughter buried in the dome, he himself in the Northern Cemetery.
summary: Built by the first Circassian sultan, a former slave who lost his throne and won it back, it hides one of Cairo's finest painted ceilings.
look: The northernmost of the three great façades of Bayn al-Qasrayn, with a tall portal and bronze-plated doors patterned with stars. A vaulted vestibule leads to a courtyard with four iwans and striped stone. The largest iwan, the prayer hall, is divided by reused ancient columns into three aisles under a painted and gilded wooden ceiling; the domed tomb chamber opens off it.
story:
Barquq was a Circassian from the Caucasus, enslaved as a boy and bought into the household of the emir Yalbugha around 1363. In November 1382 he deposed the last of Qalawun's line and took the throne, opening the Circassian, or Burji, period of Mamluk rule. In 1389 rebels captured him and locked him in the castle of Kerak, in today's Jordan, but he was back in Cairo by February 1390 and reigned until his death in 1399.

The façade inscription dates the building from December 1384 to April 1386. The supervisor was Jarkas al-Khalili, the emir who founded Khan el-Khalili, and the architect Ahmad al-Tuluni, whose relatives Barquq married. The workers were paid, unlike Qalawun's. The foundation deed lists a Friday mosque, a college teaching the four Sunni law schools to 125 students, and a khanqah, a lodge for sixty Sufis.

The tomb chamber holds Barquq's daughter Fatima, and his father's remains were moved here. Barquq himself lies in the Northern Cemetery, in the great khanqah completed by his son Faraj. Thieves stripped much of the ornament from the minbar and the door in 2012 and 2013.
details: The bronze-plated doors: geometric patterns built on 18- and 12-pointed stars.
Around the doorway: a Quranic inscription whose letter tops are knotted like flowers.
The prayer hall ceiling: painted and gilded wood like an illuminated Quran page, the largest single Mamluk wooden roof.
The marble floor of the prayer hall, with mosaic panels shaped like little mihrabs.
The tomb chamber: the dome was rebuilt in 1893, but the wooden pendentives at its base are original.
fun_fact: The emir who supervised this building, Jarkas al-Khalili, is the same man whose khan gave Khan el-Khalili its name, a few minutes' walk away.
narration: This is the madrasa and khanqah of Sultan Barquq, finished in 1386. Barquq was a Circassian from the Caucasus, sold as a boy into slavery, and in 1382 he became the first of a new line of Mamluk sultans. His career had a twist: in 1389 rebels overthrew him and locked him in the castle of Kerak, in today's Jordan, but within a year he was back on the throne. The building did three jobs. It was a Friday mosque, a college for 125 students of Islamic law, and a khanqah, a lodge where 60 Sufi mystics lived and prayed on a stipend. The man who supervised the work was Jarkas al-Khalili, the same emir who gave his name to Khan el-Khalili. The domed tomb holds Barquq's daughter, not Barquq himself: he lies in the Northern Cemetery, in a complex finished by his son. Walk through to the prayer hall and look up. The painted and gilded wooden ceiling, patterned like a page of an illuminated Quran, is the largest single wooden roof of the Mamluk age.

name: Al-Ghuri complex and Wikala: the last Mamluk sultan
note: 1503-05, mosque-madrasa and mausoleum facing each other across the street (the roof once covered the silk market); Qansuh al-Ghuri died at Marj Dabiq 1516 fighting the Ottomans, body never found; the Wikala al-Ghuri caravanserai (five storeys, merchants below, lodgings above) now hosts the Tannoura Sufi whirling show (Wed/Sat evenings).
period: Late Mamluk, 1503-1505
summary: The last great Mamluk sultan built a mosque and a tomb facing each other across the street, then died in battle and never lay in his tomb.
look: Just south of al-Azhar Street, two buildings face each other across al-Muizz, joined by a wooden roof over the cloth market between them. On the west stands the mosque-madrasa with its tall square minaret; on the east, the mausoleum and Sufi hall, with a sabil-kuttab on the corner. His caravanserai, the Wikala al-Ghuri, is a short walk east along al-Azhar Street.
story:
Qansuh al-Ghuri ruled from 1501 to 1516. He had been governor of Tarsus and chamberlain of Aleppo, loved music, poetry, flowers and Sufis, and paid for his showcase buildings partly by confiscating property. His mosque opened with a banquet in May 1503; relics of the Prophet were moved into the mausoleum in 1504. The tomb's dome was covered in tiles described as lapis blue, so unstable that it was rebuilt in 1512-13 and finally pulled down in 1860.

In 1516 he marched north against the Ottoman sultan Selim I. At Marj Dabiq near Aleppo his governor Khayrbak changed sides mid-battle, the old sultan collapsed and died, and his body was never found. Within months the Ottomans held Cairo, and Selim shipped the building's marble to Istanbul.

Nearby, the Wikala al-Ghuri (1504-05) rises five storeys round a courtyard: animals and goods on the ground floor, merchants above, and three floors of rented apartments on top. Its rents helped pay for the complex. Today it houses craft workshops and evening shows of Sufi whirling, the tannoura.
details: The minaret: a square shaft ending in five little domed heads, a 19th-century replacement for al-Ghuri's original four.
The sabil-kuttab on the corner of the eastern building: water below, school above, marble star paving inside.
Under the wooden roof: clothes and cloth stalls continue the textile market whose rents paid for the buildings.
Wikala al-Ghuri: five storeys round a courtyard. The tannoura show runs only on certain evenings, so check; the 16th is a Friday.
fun_fact: In 1945 the young civil servant Naguib Mahfouz asked to be posted to the library in this mausoleum, and used the job to interview people from his old neighbourhood.
narration: The two buildings facing each other here are the complex of Qansuh al-Ghuri, the last great Mamluk sultan, built between 1503 and 1505. On one side is his mosque and college, with the tall square minaret. On the other is his mausoleum and a hall for Sufis. The wooden roof between them shades the cloth market, whose rents helped pay for it all. Al-Ghuri loved music, poetry and flowers, and he paid for his buildings partly by confiscating other people's property. In 1516 he marched north to fight the Ottoman sultan Selim. Near Aleppo, in the middle of the battle, one of his governors switched sides. The old sultan collapsed and died, and his body was never found. So the splendid tomb he built here never received him. A few months later the Ottomans took Cairo. A short walk east is his caravanserai, the Wikala al-Ghuri, where Sufi whirling dancers perform on some evenings. Now look up at the minaret: its top ends in a cluster of little domed heads, a late Mamluk flourish.

name: Mosque of Sultan al-Mu'ayyad and Bab Zuwayla
note: The 1092 southern Fatimid gate where heads were displayed and the last Mamluk sultan Tumanbay was hanged by the Ottomans in 1517 (rope broke twice); al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh built his mosque 1415-21 on the site of the prison where he had been held, and put his twin minarets on top of the gate: climb them for the best view of the street; the door was taken from Sultan Hassan's mosque.
period: Bab Zuwayla 1092; Mosque of al-Mu'ayyad 1415-1421
summary: A sultan who once suffered in a prison here tore it down and built his mosque on the spot, with two minarets planted on top of the city gate.
look: Bab Zuwayla is the southern gate of the Fatimid city: two rounded stone towers with a vaulted passage between them, topped since 1419-1420 by the two slim minarets of the mosque next door. The mosque of al-Mu'ayyad stands just inside the gate on the west side of the street, its tall façade and great bronze door facing al-Muizz. A ticket usually lets you climb onto the gate and up the minarets.
story:
The vizier Badr al-Jamali built the gate in 1092, naming it after Fatimid soldiers of the Zawila Berber tribe from the Libyan Sahara. For centuries it was Cairo's place of execution. In 1260 Sultan Qutuz hung the heads of Mongol envoys here before marching to victory at Ain Jalut. In 1517 the Ottomans hanged Tumanbay, the last Mamluk sultan, in this gateway; the story goes that the rope broke twice.

Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh, bought as a boy by Sultan Barquq, was once jailed in a prison on this site. Al-Maqrizi says he suffered from fleas and lice there and vowed to turn it into a place of learning if he ever came to power. He took the throne in 1412, demolished the prison, and from 1415 built this mosque and college for 40,000 dinars, perching its two minarets on the gate's towers. Inscriptions inside them name the builder, Muhammad ibn al-Qazzaz. He also took the bronze door and a chandelier from Sultan Hassan's mosque. He lies in the domed mausoleum with his son.

Later the gate gained a saint, Mitwalli al-Qutb, and people nailed hair or scraps of clothing to its doors to ask for help against illness.
details: The gate's wooden doors: each leaf weighs about three and a half tonnes.
The mosque's bronze-covered door: made for Sultan Hassan's mosque, taken by al-Mu'ayyad.
The mausoleum dome beside the gate: carved stone with a zigzag pattern, typical of the early 1400s.
From the minaret tops: al-Muizz Street running north, and the Citadel and Muhammad Ali's mosque to the south-east.
fun_fact: The prisoner kept his vow with interest: the lice-ridden jail became one of 15th-century Cairo's leading colleges, where the great scholar Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani taught law.
narration: In front of you is Bab Zuwayla, the southern gate of Fatimid Cairo, built in 1092 and named after a regiment of Berber soldiers from the Libyan desert who camped here. For centuries this was where Cairo hanged criminals and displayed heads. In 1260 the Mamluk sultan hung the heads of Mongol envoys here before beating the Mongols in battle. And in 1517 the conquering Ottomans hanged the last Mamluk sultan, Tumanbay, in this gateway; the story goes that the rope broke twice. The two minarets on top belong to the mosque next door. Its founder, Sultan al-Muayyad, had once been a prisoner in a jail on this very spot, tormented by fleas and lice. He swore that if he ever came to power he would turn the prison into a holy place. He did, between 1415 and 1421, and he even took his great bronze door from the mosque of Sultan Hassan. If the ticket office is open, climb up to the minarets: from the top you look straight down al-Muizz Street, the whole Fatimid city at your feet.

name: Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan
note: 1356-63, built with Black Death inheritances; 36 m portal, the four iwans for the four Sunni law schools with student cells behind; the cruciform plan, the chains of lamps, the mausoleum behind the qibla (Hassan's body never found, two sons buried there); the minaret that collapsed killing 300; used as a fortress to bombard the Citadel; scale: 150 m long, 8,000 m2.
summary: Medieval Cairo's biggest and most expensive mosque, paid for partly with the estates of plague victims, and so massive it served as a fortress.
look: Facing the Citadel across the square, a cliff of stone about 150 metres long, 68 wide and 36 high. The entrance portal rises 38 metres, and much of its decoration was never finished. Inside, a dark bent passage opens into a huge courtyard with four vaulted iwans; the biggest, facing Mecca, has the domed mausoleum directly behind it. The surviving tall minaret reaches about 84 metres above the street.
story:
An-Nasir Hasan, a son of al-Nasir Muhammad, became sultan at thirteen in 1347, a puppet of his emirs. He was deposed in 1351 and held for three years, returned to power, and in 1361 was murdered by his own mamluk Yalbugha al-Umari. His body was never found.

Work began in 1356, in the years after the Black Death had swept Cairo. The money came from austerity, from the seized estates of plague-killed emirs and from extortion. Al-Maqrizi says it cost 30,000 dirhams a day and over a million dinars in all, the most expensive mosque of medieval Cairo. Craftsmen came from across the empire, including Anatolia, and limestone is believed to have been quarried from the Giza pyramids.

The four iwans are said to have housed the four Sunni law schools, and each corner hides its own madrasa with a courtyard and four storeys of student cells. Unusually, the mausoleum sits right behind the qibla wall; it holds two of Hassan's young sons. In 1361 one of four planned minarets collapsed and killed around 300 people, including children at a school below, and the plan was abandoned.

The building's size and position made it a fortress. In 1391 Barquq had the entrance stairs destroyed and the door blocked; in 1517 Tumanbay held out inside while the Ottomans bombarded it from the Citadel, and a 1660 account describes the dome full of cannonball holes.
details: The portal: look high up for patterns drawn onto the stone but never carved out, left as they were in the 1360s.
The long chains hanging in the iwans once held enamelled glass lamps; originals survive in museums.
The qibla iwan's band of Kufic script: the Quran's chapter of Victory, running round the hall.
Through a door beside the mihrab: the mausoleum, with Hassan's two sons buried under the dome.
Doors in the courtyard corners lead into the four madrasas: peek in at the cells stacked several storeys high.
fun_fact: The bronze-covered door you would once have walked through is now on al-Mu'ayyad's mosque by Bab Zuwayla: in the early 1400s that sultan acquired it for a modest price.
narration: You are standing under Sultan Hassan, the largest and most expensive mosque of medieval Cairo, built between 1356 and 1363. Hassan became sultan at thirteen, a puppet of his emirs, and was murdered in 1361; his body was never found. How did he pay for this? Partly with death. The Black Death had just swept through Cairo, and the estates of emirs who died of plague were seized for the treasury. A chronicler says the work cost 30,000 silver coins a day. Craftsmen came from all over the empire, and some of the stone is believed to come from the pyramids of Giza, which you saw on the 12th. Disaster struck in 1361, when one of the planned minarets collapsed and killed about 300 people, many of them children at a school below. Inside, four huge vaulted halls face the courtyard, said to be one for each of the four schools of Sunni law, with student lodgings packed into the corners. The building was so massive and so close to the Citadel that rebels used it as a fortress, and in 1517 the Ottomans bombarded it with cannon. As you go in, look high up on the great portal: parts of the carving were never finished.

name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque: royal tombs and the Shah of Iran
note: 1869-1912, commissioned by Khedive Ismail's mother Khushyar Hanim to mirror Sultan Hassan across the street; neo-Mamluk; tombs of Khedive Ismail, King Fuad I, King Farouk (died Rome 1965) and the last Shah of Iran Mohammad Reza Pahlavi (1980) whose first wife Fawzia was Farouk's sister; Sufi sheikh al-Rifa'i's shrine.
period: Khedival, 1869-1912 (neo-Mamluk)
summary: A royal mosque built to match Sultan Hassan across the lane, where Egypt's last kings and the last Shah of Iran are buried.
look: Across the narrow lane from Sultan Hassan, a building of similar height and colour with a dome and two minarets: from a distance most people cannot tell which one is medieval. Inside, the royal tombs lie in chambers around the prayer hall, richer and shinier than any Mamluk interior. Ask the guardian to point out the tombs of King Farouk and the Shah.
story:
The site once held a small Fatimid-era mosque, later a lodge of the Rifa'i Sufi order with the tomb of Ali Abu Shubbak, grandson of the order's founder, Ahmad al-Rifa'i. In 1869 Hoshiyar Qadin, mother of Khedive Ismail, commissioned a far bigger mosque to replace it and to serve as her family's mausoleum. Her architect, Hussein Fahmi Pasha, died during the first phase, work stopped after Ismail lost his throne, and Hoshiyar died in 1885. Khedive Abbas II restarted the project in 1905 under the Hungarian architect Max Herz, and it was finished in 1912.

It was designed in the neo-Mamluk style to stand level with Sultan Hassan, a way for the new dynasty to borrow medieval glory. Buried here are Hoshiyar, Khedive Ismail, Sultan Hussein Kamel, King Fuad I and King Farouk, the last king of Egypt, who died in exile in Rome in 1965. So is Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah of Iran, who died in Cairo in July 1980. His father, Reza Shah, also lay here from 1944 until 1950, when he was taken home to Iran.
details: Stand in the lane between the two mosques: the profiles match on purpose, built about 550 years apart.
King Farouk's tomb: the last reigning king of Egypt, who died in Rome in 1965.
The tomb of the last Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who died in Cairo in July 1980.
The shrine of the Sufi saint Ali Abu Shubbak al-Rifa'i, still visited by followers of the order.
fun_fact: The Shah's first wife was Princess Fawzia, King Farouk's sister; she and her father, King Fuad, are also listed among those buried here.
narration: The mosque facing Sultan Hassan looks medieval, but it was finished in 1912. It was commissioned in 1869 by Hoshiyar, the mother of Khedive Ismail, on the site of a small Sufi shrine, to be a mosque and a mausoleum for her family. Work stopped when Ismail lost his throne, and it was completed decades later under the Hungarian architect Max Herz. The builders deliberately matched the scale and style of Sultan Hassan across the lane, so that the new dynasty would stand shoulder to shoulder with Mamluk glory. Inside lie Hoshiyar herself, Khedive Ismail, King Fuad, and King Farouk, the last king of Egypt, who died in exile in Rome in 1965. And here too lies an unexpected guest: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah of Iran. After the revolution of 1979 he moved from country to country until Egypt took him in, and he died in Cairo in 1980. His first wife was Farouk's sister. Stand in the lane between the two mosques and compare them: the same height, the same mood, but about 550 years apart.

name: The Citadel of Saladin
note: Begun 1176 by Saladin with Crusader prisoners and stones from small Giza pyramids; seat of government for 700 years until Khedive Ismail moved to Abdeen 1874; Muhammad Ali's 1811 massacre of the Mamluks at the Bab al-Azab gate (the legend of the one who jumped his horse over the wall); Northern vs Southern enclosures; what to see in 90 minutes; the view over Cairo to the pyramids on a clear day.
period: Ayyubid, begun 1176; Mamluk and 19th-century additions
summary: For almost 700 years Egypt was ruled from this hilltop fortress, from Saladin to Khedive Ismail, and in 1811 it saw the massacre that ended the Mamluks.
look: The Citadel sits on a spur of the Muqattam hills above the old city. The Southern Enclosure holds the Muhammad Ali mosque, al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque, the Gawhara Palace and Joseph's Well; the Northern Enclosure, once the soldiers' quarter, holds the Military Museum. The terrace beside the Muhammad Ali mosque gives the great view west over Cairo. In 90 minutes: the Alabaster Mosque, al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque, the terrace, then the Gawhara Palace or the Military Museum.
story:
Saladin began the Citadel in 1176, a few years after abolishing the Fatimid caliphate, to defend Cairo against the Crusaders and give his new regime a safe seat. His eunuch and confidant Baha al-Din Qaraqush ran the works. Christian prisoners of war provided labour, and besides stone from the Muqattam hills Qaraqush quarried several of the small pyramids at Giza. An inscription on Bab al-Mudarraj, the only surviving original gate, dates completion to 1183-84.

Saladin's successors moved in, and the Mamluks filled the hill with palaces. Al-Nasir Muhammad built the striped Ablaq Palace, the domed Great Iwan and his mosque of 1318. After 1517 Selim I stripped the marble and shipped it to Istanbul, and the Citadel was divided between Ottoman garrison corps.

On 1 March 1811 Muhammad Ali invited the Mamluk leaders to a ceremony up here. As they rode down the narrow lane towards Bab al-Azab, his Albanian soldiers fired on them from above, and several hundred died. Legend says one bey leapt his horse over the wall and escaped. Muhammad Ali then demolished the Mamluk palaces and built his own mosque and palaces. In 1874 Khedive Ismail moved the government to Abdeen Palace, ending the Citadel's role as the seat of power. The British garrisoned it until 1946, and from 1983 it opened to visitors as a group of museums.
details: The terrace by the Muhammad Ali mosque: Sultan Hassan and al-Rifa'i right below, the old city beyond, Giza on the horizon.
Bab al-Azab (1754), the lower western gate: the sunken lane leading to it is where the Mamluks were shot in 1811.
Al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque (1318): the only major Mamluk building left on the hill.
Northern Enclosure: the Military Museum in Muhammad Ali's Harem Palace, with a MiG-21 jet outside.
Also inside: the Carriage Museum and the Police Museum in the old prison. Skip them if time is short.
fun_fact: Saladin's builders took stone from small pyramids at Giza, so some of the walls around you are recycled from the plateau you saw on the 12th.
narration: You are on the Citadel, the fortress from which Egypt was ruled for almost 700 years. Saladin began it in 1176, a few years after ending the Fatimid caliphate, to protect Cairo from the Crusaders and to keep his own new regime safe. His right-hand man, the eunuch Qaraqush, ran the works. Christian prisoners of war did much of the labour, and Qaraqush took stone from several of the small pyramids at Giza, so some of these walls are made of what you saw on the 12th. Mamluk sultans later filled the hilltop with palaces, and the Ottomans shipped their marble off to Istanbul. Then, on the first of March 1811, came the Citadel's darkest day. Muhammad Ali, the new ruler, invited the Mamluk leaders to a ceremony up here. As they rode down the narrow lane to the lower gate, his soldiers opened fire from above, and several hundred were killed. Legend says one bey leapt his horse over the wall and escaped. With his rivals gone, Muhammad Ali rebuilt the Citadel in his own image, and his family ruled from here until 1874. Now walk to the terrace beside the great mosque and look west: the old city lies below you, and on a clear day the pyramids stand on the horizon.

name: Mosque of Muhammad Ali (the Alabaster Mosque)
aliases: big Ottoman mosque on the Citadel
note: 1830-48 by Yusuf Bushnaq, an Istanbul-style Ottoman mosque (like Sultan Ahmed) deliberately un-Mamluk to mark the new dynasty; alabaster cladding from Beni Suef; the clock tower a 1845 gift from Louis-Philippe in exchange for the Luxor obelisk (now in Paris), reportedly never worked; Muhammad Ali's tomb (moved 1857); the chandeliers and the 365 lamps.
period: Muhammad Ali dynasty, founded 1830, built 1832-1857
summary: Cairo's skyline signature is an Istanbul-style mosque, built by an Ottoman officer from Kavala to show Egypt it had a new, non-Mamluk master.
look: Visitors usually come in through a side gate into a big arcaded courtyard faced with alabaster, with a domed ablution fountain in the middle and an iron clock tower over the wall opposite the prayer hall. The prayer hall is almost square, about 45 by 46 metres, under a central dome 52 metres high, with four half-domes, four corner domes and rings of hanging lamps. Muhammad Ali's tomb is in its western corner, near the courtyard wall, behind a bronze screen.
story:
Muhammad Ali was born in 1769 in Kavala, in today's northern Greece. He came to Egypt with the Albanian troops of the Ottoman army sent against the French, made himself ruler in 1805, destroyed the Mamluks in 1811 and set about building a modern army and state. On the highest point of Cairo, after clearing the ruined Mamluk palaces, he began a mosque in 1830 that would look nothing like the Mamluk city below. A neo-Mamluk design by the French architect Pascal Coste was rejected; the building took the form of Istanbul's imperial mosques, such as the Sultan Ahmed and Şehzade mosques. The architect is uncertain: some sources name Yusuf Bushnaq from Istanbul, others suggest a Greek or an Armenian.

Muhammad Ali insisted on alabaster, partly to revive a declining local industry, so the lower walls and courtyard are faced with it. The upper panels were removed before completion and reused in the palaces of his successor Abbas I. The minarets rise over 80 metres.

The clock tower was a gift from King Louis-Philippe of France around 1846, in exchange for the Luxor obelisk that has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since 1836. The clock was long out of order until King Farouk had it repaired.

Muhammad Ali died in 1849; his body was moved here in 1857, when the decoration was finished under his son Said. By the 1930s the domes were cracking, and between 1935 and 1939 they were dismantled and rebuilt to the original design.
details: Muhammad Ali's tomb: Carrara marble behind a bronze openwork screen, in the prayer hall's western corner by the courtyard wall.
The clock tower over the courtyard: Louis-Philippe's gift of about 1846, paid for with a Luxor obelisk.
Two pencil minarets of over 80 metres, Ottoman style, each with two balconies and a conical cap.
Two pulpits: the tall original wooden minbar, and King Farouk's smaller alabaster one of 1939.
The ablution fountain in the courtyard: carved marble under a wooden canopy, in a Baroque taste.
fun_fact: France got a Ramesses II obelisk more than 3,000 years old; Egypt got a clock that did not keep working for long. You will see the obelisk's twin at Luxor Temple on the 22nd.
narration: This is the mosque of Muhammad Ali, the domes and pencil minarets you see from all over Cairo. Muhammad Ali was an Ottoman officer born in 1769 in Kavala, in today's northern Greece. He came to Egypt with Albanian troops to fight the French, made himself ruler in 1805, and in 1811 wiped out the Mamluks just below this hilltop. Then he cleared their ruined palaces away and, from 1830, built a mosque that looks like nothing the Mamluks built: a pure Istanbul design, modelled on the imperial mosques of the Ottoman capital. The message was clear. Egypt had a new dynasty, and it looked to Istanbul and to Europe. He insisted on facing it with Egyptian alabaster, to revive a local craft, which is why people call it the Alabaster Mosque. Out in the courtyard, the iron clock tower was a gift from King Louis-Philippe of France, given in return for an obelisk from Luxor Temple that now stands in Paris. Cairenes like to say the clock never worked properly. Muhammad Ali died in 1849 and lies inside. Go into the prayer hall and look for the bronze screen in the corner by the courtyard wall: behind it stands his marble tomb.

name: Mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad on the Citadel
note: 1318-35, the only Mamluk building left on the Citadel, royal mosque of the sultans; reused Pharaonic and Roman columns in the arcades; the two minarets with Persian-style green faience tops (Tabriz craftsmen); the Ottomans used it as a stable; the Selim I Ottoman conquest.
period: Mamluk, 1318, enlarged 1335
summary: The royal mosque of the Mamluk sultans, the only major Mamluk building left on the Citadel, with a minaret top tiled like a Persian mosque.
look: A short walk from the Muhammad Ali mosque stands a plain, crenellated block about 63 by 57 metres around an open courtyard. Inside, the arcades rest on reused columns of every size and style, and the dome over the prayer niche stands on red granite columns. The minaret above the main entrance ends in a bulbous, garlic-shaped top sheathed in green, white and blue faience.
story:
Al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun, finished the mosque in 1318 as the Citadel's royal mosque, where the sultans came for Friday prayers. He prayed here daily, using a side room behind an iron grille as his private retreat, and he chose preachers by making each candidate preach in front of him. The endowment was so generous that the surplus bought land and shops. Ibn Battuta praised his virtue; the chronicles add that he was short and lame, with a cataract in one eye.

In 1335 the walls were raised, the roof rebuilt, and a green-tiled dome set over the prayer niche. The walls are said to use limestone taken from the pyramids, and the ten red granite columns came from ancient temples. The faience-covered minaret top is unique in Cairo; it was probably made by a craftsman from Tabriz, in Mongol-ruled Iran, at a time when al-Nasir was on friendly terms with the Mongols.

After 1517 Selim I carried off its marble panelling to Istanbul, the dome collapsed, and the arcades were walled up as prison cells and storerooms. In the British period an army officer, Charles Moore Watson, had prisoners strip out the plaster walls. Today it is open but seldom crowded.
details: The minaret over the main entrance: a garlic-shaped top in green, white and blue faience, unique in Cairo.
The arcades: columns of every size and style, pulled from older buildings. Compare the mismatched capitals.
Under the dome by the mihrab: red granite columns taken from ancient Egyptian temples.
Over the doors: inscriptions naming al-Nasir Muhammad son of Qalawun and the Hijra year 718, that is 1318.
The bare upper walls: the marble dado was stripped and shipped to Istanbul by Selim I after 1517.
fun_fact: This was the sultans' Friday mosque, and al-Nasir Muhammad auditioned his preachers personally: every candidate had to give a sermon in front of him.
narration: While everyone queues for the Alabaster Mosque, this plainer building is the real survivor: the mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad, the only major Mamluk monument left on the Citadel. Al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun, finished it in 1318 as the royal mosque of the palace, where the sultans came for Friday prayers, and he enlarged it in 1335. He chose his preachers in person, making each candidate deliver a sermon in front of him. Chroniclers describe him as short and lame, with a cataract in one eye, yet his reign was the high point of Mamluk Cairo. Inside, the arcades stand on columns of every size, collected from older buildings, and the dome rests on red granite columns from ancient temples. After the Ottoman conquest of 1517, Sultan Selim stripped its marble panelling and shipped it to Istanbul, and later the mosque served as a prison and storehouse. Now look up at the minaret over the main entrance: its bulging top is covered in green, white and blue tiles, a Persian touch probably brought by a craftsman from Tabriz.

name: Gawhara Palace and the Mamluk massacre site
note: Short. 1814 palace of Muhammad Ali (named after his last wife Gawhara), French-Ottoman style, where he received envoys; his portrait, the throne; fire in 1972; near the Bab al-Azab where the 470 Mamluk beys were shot in 1811 after a banquet.
period: Muhammad Ali dynasty, 1814
summary: Muhammad Ali's reception palace, built by craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania, where he received envoys on a throne from Italy.
look: A two-storey Ottoman-style pavilion just south of the Muhammad Ali mosque, with European windows and terraces looking west over the city. Inside, the reception hall holds his throne, a huge chandelier and paintings of foreign ambassadors being received.
story:
Muhammad Ali commissioned the palace in 1814, three years after the massacre of the Mamluks a short way down the hill. Craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania built it as a Turkish-style kiosk, and the French architect Pascal Coste later added quarters for servants and officials. The name, Gawhara, means 'jewel', and it is often said to honour one of his wives.

Fire destroyed the wooden building in 1822, and gunpowder explosions caused another in 1824. Each time he rebuilt it grander, with Italian marble, terraces, orange groves and a menagerie with a lion, two tigers and an elephant. In the divan, the reception hall, he received guests under a 1,000 kg chandelier sent by King Louis-Philippe of France. The palace was damaged again by fire in 1972.
details: The throne: a gift to Muhammad Ali from the King of Italy.
The 1,000 kg chandelier in the reception hall, sent by Louis-Philippe of France.
Paintings of foreign ambassadors being presented to the pasha.
From the terraces: the old city and, on clear days, the pyramids.
fun_fact: In 1825 an English visitor, Anne Elwood, described a grand room here for dancing, with deep niches for conversation and side rooms for music, reading, games and refreshments.
narration: This elegant pavilion is the Gawhara Palace, built in 1814 for Muhammad Ali, three years after he massacred the Mamluks a short way down this hill. Craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania built it in Turkish style, with European windows and a view over the whole city. Here the pasha received foreign ambassadors, sitting on a throne given by the King of Italy, under a huge chandelier sent by the King of France. Fire damaged the palace more than once, and each time he rebuilt it grander. Inside, look for the throne and the paintings of envoys being presented to him.

name: Joseph's Well (Bir Yusuf)
note: Short. 87 m spiral well cut through rock by Crusader prisoners c. 1176 to give the Citadel water in a siege; oxen walked down the ramp to turn the waterwheels; named after Saladin (Yusuf), not the biblical Joseph; usually closed, viewable from above.
period: Ayyubid, about 1176-1183
summary: A well about 85 metres deep, cut through the rock for Saladin's Citadel, where oxen walked down a spiral ramp to turn the waterwheels.
look: In the Southern Enclosure, a square opening in the rock with a wide upper shaft wrapped by a spiral passage. It is usually closed to visitors, but you may be able to look down from the top.
story:
A fortress on a dry hill needs water that no besieger can cut off. Saladin's overseer Baha al-Din Qaraqush, who also built the walls, had a well dug through the rock, about 85 metres deep. It is called Bir Yusuf, after Saladin's own first name, Yusuf, the Arabic form of Joseph, not after the Joseph of the Bible, though guides happily tell both stories.

The well works in two stages. A spiral stair winds round the wide upper shaft, and it could be covered with earth to make a ramp for oxen. At the bottom of the upper section two oxen turned a waterwheel; a second wheel at the top, also driven by oxen, lifted the water the rest of the way.
details: The spiral passage round the upper shaft: oxen once walked down it to their waterwheel.
The name: Yusuf was Saladin's birth name, the Arabic form of Joseph.
Usually locked: ask at the gate, but do not count on going down.
fun_fact: Its other name, Bir al-Halazon, means the Snail Well, after the spiral passage coiled round the shaft.
narration: This opening in the rock is Joseph's Well, one of the cleverest works on the Citadel. A fortress on a dry hill needs water that no besieger can cut off, so Saladin's builder Qaraqush had a shaft cut down through the rock, about 85 metres deep. It is called Bir Yusuf after Saladin himself, whose first name was Yusuf, the Arabic Joseph, not after the Joseph of the Bible. A spiral ramp winds around the upper shaft, and oxen walked down it to turn a waterwheel deep inside, while a second team at the top lifted the water the rest of the way. It is usually closed, but if you can, look down into the spiral.

name: The Egyptian Military Museum (Harim Palace)
note: Short. In Muhammad Ali's Harim Palace (1827); dioramas from Pharaonic armies to 1973; the Korean-made panoramas; mainly for the palace interiors; the tanks outside; skip if short on time.
period: Harem Palace 1812; museum here since 1949
summary: Egypt's army museum fills Muhammad Ali's old harem palace: come as much for the 19th-century rooms as for the cannons.
look: In the Northern Enclosure of the Citadel, a long 19th-century palace with tanks, guns and a MiG-21 jet parked outside. Inside, hall after hall of weapons, uniforms and battle scenes, set in the rooms of Muhammad Ali's household palace.
story:
Muhammad Ali built the Haram, or Harem, Palaces in the Northern Enclosure in 1812 as private quarters for his household. The army museum was founded in 1937 in the old War Ministry building downtown, moved to a temporary home in Garden City, and came here in November 1949. It was renovated in 1982, 1993 and 2011.

The halls run from Ottoman and Muhammad Ali-era militaria through the wars of 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973 and the revolution of 1952. The 1973 war is covered only briefly, because a separate museum, the 6th of October Panorama, is devoted to it. If time is short, skip this one: the Citadel's mosques and view come first.
details: Outside: tanks, artillery and a MiG-21 jet fighter on display.
The Ottoman and Muhammad Ali militaria hall: swords, firearms and uniforms of the pasha's new army.
Look up and around: the rooms of Muhammad Ali's household palace are often more interesting than the displays.
fun_fact: The museum moved twice before settling in a harem: the private family quarters of the man who built Egypt's first modern conscript army.
narration: This long palace in the Northern Enclosure was built in 1812 for Muhammad Ali's household, the Harem Palace, and since 1949 it has housed Egypt's National Military Museum. Outside stand tanks, guns and a MiG-21 jet. Inside, the halls run from the swords and uniforms of the Ottoman and Muhammad Ali era to the wars of the 20th century. Fair warning: unless you love military history, the building is the main attraction, so walk through at your own pace and enjoy the palace rooms themselves. If time is short, skip it and spend the time on the view instead. Before you leave, take a look at the MiG parked outside.

name: Abdeen Palace
note: Built 1863-74 by Khedive Ismail to move government from the Citadel and make Cairo 'Paris on the Nile'; 500 rooms; the 1942 Abdeen incident when British tanks forced King Farouk to appoint a prime minister; the 1952 revolution; museums open to visitors: arms, royal family, silver, presidential gifts; still a presidential palace: strict security, no photos in parts.
period: Khedival, 1863-1874
summary: The palace that replaced the Citadel as Egypt's seat of power in 1874: 500 rooms, the royal home until 1952, and still a presidential palace.
look: A long European-style façade on Abdeen Square, in the 19th-century city west of the old town. Visitors see only the museums on the lower floors: arms, silver, the royal family, presidential gifts and historical documents. Security is strict: expect bag checks, have your passport with you, and ask before taking photographs.
story:
Khedive Ismail, Muhammad Ali's grandson, wanted a modern capital and a modern seat of government, away from the medieval Citadel. He built on the site of a small mansion belonging to one Abdeen Bey, whose name the palace keeps. Work began in 1863 and the palace was inaugurated in 1874. The French architect Léon Rousseau designed it with a crowd of Egyptian, Italian and French decorators. It cost 700,000 Egyptian pounds to build and two million more to furnish, and it has about 500 rooms. Joseph Urban added a wing in 1891, and Fuad I a garden in 1921.

From 1874 until the revolution of 1952 it was the main official residence of the royal family. Its most dramatic day was 4 February 1942, when British tanks surrounded the palace and the ambassador, Sir Miles Lampson, forced King Farouk to appoint Mustafa el-Nahhas as prime minister. Since 1952 it has been one of the presidential palaces, and the upper floors are kept for visiting dignitaries.

The Historical Documents Museum, opened in 2005, holds the Ottoman firman that made Egypt hereditary in Muhammad Ali's family.
details: The Arms, Silver, Royal Family and Presidential Gifts museums fill the lower floors; allow about an hour.
The Historical Documents Museum (2005): the Ottoman firman that founded Muhammad Ali's dynasty.
Look out for the clocks: the palace is full of them, most decorated with gold.
Abdeen Square in front: where British tanks drew up on 4 February 1942.
fun_fact: The documents include a certificate of the Order of the Iron Crown from the Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia, a short-lived South American kingdom almost nobody has heard of.
narration: Abdeen Palace marks the moment Egypt's rulers came down from the hill. For nearly 700 years they had governed from the Citadel. Then Khedive Ismail, Muhammad Ali's grandson, who wanted a modern, European-looking capital, built this palace on the site of a small mansion that belonged to one Abdeen Bey, and in 1874 moved the government here. It has about 500 rooms, a French architect, and cost 2.7 million Egyptian pounds with its furniture. Kings lived here until 1952. Its most dramatic day came on the 4th of February 1942, when British tanks surrounded the palace and the British ambassador forced King Farouk to appoint the prime minister Britain wanted. Today it is still a presidential palace, so security is tight and only the museums on the lower floors are open: arms, silver, the royal family and presidential gifts. As you walk through, look out for the clocks: the palace is full of them, most decorated with gold.

name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun (if you have time)
note: 876-879, Cairo's oldest mosque in original form, Samarra-style brick with the spiral minaret (legend: Ibn Tulun twisted a piece of parchment); 2 km from the Citadel, Gayer-Anderson house next door (Bond's 'The Spy Who Loved Me' scene). Optional detour.
period: Tulunid, 876-879
summary: Cairo's oldest mosque still in its original form: a vast brick courtyard of 879 and a minaret you climb by a stair that spirals round the outside.
look: About 2 km west of the Citadel, a huge square courtyard ringed by brick arcades on piers, with a domed fountain in the middle, all inside an outer enclosure. The minaret stands in that enclosure on the side away from Mecca, its stair winding round the outside. The Gayer-Anderson Museum adjoins the south-east corner.
story:
Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish officer who had spent his early career at the Abbasid capital of Samarra in Iraq, became governor of Egypt in 868 and soon ruled it as his own. He built this mosque in 876-879 as the centrepiece of his new city, al-Qata'i, in the Samarra style: brick piers, carved stucco and an outer enclosure. When the Abbasids razed the city in 905, they spared the mosque.

The minaret's date is debated. Some scholars credit it to Sultan Lajin, who hid in the ruined mosque after a sultan's murder, vowed to restore it, and did so in 1296. Next door, two 16th- and 17th-century houses form the Gayer-Anderson Museum, and parts of the Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me were shot at the mosque.
details: The minaret's outside spiral stair: the historian Ibn Duqmaq said it was wide enough for two camels.
Lajin's domed fountain of 1296 in the centre of the courtyard.
Under the ceiling: a wooden frieze of Kufic Quran text, nearly 2 km long in total.
The 128 stucco window grilles: a few of the simplest are original, the rest later.
fun_fact: Legend says Ibn Tulun was absent-mindedly twisting a strip of parchment round his finger in a meeting, and when asked what he was doing, said he was designing his minaret.
narration: If you have time for one detour, make it the mosque of Ibn Tulun, the oldest mosque in Cairo that still looks the way it was built, between 876 and 879. Ahmad ibn Tulun was a Turkish officer who had served the caliphs in Samarra, in Iraq, and he built in the Samarra style: brick piers, carved plaster and a huge open courtyard. When his city was burned in 905, only this mosque was spared. Legend says he designed the minaret by twisting a strip of parchment round his finger. Walk out to it and look at the staircase spiralling around the outside; if it is open, climb it for a wide view over the domes.

name: How to read a Mamluk building: ablaq, muqarnas, mashrabiya
note: Visual glossary: ablaq striped masonry, muqarnas stalactite vaults over portals, mashrabiya turned-wood screens, iwan vaulted hall, qibla/mihrab/minbar, dikka, sabil, kuttab, madrasa, khanqah, wikala, carved stone domes (zigzag, star), the tiraz inscription band; and the Mamluk blazons (cup for cupbearer, pen box for secretary).
period: Mamluk, 1250-1517, and after
summary: A handful of words unlocks every building today: learn ablaq, muqarnas, iwan and sabil, and the façades start talking.
look: A glossary for the street. Start at the portal: a tall recess crowned by honeycomb muqarnas, often with striped ablaq stone around the arch. Then look up at the dome, which may be carved stone, and the minaret, usually built in three different tiers. Inside a madrasa, find the courtyard and its iwans.
story:
Ablaq is masonry in alternating courses of light and dark stone, as on the arch over Qalawun's entrance. Muqarnas are small niches stacked in tiers like honeycomb or stalactites; they carry portal hoods, minaret balconies and the corners of domes. By the late 13th century Mamluk portals had become tall recesses crowned with muqarnas, and Sultan Hassan's is the grandest. Mashrabiya is a lattice of small turned-wood pieces for windows and balconies: air in, eyes out.

An iwan is a hall open on one side to a courtyard; the four-iwan plan became standard for Mamluk madrasas. The qibla is the direction of Mecca, the mihrab the niche marking it, the minbar the stepped pulpit, and the dikka a platform for those who repeated the prayers to the crowd. A madrasa is a college, a khanqah a Sufi lodge, a sabil a charity fountain, a kuttab a Quran school, a wikala a merchants' inn, and a waqf the endowment that paid for it all.

From around 1400 domes were built of carved stone, first with zigzags, as on al-Mu'ayyad's mosque, then geometric and floral patterns, peaking under Qaytbay. Later Mamluk minarets usually had an octagonal first tier, a round second and a lantern with a bulb on top. The Ottomans brought pencil-shaped minarets.
details: Portals: a tall recess with a muqarnas hood. Sultan Hassan's is the grandest; Barquq's is a classic.
Ablaq: the striped stone of the arch over Qalawun's entrance.
Mashrabiya: the turned-wood screens at Bayt al-Suhaymi and on the Katkhuda kuttab.
Dome carving: zigzags on al-Mu'ayyad's dome by Bab Zuwayla; later domes carry stars and flowers.
Blazons: al-Ghuri's name in round medallions over the side iwan arches of his mosque.
fun_fact: Mamluk emirs put their old palace jobs on their coats of arms: a cup meant a former cupbearer, a pen box a secretary, crossed polo sticks the master of polo.
narration: Here is a pocket glossary for the buildings around you. Start at the door. Mamluk portals are tall recesses topped by muqarnas, little niches stacked in rows like honeycomb or stone stalactites. Around the arch you often see ablaq, bands of light and dark stone in alternation. On windows and balconies, the wooden lattices of small turned spindles are mashrabiya, letting the breeze in and keeping eyes out. Inside a madrasa, which is a college, the courtyard is usually framed by iwans, great halls open on one side. The biggest faces Mecca and holds the mihrab, the prayer niche, and beside it the minbar, the stepped pulpit. A khanqah is a lodge for Sufis, a sabil gives free water, a kuttab is a primary school, and a wikala is an inn for merchants. Now look up. From about 1400 domes were built in stone and carved, first with zigzags, later with stars and flowers. Minarets usually have three tiers of different shapes.
