The tomb held more than 80 pieces of footwear, from simple sewn sandals of plant fibre to decorated shoes; a study by André Veldmeijer examined 81 of them. One wooden pair shows bound foreigners, an Asiatic and a Nubian, on the insoles: every step was a small daily conquest. On the mummy itself, the feet wore gold sandals and each toe had its own gold cap.

The feet also feed a medical argument. A 2010 study of the mummy reported a clubfoot and bone disease in the left foot and pointed to the many walking sticks in the tomb. Other experts argue the damage happened after death. The debate is open.
details: Find the sandals with bound captives on the insoles: an Asiatic and a Nubian under the royal heel.
Look for the gold sandals and the gold toe caps that were on the mummy's feet.
Notice the plain plant-fibre sandals: everyday royal footwear, not so different from anyone else's.
fun_fact: Even in death the king's toes were dressed individually: each toe and finger of the mummy had its own gold cap.
narration: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 80 pieces of footwear, from plain sandals of plant fibre to gold. Look for the wooden pair with bound prisoners on the insoles, a foreigner from Asia and one from Nubia. Every time the king took a step, he trod on his enemies. The mummy itself wore gold sandals, and each of his toes had its own gold cap. His feet are also part of a medical puzzle. A 2010 study reported a clubfoot and bone disease in his left foot, and pointed to the many walking sticks found in the tomb. Other experts think the damage happened after death. Now find the captives on the soles, and look at their faces.

name: The wooden 'mannequin' bust
note: Painted wooden torso with a flat-topped crown, no arms, found in the Antechamber; perhaps a dress form for the king's clothes and jewellery, or a ritual figure. Gives his face without idealisation.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: A painted wooden torso of the king with no arms and a flat-topped crown: maybe a dummy for his clothes, maybe something more magical.
look: This life-size head and torso is carved in wood, plastered and painted, and ends at the waist with no arms. The king wears a flat-topped crown, and the face is young and soft. It was found in the Antechamber.
story:
Carter found the figure in the Antechamber, the room where boxes of the king's clothes were stacked, and he thought it was a mannequin: a dummy on which the king's robes or jewellery were fitted. The shape fits the idea, life-size, armless and cut off at the waist like a modern dress form. And there was plenty to dress: tunics, shirts, kilts, gloves and sandals came out of the Antechamber boxes alone.

Other Egyptologists prefer a ritual explanation, a stand-in body for the king's ka or an image used in ceremonies. Nothing written on it settles the question.

What makes it special is the face. Royal portraits are usually polished into an ideal. This one, life-size and painted, feels closer to a real young man. Compare it with the gold mask, the same features turned into a god, and with the lotus head, which shows him as a small child. Three portraits, three ages, one boy.
details: Look at the crown: flat-topped, an unusual shape among the king's many headdresses.
Notice the shoulders and chest end abruptly with no arms: exactly the shape of a dress form.
Compare the face with the gold mask: same features, but here the painted skin feels more human.
Walk round the side and look at the profile, the line of lips and chin.
fun_fact: The Antechamber boxes held tunics, shirts, kilts and even gloves. If Carter was right, this was the fitting dummy for the whole royal wardrobe.
narration: This painted wooden figure is a life-size head and torso of Tutankhamun, with no arms, ending at the waist, wearing a flat-topped crown. Carter found it in the Antechamber, the room stacked with furniture and boxes of clothes, and he thought it was a mannequin: a dummy on which the king's robes or jewellery were fitted. Life-size, armless, cut off at the waist, it is basically a dress form. And the tomb had plenty to dress: tunics, shirts, kilts, even gloves. Other Egyptologists suspect a ritual role, perhaps a stand-in body for the king's spirit, used in ceremonies. What makes it special is the face. Royal portraits are usually polished into perfection. This one feels closer to a real young man. You have three portraits of him in these halls: the golden mask, made as a god; the lotus head, as a little child; and this one, somewhere in between. Look now at the face from the side, at the line of the lips and the chin, and compare it in your mind with the gold mask.

name: The alabaster 'Wishing Cup'
note: Calcite chalice shaped as an open lotus with Heh figures on the handles; its inscription wishing the king 'millions of years... his eyes beholding happiness' is on Carter's grave in Putney Vale.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1332-1323 BC
summary: An alabaster cup shaped like an open lotus, whose wish for 'millions of years' ended up carved on Howard Carter's own gravestone.
look: The chalice is carved from a single piece of alabaster, 18.3 centimetres high, in the shape of a white lotus in full bloom. The handles are blue lotus flowers and buds topped by the kneeling god Heh, who holds notched palm ribs that count years, each resting on a tadpole and a shen ring. An inscription runs round the rim from a central ankh.
story:
It lay on the floor just inside the Antechamber, among the first things Carter's team saw, though not in its original place. Carter called it the Wishing Cup, because of its text.

The white lotus with its rounded petals is the cup; blue lotus flowers and buds form the handles. On each, Heh, the god of infinity, kneels on a basket, the sign for 'all', holding palm ribs notched to count years. Under each rib sits a tadpole, the hieroglyph for 100,000, on a shen ring, the sign of eternity. Together they say: endless time, forever.

The rim inscription runs two ways from a central ankh. One way gives the king's full titles. The other is the wish: may his ka live, may he spend millions of years, he who loves Thebes, sitting with his face to the north wind, his eyes beholding happiness. Alan Gardiner provided the translation for Carter's publication.

Carter clearly loved it. When he died in London in 1939, only nine people attended his funeral. His gravestone in Putney Vale Cemetery carries the cup's words: 'May your spirit live, may you spend millions of years, you who love Thebes, sitting with your face to the north wind, your eyes beholding happiness.'
details: Find the ankh in the middle of the rim: from there the text runs one way for his titles, the other for the wish.
On each handle, find Heh kneeling on a basket and holding notched palm ribs, the sign for years.
Look for the tadpole under each palm rib: it is the hieroglyph for 100,000.
Compare the rounded petals of the white lotus cup with the pointed blue lotus flowers on the handles.
fun_fact: The cup's wish is carved on Howard Carter's grave in Putney Vale Cemetery in London: the pharaoh's blessing became his discoverer's epitaph.
narration: This lotus-shaped cup is carved from a single piece of alabaster. Carter called it the Wishing Cup, and it was one of the first things his team saw, lying on the floor just inside the Antechamber. The cup is a white lotus in full bloom, a flower of rebirth. On each handle kneels Heh, the god of infinity, holding palm ribs notched to count the years, and under each rib sits a tadpole, the hieroglyph for 100,000. In other words: endless time. Around the rim runs the wish: may your spirit live, may you spend millions of years, you who love Thebes, sitting with your face to the north wind, your eyes beholding happiness. The north wind was the cool breath of life in a hot country. Howard Carter loved this text. When he died in London in 1939, only nine people came to his funeral, and his gravestone in Putney Vale Cemetery carries these very words. The pharaoh's wish became his discoverer's epitaph. Now find the little ankh in the middle of the rim inscription: from there, the words run one way for his titles and the other way for the wish.

name: Head of Tutankhamun as Nefertem on the lotus
note: Painted wood head of the boy king rising from a blue lotus like the sun god at creation; found in the tomb corridor rubble; Carter nearly got into trouble as it was not registered (found later in a Fortnum & Mason crate).
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, probably Amarna period, c. 1335-1323 BC
summary: The child king rising from a blue lotus like the newborn sun: the only known image of Tutankhamun as a child, with a whiff of scandal attached.
look: A head of painted wood and stucco, 30 centimetres tall, rising from a blue lotus flower on a blue base that stands for the primeval waters. The head is shaved, with painted black stubble, dark blue eyebrows and eyeliner, pierced ears and the long skull and neck creases of Amarna art. The red paint of the skin is damaged in large patches.
story:
Egyptian myth told that at the beginning of time a lotus rose from the dark waters, and from it came the young sun, as the child-god Nefertem. The lotus closes at night and opens again at dawn, so it became the flower of the sun's daily rebirth. Showing the king as Nefertem was a magical guarantee that he, too, would be reborn.

It is the only known image of Tutankhamun as a child. The elongated head and wrinkled neck are typical of Amarna art, which suggests it was made in the Amarna period, when he was still called Tutankhaten.

Then the scandal. Carter did not record it in his first-season notes, and there is no photograph of it in the tomb, unlike almost everything else. In 1924, while Carter was locked in a dispute with the authorities and away from Egypt, Pierre Lacau and Rex Engelbach of the Antiquities Service found it in KV4, the tomb of Ramesses XI, which Carter used as a storeroom. It was packed among bottles in a box of red wine. Carter later said it came from the rubble of the entrance corridor and simply had not been registered yet. Some still suspect he meant to keep it. Carter blamed the damage to its paint on the seizure.
details: Look at the ears: pierced, just like those of the gold mask.
Look closely at the scalp: black painted dots for stubble on a shaved head.
Find the blue base under the lotus: the primeval waters from which the world began.
Notice the long skull and creased neck, hallmarks of the Amarna style of Akhenaten's reign.
fun_fact: In 1924 inspectors found this head in a tomb Carter used as a storeroom, packed in a box of red wine bottles. Carter's explanation: he simply hadn't registered it yet.
narration: This is the boy king as the newborn sun. A child's head rises from an opening blue lotus, in painted wood and stucco, about 30 centimetres tall. Egyptian myth said that at the start of time a lotus rose out of the dark waters, and from it came the young sun god, Nefertem. Because the lotus closes at night and opens at dawn, it promised rebirth every morning. Showing Tutankhamun as Nefertem guaranteed that he too would be reborn. It is the only known image of him as a child, and the long head and creased neck are Amarna style, so it was probably made when he was still called Tutankhaten. Now the scandal. Carter never recorded it in his notes. In 1924, during a quarrel between Carter and the authorities, inspectors found it in a side tomb Carter used as a storeroom, packed in a box of red wine bottles. Carter said it came from the rubble in the entrance corridor and simply had not been registered yet. Some still suspect he meant to keep it. Look at the ears: they are pierced, just like those on the gold mask.

name: Pectorals, collars and the desert-glass scarab
note: Over 140 pieces on the mummy and in boxes; the winged scarab pectoral whose yellow-green scarab is Libyan desert glass formed by a meteorite impact in the Great Sand Sea (link to Siwa); gold collars, earrings showing pierced ears.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: More than 200 jewels, 143 objects on the body alone, and a pectoral whose green scarab is glass made by a cosmic impact in the Sahara.
look: The cases hold pectorals, collars, bracelets, rings and earrings in gold, inlaid with carnelian, lapis lazuli, turquoise and coloured glass. Find the chest ornament with a winged scarab at its centre: the scarab is pale yellow-green Libyan desert glass. Above it, a little boat carries the eye of Horus beneath the moon.
story:
The tomb held more than 200 pieces of jewellery. The mummy alone carried 143 objects in its wrappings: amulets, collars, bracelets, rings, two daggers, sandals and gold caps for fingers and toes. Many more lay in boxes in the Treasury and elsewhere, though ancient robbers had rifled them. Carter found a bundle of gold rings knotted into a cloth, apparently loot abandoned by a thief in a hurry.

The star is the pectoral with the winged scarab. Its body is carved from Libyan desert glass, a natural glass found in the eastern Sahara, in the deserts of western Egypt and eastern Libya. It formed about 29 million years ago. Its origin was long argued over, but recent research ties it to a meteorite impact: grains inside the glass show a mineral transformation that has only been found at impact sites. The Italian mineralogist Vincenzo de Michele published the identification of the scarab in 1998. Prehistoric people knapped the same glass into tools.

The scarab beetle rolls its ball of dung the way the sun god rolls the sun into the sky each morning, so a winged scarab is sunrise itself. Above it, a boat carries the eye of Horus under the moon. Sun below, moon above: day and night guarding the king.

The jewellery also tells you about the person. His ears were pierced, as you can see on the gold mask, and earrings were among the finds.
details: Find the winged scarab pectoral: the yellow-green scarab is Libyan desert glass, about 29 million years old.
Above the scarab, look for the boat carrying the eye of Horus under a moon disc and crescent.
Look for the broad gold collars in the shape of a vulture and a falcon, laid on the mummy for protection.
Spot the earrings: Tutankhamun's ears were pierced, as the gold mask shows.
Look for the gold finger and toe caps that were fitted to each finger and toe of the mummy.
fun_fact: The scarab on the king's chest is glass born about 29 million years ago when something from space struck the Sahara: Tutankhamun wore a piece of a cosmic accident.
narration: These cases hold Tutankhamun's jewellery, and there is a lot of it: more than 200 pieces in the tomb, and 143 objects on the mummy alone, tucked into the layers of linen. Collars, amulets, bracelets, rings, even gold caps for each finger and toe. Robbers got into the jewellery boxes in antiquity, and some loot never left the tomb: Carter found gold rings knotted into a cloth, apparently dropped in a hurry. Now look for the chest ornament with a winged scarab in the middle. The scarab beetle rolls its ball of dung the way the sun god rolls the sun into the sky each morning, so a scarab with wings is sunrise itself. But this scarab is special. Its pale yellow-green body is not a gemstone. It is Libyan desert glass, a natural glass from the Sahara between Egypt and Libya. It formed about 29 million years ago, and recent research ties it to the impact of a meteorite. So the king wore a piece of a cosmic accident on his chest. You will be in the Western Desert yourselves, at Siwa, in a couple of days. Above the scarab, a little boat carries the eye of Horus under the moon: sun below, moon above, day and night protecting him. One last detail: Tutankhamun's ears were pierced, and earrings were found in the tomb. Look at the scarab again and notice its soft green colour, the colour of glass born in fire.

name: The 413 shabtis
note: 365 workers + 36 overseers + 12 monthly overseers = 413, in wood, faience, stone; some gifted by officials Maya and Nakhtmin; the spell 6 text; what they were for.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: Tutankhamun took 413 little servants into the afterlife: a worker for every day of the year, plus foremen with whips to keep them at it.
look: Rows of small mummy-shaped figures in gilded wood, blue faience and stone, most between the length of your hand and your forearm. Many hold a hoe and a pick, or have a basket on the back, ready for field work. A few look different: men dressed as the living, in a kilt, holding a whip. Those are the overseers.
story:
The Egyptian afterlife was not a holiday. The Field of Reeds looked like a perfect Egypt, and a perfect Egypt still had fields to plough and canals to clear. From the Middle Kingdom onwards the answer was a stand-in: a figure inscribed with a spell that steps forward when the gods call the dead person up for labour. The spell became Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead, and its key line is the figure's reply: 'I will do it, here I am.' The word changed over the centuries, shabti, shawabti, ushabti, and scholars still argue whether it meant 'answerer'.

Carter counted 413 in Tutankhamun's tomb, most in the Annexe and the Treasury, packed in black shrine-shaped boxes with miniature tools of copper and faience. The usual reading of the number is neat: 365 workers, one per day, 36 overseers, one for each gang of ten, and 12 more, one for each month.

Not all came from the royal workshop. Some carry dedications from powerful men at court, the general Nakhtmin and the treasurer Maya among them. A gift to the dead king was also a way of being seen at his funeral. The finest figures are small portrait sculptures with the king's full cheeks and heavy-lidded eyes.
details: The overseers: figures in a kilt, as living men, often with a whip. Count how few they are next to the workers.
Miniature hoes, picks and baskets in copper and faience, made for the shabtis to work with.
Horizontal bands of text round the legs: usually the shabti spell, Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead.
Compare materials: gilded wood, blue faience, dark stone, pale calcite. The best are true portraits of the king.
A few carry a short line naming the giver, such as the general Nakhtmin. Check the labels.
fun_fact: One overseer for every ten workers, and a dozen monthly bosses on top: Tutankhamun's afterlife farm came with middle management.
narration: These little mummy-shaped figures are Tutankhamun's workforce for eternity. The Egyptian afterlife looked like a perfect Egypt, and a perfect Egypt still needed fields ploughed and canals cleared. So people took stand-ins. Each figure carries a spell, Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead. When the gods call the dead man to work, the figure answers: I will do it, here I am. That may be where the name comes from, ushabti, the answerer, though scholars still argue. Howard Carter counted 413 of them. The neat reading is 365 workers, one for every day of the year, 36 overseers, one for every gang of ten, and 12 more, one for each month. Most were packed in black boxes in the Annexe and the Treasury, with tiny tools of copper and faience. Not all came from the palace. Some were gifts from powerful men at court, like the general Nakhtmin and the treasurer Maya, a way of being seen at the king's funeral. Look now for the odd ones out: figures in a kilt, dressed as living men, holding a whip. Those are the bosses.

name: Gilded statuettes: the king on a panther, harpooning, and the gods
note: Wrapped in linen in black shrines: Tut riding a black leopard, Tut on a papyrus skiff harpooning (an invisible Seth-hippo), and some 30 gilded deities (Ptah, Sekhmet, Duamutef...). Some are thought reused from Neferneferuaten's planned burial.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: Gilded figures sealed in black shrines: the king striding on a leopard, the king spearing an invisible hippo, and a crowd of gods to escort him.
look: Gold-covered wooden figures, most well under a metre tall, standing on black bases. Find the king walking on the back of a black leopard, and the king on a little papyrus boat with a harpoon raised. Around them stand gilded gods and goddesses, some with the king's own face.
story:
In the Treasury, Carter found a row of black wooden chests shaped like shrines, their doors tied shut and sealed. Inside, each gilded statuette stood wrapped in linen, as if dressed for a journey. Together they are a cast for the king's night voyage through the underworld.

Two figures show the king in the White Crown striding along the back of a black leopard. The same image is painted in the tomb of Seti II, so it belonged to the royal underworld, not to a hunting trip; the cat may stand for the dark realm the king must cross. Two more show him on a papyrus skiff, arm raised, a coil of rope in the other hand. The target is missing on purpose. In temple reliefs it is a hippopotamus, the animal of Seth, god of chaos. Here the enemy is left to your imagination.

The gods include Ptah, with Tutankhamun's features, Sekhmet, Duamutef, one of the four sons of Horus, and the goddess Menkaret carrying the small king on her head. Not everything was made for him. Some Egyptologists point to one leopard figure with a soft, almost female chest and argue it was first made for Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler before him, then reused.
details: The leopard figures: a black cat, a gilded king in the tall White Crown. Compare the two chests; one looks softer, almost female.
The harpooner: rope coiled in one hand, harpoon raised in the other, and no hippo anywhere. That is deliberate.
Ptah, wrapped tight like a mummy, with Tutankhamun's face.
Menkaret, a goddess carrying a small figure of the king on her head.
The black shrine-shaped chests, if shown: each figure was sealed inside one.
fun_fact: When the shrines were opened, the gilded figures were found wrapped in linen like passengers in travelling cloaks.
narration: Here is the king's escort for the night journey. In the Treasury, Howard Carter found a row of black wooden chests shaped like little shrines, all sealed. Inside stood gilded figures, each wrapped in linen like a traveller in a cloak. Start with the leopard. The king, in the tall White Crown, strides along the back of a black cat. It is not a hunting trophy. The same image is painted in the tomb of Seti the Second, so it belongs to the underworld, perhaps the dark realm the king had to cross. Some Egyptologists think one of the two leopard figures, with its soft, almost female chest, was first made for Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler before Tutankhamun. Then the harpooner: the king on a papyrus skiff, arm raised, rope coiled in his hand. His target is missing on purpose. In temple scenes it is a hippopotamus, the creature of Seth, god of chaos. Here the enemy is left to your imagination. Around him stand the gods, Ptah with the king's own face, Sekhmet and more. Look now at the empty water before the harpooner.

name: Ostrich-feather fans and walking sticks
note: Gold fan showing the king hunting ostriches at Heliopolis; the 130 walking sticks, some worn with use, feeding the theory he limped.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: A gold fan shows the king hunting the very ostriches whose feathers it once held, and 130 sticks raise the question: did Tutankhamun limp?
look: The gold fan is a half-round head on a long handle, with holes along the curved edge where ostrich feathers were fixed; the feathers have mostly perished. One face shows the king hunting ostriches from his chariot, the other his return with the catch. Nearby are walking sticks: plain reeds, gilded canes, and canes whose curved handles are bound foreign captives.
story:
The fan was found between the gilded shrines in the burial chamber. Its inscription says the feathers came from ostriches the king hunted himself in the desert near Heliopolis, so the gold tells the fan's own origin story.

The sticks are a puzzle. More than 130 canes and staffs went into the tomb, one labelled as a reed His Majesty cut with his own hand. When a 2010 DNA study suggested a clubfoot, the canes were offered as proof that he limped. A later study found very little wear on them, and canes were also badges of rank. The jury is still out.
details: Fan, hunting side: the king draws his bow from a racing chariot as ostriches flee.
Fan, other side: servants carry the dead birds home; the king holds the plumes under his arm.
The holes along the fan's curved edge, where the feathers were fixed.
Canes with handles carved as bound foreign captives: the king held his enemies in his hand.
fun_fact: The fan is a souvenir of its own making: the gold shows the hunt that supplied its feathers.
narration: This gold fan tells its own origin story. On one face the young king races his chariot and draws his bow at fleeing ostriches. On the other, servants carry the birds home and the king holds the plumes under his arm. The inscription says the feathers came from his own hunt in the desert near Heliopolis. The feathers have mostly perished, but you can see the holes where they were fixed. Now the sticks. More than 130 canes and staffs were buried with him. After a DNA study suggested a clubfoot, people said: there is the proof he limped. A later study found the sticks show very little wear, and canes were badges of rank. Look now for the canes whose handles are bound foreign captives.

name: The Little Golden Shrine
note: Small gilded shrine covered in tender scenes of Tut and Ankhesenamun (she hands him arrows, anoints him, ties his collar); the statue inside was stolen in antiquity; the themes of fertility and kingship.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1332-1323 BC
summary: A small gold shrine covered in tender scenes of a teenage king and queen. The statue it was made for was stolen over 3,000 years ago.
look: A wooden shrine about half a metre tall, sheathed in gold and set on a sledge, with a roof sloping down towards the back like the ancient shrine of Upper Egypt. Every outside panel shows Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun together. Walk all the way round and read it like a comic strip.
story:
Carter found it in the Antechamber. Inside was a base for a small statue, but the statue itself was gone, taken by robbers soon after the funeral. They missed a necklace with a pendant of Weret-Hekau, 'Great of Magic', a snake goddess with a woman's head, nursing the king.

The panels are some of the most intimate royal images from ancient Egypt. Ankhesenamun hands her husband arrows as he shoots at birds from a seat. She ties a collar round his neck, offers him flowers, and perfume passes between their hands. She was his wife and probably his half-sister, a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, born Ankhesenpaaten.

These are not holiday snapshots. The queen plays the role of goddesses such as Hathor and Weret-Hekau, who renew the king's power and promise new life, so the shrine is about kingship and fertility as much as love. Still, the soft, curving lines are the Amarna style the couple grew up with, and they make two teenagers look like real people.
details: The panel where the king sits shooting at birds and the queen holds out an arrow.
The queen fastening a broad collar round the king's neck.
Scenes where perfume or water passes between their hands: who serves whom changes from panel to panel.
The cartouches of king and queen in the text columns framing each scene.
If the doors are open: the empty base where the stolen statue once stood.
fun_fact: Ankhesenamun means 'She lives for Amun'. She was born Ankhesenpaaten, 'She lives for the Aten', and changed her name when the court abandoned her father's god.
narration: This small shrine of gold is the closest thing to a family album that Tutankhamun left. Every panel shows the young king with his queen, Ankhesenamun, probably his half-sister and a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti. Walk around it slowly. She hands him arrows as he shoots at birds from a seat. She ties a collar round his neck. She offers him flowers. Perfume passes between their hands. Howard Carter found the shrine in the Antechamber. Inside was a base for a small statue, but the statue was gone, stolen soon after the funeral. The robbers missed a necklace showing a snake goddess called Great of Magic, nursing the king. That is the key. These are not holiday snapshots. The queen plays goddesses like Hathor, who renew the king's power and promise new life. Still, the soft curving lines are the Amarna style they grew up with, and they make two teenagers look real. Look now for the panel where she holds out an arrow and he draws his bow.

name: The king's wardrobe: tunics, gloves, loincloths
note: Hundreds of textiles incl. a tapestry-woven tunic, gloves, 145 loincloths, and a 'dalmatic' with duck motifs; rarely surviving evidence of royal dress. Short.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: Royal clothes almost never survive from ancient Egypt. Tutankhamun's tomb kept his tunics, his gloves and a pile of linen underwear.
look: Folded linen garments behind glass: a tunic with woven and embroidered bands at the neck and hem, small linen gloves, sashes, and triangular loincloths with ties. The linen is brown and brittle now. Imagine it bright white, with coloured borders.
story:
Egyptian art shows kings in crisp white linen, but real royal clothes almost never survive. Tutankhamun's tomb is the exception. Carter found hundreds of textiles, many stuffed back into boxes by officials who tidied up after ancient robbers: tunics, kilts, shirts, sashes, gloves and around 145 loincloths.

The showpieces are tunics with tapestry-woven and embroidered decoration; Carter nicknamed one ceremonial robe a 'dalmatic', after a church vestment. Gloves may have been for gripping a chariot's reins. Some pieces are small enough for a boy, as if clothes from his childhood were kept and buried with him.
details: The tunic's neck opening and hem: woven bands and embroidery in coloured thread.
The gloves: linen, sized for a young man's hands, perhaps for driving a chariot.
Triangular loincloths with ties: the basic underwear of ancient Egypt.
The brown colour: linen darkens with age. It was once white.
fun_fact: Around 145 loincloths went into the tomb. Even a god-king needed clean underwear for eternity.
narration: Here is something almost nothing else in Egypt can show you: a king's actual clothes. Paintings show pharaohs in crisp white linen, but real royal garments almost never survive. Tutankhamun's tomb kept hundreds of textiles, many stuffed back into boxes by officials tidying up after ancient robbers. There are tunics with woven and embroidered borders, sashes, gloves that may have been for driving a chariot, and around 145 loincloths. Some pieces are small enough for a boy, as if clothes from his childhood were kept. The linen has turned brown with age. Imagine it bright white. Look now at the gloves, and at how small those hands were.

name: What stayed in the tomb: the mummy, the sarcophagus, the paintings
note: Explain that the mummy, the quartzite sarcophagus and the outermost coffin are still in KV62 in Luxor (visited 21 Oct), so the user understands the split. Carter's rough handling of the body, the 2005 CT scan, the cause-of-death theories (leg fracture + malaria), the 2010 DNA study (Akhenaten's son).
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC; tomb found 1922
summary: The gold is here, but the king is not. His mummy and his stone sarcophagus are still in KV62 in the Valley of the Kings.
look: Nothing to look at in this gallery: this entry explains the split. On 21 October, in the burial chamber of KV62, you will see what stayed: the quartzite sarcophagus with a winged goddess at each corner, the mummy in a glass case, and the painted walls. The outermost gilded coffin also stayed in the tomb until July 2019, when it came to the Grand Egyptian Museum for restoration, to be shown with the other two.
story:
When Carter cleared the tomb, between 1922 and 1932, nearly everything went to Cairo. The king stayed, in his quartzite sarcophagus, whose lid was replaced by glass, inside his outermost coffin. Since 4 November 2007 the mummy has lain in a climate-controlled glass case in the tomb.

It is not a pretty story. In November 1925 the anatomist Douglas Derry unwrapped the body. Resins had glued it to the gold coffin, so the team chiselled it out, used hot knives to free the head from the mask, cut the torso at the hips and took the arms apart. It went back to the tomb on a tray of sand in 1926. When R. G. Harrison X-rayed it in 1968, parts of the chest were missing, probably taken by thieves after the reburial.

A CT scan in 2005 confirmed an age of about 19, ruled out the old theory of a fatal blow to the head, and found a leg fracture that never healed. A DNA study published in 2010 named the KV55 mummy, probably Akhenaten, as his father and the 'Younger Lady' from KV35 as his mother, found malaria parasites, and proposed malaria plus the fracture as the cause of death. Other experts dispute parts of the genetics and the clubfoot diagnosis: it is the best current guess.
details: In the tomb, north wall: Ay, the next king, performs the Opening of the Mouth on Tutankhamun's mummy.
East wall: the funeral procession dragging the coffin, a private-tomb scene found in no other royal tomb.
West wall: twelve baboons from the Amduat, the book of the sun's night journey.
The sarcophagus: quartzite box, red granite lid painted to match, goddesses spreading their wings at the corners.
If the real tomb is crowded, a full-size replica of the burial chamber was opened near Carter's house in 2014.
fun_fact: The king was found with 143 objects tucked into his wrappings, from amulets to two daggers, one with a blade of meteoric iron.
narration: Nothing in this gallery is the king himself, and that is the point of this stop. When Howard Carter emptied the tomb, almost everything came to Cairo, but the mummy and the stone sarcophagus stayed in K V 62 in the Valley of the Kings, where you will see them on the 21st. The mummy's story is rough. In November 1925 the anatomist Douglas Derry unwrapped it. Resins had glued the body to the gold coffin, so the team chiselled it out, used hot knives to free the head from the mask, and cut the body into pieces. It went back into the tomb on a tray of sand. A CT scan in 2005 put his age at about 19, ruled out the old theory of a blow to the head, and found a broken leg that never healed. In 2010 a DNA study named the K V 55 mummy, probably Akhenaten, as his father, found malaria, and suggested malaria plus the fracture as the cause of death. Other experts dispute parts of it, so call it the best current guess. When you stand in the tomb, look for Ay on the north wall, performing the last rites for the king.

name: Narmer Palette
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN: historically Egyptian Museum Tahrir; may be at GEM. Say 'if you find it'. c. 3100 BC, Hierakonpolis, earliest hieroglyphs, smiting pose, the 'unification of Two Lands', serpopards, Hathor/Bat heads.
period: Late Predynastic to 1st Dynasty, c. 3100 BC
summary: A make-up palette far too big to use, carved around 3100 BC with a king smiting his enemy: the pose every pharaoh copied for 3,000 years.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. If you find it: a shield-shaped slab of dark grey-green siltstone about 63 cm tall, carved on both faces. One side shows the king in the tall White Crown, mace raised over a kneeling captive. The other has two long-necked beasts whose necks curl round a shallow circle: the grinding dish.
story:
In the 1897-98 season James Quibell and Frederick Green were digging at Hierakonpolis, ancient Nekhen, a centre of the falcon god Horus; the Greek name means 'falcon city'. In a buried cache of old temple offerings, the 'Main Deposit', they found this palette. Palettes were normally small slabs for grinding eye paint. This one is too big and heavy for any dressing table. It was a temple gift, perhaps used to grind cosmetics for a god's statue.

At the top of both sides the king's name sits in a palace-façade box: a catfish and a chisel, read Nar-mer, between cow heads usually identified as the goddess Bat. On one side Narmer, in the White Crown of Upper Egypt, raises a mace over a kneeling enemy, while a falcon holds a captive head rising from a papyrus marsh on a rope and a servant carries the king's sandals. On the other side, in the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, he marches to view ten beheaded enemies, each head placed between the feet. Below, two serpopards, leopards with snake necks, are held on leashes. At the bottom a bull, the king, smashes a walled town.

For a century this was read as a news report: the south conquers the north, Egypt is united. Many Egyptologists now see it less as one event than as a statement of what kings do: crush disorder, rule both lands. Either way, the smiting pose lasted until the Roman emperors.
details: Top of both sides: catfish and chisel in a box, Narmer's name, flanked by cow heads with curling horns.
Smiting side: the small sandal-bearer behind the king, carrying his sandals.
Other side, top right: ten headless bodies laid in rows, each head between its feet.
The serpopards: long-necked beasts on leashes, their necks framing the grinding dish.
The king's belt: tassels capped with little cow-goddess heads, and a bull's tail hanging behind.
fun_fact: Narmer wears a bull's tail hanging from his belt. Pharaohs kept wearing one for the next 3,000 years.
narration: If you have found it, you are looking at the slab where Egyptian kingship begins. The Narmer Palette was carved about 3100 BC from dark siltstone, and found in the 1890s by James Quibell and Frederick Green at Hierakonpolis, a Greek name meaning city of the falcon, in a buried pile of old temple offerings. Palettes were small slabs for grinding eye paint. This one is far too big for any dressing table. It was a gift to a god. At the top of both faces, between two cow heads, is the king's name in a little box: a catfish and a chisel, read Nar and Mer. On one side Narmer wears the tall White Crown of the south and raises a mace over a kneeling enemy, held by the hair. Behind him a servant carries his sandals. On the other side he wears the Red Crown of the north and marches to inspect ten headless enemies, each head placed between the feet. Below, two monsters with leopard bodies and snake necks curl around the dish where paint was ground. At the bottom, a bull, the king himself, smashes a walled town. For a century people read this as the unification of Egypt in one war. Many Egyptologists now see it as a statement of what kings do. Either way, that smiting pose lasted 3,000 years, and you will see Ramesses doing the same at Abu Simbel. Look now for the catfish at the top.

name: Khafre Enthroned (diorite statue with Horus)
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN (Tahrir or GEM). Gneiss/diorite from Nubia found 1860 by Mariette in a pit in the Valley Temple at Giza (seen 12 Oct); Horus embracing the king's head; sema-tawy on throne; 23 statues originally.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2550 BC
summary: The builder of the second Giza pyramid, sitting in stone so hard it barely takes a chisel, with the falcon god folding its wings round his head.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A life-size seated king, about 1.68 m tall, in dark stone flecked with pale crystals. From the front you see a calm man in the striped nemes headcloth and false beard. Now walk to the side: a falcon perches on the back of the throne and wraps its wings round the back of his head.
story:
Auguste Mariette found the statue in 1860 in Khafre's valley temple at Giza, the granite building beside the Sphinx that you visit on the 12th. It had been thrown into a pit in the temple. The temple's hall has sockets in the floor for 23 statues of the king; this is the one that survived whole.

The stone matters. It is anorthosite gneiss, often loosely called diorite, brought from the 'Khafre quarries' deep in the Nubian desert west of Gebel el-Asr, about 1,000 km up the Nile from Giza. It is extremely hard, so every smooth curve was won by grinding with abrasive sand.

Now read the composition. The throne's sides are lions. Between the legs, the lily of the south and the papyrus of the north are tied around the hieroglyph for 'unite': this king holds the Two Lands together. The falcon is Horus, and the king is Horus on earth. From the front you hardly notice the bird; from the side, king and god become one being.

Khafre is the Chephren of Herodotus, who heard that he and his father Khufu closed the temples and were so hated that Egyptians avoided saying their names. This face does not look like a tyrant. It is an ideal, calm and ageless, a permanent home for the king's ka, the life-force that needed a body that would never decay.
details: The falcon: walk to the side and look behind the king's head. Its wings wrap round the back of the nemes.
The throne sides: lion legs, and the lily and papyrus knotted together, the sign of the united Two Lands.
His hands: the right is clenched, the left lies flat on his knee.
The stone: dark gneiss with pale flecks, from a Nubian quarry about 1,000 km to the south.
fun_fact: In the Valley Temple on the 12th, you can still see the sockets in the floor where 23 statues of Khafre once sat. You have just met the survivor.
narration: If you have found him, you are looking at Khafre, king of the second pyramid at Giza, whose face most Egyptologists see on the Sphinx. He sits life-size in stone so hard it barely takes a chisel. Auguste Mariette found him in 1860 in Khafre's valley temple, the granite building beside the Sphinx that you will walk through on the 12th. He had been thrown into a pit. The floor of that temple has sockets for 23 statues of the king; this is the one that survived whole. The stone is anorthosite gneiss, often called diorite, dark with pale flecks. It came from quarries deep in the Nubian desert, about 1,000 kilometres up the Nile, and every smooth curve was ground with sand. Now walk slowly to the side. A falcon perches on the back of the throne and folds its wings round the king's head. That is Horus, and the king is Horus on earth. From the front you hardly see the bird. From the side, king and god become one. Look at the throne too: lions for legs, and the lily of the south and the papyrus of the north tied together, the sign for a united Egypt. The Greeks called him Chephren, and Herodotus heard that he was a tyrant who shut the temples. This face does not look like a tyrant. It is an ideal, calm and ageless, a home for the king's spirit forever. Look now for the falcon's wings behind his headcloth.

name: The Menkaure triads
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
aliases: king with Hathor and nome goddess
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Greywacke triads of Menkaure with Hathor and a nome goddess from his valley temple (Reisner 1908); the 'dyad' with his queen is in Boston.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2500 BC
summary: The owner of the smallest Giza pyramid stands with the goddess Hathor and the spirit of a province: kingship shown as a team.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Each triad is a slab of dark greywacke with three figures standing against a back slab. The king, usually in the middle, wears the tall White Crown and steps forward; Hathor wears cow horns around a sun disc; the third figure carries the emblem of a province on the head.
story:
In 1908 George Reisner, digging for Harvard and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, cleared Menkaure's valley temple at Giza. The king had not lived to finish it, and it was completed largely in mud brick. In its rooms Reisner found the triads: Menkaure with Hathor, 'Mistress of the Sycamore', and a figure personifying one of Egypt's provinces, which the Greeks called nomes. Each wears its emblem: a jackal, a hare, the emblem of the cow goddess Bat, the sceptre of Thebes.

Finds were divided, so some triads are in Cairo and others in Boston, together with the famous pair statue of Menkaure and his queen, usually identified as Khamerernebty II. Some scholars thought there was once a triad for every province; others think only a handful were made.

The message is practical as well as religious: the provinces feed the king's cult forever, under Hathor's protection. Herodotus, who calls him Mycerinus, remembered a gentle king after harsh ones. An oracle gave him six years to live, so he lit lamps and partied every night to turn six years into twelve.
details: Hathor's headdress: cow horns cradling a sun disc. Look for her arm around the king or her hand in his.
The third figure's head: a province emblem. Jackal, the cow-faced Bat emblem or a Theban sceptre?
The king's pose: left foot forward, fists clenched, tall White Crown of the south.
The stone left between legs and behind bodies: the figures were never fully freed from the block.
fun_fact: Herodotus heard that Menkaure, told he had six years left, partied by lamplight every night to make six years into twelve.
narration: Three figures stand shoulder to shoulder in dark greywacke, and this is how a pharaoh liked to be seen: never alone. The king is Menkaure, owner of the third and smallest pyramid at Giza, in the tall White Crown, left foot forward. Beside him is Hathor, with cow horns cradling a sun disc. The third figure stands for one of Egypt's provinces, which the Greeks called nomes, and wears its emblem on the head: a jackal, a cow-faced emblem, or the sign of Thebes. George Reisner, digging for Harvard and Boston, found these in 1908 in Menkaure's valley temple, which the king had not lived to finish. The finds were divided, so some triads stayed in Cairo and others went to Boston, with the famous pair statue of Menkaure and his queen. The message is practical: the provinces will feed the king's cult forever, with Hathor's blessing. Herodotus, who calls him Mycerinus, heard that an oracle gave him six years to live, so he partied by lamplight every night to turn six years into twelve. Look now at the third figure's head: which province is it?

name: The tiny ivory statuette of Khufu
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. 7.5 cm ivory from Abydos, found by Petrie 1903 (the head found later after sieving for weeks); the only complete portrait of the builder of the Great Pyramid; red crown, Horus name on the throne.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2580 BC (date debated)
summary: The man who built the Great Pyramid survives in a portrait 7.5 centimetres tall. It is the only complete statue of him we have.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Look for something smaller than your palm: a seated ivory figure 7.5 cm high, usually in a case of its own. The king wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, holds a flail against his right shoulder and rests his left hand on his knee. The feet and base are broken off.
story:
Khufu built the largest pyramid ever made, yet almost nothing of his own image survives: a few heads that might be his, fragments of statues smashed long ago. This ivory statuette is the only complete figure of him that most Egyptologists accept.

Flinders Petrie found it in 1903 at Abydos, in a storeroom of the temple of Osiris-Khentiamentiu at Kom el-Sultan, far south of Giza. It came out of the ground headless. Petrie stopped the work, offered a reward and had the debris of the room sieved. Three weeks later the head turned up.

Look at the face: round, fleshy, determined, not the calm mask of later royal sculpture. The crown has lost its back spike and front curl. On the right side of the throne, by the knee, is his Horus name, Medjedu; faint traces of the cartouche Khnum-Khufu are on the left.

Not everyone accepts the date. Zahi Hawass has argued it was made nearly 2,000 years later, in the 26th Dynasty, as a votive offering to a revered ancestor, pointing to the shape of the throne and the flail. Few have followed him, but nobody has disproved him. Herodotus, who called the king Cheops, heard that he shut the temples and forced all Egypt to labour on his pyramid. The little man in front of you does not look like a monster.
details: The Red Crown of Lower Egypt, with its back spike and front curl broken away.
The flail held against his right shoulder.
The Horus name Medjedu cut on the right side of the throne, by the knee.
The neck: the head was found three weeks after the body, after the rubble was sieved.
Scale: 7.5 cm here against about 146 m for the Great Pyramid you see on the 12th.
fun_fact: The Great Pyramid is nearly 2,000 times taller than this portrait of the man who built it.
narration: Lean in close: this little ivory king, 7.5 centimetres tall, is Khufu, the man who built the Great Pyramid. It is the only complete statue of him that most Egyptologists accept. The pyramid you will see on the 12th is nearly 2,000 times taller than its owner here. Flinders Petrie found him in 1903 at Abydos, the holy city of Osiris, far south of Giza. He came out of the ground without a head. Petrie stopped work, offered a reward, and had the rubble of the room sieved. Three weeks later, the head turned up. Look at it now. He wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, though its back spike has broken off. He holds a flail against his right shoulder, and his left hand rests on his knee. On the side of the throne, by his right knee, is his Horus name, Medjedu. The face is round, fleshy and determined, not the calm mask of later kings. Is it really from his lifetime? Most specialists say yes. Zahi Hawass has argued it was made nearly 2,000 years later as an offering to a famous ancestor, because of the shape of the throne and the flail. Few have followed him, but nobody has proved him wrong. The Greeks called Khufu Cheops, and Herodotus heard that he was a tyrant who shut the temples and worked his people to the bone. This tiny man does not look like a monster. Look now for the Horus name by his knee.

name: Rahotep and Nofret
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Painted limestone pair from Meidum (Mariette 1871); inlaid rock-crystal eyes so lifelike the workmen fled; skin-colour conventions (men red-brown, women pale); Rahotep son of Sneferu.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2600 BC
summary: A prince and his wife, painted about 4,600 years ago, with crystal eyes so alive that the men who found them are said to have fled.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Two seated statues in painted limestone, side by side, each a little over a metre tall. He has red-brown skin, a thin moustache and short dark hair; she is pale cream, in a white cloak, with a heavy wig and a flowered headband. Their names and titles are painted in black hieroglyphs on the high chair backs beside their heads.
story:
In 1871 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette at Meidum, under Albert Daninos, broke into mastaba 6, the brick tomb of Rahotep and Nofret near the collapsed pyramid of Sneferu. The story goes that when their lamps fell on two faces staring back with shining eyes, the workmen ran. The eyes are inlaid with rock crystal and quartz in copper rims, and they still catch the light.

Rahotep was a king's son, most likely of Sneferu, the first great pyramid builder, which would make him a brother of Khufu. His titles, painted beside his head, include High Priest of Ra at Heliopolis, Director of Expeditions and Overseer of Works. Nofret's title is 'King's Acquaintance', a rank at court. The couple had six children, three sons and three daughters.

The colours are almost untouched, and they show the rules of Egyptian art at their purest. Men are painted reddish brown, women a pale yellowish cream. It is a convention, not a skin chart, often explained as the ideal of the outdoor man and the indoor woman. Yet the details are startlingly real: Rahotep's moustache, the dark natural hairline showing under Nofret's thick wig, her floral diadem like the gold ones found at Giza, the cloak she pulls around her.
details: The eyes: rock crystal and quartz set in copper. Move your head and watch them catch the light.
Nofret's forehead: her own straight dark hair shows under the edge of the heavy wig.
Her headband: a diadem of painted flowers, like real gold diadems with inlays.
Rahotep's thin moustache, and his amulet on a cord round the neck.
The black hieroglyphs beside each head: names, and Rahotep's titles such as High Priest at Heliopolis.
fun_fact: Their names mean 'Ra is satisfied' and 'the beautiful one'. After 4,600 years, both still seem to apply.
narration: If you have found them, meet Prince Rahotep and his wife Nofret, painted about 4,600 years ago and still in their original colours. In 1871 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette at Meidum broke into the couple's tomb, near the collapsed pyramid of King Sneferu. The story goes that when their lamps fell on two faces staring back with shining eyes, the workmen dropped everything and ran. Look at those eyes now. They are rock crystal and quartz set in copper, and they still catch the light when you move. Rahotep was a king's son, most likely of Sneferu, which would make him a brother of Khufu, the builder of the Great Pyramid. His titles are painted in black beside his head: High Priest of Ra at Heliopolis, Director of Expeditions, Overseer of Works. Nofret was a lady of the court. They had six children. Now the colours. He is reddish brown, she is pale cream. That is a rule of Egyptian art, not a skin chart, usually explained as the outdoor man and the indoor woman. Yet everything else feels real: his little moustache, her heavy wig with her own dark hair peeping out underneath, the band of painted flowers around her head, the cloak she pulls close. Look now at Nofret's forehead, and find her real hairline under the wig.

name: The Meidum Geese
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Painted plaster frieze from the mastaba of Nefermaat and Itet at Meidum, c. 2600 BC; 2015 forgery claim and rebuttal; identifying the species.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2600 BC
summary: Six geese painted on plaster 4,600 years ago, so precise that ornithologists can name the species, and so perfect that someone called them a fake.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A long, low strip of painted plaster under glass. Six geese stand and graze on a pale ground with tufts of plants, three facing left and three facing right, mirrored around the centre. Look for the joins where the plaster was cut from a tomb wall.
story:
The frieze comes from the tomb chapel of Itet, wife of Prince Nefermaat, in their mastaba at Meidum, a short walk from the tomb of Rahotep and Nofret. Auguste Mariette and Luigi Vassalli found it in 1871; it was cut from the wall and reassembled in the museum. The tomb was experimental in other ways too: elsewhere in it, figures were cut deep and filled with coloured paste, a technique known from no other tomb.

The birds are real. Ornithologists recognise greylag geese and greater white-fronted geese, and the boldly patterned pair look like red-breasted geese. In 2021 Anthony Romilio argued that those did not match the living species well and might show an extinct goose; in 2022 other scientists replied that they fall within natural variation and artistic licence.

In 2015 the Italian Egyptologist Francesco Tiradritti suggested that the whole frieze was a 19th-century forgery, possibly by Vassalli himself. Zahi Hawass and other Egyptian authorities dismissed the claim at once, and the geese stayed in the museum and in the textbooks.
details: The red-breasted pair: brick-red necks with black and white patches, the birds in the extinct-goose debate.
The grey geese: greylags, the wild ancestors of the farmyard goose.
The symmetry: three birds face left, three face right.
Cracks and joins: the plaster was cut from a tomb wall in the 1870s and pieced together again.
fun_fact: One scientist wondered whether the red-breasted geese show a species that is now extinct. If so, this would be its only portrait.
narration: If you have found them, you are looking at six geese painted on plaster about 4,600 years ago. They come from the tomb chapel of Itet, wife of Prince Nefermaat, at Meidum, close to the tomb of Rahotep and Nofret. Auguste Mariette and Luigi Vassalli found the frieze in 1871, cut it from the wall and pieced it together in the museum. Three birds face left, three face right, grazing on a strip of marsh. They are real species. Bird experts recognise greylag geese, the wild ancestors of the farmyard goose, and greater white-fronted geese. The pair with bold red, black and white patterns look like red-breasted geese, and in 2021 one scientist suggested they might show an extinct species. Others replied that it is just artistic licence. The painting is so good it even had a forgery scare. In 2015 an Italian Egyptologist suggested it was faked in the 19th century, possibly by Vassalli himself. Egyptian authorities dismissed the idea at once. Look now for the red-breasted pair and decide for yourself.

name: Ka-aper, the 'Sheikh el-Balad'
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Sycamore wood, c. 2450 BC, Saqqara; workers nicknamed him after their village headman; rock-crystal eyes in copper frames; a real paunchy middle-aged man.
period: Old Kingdom, late 4th to early 5th Dynasty, c. 2500 BC
summary: A wooden priest so lifelike that the men who dug him up named him after their village headman. The nickname has stuck for over 160 years.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A standing man carved in sycamore wood, about 1.12 m tall, striding forward with a staff. Round face, double chin, a comfortable belly over a long kilt. The eyes are rock crystal set in copper, and they seem to follow you.
story:
In 1860 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette opened a mastaba at Saqqara, just north of Djoser's Step Pyramid. When this statue came out of the sand and stood upright, they cried out that it was their 'sheikh el-balad', the headman of their village. The name stuck, and guides still use it.

His real name was Ka-aper. He was a lector priest, who read the sacred texts aloud at rituals, and an army scribe of the king, a title that may link him with campaigns in the southern Levant. He lived around 2500 BC, as the 4th Dynasty gave way to the 5th.

The sculptor built him from at least six pieces of sycamore. Wooden statues were usually finished with a coat of plaster and paint, now mostly gone, so the grain shows. What remains is one of the most honest portraits in Egyptian art: not a god-like ideal but a well-fed, middle-aged official. A wooden statue of a woman from the same tomb is usually thought to be his wife.
details: The eyes: rock crystal with small copper plates. Step to one side and they still seem to watch you.
The belly and double chin: an official who ate well, and wanted to be remembered that way.
Joins in the wood at the shoulders and arms: he was built from several pieces of sycamore.
His left foot steps forward: the standard pose for a living man on the move.
fun_fact: Sheikh el-Balad is Arabic for 'village headman'. Ka-aper has been Egypt's most famous mayor for over 160 years without winning a single vote.
narration: If you have found him, this wooden man is Ka-aper, and he has one of the best nicknames in Egypt. In 1860 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette at Saqqara, just north of the Step Pyramid, pulled him out of a tomb and stood him up. They took one look and cried out: it is our sheikh el-balad, the headman of our village. The name stuck. His real titles were grander. Ka-aper was a lector priest, who read the sacred texts aloud at rituals, and a scribe of the king's army, around 2500 BC. He is carved from sycamore wood, in several pieces joined together, and he probably once wore a coat of plaster and paint, now mostly gone. What is left is an honest portrait: a round face, a double chin, a comfortable belly over his kilt. This is not a god-like ideal. It is a successful middle-aged official who ate well and wanted to be remembered that way. Now look at the eyes. They are rock crystal set in copper, and from a step to one side they still seem to follow you.

name: Seneb the dwarf and his family
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Painted limestone group from Giza; the sculptor's solution of placing the children where legs would be; Seneb's high offices; attitudes to dwarfism in Egypt (Bes, Ptah).
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2520 BC
summary: A dwarf who rose to high office sits beside his wife, and the sculptor used the children to make the family look perfectly balanced.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A small painted limestone group, only about 22 cm high. Seneb sits cross-legged on a block, his wife Senetites beside him with her arm around him. In front, exactly where a seated man's legs would hang, stand their son and daughter, fingers to their lips.
story:
Seneb lived around 2520 BC and was buried in tomb G 1036 in the Western Cemetery at Giza, among the officials of the pyramid age. Hermann Junker found the tomb in 1926. It had been robbed long ago and no trace of the bodies remained, but this group survived.

Seneb was a man of rank. His monuments list about twenty titles, among them overseer of dwarfs and overseer of weaving in the palace, and he took part in the funeral services of Khufu and Djedefre. His wife Senetites, of normal height, was a priestess of Hathor and Neith. Three children are named; only two are shown, probably for symmetry.

The sculptor faced a puzzle: how to show a short man beside a taller wife with dignity. The answer was to seat him cross-legged, like a scribe, with his head level with hers, and to fill the space below him with the children. Nothing here mocks him. Dwarfism was not treated as a defect in ancient Egypt: texts advised respect for people with disabilities, some dwarfs held prestigious posts, and two gods, Bes and Ptah, could take dwarf form.
details: The children where Seneb's legs would be: a boy and a girl, each with a finger to the mouth, the sign of a child.
Skin colours: Seneb red-brown, Senetites pale. The usual male and female convention.
Senetites' arm around her husband: a gesture of partnership found in many Old Kingdom couples.
The hieroglyphs on the base naming the family.
fun_fact: Among Seneb's twenty titles is 'overseer of dwarfs'. The man in charge of the palace dwarfs was one himself, and he put it on his tomb.
narration: If you have found it, this small painted family group is Seneb, his wife Senetites and two of their children, carved around 2520 BC. Seneb was a dwarf, and he was also a man of rank. His tomb at Giza, among the officials of the pyramid age, lists about twenty titles, among them overseer of weaving in the palace and overseer of dwarfs, and he took part in the funeral rites of King Khufu and King Djedefre. Senetites, of normal height, was a priestess of Hathor and Neith. Now look at how the sculptor solved his puzzle: how to show a short man beside a taller wife, with dignity. Seneb sits cross-legged, like a scribe, so his head is level with hers. And in the space where a seated man's legs would hang, the sculptor placed the children, a boy and a girl, fingers to their lips, the Egyptian sign for a child. Senetites puts her arm around him. Egyptian texts urged respect for people with disabilities, and two gods, Bes and Ptah, could take the form of dwarfs. Look now at the children, standing exactly where their father's legs would be.

name: Queen Hetepheres' furniture
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Gilded bed, canopy, carrying chair and curtain box from a shaft (G7000X) near the Great Pyramid found by Reisner 1925; the empty sarcophagus mystery; the canopic chest with the earliest known embalming remains.
period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2600-2570 BC
summary: The mother of the Great Pyramid's builder left gold-covered furniture, a sealed stone coffin and no body. Nobody knows where she went.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A bed sloping down to a footboard, a headrest, a carrying chair, armchairs, a curtain box and a tall frame of poles for a bed canopy, all sheathed in gold. Most of the wood is modern: the original had rotted away, and restorers rebuilt it inside the surviving gold and inlay.
story:
On 9 March 1925 a photographer with George Reisner's Harvard and Boston expedition noticed a patch of plaster just east of the Great Pyramid, where he expected bare limestone. Beneath it was a shaft filled with masonry, about 26 metres deep. At the bottom lay a jumble of gold sheet and decayed wood, the remains of royal furniture, and a sealed alabaster sarcophagus. Inscriptions named Hetepheres, a wife of King Sneferu and mother of Khufu.

The team recorded every fragment before lifting it. In 1927 they opened the sarcophagus. It was empty.

Where was the queen? Reisner thought she had first been buried near Sneferu's pyramids at Dahshur, that robbers violated that tomb, and that Khufu had the rest reburied at Giza without knowing the body was gone. Mark Lehner proposed the reverse: this shaft first, a small pyramid nearby second. Others suggest different sequences. Nobody has settled it.

One thing was intact: her alabaster canopic chest. Its four compartments still held organic remains, two in a weak natron solution. It is one of the oldest canopic chests known, and a hint that royal embalming was well under way.
details: The canopy frame: gold-cased poles that held curtains round the bed, a gift from Sneferu according to its inscription.
The carrying chair: gold hieroglyphs on the back give the queen's titles.
The armchairs: one with papyrus flowers, one with the emblem of the goddess Neith.
The headrest at the head of the bed: Egyptians slept on these instead of pillows.
Her silver bracelets with butterflies, if displayed. Silver was rarer than gold in Egypt.
fun_fact: Her bed slopes downhill towards a footboard, and the 'pillow' is a hard headrest. Royal comfort, 4,500 years ago.
narration: If you have found it, this gold-covered furniture belonged to Queen Hetepheres, wife of King Sneferu and mother of Khufu, the builder of the Great Pyramid. In March 1925 a photographer on George Reisner's Harvard and Boston team noticed a patch of plaster beside the Great Pyramid where there should have been bare rock. Under it was a shaft packed with stone, about 26 metres deep. At the bottom lay a heap of gold sheet and crumbling wood: a bed, a canopy, chairs, a curtain box, all collapsed. The team recorded every fragment, and restorers later rebuilt the furniture in new wood inside the original gold. In 1927 they opened her alabaster sarcophagus. It was empty. Reisner thought robbers had wrecked her first tomb at Dahshur, and that Khufu reburied what was left, never told the body was gone. Others reverse the order. Nobody knows. One thing was intact: her canopic chest, still holding her embalmed organs, one of the oldest known. Look now at the bed: it slopes down to the footboard, and the pillow is a hard headrest.

name: The wooden panels of Hesy-Ra
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Cedar relief panels from his Saqqara mastaba, 3rd Dynasty; 'chief of dentists and physicians'; the scribal kit on his shoulder; his tomb the earliest with painted walls.
period: Old Kingdom, 3rd Dynasty, reign of Djoser, c. 2650 BC
summary: Carved wooden panels of a 3rd Dynasty official, often billed as the world's first named dentist. The title may really mean 'ivory carver'.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Tall, narrow panels of cedar carved in low relief. Each shows Hesy-Ra standing or seated, holding a staff and sceptre, with a scribe's kit slung over his shoulder: palette, water pot and pen case. Above him, crisp hieroglyphs give his name and titles.
story:
Hesy-Ra served King Djoser, builder of the Step Pyramid, around 2650 BC. His big mud-brick mastaba lies about 260 metres north-east of the pyramid at Saqqara. Mariette found it in 1861, and James Quibell excavated it in 1910-1912. These cedar panels stood in niches along a long corridor, showing him young, middle-aged and old. The corridor walls were painted with patterned mats, furniture and game boards, among the earliest painted tomb decoration known.

One of his titles is often translated 'greatest of the dentists'. The same signs can be read 'greatest of the ivory carvers', so the first-dentist label deserves a raised eyebrow.
details: The scribe's kit on his shoulder: palette, water pot and pen case, the badge of a literate official.
Compare the faces: younger and older versions of the same man across the panels.
The hieroglyphs above him: some of the finest early relief carving anywhere.
fun_fact: His most famous title may be a misreading: 'greatest of the dentists' and 'greatest of the ivory carvers' are written with the same signs.
narration: If you have found them, these carved cedar panels show Hesy-Ra, an official of King Djoser, builder of the Step Pyramid, about 2650 BC. They stood in niches along a corridor of his mud-brick tomb at Saqqara, found by Auguste Mariette in 1861. They show him at different ages, young, middle-aged and old, holding a staff and a sceptre. Over his shoulder hangs his scribe's kit: a palette, a water pot and a pen case. One of his titles is usually translated greatest of the dentists, and it made him famous as the first named dentist in history. But the same signs can mean greatest of the ivory carvers, so be a little sceptical. Look now for the scribe's kit on his shoulder.

name: The seated statue of Djoser
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Oldest life-size Egyptian royal statue, from the serdab of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara; the hollowed eyes robbed of inlay; the replica still sits in the serdab facing the stars.
period: Old Kingdom, 3rd Dynasty, c. 2650 BC
summary: The oldest known life-size Egyptian statue: the king of the Step Pyramid, who sat in a sealed room watching the world through two holes.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A seated king in painted limestone, life-size, wrapped in a long close-fitting robe, right arm across his chest, left hand on his thigh. A heavy wig shows under a striped headcloth, and he wears a long beard. The eye sockets are empty: the inlaid eyes were prised out long ago.
story:
The statue was found in 1924-25, during excavations by the Antiquities Service at Saqqara, inside the serdab of the Step Pyramid: a small sealed chamber built against the pyramid's north side. A serdab had no door. Its only openings were two small holes in the front wall, at the height of the statue's eyes, so the king's spirit could look out on the rituals performed there and, many think, at the northern stars that never set. A plaster copy now sits in the serdab in his place.

Djoser ruled around 2650 BC. His official Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid, the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt, which began as a square mastaba and grew in stages into a stack of steps.

The robe is probably the one worn for the Sed festival, the jubilee that renewed a king's power, which his pyramid complex celebrates in stone. His feet rest on the Nine Bows, the traditional enemies of Egypt. Even without its eyes, the face is heavy, stern and very human. In his lifetime his monuments called him Netjerikhet; the name Djoser is known from later Egyptian sources.
details: The empty eye sockets: once inlaid, robbed long ago.
The long close-fitting robe, probably the Sed festival garment of royal renewal.
His feet resting on the Nine Bows, the symbolic enemies of Egypt.
The base: look for his Horus name, Netjerikhet, 'divine of body'.
The striped headcloth over a heavy wig, and the long false beard.
fun_fact: Visitors to Saqqara can still peer through the two holes in the serdab and meet the gaze of Djoser's plaster double.
narration: If you have found him, this is King Djoser, from about 2650 BC, and he is the oldest known life-size statue in Egypt. He sat in the dark for more than 4,000 years. His official Imhotep is credited with building him the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first great stone building in Egypt. Against its north side stood a serdab, a tiny sealed room with no door. Its only openings were two small holes in the front wall, at the height of the statue's eyes. Through them the king's spirit could watch the rituals outside and, many think, the northern stars that never set. The Antiquities Service found him there in 1924. A plaster copy now sits in the serdab, still peering through the holes. Look at him. He wears a long, tight robe, probably the cloak of the jubilee festival that renewed a king's power. A heavy wig shows under his striped headcloth, and his feet rest on the nine bows, the symbol of Egypt's enemies. In his own time he was called Netjerikhet. Now look at his eyes. The sockets are empty: robbers dug out the inlays long ago.

name: Black seated statue of Mentuhotep II
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Found by Carter in 1900 when his horse stumbled into the 'Bab el-Hosan' shaft at Deir el-Bahari; black skin = Osiris; Sed-festival cloak; reunifier of Egypt after the First Intermediate Period.
period: Middle Kingdom, 11th Dynasty, c. 2060-2009 BC
summary: Black-skinned, red-crowned and arms crossed like Osiris: the king who reunited Egypt, found because Howard Carter's horse tripped.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A seated king in painted sandstone with jet-black skin, the tall Red Crown of Lower Egypt, a beard and a short white cloak. His arms are crossed over his chest, fists clenched. Heavy legs, big feet, a blunt face: a bold, new style compared with the Old Kingdom.
story:
When Mentuhotep II came to the throne, around 2060 BC, Egypt was split between Thebes in the south and Herakleopolis in the north. He was a Theban, and by about the 39th year of his reign, which lasted 51 years, he had reunited the country and taken a new name, 'He who unites the Two Lands'. Later Egyptians honoured him as a founder of a new age.

His temple at Deir el-Bahari, right beside the temple of Hatshepsut you see on the 21st, was the model for hers. One day Howard Carter, then a young inspector, was riding there when his horse stumbled into a hollow in the forecourt. When he dug it out in 1900, a long tunnel led to a chamber with an empty coffin and this statue, wrapped in linen. The place is still called Bab el-Hosan, the Gate of the Horse.

Why black? Black was the colour of the fertile Nile mud and of Osiris, god of the dead and of rebirth. The crossed arms are Osiris's pose. The white garment is the cloak of the Sed festival, the jubilee that renewed a king's power. Many see the hidden chamber as a symbolic burial: the king as Osiris, waiting to be reborn.
details: The Red Crown of the north, worn by the southern king who conquered it.
Black skin: the colour of Nile mud and of Osiris, god of rebirth, not a portrait of a real complexion.
Arms crossed over the chest: the classic pose of Osiris.
The short white garment: the Sed festival cloak of royal renewal.
The heavy legs and big feet: the bold Theban style of the early Middle Kingdom.
fun_fact: A stumble by Carter's horse named this site, Bab el-Hosan, the Gate of the Horse, more than 20 years before Carter found Tutankhamun.
narration: If you have found him, this black-skinned king with crossed arms is Mentuhotep the Second, and he put Egypt back together. When he came to the throne, around 2060 BC, the country was split between Thebes in the south and rival kings in the north. Mentuhotep, a Theban, reunited it during a reign of 51 years, and later Egyptians remembered him as a founder. His temple at Deir el-Bahari stands right beside Hatshepsut's, which you will see on the 21st, and hers copied his. The way this statue was found is a gift to any guide. One day Howard Carter, then a young inspector, was riding there when his horse stumbled into a hollow. When he dug it out in 1900, a long tunnel led to a chamber holding an empty coffin and this statue, wrapped in linen. The place is still called Bab el Hosan, the Gate of the Horse. Why black skin? Black was the colour of fertile Nile mud and of Osiris, god of rebirth. The crossed arms are Osiris's pose too. Look now at his crown: the Red Crown of the north, worn by a king from the south.

name: The colossi of Akhenaten from Karnak
area: Masterpieces: GEM or Tahrir, check label
note: LOCATION UNCERTAIN. Sandstone colossi from the Gempaaten at East Karnak (found 1925); the elongated face, belly, thighs; the sexless one; theories: Marfan, Froehlich, or deliberate theology of the Aten as mother and father.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, early reign of Akhenaten, c. 1350 BC
summary: The strangest royal portraits Egypt ever made: a king with a long face, a pot belly and wide hips, carved for a temple to the sun disc.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Huge sandstone figures of the king, arms crossed, holding the crook and flail, many broken off around the knees. The face is long and narrow, with slanting eyes, full lips and a drooping chin; below a pinched waist the belly swells and the hips and thighs spread. Small cartouches are carved on his body like jewellery.
story:
In 1925 workers digging a drainage ditch east of the great temple of Amun at Karnak hit fallen sandstone statues, lying face down and inscribed with the name Amenhotep IV. That was Akhenaten's name in the first years of his reign, before he moved the court to Amarna. Henri Chevrier, chief inspector at Karnak, excavated there on and off for 25 years and found 28 bases. The site belonged to the Gempaaten, 'the Aten is found', a roofless temple to the sun disc whose open court was lined with pillars and colossi.

Nothing in Egyptian art before looks like this. Kings had always been strong, youthful, ideal men. Here the face is stretched, the lips thick, the belly sags, the hips are wide. One colossus seems naked and has no genitals at all.

Why? Doctors have offered diagnoses. Froehlich's syndrome is generally rejected, because sufferers are usually infertile and Akhenaten fathered at least six daughters. Marfan syndrome has never been confirmed. Most Egyptologists prefer a religious reading: the Aten was creator of all life, father and mother at once, and the king, its only son and prophet, took on that double nature. One scholar argued that the naked figure is really Nefertiti in a clinging dress; its feet, which might settle the matter, are lost.
