fun_fact: The famous tomb-robbery trials of about 1110 BC were heard in a little temple of Maat, the goddess of truth, inside this precinct.
narration: Beyond the north wall of Amun's precinct lies the Precinct of Montu, the falcon-headed war god who was lord of Thebes before Amun took over. The kings who reunited Egypt around 2000 BC were named after him: Mentuhotep means Montu is content. Amenhotep the Third rebuilt his temple here, Ramesses the Second added obelisks, and Ptolemy the Third and Fourth built the tall gateway that rises above the wall. In a small temple of Maat, goddess of truth, judges once tried the men who robbed royal tombs. The precinct is usually closed. Look north over the enclosure wall for the top of that Ptolemaic gate.

name: Luxor Museum: small, dark and perfect
note: Opened 1975, a model of restraint: a few hundred objects, superbly lit, labelled; two floors plus the cachette hall and the 'Thebes Glory' military wing (2004) with two royal mummies; what to see in order: the ground-floor giants (Amenhotep III, Sobek, Thutmose III), the Akhenaten talatat wall, Tut's cow head and chariot, the Luxor cachette hall; air-conditioned refuge at midday; 1-1.5 hours.
period: Opened 1975; new wing 2004
summary: A small museum that chose quality over quantity: a few hundred masterpieces, lit like jewels, and an air-conditioned break from the midday sun.
look: A low modern building on the Corniche, between Luxor Temple and Karnak, facing the Nile. Inside: a dark, calm ground floor of big statues, an upper floor, the hall of the 1989 Luxor Temple statues, and a newer wing on the early New Kingdom army with two royal mummies. Plan 1 to 1.5 hours.
story:
The Ministry of Culture commissioned the architect Mahmoud El-Hakim in 1962; the objects were installed between 1972 and 1975, and the museum opened in 1975. The idea was the opposite of the crowded old Cairo museum: fewer pieces, each with space, good light and clear labels. It works. You can see everything that matters without museum fatigue.

Two additions changed it. In 1989 workers at Luxor Temple found a pit of buried statues, and a hall was built for them here. In March 2004 a new wing opened on the military glory of the early New Kingdom, with chariots and weapons, and two royal mummies: Ahmose I, who drove out the Hyksos, and the mummy believed to be Ramesses I, back from more than a century at Niagara Falls.

A good route: the calcite Sobek with Amenhotep III; the tall limestone stela of Kamose from Karnak, telling of the war against the Hyksos; Thutmose III in greywacke; the Akhenaten wall; the scribe statue of Amenhotep son of Hapu; any Tutankhamun pieces still here; the cachette hall; and the mummies in the new wing. Come in the midday heat, between Karnak in the morning and Luxor Temple at dusk.
details: The calcite Sobek and Amenhotep III: the crocodile god and the king side by side, a good place to start.
The Kamose stela: 2.3 m of limestone from Karnak, the war on the Hyksos told for the king just before Ahmose.
The Akhenaten wall: hundreds of small blocks from his Karnak temple, reassembled into one long painted wall.
The cachette hall: the 1989 statues from under Luxor Temple, with Amenhotep III on his sledge.
The military wing: chariots, weapons and two royal mummies in a dim room.
fun_fact: One of the kings in the new wing spent more than 130 years in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls before researchers worked out who he probably was.
narration: Welcome to the Luxor Museum, opened in 1975 and designed around a simple idea: show fewer things, and show them beautifully. Dark walls, careful spotlights, plenty of space. You can see everything that matters in an hour or so, and it is the best place in Luxor to spend the hottest part of the day. Here is a route. Near the start, the white calcite statue of the crocodile god Sobek with King Amenhotep the Third. Look for the tall stela of Kamose, the king who fought the Hyksos invaders just before Ahmose finished the job. Then Thutmose the Third, the conqueror, in dark polished stone, and the long wall of small painted blocks from Akhenaten's lost temple at Karnak. Find the scribe statue of Amenhotep son of Hapu, the architect who became a god. In 1989 workers at Luxor Temple found a pit full of buried statues, and a special hall was built here for them; its star is Amenhotep the Third in red quartzite, standing on a sledge. Finally, in the newer wing opened in 2004, chariots, weapons and two royal mummies: Ahmose the First, and the man believed to be Ramesses the First, who spent more than a century in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls. Start with Sobek: look for the crocodile head, and the small king at his side.

name: Sobek and Amenhotep III: the calcite pair
note: Life-size calcite (Egyptian alabaster) group of the crocodile god Sobek with a human body handing the ankh to the young Amenhotep III, found in 1967 in a water-filled shaft at Dahamsha (Armant) by chance; usurped by Ramesses II who recut the king's face; the translucent stone; one of the greatest statues of the New Kingdom; at the entrance.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC; later inscribed by Ramesses II
summary: A crocodile-headed god and a young king carved from one block of glowing calcite, found by chance in 1967 at the bottom of a water-filled shaft.
look: A group carved from a single block of calcite, the stone called Egyptian alabaster. Sobek, with a man's body and a crocodile's head under a tall crown, sits on a throne, with Amenhotep III beside him at a much smaller scale. Step to one side where the light passes into the stone's thin edges: it glows.
story:
Sobek was the crocodile god, lord of the waters and of the fertility the Nile brought, and crocodiles were a real danger on every riverbank. At Sumenu, south of Thebes near Armant, he had an important cult centre, and this statue comes from there. The king is beside the seated god at a much smaller scale, like a protected son: the power belongs to Sobek, and the king receives it.

It was found by chance in 1967 at Dahamsha, the site of ancient Sumenu, at the bottom of a shaft full of water, where it had lain since antiquity. Ramesses II later carved his own name on it, as he did on so many of his predecessors' statues: taking over a masterpiece was cheaper than commissioning one, and just as glorious.

Calcite is soft enough to carve fine detail and translucent enough to glow when light gets into it. Look at the king's face, round-cheeked with the almond eyes favoured by Amenhotep III's sculptors, and at the fine pleating of his kilt. Few statues put a god and a king so close together, and fewer still survive in this condition.
details: Sobek's head: a crocodile's long snout under a tall crown, on a muscular man's body.
Amenhotep III's face: round cheeks and almond eyes, the house style of his reign.
Stand where a light is behind a thin edge of stone: calcite is translucent and seems to glow from inside.
Search the inscriptions for Ramesses II's cartouches, added long after Amenhotep III's death.
Compare with the crocodile mummies you saw at Kom Ombo's Crocodile Museum on the 20th.
fun_fact: Herodotus, visiting Egypt in the 5th century BC, describes tame sacred crocodiles wearing earrings of glass and gold, with bracelets on their front feet.
narration: Here is one of the finest statues of the New Kingdom: the crocodile god Sobek, seated on a throne, with King Amenhotep the Third beside him, both carved from a single block of calcite, the stone often called Egyptian alabaster. Sobek has a man's body and a crocodile's head under a tall crown. The king is smaller and young-faced, close to the god like a protected son. The message is clear: the power comes from the god, and the king receives it. Sobek ruled the Nile's waters and the crocodiles that lived in them, a very real danger on every riverbank. One of his cult centres was Sumenu, south of Thebes, and that is where this statue comes from. It was found by chance in 1967 at Dahamsha, the site of Sumenu, at the bottom of a shaft full of water, where it had lain since antiquity. Later, Ramesses the Second added his own name to it, as he did to so many of his predecessors' statues. The Greek historian Herodotus, visiting Egypt in the fifth century BC, saw tame sacred crocodiles wearing earrings of glass and gold, with bracelets on their front feet. Now look at the king's face, round-cheeked with almond eyes, then step to the side, where the light passes into the thin stone and makes it glow.

name: Thutmose III in greywacke
note: The famous dark greywacke standing statue of Thutmose III from the Karnak cachette, the serene 'Thutmoside smile', the nemes and the fine polished torso, the Horus falcon name on the belt; the man behind the face: 17 campaigns to Megiddo and the Euphrates, Hatshepsut's stepson; look at the belt buckle cartouche Menkheperre: the most common name on scarabs in Egypt.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose III, 1479-1425 BC
summary: The face of Egypt's greatest conqueror, carved in dark greywacke with a gentle half-smile you would never expect from a man who spent twenty years at war.
look: A statue of Thutmose III in dark, fine-grained greywacke, polished to a soft sheen, from the Karnak cachette. He wears the striped nemes headcloth with the cobra on his brow and a pleated kilt. Look at the face first, then search the belt and inscriptions for his name in a cartouche.
story:
Thutmose III came to the throne as a child in 1479 BC, and for about 22 years his stepmother and aunt Hatshepsut ruled beside him, in the end as senior king. When she died around 1458 BC he went to war almost at once. In his year 23 he led his army through a narrow mountain pass his generals thought too dangerous, routed a coalition of Canaanite princes at Megiddo, and then besieged the city for seven or eight months. Over the next twenty years he campaigned again and again, at least sixteen times by most counts, and in year 33 he carried boats overland to cross the Euphrates and strike at Mitanni. The American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt. His annals are carved on the walls of the Amun temple at Karnak.

None of that shows in this face. The sculptors of his family gave their kings a calm, youthful look: almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and a faint smile. It is an ideal, not a photograph, but the family likeness runs through the dynasty.

The statue was found in the Karnak cachette, the great hoard of buried statues that Georges Legrain recovered from 1903. Greywacke, a hard dark stone from the Wadi Hammamat in the Eastern Desert, takes a polish that catches the light.

His throne name, Menkheperre, roughly 'the manifestation of Ra is established', became the favourite royal name on scarab amulets, copied for centuries after his death.
details: The face: almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and the closed half-smile of the Thutmoside kings.
The nemes headcloth with its stripes, and the cobra rising on his brow.
Menkheperre in a cartouche: a sun disc, a scarab beetle and a sign like a game board. Look for it on the statue.
The polish: hard greywacke from the Eastern Desert takes a sheen that sandstone never could.
fun_fact: Menkheperre was such a lucky name that Egyptians kept putting it on scarab amulets for centuries after his death, and you will still see it on souvenir scarabs today.
narration: Meet Thutmose the Third, carved in dark greywacke and polished until it shines. He came to the throne as a small child in 1479 BC. For about twenty years his stepmother and aunt, Hatshepsut, ruled beside him, and in the end above him. When she died, he went to war. In his twenty-third year he led his army through a narrow mountain pass that his generals called too dangerous, surprised an alliance of Canaanite princes at Megiddo, and then besieged the city for seven months or more. Over the next twenty years he campaigned again and again, at least sixteen times, and once he carried boats overland so his army could cross the Euphrates. The American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt. Yet look at this face. Calm, young, with almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and a faint smile. The sculptors of his family gave every king this serene look; it is an ideal, not a photograph. The statue comes from the Karnak cachette, the pit of buried statues found by Georges Legrain in 1903. Now look for his throne name, Menkheperre, written in a cartouche with a sun disc, a scarab beetle and a sign shaped like a game board. It became the favourite name on lucky scarab amulets for centuries, and you will still see it on souvenir scarabs today.

name: The Luxor cachette hall: Amenhotep III on his sledge
note: The hall built for the 26 statues found under Luxor Temple's court in 1989: the 2.5 m red quartzite Amenhotep III standing on a sledge in perfect condition (the king as a cult statue to be dragged in procession), Horemheb kneeling before Atum in diorite, the Hathor-cow-eared goddess, Iunyt, the Amun with Tutankhamun's features; why priests buried statues (sacred, cannot be thrown away) and why the Roman legion needed the space.
period: New Kingdom statues, mostly 18th Dynasty; buried probably in the Roman period; found 1989
summary: In 1989 a routine check of the ground under Luxor Temple turned up a pit of near-perfect statues buried by priests; the king on his sledge is the star.
look: A hall built for the statues found in 1989 under the sun court of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple. The tallest is Amenhotep III in red quartzite, about 2.5 m high, standing on a sledge. Around him are gods, goddesses and kings, including Horemheb kneeling before the god Atum, Hathor, and Iunyt, a local goddess of Armant.
story:
In 1989 Egyptian workers were testing the ground beneath the sun court of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple, checking the foundations, when they broke into a pit. Inside, laid down with care, were statues: 26 came out, many in near-perfect condition.

Why were they buried? A statue in a temple was sacred; you could not simply throw away the image of a god or a king. When priests needed space, they buried such statues in holy ground, as they did on a far bigger scale in the Karnak cachette. The most likely moment here is the Roman period: around 300 AD Diocletian turned Luxor Temple into the heart of a legionary fortress, and the old cult was squeezed into a corner. Burying the statues may have protected them, or simply made room.

The centrepiece shows Amenhotep III in red quartzite, wearing the double crown and standing on a sledge. The sledge is the clue. This is not just a portrait: it is the king as a divine image, a cult statue to be dragged in procession and worshipped, fitting for a temple devoted to the king's divine ka. Nearby, Horemheb, the general who became the last king of the dynasty, kneels before Atum, the creator. Iunyt was a goddess of Armant, just south of Thebes. Another figure of Amun is thought to carry the features of Tutankhamun: kings liked to lend their faces to gods.
details: Amenhotep III on his sledge: red quartzite, about 2.5 m tall. Look down at the runners under his feet.
Horemheb kneeling before Atum: the general turned king, presenting offerings to the creator god.
Look for Hathor and Iunyt: goddesses who spent many centuries in the dark under the temple court.
Surfaces: buried in sand, these statues kept crisp detail that statues left standing outside lost.
At Luxor Temple today, find the sun court of Amenhotep III: the pit was under its floor.
fun_fact: The discovery was an accident of engineering: the workers were only checking the soil under the court, and found a pit of kings and gods.
narration: This hall was built for one discovery. In 1989 Egyptian workers were testing the ground beneath the sun court of Amenhotep the Third at Luxor Temple, checking the foundations, when they broke into a pit full of statues. Twenty-six came out, many in near-perfect condition. They had been buried on purpose. A statue in a temple was sacred: you could not throw away the image of a god or a king. When space was needed, priests buried them in holy ground. The most likely moment is the Roman period, when around 300 AD the emperor Diocletian turned Luxor Temple into a fortress for his legion. The star is Amenhotep the Third in red quartzite, about two and a half metres tall, wearing the double crown and standing on a sledge. That sledge is the key. This is not just a portrait of the king, it is the king as a divine image, to be dragged in procession and worshipped. Around him stand gods and goddesses, including Hathor and Iunyt, a local goddess of Armant, and Horemheb, the general who became king, kneeling before the creator god Atum. At Luxor Temple, stand in the court where they were found. For now, walk round Amenhotep, and look down at the runners of the sledge beneath his feet.

name: The Akhenaten talatat wall and the Amarna heads
note: A reassembled 18 m wall of 283 small sandstone 'talatat' blocks (a hand-sized building block for fast construction) from Akhenaten's Gempaaten temple at Karnak, found as fill inside the ninth pylon: daily life in the palace, Nefertiti offering to the Aten, workshops, brewing, the royal couple's intimacy; upstairs the sandstone heads of Akhenaten from his Karnak colossi with the elongated face; the Amarna revolution in five minutes and the Akhenaten Temple Project's 45,000 blocks.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Akhenaten, c. 1350 BC
summary: Akhenaten's lost temple at Karnak, rebuilt from small blocks his successors used as rubble: palace life, workshops and the royal couple under the sun's hands.
look: A long wall of small painted sandstone blocks, 283 of them, reassembled along the gallery. The colours survive in places. Read it in bands: the Aten disc with its rays ending in hands, the royal couple offering, and below them storerooms, workshops and people at work. Colossal sandstone heads of Akhenaten nearby show his long face.
story:
Early in his reign, before he founded his new city at Amarna, Amenhotep IV, soon to call himself Akhenaten, built temples to the Aten, the sun disc, at Karnak. To build fast he used talatat: standard blocks about 27 by 27 by 54 cm, half a cubit by half a cubit by one, light enough for one man to carry.

After his death his religion was abandoned and his name cursed. Horemheb and the Ramesside kings pulled down his temples and used the blocks as fill and foundations at Karnak, inside pylons such as the Ninth and under the Hypostyle Hall. Inside the pylons the paint survived. Tens of thousands of talatat have been recovered. From the 1960s the Akhenaten Temple Project photographed them and used computers to help match scenes, one of the first such uses in archaeology. This wall is one of the results.

The scenes break with everything before them. The king and Nefertiti offer to the Aten, whose rays end in little hands holding the sign of life to their faces. Below, the life of the temple and palace: storerooms stacked with jars, bakers, brewers, workmen, servants. The figures are loose and lively, the bodies stretched in the Amarna style.

The colossal heads nearby come from statues of Akhenaten at Karnak: the long chin, the full lips, the narrow slanting eyes. Whether that face was a portrait, a style or a statement of religion is still argued.
details: Find the Aten: a disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding an ankh to the royal faces.
Look for Nefertiti offering alongside the king: she appears in these scenes as an active partner.
Lower rows: storerooms of jars, bakers and brewers, everyday work in Akhenaten's temple.
Size up one block: each is about three hand-spans long, a load one man could carry alone.
The sandstone heads of Akhenaten: long chin, full lips and narrow slanting eyes.
fun_fact: Talatat may simply mean 'threes': one theory says Egyptian workmen named the blocks because each is about three hand-spans long.
narration: This long painted wall was rebuilt from 283 small blocks taken out of Karnak's pylons. They come from temples that Akhenaten, the heretic king, built to the Aten, the sun disc, at Karnak about 1350 BC, before he left Thebes for his new city at Amarna. To build fast he used standard little blocks, each about three hand-spans long, light enough for one man to carry. Archaeologists call them talatat. When Akhenaten died, his religion was abandoned and his name cursed. Later kings pulled down his temples and packed the blocks inside their own pylons as rubble, among them Karnak's Ninth Pylon. That insult turned out to be lucky: inside the pylons, the paint survived. Tens of thousands of these blocks have been found, and in the 1960s a project began to photograph them and match them like a giant jigsaw, one of the first uses of computers in archaeology. Look at the top. The Aten is a disc whose rays end in little hands, holding the sign of life to the faces of the king and Nefertiti. Lower down, the life of the temple: storerooms full of jars, bakers, brewers, people at work. Nearby stand colossal heads of Akhenaten from the same temples. Find a ray ending in a hand, and follow it down to a royal face.

name: Tutankhamun's cow head of Mehet-Weret and the KV62 objects
note: A few KV62 pieces kept in Luxor: the gilded wooden cow head of Mehet-Weret ('great flood', the celestial cow who carried the sun) with copper horns and lapis eyes, a boat, sandals, arrows, the chariot (in the military wing): the only Tut objects outside GEM; link back to 11 Oct.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Tutankhamun, c. 1323 BC
summary: A gilded cow's head from Tutankhamun's treasury: the celestial cow who lifted the sun into the sky, one of the few pieces of his tomb kept in Luxor.
look: A cow's head of gilded wood, with dark horns and inlaid eyes, made for Tutankhamun's tomb, KV62. The Grand Egyptian Museum has been gathering the king's whole treasure, so if it is not on display, that is probably where it went; trust the labels for what is still here.
story:
Mehet-Weret, 'the Great Flood', was the celestial cow: a goddess of water, creation and rebirth who lifted the newborn sun into the sky every day, carrying it between her horns. In the Book of the Dead she is credited with the birth of Ra, and she helps the dead reach the afterlife. A cow who carries the sun up out of the dark was exactly what a dead king needed. She overlaps with Hathor, and labels often use both names.

The head was found in the Treasury of KV62, the small room beyond the burial chamber that Howard Carter cleared after the coffins. Almost all of Tutankhamun's objects went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and are now at the Grand Egyptian Museum, which you visited on 11 October. A handful were kept in Luxor, near the tomb itself.

One of the three ritual beds from the tomb is shaped as the same celestial cow, with lyre-shaped horns and a sun disc between them. If you saw it at GEM, this head is its small sister.
details: The horns: curved like a lyre, the cradle for the sun the celestial cow lifted into the sky.
The gilding: a thin skin of gold over carved wood, the technique used for most of the tomb's furniture.
Look for other Tutankhamun pieces nearby: labels will say KV62 or 'tomb of Tutankhamun'.
Compare it in memory with the cow-headed ritual bed at GEM: same goddess, same lyre horns.
fun_fact: Her name means 'Great Flood', and one scholar links her to the Milky Way, a river of stars flowing across the night sky.
narration: This golden cow's head comes from the tomb of Tutankhamun, K V 62. It shows Mehet Weret, whose name means the Great Flood: the celestial cow who lifted the newborn sun into the sky between her horns. For a dead king that was the right companion, a goddess who carries the sun up out of the darkness every morning. In the Book of the Dead she is credited with the birth of the sun god, and she helps the dead reach the next world. She shares a lot with Hathor, so labels sometimes use both names. The head is carved wood covered in gold, with dark horns and inlaid eyes, and it was found in the Treasury, the small room beyond the burial chamber. Almost all of Tutankhamun's treasure went to Cairo and is now gathered at the Grand Egyptian Museum, which you visited on the 11th. A few pieces were kept here in Luxor, near the tomb, though some may have moved, so if the cow is not on display she is probably in Giza. If she is here, look at her horns: they curve like a lyre, a cradle for the sun.

name: Two royal mummies: Ahmose I and Ramesses I
note: In the 'Thebes Glory' military wing, dimly lit: Ahmose I, founder of the New Kingdom who expelled the Hyksos (from the DB320 cache; the identification debated), and the mummy believed to be Ramesses I, which spent 130 years in a Niagara Falls freak museum after being sold by the Abd el-Rassuls c. 1860, bought by the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta in 1999 and returned to Egypt in 2003 with honours; the weapons, chariot and Ahmose's axe from Ahhotep's burial.
period: Ahmose I, mid-16th century BC; Ramesses I, c. 1292-1290 BC
summary: The founder of the New Kingdom and the founder of the Ramesside line lie here, one of them after more than 130 years in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls.
look: In the newer wing devoted to the armies of the early New Kingdom, a dim room holds two royal mummies in glass cases. Keep your voice low. Around them in the wing: chariots, weapons and the story of the war against the Hyksos.
story:
Ahmose I finished the war that his predecessors Seqenenre and Kamose had begun against the Hyksos, foreign kings who ruled the north from Avaris. He attacked Avaris several times before it fell, then besieged Sharuhen near Gaza for three years, reunited Egypt and opened the New Kingdom. His mummy was found in 1881 in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari, in a coffin bearing his name, and unwrapped by Gaston Maspero in 1887. The identification is not certain: in 1980 James Harris and Edward Wente questioned it, partly because the arms are not crossed over the chest.

The second mummy has a stranger story. Members of the Abd el-Rassul family, who had found the same cache, took it out, and around 1860 it was sold in Luxor to a Canadian doctor, James Douglas. It ended up in the Niagara Falls Museum, where it stayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 the collection was sold to the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta. CT scans, X-rays and radiocarbon dating, the arms crossed high on the chest, and a family resemblance convinced researchers that this was most likely Ramesses I, founder of the 19th Dynasty and grandfather of Ramesses II. On 24 October 2003 he returned to Egypt with full official honours.
details: Ahmose's arms lie at his sides, not crossed: one reason some experts doubt the identification.
Ramesses I's arms are crossed high on the chest, a royal pose that helped identify him.
Around the wing: chariots and weapons of the army that drove out the Hyksos.
Ramesses I reigned only about two years; his small tomb, KV16, was finished in a hurry.
fun_fact: Ramesses I was buried around 1290 BC and came home on 24 October 2003, after more than a century as an anonymous exhibit at Niagara Falls.
narration: In this dim room lie two kings who each founded something. The first is Ahmose the First, who finished the war against the Hyksos, the foreign rulers of northern Egypt. He besieged their capital Avaris until it fell, chased them to Sharuhen near Gaza, reunited the country and opened the New Kingdom, more than 3,500 years ago. His mummy was found in 1881 in the great royal cache at Deir el-Bahari. Some experts doubt it is really him, partly because the arms are not crossed on the chest. The second has a wilder story. Around 1860, a mummy taken from the same cache was sold in Luxor to a Canadian doctor and ended up in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls, where it stayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 a museum in Atlanta bought the collection. Scans, radiocarbon dates and a family likeness convinced researchers that this was most likely Ramesses the First, grandfather of Ramesses the Second. In October 2003 he came home with full honours. Look at his arms, crossed high on the chest, the pose of a king.

name: Amenhotep son of Hapu, the scribe who became a god
note: The granite scribe statues of Amenhotep III's architect and overseer (who moved the Colossi of Memnon), shown as a wise old man with rolls of fat and a papyrus, from Karnak; given his own mortuary temple, a privilege for a commoner, later worshipped as a healing god with Imhotep at Deir el-Bahari; 'I reached 80 years, I shall reach 110'.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: A commoner from the Delta who became Amenhotep III's master of works, got a temple next to the king's, and was prayed to as a healer a thousand years later.
look: A granodiorite statue about 1.3 m high, from Karnak: a man seated cross-legged as a scribe, a papyrus open across his lap. Look at the soft rolls of fat on his chest and belly: in Egyptian art, the mark of a successful, well-fed official.
story:
Amenhotep son of Hapu was born around 1425 BC at Athribis in the Delta, son of Hapu and Itu, with no royal blood. He rose late, in middle age, under Amenhotep III: Scribe of Recruits, organising manpower for the king's projects, then overseer of works. He supervised the king's huge mortuary temple on the west bank, of which only the Colossi of Memnon remain, and took part in the king's first jubilee in year 30.

His reward was extraordinary: his own mortuary temple beside the king's, the only private cult temple among the royal ones. His statues stood at Karnak, where people approached him as an intermediary with Amun. On one of them, now in Cairo, he says he has reached 80 years and hopes to reach 110, the ideal lifespan of Egyptian wisdom literature.

After his death he became a sage and a healer. In Ptolemaic times he had chapels at Deir el-Medina and in Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari, where he was honoured with Imhotep, the builder of the Step Pyramid. Greek-speaking pilgrims called him Amenothes.
details: The rolls of fat on his chest: not an insult but a boast. Only a rich man ate well enough to have them.
The papyrus across his lap, the badge of a scribe: literacy was the key to his whole career.
The cross-legged scribe pose echoes Old Kingdom scribe statues, chosen to look wise and traditional.
His mortuary temple stood beside Amenhotep III's on the west bank, near the Colossi of Memnon you saw on the 21st.
fun_fact: His mortuary temple carried a long, detailed curse against anyone who disturbed or robbed it.
narration: This seated scribe is Amenhotep son of Hapu, one of the very few ordinary Egyptians who became a god. He was born about 1425 BC at Athribis in the Delta, son of a man called Hapu, with no royal blood. He rose late, in middle age, under King Amenhotep the Third: first as scribe of recruits, organising the workforce, then as the king's master of works. He supervised the king's vast temple on the west bank, of which only the Colossi of Memnon remain; you passed them on the 21st. His reward was unheard of: his own mortuary temple, built next to the king's. His statues stood at Karnak, where people asked him to pass their prayers on to Amun. On one, now in Cairo, he says he has reached 80 years and hopes to reach 110, the perfect lifespan. After his death he became a healer and a sage. Over a thousand years later, in Ptolemaic times, the sick still came to him at Deir el-Bahari, together with Imhotep. Look at the rolls of fat on his chest: here, that means success.

name: Senusret III and the Middle Kingdom faces
note: Short. Red granite head with the heavy-lidded, careworn face typical of the 12th Dynasty 'realistic' royal portraits (the burdened shepherd of his people), from Karnak; compare with the idealised New Kingdom smiles around it; the conqueror of Nubia who built the forts now under Lake Nasser.
period: Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, Senusret III, c. 1878-1839 BC
summary: A king who chose to look tired: Senusret III's heavy-lidded, careworn face is one of the most human portraits in Egyptian art.
look: A red granite head of Senusret III with deep-set eyes, heavy lids, pouches beneath them, a downturned mouth and big ears turned forward. Follow the labels to find it, then compare it with the smooth, smiling New Kingdom faces around the museum.
story:
Senusret III ruled from about 1878 to 1839 BC and pushed Egypt's border deep into Nubia. He campaigned there in his years 8, 10, 16 and 19, cleared a navigable canal through the First Cataract at Aswan, and built a chain of forts at the Second Cataract, Buhen, Semna, Uronarti and others, now under Lake Nasser. His boundary stela at Semna tells his successors that a son who keeps the border is his true son.

His sculptors broke with tradition. Instead of an ageless mask, they gave him hollow eyes, heavy lids and a weary mouth on a young, muscular body. Some read it as a ruler burdened by care; others as a stern king meant to be feared. He was worshipped as a god in Nubia long after his death.
details: The eyes: deep sockets, heavy upper lids and pouches below. No earlier king was carved like this.
The ears: big and set forward, perhaps a king who hears everything.
Find a New Kingdom face nearby and compare: the 12th Dynasty frown against the 18th Dynasty smile.
fun_fact: Herodotus tells of Sesostris, a pharaoh who conquered half the world; that Greek legend is partly built on memories of this king.
narration: This red granite head belongs to Senusret the Third, a king of the Middle Kingdom who ruled about 1850 BC. Look at the face: deep-set eyes, heavy lids, pouches beneath them, a mouth that turns down, and big ears pushed forward. Earlier kings had smooth, ageless faces. Senusret chose to look tired. Some see a ruler weighed down by care for his people, others a stern king who sees and hears everything. He pushed Egypt's border deep into Nubia and built forts at the Second Cataract that now lie under Lake Nasser. Herodotus tells of a conquering pharaoh called Sesostris, a legend partly built on his memory. Now compare his eyes with any smiling New Kingdom face nearby.

name: Mummification Museum
note: Small 1997 museum below the Corniche: the process in order (the 70 days, natron, the hook through the nose, the four organs, the heart left in place, resin, linen, amulets), the tools, materials, canopic jars, amulets with their positions on the body, the painted coffin and mummy of Masaharta, mummified animals; 30-45 minutes; good before seeing tombs; dim and cool.
period: Museum opened 1997
summary: A small, cool museum on the Corniche that explains step by step how the Egyptians turned a body into a mummy, with the real materials, tools and a high priest.
look: On the Corniche in front of the Mina Palace Hotel, north of Luxor Temple, facing the Nile. A corridor with ten panels copied from the Book of the Dead papyri of Ani and Hunefer leads into one dim hall with 19 cases and over 60 objects. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.
story:
President Hosni Mubarak opened the museum in 1997 in a former visitor centre. It is small, 2,035 square metres including a lecture hall and a video room, and that is its strength: everything is about one subject.

The corridor at the start sets the scene with copies of vignettes from the papyri of Ani and Hunefer, both in the British Museum, following a burial from death to tomb. Then the cases are arranged by theme: the gods of embalming, the materials (natron, organic materials, embalming fluid), the tools, canopic jars, shabtis, amulets, the coffin of a man called Padiamun, the mummy of Masaharta, a High Priest of Amun around 1050 BC, and mummified animals.

After yesterday's tombs on the West Bank, this is where it all makes sense: the jackal-headed Anubis leaning over a mummy, the four jars by the coffin, the priest with the adze at the tomb door.
details: Canopic jars with lids shaped as the four sons of Horus: human, baboon, jackal and falcon.
The mummy of Masaharta, High Priest of Amun about 1050 BC, son of the priest-king Pinedjem I.
The coffin of Padiamun: painted wood covered with protective gods and texts.
Mummified animals: cats, fish and a crocodile among them.
The amulet case: small charms that were tucked between the bandages, each with a job.
fun_fact: The whole process took about 70 days, which the Egyptians linked to the time the star Sirius stays hidden from the sky each year.
narration: This small museum on the Corniche explains one thing: how the Egyptians made a mummy. It opened in 1997 and fits into a single dim, cool hall. The corridor at the start shows scenes copied from two famous Book of the Dead papyri, those of Ani and Hunefer, following a funeral from death to the tomb. Then come the cases, arranged like a lesson. The gods of embalming, with Anubis the jackal in charge. The materials: natron salt to dry the body, resins, oils and linen. The tools. The canopic jars that held the organs, with lids shaped as the four sons of Horus. The amulets tucked between the bandages, and the little shabti figures that worked for the dead. At the heart of the room lies a real person: Masaharta, High Priest of Amun about 1050 BC, son of the priest-king Pinedjem, whose name you saw on the colossus at Karnak. There is a painted coffin of a man called Padiamun, and mummified animals: cats, fish, a crocodile. The whole process took about 70 days. Start at the canopic jars: a human head, a baboon, a jackal and a falcon.

name: Masaharta: the high priest in his coffin
note: Son of the priest-king Pinedjem I (see the Karnak colossus), High Priest of Amun c. 1050 BC, a large man, his mummy in a fine 21st Dynasty yellow coffin from the DB320 cache; the 21st Dynasty embalmers' peak: subcutaneous packing with sawdust and mud to restore the shape of the face and limbs, artificial eyes, painted skin; the priest-kings who hid the royal mummies and quietly 'recycled' their gold.
period: Third Intermediate Period, 21st Dynasty, High Priest c. 1054-1045 BC
summary: Son of a priest-king and brother of a pharaoh, Masaharta ran Thebes for Amun, and his family were the ones who hid Egypt's royal mummies.
look: The mummy of Masaharta, High Priest of Amun, in its own case at the heart of the hall. He died around 3,000 years ago. The painted coffin nearby belongs to a different man, Padiamun; read the labels so you do not mix them up.
story:
Masaharta was High Priest of Amun at Thebes from about 1054 to 1045 BC. His father was Pinedjem I, the high priest who ruled Upper Egypt and in 1054 BC declared himself king; Pinedjem's name is carved on the colossus at Karnak's second pylon. His mother was probably Duathathor-Henuttawy, a daughter of Ramesses XI, the last Ramesside. His brother Psusennes I became pharaoh at Tanis in the Delta, and another brother, Menkheperre, later held the high priesthood. His sister Maatkare was probably God's Wife of Amun. It was a family business: the north had the crown, the south had the god.

These priest-kings also managed the royal dead. Robbers had plundered the Valley of the Kings, so the priests gathered the kings' mummies, rewrapped them and moved them into hiding; many scholars think much of the old gold went back into circulation along the way. Masaharta himself restored the mummy of Amenhotep I, in year 16 of King Smendes. In the end his own body was found with members of his family in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari, DB320, discovered in 1881. It was later moved from the Egyptian Museum in Cairo to this museum.
details: The mummy itself: a High Priest of Amun from the family that hid Egypt's royal mummies.
The coffin of Padiamun nearby is a different man's; a good example of a painted wooden coffin.
Pinedjem I, his father, is the name carved on the colossus in front of Karnak's second pylon.
His brother Psusennes I was buried at Tanis in a silver coffin with a gold mask, one of Egypt's great treasures.
fun_fact: His family ran both ends of Egypt: one brother was pharaoh in the Delta, another succeeded to the high priesthood at Thebes, and a sister was God's Wife of Amun.
narration: Here lies Masaharta, High Priest of Amun at Thebes about 3,000 years ago. Picture Egypt split in two. In the north a king ruled from the Delta. In the south the High Priests of Amun ruled Thebes in the god's name. Masaharta's father was Pinedjem, the high priest who declared himself king; you saw his name carved on the colossus at Karnak's second pylon. His mother was probably a daughter of Ramesses the Eleventh, the last of the Ramesside kings. His brother Psusennes became pharaoh in the north and was buried at Tanis in a silver coffin. These priest-kings also looked after the royal dead. Robbers had plundered the Valley of the Kings, so the priests rewrapped the royal mummies and moved them into hiding, and many scholars think much of the kings' gold went back into circulation on the way. Masaharta himself restored the mummy of Amenhotep the First. In the end his own body lay in the great hiding place at Deir el-Bahari, found in 1881. Look closely at him: this was a member of Egypt's ruling family.

name: Mummified animals: cat, crocodile, ram, fish, ibis
note: Why millions of animals were mummified: sacred animals (one Apis bull, one ram of Khnum), votive offerings bought by pilgrims (ibises for Thoth: 4 million at Tuna el-Gebel; cats for Bastet: 19 tons shipped to Liverpool as fertiliser in 1890), pets, and food for the dead (victual mummies); the fake votives stuffed with a single bone; CT scanning today; the Nile perch and the ram with gilded horns here.
period: Mostly Late Period to Roman times
summary: Cats, crocodiles and fish: the Egyptians mummified millions of animals, as pets, food, sacred beasts and offerings, and plenty of them were fakes.
look: A few cases of animal mummies, including cats, fish and a crocodile. Look at the shapes of the wrappings: some follow the animal's body, others are neat geometric parcels. The labels say what each one was for.
story:
Most animal mummies fall into four groups. Pets, buried to keep their owners company: cats, dogs, monkeys, gazelles. Food, the 'victual mummies' of meat and ducks for the dead to eat; Tutankhamun had boxes of them. Sacred animals, a single chosen creature that lived in a temple as the god's living image, like the Apis bull at Memphis or the rams of Khnum at Elephantine, pampered in life and buried with honours. And above all votive offerings: pilgrims bought a mummified animal at a temple and dedicated it to the god.

That last trade became an industry in the Late Period and under the Ptolemies and Romans. Animals were raised on temple grounds for it. About four million ibises, Thoth's bird, were buried at Tuna el-Gebel. Cats went to Bastet, crocodiles to Sobek, Nile perch to the goddess Neith near Esna. Quality fell as demand rose: scans show many bundles hold only a few bones, feathers or reeds. The pilgrim never knew.

Modern people were not kinder. In 1888 a farmer found a vast cat cemetery in Middle Egypt, and around 1890 some 19 tons of cat mummies were shipped to Liverpool and sold as fertiliser.
details: The cat: look at the wrapping pattern. The best cat mummies have geometric bands and modelled ears.
The crocodile: Sobek's animal. You met his sacred crocodiles at Kom Ombo on the 20th.
The fish: Nile perch were sacred to Neith, and thousands were buried near Esna, which you visited on the 20th.
Think about what is inside: the label may say whether scans found a whole animal or only fragments.
fun_fact: Many votive mummies were fakes: scans show bundles holding a few bones, feathers or reeds, sold to pilgrims who never knew the difference.
narration: These are the animals. The Egyptians mummified millions of them, for four reasons. Some were pets, buried to keep their owners company. Some were food for the dead. Some were sacred animals, a single chosen creature that lived in a temple as the living image of a god, like the Apis bull at Memphis or the ram of Khnum at Elephantine. But most were offerings. A pilgrim bought a mummified animal at the temple and gave it to the god, the way you might light a candle. Under the last pharaohs, the Ptolemies and the Romans, it became an industry, with animals raised on temple grounds. About four million ibises, the bird of Thoth, were buried at Tuna el-Gebel. Cats went to Bastet, crocodiles to Sobek, Nile perch to the goddess Neith near Esna. Quality fell as demand grew, and scans show that many bundles hold only a few bones, feathers or reeds. Modern people were worse: around 1890 a ship carried tons of cat mummies to Liverpool to be sold as fertiliser. Find the cat, and look at the neat pattern of its wrapping.

name: The embalmer's kit: natron, hooks, resins and amulets
note: The Herodotus three price tiers; the ibu tent and the wabet workshop; the brain hook through the ethmoid bone, the Ethiopian stone knife, the ripper-up who was ritually chased; natron from Wadi Natrun, 40 days of drying; cedar oil, resins, beeswax; the 20 layers of linen and the 100+ amulets (heart scarab over the heart with spell 30B, the djed, the tyet, the headrest); the Opening of the Mouth with the adze; Anubis masks worn by the priests; the 2019 Saqqara embalming workshop discovery.
period: Old Kingdom to Roman period
summary: Hooks, natron, resin and amulets: the 70-day recipe for eternity, as a Greek tourist described it 2,500 years ago and as the embalmers' own pots confirm.
look: Cases of embalming materials and tools: natron, resins and oils, linen, instruments, canopic jars and amulets. Read them as a sequence: drying, emptying, filling, wrapping, protecting. The amulets show the charms that went between the bandages.
story:
The Greek historian Herodotus, writing around 450 BC, describes three price levels. The best: the brain drawn out through the nose with an iron hook, the belly opened along the flank with a sharp Ethiopian stone, the cavity rinsed with palm wine and spices, and the body laid in natron for 70 days. The middle: cedar oil injected to dissolve the organs, drained after the natron. The cheapest: a purge and the natron. Modern study adds that the brain was often liquefied with a rod, and the drying took about 40 days of the 70.

The body was washed in a purification tent, the ibu, and worked on in the 'House of Beauty'. Lungs, liver, stomach and intestines went into canopic jars protected by the four sons of Horus. The heart stayed, to be weighed against the feather of Maat. Over it lay a heart scarab with a spell asking the heart not to testify against its owner. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with amulets between them.

Last came the Opening of the Mouth: a priest touched the mummy's mouth with an adze so the dead could breathe and speak. Pots from a 26th Dynasty embalming workshop at Saqqara still held residues of cedar, juniper, Dead Sea bitumen, beeswax and imported resins.
details: Natron: a natural mix of salts from desert lakes such as the Wadi Natrun, packed in and around the body.
Canopic lids: human Imsety for the liver, baboon Hapy for the lungs, jackal Duamutef for the stomach, falcon Qebehsenuef for the gut.
Amulets: the djed pillar for stability, the Eye of Horus for healing, the heart scarab over the heart.
Resin: the dark, glassy coating that sealed the wrappings and made many old mummies look black.
fun_fact: The Greek historian Diodorus says the man who made the first cut was chased away with stones and curses, because wounding a body was an offence, even when it was your job.
narration: Here is the embalmer's kit, and the recipe for eternity. The Greek historian Herodotus described it around 450 BC, with three price levels. In the best, the brain was drawn out through the nose with a hook, the belly was cut open on the left side with a sharp stone blade, the cavity rinsed with palm wine and spices, and the body buried in natron, a natural salt from the desert lakes. Modern studies show the drying took about 40 days, inside a 70-day ritual. Lungs, liver, stomach and intestines went into four canopic jars. The heart stayed in the body, because it would be weighed in the judgment of the dead. Over it lay a heart scarab with a spell asking the heart not to testify against its owner. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with amulets tucked between them while a priest recited spells. Last, the Opening of the Mouth: a priest touched the mummy's lips with an adze, so the dead could breathe and speak again. Look for the natron in its case: plain whitish salt, the most important ingredient of all.

name: How to tell real papyrus from banana leaf (and what to pay)
note: Practical: real papyrus has a crosshatched, slightly translucent fibrous weave visible against light, is stiff, does not crack when rolled; banana-leaf fakes are soft, uniform, crack and are often printed, not painted; the 'institute' demonstration is a sales pitch, fine but bargain hard (start at a third); ask for hand-painted, check the back for brush marks; ancient method: Cyperus papyrus pith sliced, laid in two layers, pressed; the plant nearly extinct in Egypt until Hassan Ragab replanted it in the 1960s; how the Egyptians made books 5,000 years before paper; the 'cartouche with your name' trick.
period: Papyrus used from at least c. 2560 BC; modern craft revived in 1962
summary: Real papyrus is a woven sheet of plant pith you can see through; the cheap stuff is often banana leaf. Here is how to tell, and how to bargain.
look: Hold the sheet up to the light. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross of strips, darker lines where they overlap, running one way on the front and the other way behind. Banana-leaf fakes look uniform, with veins in one direction only, and feel soft and floppy.
story:
Papyrus, Cyperus papyrus, is a tall sedge that once filled the Delta marshes. To make a sheet, the Egyptians peeled the stem, cut the white pith into strips about 40 cm long, laid one layer side by side and a second across it at right angles, then hammered and pressed them while moist and dried them under pressure. Polished sheets were glued into rolls. The oldest inscribed papyri yet found, the Diary of Merer from Wadi al-Jarf, date to about 2560 BC and describe moving stone for the Great Pyramid.

Our words come through Greek: papyros gave 'paper', and byblos, named after the Phoenician port of Byblos, gave 'Bible'.

By the late 1700s the plant had died out in Egypt. The modern craft was revived in 1962 by Hassan Ragab, an Egyptian engineer and diplomat, and today's 'papyrus institutes' grew from his work. The demonstration you will be shown, slicing, soaking and pressing, is real. So is the sales pitch afterwards.

On price: hand-painted work on real papyrus costs more than a print, and the first price is high. Decide what you would pay before you ask, offer about a third, settle somewhere in the middle, and walk away smiling if it does not work.
details: Light test: hold it up. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross grid of strips; banana leaf shows parallel veins only.
Roll test: real papyrus rolls gently without cracking; banana leaf is brittle and splits along its veins.
Paint test: hand-painted work shows brush marks and uneven colour; prints are flat and perfect.
Your name in a cartouche is fun, but agree the price, name included, before anyone starts painting.
Opening offer: about a third of the first price is normal. Meet in the middle and part friends either way.
fun_fact: The words paper and Bible both come from papyrus: paper from the Greek papyros, Bible from byblos, the name of the Phoenician port it was traded through.
narration: A quick guide before you buy papyrus. Real papyrus is made from the pith of a tall marsh plant. The stem is peeled, the white pith cut into strips, one layer laid across another at right angles, then pressed and dried. So hold a sheet up to the light. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross grid of strips, darker where they overlap. Fakes made of banana leaf look even, with veins running one way only, and they feel soft. Roll it gently: real papyrus bends without cracking, banana leaf splits. Look at the paint: hand-painted work shows brush marks and uneven colour, prints are flat and perfect. The oldest written rolls, about 4,500 years old, record the building of the Great Pyramid. The plant died out in Egypt, and an engineer called Hassan Ragab revived the craft in 1962. The shop demonstration is real; so is the sales pitch. Offer about a third of the first price, settle in the middle, and smile. The word paper, and even the word Bible, come from Greek names for papyrus. Now hold a sheet up to the light, and look for the grid.

name: The Opet Festival: Amun's annual journey to Luxor
note: Held in the second month of the inundation (around now in the ancient calendar, Sept-Oct): the statues of Amun, Mut and Khonsu carried in their barques from Karnak, by land along the sphinx avenue or towed on the river, to Luxor Temple where Amun 'married' Mut and the king merged with his royal ka, emerging reborn; 11 days under Hatshepsut, 27 under Ramesses III, with 11,341 loaves and 385 jars of beer distributed; the public's one chance to ask the god oracle questions as the barque dipped; the reliefs in the colonnade; the Abu el-Haggag moulid as its ghost.
period: New Kingdom and later, from the 18th Dynasty, c. 1500 BC
summary: Once a year Amun left Karnak in his golden boat and travelled to Luxor to renew the king's divine power, and the city celebrated for weeks.
look: Nothing single to look at: this festival is the reason Luxor Temple and the Avenue of Sphinxes exist. Its best picture is the procession carved in the Colonnade of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple, and the barque scenes on Hatshepsut's Red Chapel at Karnak. Walk any stretch of the Avenue of Sphinxes and you are on the route.
story:
Opet was celebrated in the second month of Akhet, the flood season, roughly the time of year you are travelling. Under Thutmose III it lasted 11 days; by the start of Ramesses III's reign it had stretched to 24, and by his death to 27.

Priests lifted the barques of the Theban triad, Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, gilded boats with a veiled shrine in the middle, onto their shoulders and carried them out of Karnak. Some years they went by land along the Avenue of Sphinxes; other years the god sailed in his great river barge, Userhat-Amun, 'mighty of prow is Amun', built of Lebanese cedar covered in gold, with ram heads at prow and stern. Soldiers, musicians, dancers and acrobats went with them, and officials from all over the country helped run it.

At Luxor Temple the king met the god in the inner rooms. In a ritual of union and rebirth he was renewed as the son of Amun and recrowned, his royal ka, the divine power of kingship, refreshed for another year. Then the gods returned to Karnak.

Ordinary people did not enter the sanctuary. They watched from the route and the riverbanks, shared in bread and beer, and could put questions to the god as the barque passed. Today the moulid of Sheikh Yusuf Abu el-Haggag, whose boat is carried around Luxor, is widely seen as a distant echo of Opet.
details: Luxor Temple colonnade: the full procession, barques, soldiers, acrobats and musicians, carved under Tutankhamun.
The Avenue of Sphinxes: the land route of the procession between Karnak and Luxor Temple.
Red Chapel at Karnak: Hatshepsut's version, with the barque carried on poles by priests.
Spot Amun's barque in any relief: a boat with a ram's head at prow and stern and a veiled cabin in the middle.
The Abu el-Haggag mosque on top of Luxor Temple: its saint's moulid parades a boat through town.
fun_fact: Oracle questions were answered by the barque itself: Egyptologists think a lurch forward on the priests' shoulders meant yes, a step back meant no.
narration: Imagine Thebes in the flood season, around this time of year, more than 3,000 years ago. The Opet Festival has begun. At Karnak, priests lift the sacred boats of the gods onto their shoulders: Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, each in a gilded barque with a veiled shrine in the middle. Some years they carried them along the Avenue of Sphinxes to Luxor Temple. Other years Amun sailed upriver in his great river barge, Userhat Amun, mighty of prow is Amun, built of Lebanese cedar covered in gold, with ram heads at each end. Soldiers marched, musicians played, acrobats bent over backwards. At Luxor Temple, in the inner rooms, the king met the god. In a ritual of union and rebirth he was renewed as Amun's son, and his royal power, his ka, was refreshed for another year. Then the gods went home. Under Thutmose the Third the festival lasted 11 days. Under Ramesses the Third it stretched to 27. Ordinary people never entered the sanctuary, but they lined the route, shared bread and beer, and could ask the god questions; a lurch of the barque on the priests' shoulders was an answer. Today the moulid of Abu el-Haggag, whose boat is carried around Luxor, may be its distant echo. Walk a stretch of the Avenue of Sphinxes, and you are on the route.

name: The Theban West Bank: city of the dead
note: Orientation: east bank for the living and the gods' temples, west bank where the sun sets for the dead: royal tombs hidden in the Valleys, 'mansions of millions of years' (mortuary temples) on the edge of the fields, nobles' tombs in the hills, the workmen's village; the Qurn peak as a natural pyramid; the day's route and ticket logic (separate tickets, 3 tombs per VoK ticket, extras for Tut/Seti I/Ramesses V-VI/Nefertari); heat and water; no flash.
period: Mainly New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC
summary: The west bank was Thebes' city of the dead: hidden royal tombs, temples for dead kings, nobles' tombs and the village of the men who built them.
look: Face west from the road coming off the river: first green fields, then a line of ruined temples along the edge of the farmland, then bare limestone hills full of tomb doorways. The pointed peak on the skyline is the Qurn. The Valley of the Kings hides behind the cliffs north of it, Deir el-Bahari sits at the foot of those cliffs on the near side, and Deir el-Medina and the Valley of the Queens lie further south.
story:
Egyptians lived on the east bank, where the sun rises, and buried their dead in the west, where it sets. Across the river from Karnak and Luxor Temple, Thebes kept a second city with its own priests, embalmers, police and craftsmen, all working for the dead. UNESCO lists the whole thing as 'Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis'.

The layout follows one big decision. From about 1539 BC the New Kingdom pharaohs gave up pyramids, which had all been robbed, and cut their tombs in a hidden desert valley behind the cliffs, under a peak shaped like a natural pyramid. Their temples moved away from the tombs to the edge of the fields, facing Thebes. The Egyptians called them 'mansions of millions of years': places where priests kept a dead king's cult alive every day. From north to south you can still trace them: Seti I at Qurna, Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, the Ramesseum, Amenhotep III behind the Colossi of Memnon, and Ramesses III at Medinet Habu.

Between the temples and the valley, officials cut decorated tombs into the hills at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna and its neighbours, full of banquets and harvests. The workmen who dug and painted the royal tombs lived in a walled village at Deir el-Medina and walked to work over the hill.

The practical logic: each site has its own ticket. The standard Valley of the Kings ticket covers three tombs; Tutankhamun, Seti I and Ramesses V and VI each need an extra one, and Nefertari's tomb in the Valley of the Queens has its own, pricier ticket. Prices and rules change, so check at the window. Start early, carry more water than seems sensible, wear a hat, and never use flash.
details: The Qurn: the pyramid-shaped peak on the western skyline. Every royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings lies beneath it.
The Colossi of Memnon by the road: all that stands of Amenhotep III's temple, once the largest on this bank.
Dark square doorways in the hillside at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna: the Tombs of the Nobles.
Hatshepsut's terraced temple: a pale stripe of colonnades against the cliff below the Qurn, visible from the road.
fun_fact: The ancient Egyptians called the dead 'the westerners', so a funeral here really was a trip to the other side.
narration: You are on the west bank of Thebes, the side where the sun dies every evening, and so the side of the dead. The living city and the great temples of the gods were across the river, at Karnak and Luxor. Over here the kings built a second city: tombs, temples and workshops for eternity. Look west and read it like a map. First the green fields. Then, along the edge of the farmland, the big mortuary temples, which the Egyptians called mansions of millions of years, where priests fed a dead king's spirit every day. Then the bare limestone hills, pierced by hundreds of doorways: the tombs of officials. Behind the ridge, out of sight, is the Valley of the Kings, where the pharaohs hid their tombs after the age of pyramids. Above it all rises the Qurn, a peak shaped like a natural pyramid, probably one reason they chose the place. The men who cut and painted the royal tombs lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, tucked into the hills to the south. A practical word. Every site has its own ticket. The standard Valley ticket covers three tombs, while Tutankhamun, Seti the First and Ramesses the Sixth cost extra. Carry more water than you think you need, and never use flash. Now find the pointed peak on the skyline: that is the Qurn, your compass for the whole day.

name: Valley of the Kings: how to choose your tombs
note: 65 tombs (KV1-KV65), New Kingdom c. 1539-1075 BC, from Thutmose I to Ramesses XI; why hidden tombs replaced pyramids (robbery, the Qurn); the tomb plan evolution (bent axis to straight 'syringes'); the books of the afterlife on the walls; which tombs are usually open and a ranked suggestion: Ramesses V/VI (KV9) and Seti I (KV17) worth the extra tickets, then Ramesses IV, Merenptah, Ramesses III, Tausert/Setnakht, Ramesses IX, Thutmose III; the tram, the photo rules; ancient and modern graffiti; the Theban Mapping Project.
period: New Kingdom, Dynasties 18-20, c. 1539-1075 BC
summary: For nearly 500 years Egypt's kings were buried here in hidden, painted tombs instead of pyramids; 65 are numbered, a handful open on any day.
look: You are in the main, or East, Valley: a dry limestone gully with tomb doors cut into its sides, each with a sign giving its KV number, plan and decoration. The visitor centre at the gate has a model of the valley, and a small electric tram runs up to the tombs. The pyramid-shaped peak of the Qurn rises to the south.
story:
Thutmose I's architect Ineni boasted in his own tomb that he dug the king's tomb with 'no one seeing, no one hearing'. That was the point. Every pyramid had been robbed, so from about 1539 BC the kings hid their tombs in this remote valley, guarded by the Medjay police, and built their temples far away by the fields. The Qurn probably helped: a natural pyramid over every grave. Burials went on until about 1075 BC, from Thutmose I to Ramesses X or XI.

There are 65 numbered tombs and pits, but only about twenty held kings. John Gardner Wilkinson painted the first numbers on 21 tombs in 1827. The plan evolved: early tombs turn at a right angle, Horemheb's jogs sideways, and Ramesside tombs run straight into the hill like long pipes, which is what Greek visitors called them: syringes. The walls carry the guidebooks of the afterlife: the Amduat, the Books of Gates, Caverns and the Earth, the Litany of Ra. All tell one story: the sun dies at dusk, crosses the twelve hours of the underworld and is reborn at dawn, with the king on board.

About 18 tombs can be opened, rarely all at once, so check the board at the gate. Worth the extra tickets: Ramesses V and VI (KV9) for the sky ceilings, Seti I (KV17) for sheer quality. On the standard ticket: Ramesses IV (KV2), Merenptah (KV8), Ramesses III (KV11), Tausert and Setnakht (KV14), Ramesses IX (KV6) and, knees permitting, Thutmose III (KV34). Tutankhamun's tomb is small; you saw the treasure on the 11th.

The valley gets 4,000 to 5,000 visitors on most days, so go early. Guides may not lecture inside tombs. Ancient tourists left over 2,100 Greek and Latin graffiti, the earliest dated 278 BC.
details: The sign at each tomb door: plan, date and decoration, designed by the Theban Mapping Project in 2001.
The model of the valley in the visitor centre: see how the tombs dive into the hills and pass close to each other.
From the valley floor, look up at the Qurn: 'the Peak' that may have made this the kings' choice.
Inside any Ramesside tomb, look up: a dark blue ceiling with yellow stars, or the goddess Nut, means you are under the night sky.
Greek graffiti near the entrances of KV2 and KV9: names left by tourists in Roman times.
fun_fact: In 1912 the American excavator Theodore Davis declared the valley 'exhausted'. Ten years later Howard Carter found Tutankhamun.
narration: Welcome to the Valley of the Kings, the dry gully where Egypt's pharaohs were buried for almost 500 years. Why here, and not under pyramids? Because every pyramid had been robbed. So from about 1539 BC the kings hid their tombs deep in this valley, guarded by police, and built their temples far away by the fields. Thutmose the First's architect, Ineni, boasted that he dug the king's tomb with no one seeing and no one hearing. Look up and you will see a second reason: the peak above you, the Qurn, is shaped like a natural pyramid. There are 65 numbered tombs, but only about 20 held kings. The early ones bend sharply to the side, the later ones run straight into the hill like long pipes, which is exactly what Greek visitors called them. Their walls are guidebooks to the afterlife, and they all tell one story: the sun dies at dusk, sails through the twelve hours of the night, and is reborn at dawn, with the king on board. How to choose? If you buy the extras, take Ramesses the Sixth for the painted sky and Seti the First for the finest carving in Egypt. On the standard ticket, try Ramesses the Fourth, Merenptah, Ramesses the Third or the double tomb of Tausert and Setnakht. Now look at the sign beside the nearest tomb door: it shows the plan, so you know how deep you are about to go.

name: KV62: Tomb of Tutankhamun
note: Small, hastily adapted non-royal tomb (4 rooms); 4 November 1922, the step found by the water boy, 'wonderful things'; what you see now: the mummy in a climate case, the quartzite sarcophagus with the outer gilded coffin, the burial chamber's yellow walls (12 baboons of the Amduat first hour, Ay performing Opening of the Mouth, the funeral sledge), the brown fungus spots; the Factum Arte replica near Carter's house; the 2015-18 Reeves 'hidden chamber' radar saga; link to the GEM galleries.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC
summary: The smallest royal tomb you will enter held the only nearly intact pharaoh's burial ever found, and Tutankhamun himself still lies here.
look: Sixteen steps and an 8-metre corridor take you down into the antechamber, where Carter's 'wonderful things' were piled; today it holds Tutankhamun's mummy in a glass climate case. To your right, a step down behind a barrier, is the burial chamber, 4 by 6.4 metres, the only decorated room, with the quartzite sarcophagus in the middle. The treasury and annexe beyond are empty.
story:
Howard Carter had searched for years with money from Lord Carnarvon when, on 4 November 1922, his men found a step cut in the rock below the remains of huts used by the builders of Ramesses VI's tomb. A Qurna family tradition gives the find to a water boy, Hussein Abdel Rassoul; Carter's own account credits his workmen. On 26 November Carter made a hole in the sealed door and held up a candle. Asked if he could see anything, he answered, as he later wrote it, 'Yes, wonderful things.'

The tomb is tiny for a king: four rooms, probably a private tomb adapted in a hurry when Tutankhamun died at about 18. Robbers got in twice soon after the burial and it was resealed; later, flood debris and workmen's huts buried the entrance, which saved it. Carnarvon died of an infection in April 1923, and the 'curse' was born.

Only the burial chamber is painted. On the north wall Ay, the next king, in a leopard skin, performs the Opening of the Mouth on the mummy: by burying Tutankhamun he claimed the throne. The east wall shows the funeral sledge, the west wall twelve baboons from the first hour of the Amduat. The quartzite sarcophagus, with a granite lid painted to match, has Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serqet at its corners; the outer gilded coffin lay in it until 2019, when it went to the Grand Egyptian Museum for restoration. The brown spots on the walls are long-dead microbes that grew when the tomb was sealed with damp plaster; the Getty conservation project, finished in 2019, left them alone.

In 2015 Nicholas Reeves argued that two hidden doors lay behind the plaster, perhaps to Nefertiti's burial. Radar that year seemed to agree; scans in 2016 and 2018 found nothing. A 2026 study says chambers are still possible. Most Egyptologists remain doubtful.
details: North wall, right-hand scene: Ay in a leopard skin and blue crown, touching the mummy's mouth with a ritual adze.
West wall: twelve baboons in a grid, greeting the sun at the first hour of the night.
East wall: the mummy on a sledge under a canopy, hauled by officials with white mourning bands.
The brown spots all over the paintings: dead microbes, already there when Carter opened the tomb.
The glass case in the antechamber: Tutankhamun's face, the one pharaoh still lying in his own tomb in this valley.
fun_fact: The innermost of the three coffins is solid gold and weighs 110.4 kilograms, more than most of the men who lifted it out.
narration: You are standing in the tomb of Tutankhamun, the smallest royal tomb in the valley and the most famous. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen found a step cut in the rock, buried under the huts of the men who had built Ramesses the Sixth's tomb above. Local tradition says a water boy found it. Three weeks later Carter held a candle to a hole in the sealed door and, in his own words, saw wonderful things. This room, the antechamber, was crammed with beds, chariots and boxes. Today it holds the king himself, in the glass case: a young man who died at about 18, still lying in his own tomb. The burial chamber, a step down to your right, is the only painted room. On the north wall, Ay, the old courtier who became the next king, wears a leopard skin and touches the mummy's mouth to give back its senses. By burying the king, he was claiming the throne. Opposite, twelve baboons greet the sun at the first hour of night. The stone sarcophagus has a goddess spreading her wings at each corner. In 2015 a British Egyptologist argued that hidden doors lay behind these walls, perhaps to Nefertiti's tomb. Later radar scans found nothing, though the debate is not quite dead. Now look closely at the yellow walls: those brown spots are ancient microbes that grew when the tomb was sealed with damp plaster, and died long ago.

name: KV9: Ramesses V and VI, the astronomical ceiling
note: Extra ticket, the most spectacular open tomb: 117 m straight corridor, Book of Gates and Book of Caverns on the walls, the Book of the Day and Night with Nut swallowing and giving birth to the sun stretched twice across the burial chamber ceiling, the Book of the Earth; the shattered sarcophagus; its rubble protected KV62 below from robbers; Greek and Coptic graffiti (the 'tomb of Memnon' for Roman tourists, 1,000+ graffiti).
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1145-1137 BC
summary: The best ceiling in the valley: Nut swallows the sun and gives birth to it overhead, and Roman-era tourists left nearly a thousand graffiti.
look: One long, straight, gently sloping corridor, about 117 metres, wide enough to feel like a hall, with the Book of Gates on one side and the Book of Caverns on the other. Walk to the very end: the vaulted ceiling of the burial chamber holds the sky goddess Nut twice, stretched end to end. On the floor lie the smashed pieces of the stone sarcophagus.
story:
Ramesses V began this tomb, but he died after a few years and his uncle Ramesses VI took it over, recarving the names and digging deeper. His workmen broke by accident into an older tomb, KV12. More usefully for us, they built their huts on the rubble just below, right on top of a forgotten little tomb: Tutankhamun's, which stayed hidden until 1922.

The decoration is the richest in the valley. The corridors carry the Book of Gates and the Book of Caverns, then eleven hours of the Amduat, then spells from the Book of the Dead in the hall before the burial chamber. The burial chamber walls carry the Books of the Earth. Overhead, the Book of the Day and the Book of the Night are framed by a double figure of Nut: at evening she swallows the sun, it travels through her body by night, and at dawn she gives birth to it again.

Thieves came within decades. A papyrus records the robbery of Ramesses VI's tomb around 1118 BC, and his mummy, hacked about by robbers, was found in 1898 among the kings rewrapped and hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb.

In Greek and Roman times this was 'the tomb of Memnon', named after the Ethiopian hero of the Trojan War, and a must-see. Visitors left 995 graffiti between the 1st century BC and the 4th century AD, mostly in Greek, some in Latin, Demotic and Coptic; Polish epigraphers have studied them since 1996. A doctor named Dadouchios punned on his name, 'torch-bearer'. Another visitor grumbled: 'I did not like anything except the sarcophagus!'
details: Burial chamber ceiling: two figures of Nut back to back, the Book of the Day on one side, the Book of the Night on the other.
Red sun discs travelling along Nut's body: follow one from her mouth to her womb.
Burial chamber walls: the Book of the Earth, with the sun dragged through the underworld by rows of gods.
The pillared hall: winged cobras flank the ramp down to the second corridor.
Near the entrance: Greek graffiti in black and red ink, left by tourists of the Roman era.
fun_fact: One graffito may be signed 'Ambros', which some read as Amr ibn al-As, the Arab general who conquered Egypt in the 7th century. If so, even the conqueror stopped to look at the ceiling.
narration: Welcome to the tomb of Ramesses the Fifth and Ramesses the Sixth. Walk to the end and look up: this is the best ceiling in the valley. Ramesses the Fifth began the tomb and died young. His uncle, Ramesses the Sixth, took it over, recarved the names and pushed the corridor deeper into the hill. As they dug, his workmen built their huts on the rubble outside, right on top of a forgotten little tomb lower down. That tomb was Tutankhamun's, and those huts kept it hidden until 1922. As you walk down, the walls tell the sun's night journey, gate by gate and cavern by cavern. In the burial chamber, the vaulted ceiling shows the sky goddess Nut twice, stretched end to end. Every evening she swallows the sun. Through the night it travels inside her body, and every morning she gives birth to it again. The dead king hoped to ride along. Thieves broke in within a few decades and smashed the sarcophagus, whose pieces still lie on the floor. Then came the tourists. Greeks and Romans called this the tomb of Memnon, after the hero of the Trojan War, and left nearly 1,000 graffiti, mostly in Greek. One visitor wrote that he liked nothing here except the sarcophagus. Now look for the small red sun discs moving along Nut's body overhead, and follow one from her mouth to her womb.

name: KV17: Tomb of Seti I, Belzoni's tomb
note: Extra ticket (expensive, worth it): 137 m, the longest, deepest, most finely decorated tomb, every wall carved in raised relief and painted; found by Belzoni 1817; the Litany of Ra, Amduat, Book of Gates, the astronomical ceiling with constellations; the unfinished chamber showing the draughtsmen's grid and red sketch lines; the alabaster sarcophagus in Sir John Soane's Museum London; the mysterious tunnel descending 174 m from the burial chamber (cleared 2007-10 by Hawass); the mummy at NMEC.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1290-1279 BC
summary: The finest tomb in the valley: 137 metres of carved and painted relief under a starry vault, with a tunnel plunging 174 metres further into the rock.
look: A long descent of stairs and corridors, every wall carved in raised relief and painted, through pillared halls to the vaulted burial chamber, whose ceiling shows constellations in gold on deep blue. The sarcophagus is gone; below where it stood, a tunnel runs down into the rock, closed to visitors. It is steep and warm; give it time.
story:
On 16 October 1817 Giovanni Belzoni, a giant former circus strongman from Padua, broke into this tomb and knew at once he had something extraordinary. It belonged to Seti I, father of Ramesses II, and at 137 metres it was the longest tomb known in the valley until KV5 was explored in the 1990s. Seti was not at home: under King Shoshenq I, in the 10th century BC, priests had moved his mummy to the Deir el-Bahari cache. It is now at NMEC, with one of the best-preserved royal faces of all.

Nothing was skimped. Every wall is carved in raised relief and painted: the Litany of Ra, the Amduat, the Book of Gates, the Opening of the Mouth, and the Book of the Heavenly Cow, in which Ra nearly wipes out humankind. The vaulted burial chamber is one of the first in the valley, its ceiling painted with the constellations. In one side room the work stops at the drawing stage, figures in red and black outline.

Belzoni found a sarcophagus of translucent alabaster carved with the Book of Gates. The British consul Henry Salt sold it to the architect Sir John Soane; it has been in his London house-museum since 1824, and Soane threw a party by lamplight to show it off. The tomb paid for its fame: Belzoni's wax squeezes stripped paint, Champollion cut out a panel 2.26 metres high now in the Louvre, Lepsius took more to Berlin, and floods and later digging cracked the walls.

From beneath the sarcophagus a tunnel slopes into the mountain. A 1960 attempt cleared 136 metres before crumbling rock forced a halt. Zahi Hawass's team finished the job in 2007-10, with steel supports and a little railway: 174 metres, two staircases, then it simply stops. Nobody knows what the builders were aiming for.
details: Burial chamber vault: the constellations and gods of the night sky, in gold on deep blue.
The pillars: Seti face to face with the gods, each figure carved first and painted after.
A side room off the first pillared hall: scenes left as red and black outline drawings, the artists' first draft.
Sharp-edged gaps in some walls: where panels were cut out for the Louvre, Florence and Berlin.
Look closely at any face of Seti: eyelid, ear and lip are modelled in the stone, not just painted.
fun_fact: Belzoni rebuilt two of the tomb's halls at full size for an exhibition at London's Egyptian Hall in 1821: one of the first blockbuster museum replicas.
narration: Most Egyptologists would call this the finest tomb in the valley: the resting place of Seti the First, father of Ramesses the Second. It runs 137 metres into the rock, and nothing was skimped: every figure was carved in raised relief and then painted.
