It was found on 16 October 1817 by Giovanni Belzoni, a giant former circus strongman from Padua turned explorer. The king was not at home. Priests had moved his mummy to a hiding place near Deir el-Bahari, and today his calm, beautifully preserved face is at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo. Belzoni found only the sarcophagus, carved from translucent alabaster. It was sold to the London architect Sir John Soane, who threw a party by lamplight to show it off, and it is still in his house-museum. The tomb paid for its fame. Wax copies pulled off the paint, Champollion cut out a wall panel that is now in the Louvre, and other pieces went to Florence and Berlin. As you walk down, the walls guide Seti through the hours of the night. In the burial chamber, the vaulted ceiling is a map of the sky, gold stars on deep blue. Below where the sarcophagus stood, a tunnel slopes 174 metres into the mountain, cleared only in 2010, and then it simply stops. Before you leave, look closely at one face of Seti: the eyelid, the ear, the line of the lip, all cut by hand.

name: KV11: Ramesses III, the Harpers' Tomb
note: Begun by Setnakht, who broke into KV10 and abandoned it; Ramesses III finished it with a dog-leg; unusual side chambers showing daily life: bakers, butchers, boats, weapons, the two blind harpers singing (Bruce's 1768 drawings made it famous); the Litany of Ra, Book of Gates; the sarcophagus is in the Louvre, its lid in Cambridge; his murder in the harem conspiracy (see Medinet Habu).
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1186-1155 BC
summary: Two kings, one wrong turn and a pair of blind harpers: Ramesses III's long tomb has rare scenes of royal kitchens, boats and armouries.
look: A long tomb, 188 metres, entered from the main valley path. Small side rooms open off the first corridors, painted with scenes of royal supplies: bakers, boats, weapons. Further on, the corridor shifts sideways where the first builders hit another tomb, then runs on to an eight-pillared burial chamber.
story:
Setnakht, founder of the 20th Dynasty, started this tomb. His workmen broke straight into the older tomb of Amenmesse, KV10, so he gave up and took over Queen Tausert's tomb, KV14, instead. His son Ramesses III restarted here, shifted the axis sideways to dodge the collision and pushed on to 188 metres.

The side rooms off the first corridors are unlike anything else in the valley: bakers and butchers at work, the king's boats under sail, weapons and armour, the fields of the afterlife. In one, two blind harpers play for the gods. The Scottish traveller James Bruce copied them in 1768, and the tomb has been called 'Bruce's tomb' or the Harpers' Tomb ever since.

The main corridors carry the Litany of Ra, the Amduat and the Book of Gates; the burial chamber has the Book of the Earth. The sarcophagus left in the 19th century: the box is in the Louvre, the lid in the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge.

Ramesses III, who beat the Sea Peoples, died in a palace plot; CT scans in 2012 showed his throat had been cut. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881 and is now at NMEC.
details: Side rooms of the first corridors: bakers, butchers and cooks preparing food for the king's afterlife.
The harpers' room: two blind musicians with tall harps, singing before the gods.
Another side room: bows, quivers, spears and armour lined up like an inventory.
Where the corridor steps sideways: the spot where the first builders broke into KV10 and had to dodge.
The burial chamber: eight pillars and the Book of the Earth on the walls.
fun_fact: James Bruce went on to find the source of the Blue Nile, and London refused to believe half his stories. His harpers, at least, are right here.
narration: You are in the tomb of Ramesses the Third, the last great warrior pharaoh, and it was not his idea. His father, Setnakht, started digging here, but the workmen broke straight into an older royal tomb next door. Setnakht gave up and moved into somebody else's tomb instead. His son restarted, shifted the corridor sideways to dodge the collision, and carried on until it was 188 metres long. Look into the small side rooms near the start. They are unlike anything else in the valley: bakers and butchers at work, the royal boats, racks of weapons and armour. In one of them two blind harpers play for the gods. A Scottish traveller, James Bruce, copied them in 1768, and ever since this has been called the Harpers' Tomb. The king himself had a grim end. He was murdered in a palace plot, and scans in 2012 showed that his throat had been cut. His mummy is now in Cairo, and his sarcophagus is split between the Louvre and Cambridge. Find the harpers, and look at their blank, closed eyes.

name: KV2: Ramesses IV
note: Short, wide, bright, easy: a good first tomb; the Turin papyrus plan of this very tomb (the ancient architect's drawing survives); the huge granite sarcophagus; Litany of Ra, Book of Caverns, Nut on the ceiling; 50+ Coptic graffiti, used as a church; open since antiquity.
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1155-1149 BC
summary: A good first tomb: short, bright and easy, and the ancient architect's plan of it survives on a papyrus in Turin.
look: Near the valley entrance, KV2 runs straight and gently downhill for about 89 metres: three corridors, a small hall, then the burial chamber, where the big granite sarcophagus still stands, almost filling the room. The sky goddess Nut stretches across the burial chamber ceiling. Coptic graffiti and painted crosses cluster on the right-hand wall by the entrance.
story:
Ramesses IV, a son of Ramesses III, came to the throne late in life and reigned about six years. He was in a hurry: an ostracon records that the site was chosen in his second year by the local governor and two royal attendants, and the gang of tomb builders at Deir el-Medina was doubled to 120 men.

The tomb is simple, straight and broad. Its walls carry the Litany of Ra, the Book of Caverns, the Amduat and spells from the Book of the Dead, and Nut arches over the sarcophagus. Robbers broke the sarcophagus, probably in antiquity; the king's mummy was rewrapped and hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb, where it was found in 1898.

What makes KV2 special is a document. A papyrus in Turin's Egyptian Museum shows this very tomb in plan, drawn to scale with measurements in hieratic, and the sarcophagus surrounded by four nested shrines: exactly what Carter found around Tutankhamun. Someone also scratched a rough plan on a limestone slab near the entrance, perhaps a workman's doodle.

KV2 has been open since antiquity. Greek and Roman tourists left 656 graffiti, second only to KV9, and Coptic monks seem to have lived here, painting saints and crosses and leaving about 50 inscriptions.
details: Right-hand wall by the entrance: Coptic graffiti, crosses and figures of saints left by monks.
Burial chamber ceiling: the sky goddess Nut stretched over the sarcophagus.
The granite sarcophagus: still in place, damaged by robbers long ago.
First corridor: Greek names scratched by visitors of the Roman era.
fun_fact: The Turin plan shows the shrines around the sarcophagus so precisely that it matches the layout Carter found intact in Tutankhamun's tomb.
narration: Short, bright and easy, the tomb of Ramesses the Fourth makes a good first tomb. Ramesses the Fourth, a son of Ramesses the Third, became king late in life and knew he had little time. In his second year the site was chosen, and the gang of tomb builders was doubled to 120 men. Walk down the gentle slope and notice how simple the plan is: three straight corridors, a small hall and the burial chamber. We know exactly what the builders intended, because the architect's plan survives. It is on a papyrus now in Turin, drawn to scale with measurements in Egyptian script, showing the sarcophagus inside four nested shrines, exactly as Carter later found them around Tutankhamun. This tomb has stood open since antiquity. Greek and Roman tourists left more than 600 graffiti, and later Coptic monks lived here. In the burial chamber, the granite sarcophagus still stands under the arching body of the sky goddess Nut. On your way out, look at the right-hand wall by the entrance for the monks' crosses and Coptic writing.

name: KV6: Ramesses IX
note: Near the entrance, open since antiquity; the king before Ra-Horakhty and Osiris, Book of Caverns, the Book of the Earth; the hurriedly painted burial chamber with Nut; during his reign the tomb-robbery trials happened (Abbott and Amherst papyri) as the state weakened; the mummy found in the DB320 cache.
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1129-1111 BC
summary: Rushed to completion after the king died, this bright tomb belongs to the reign when thieves were put on trial for robbing royal graves.
look: Near the valley entrance, just above KV5 and KV55, a gate and a gentle ramp lead into three corridors, 105 metres in all. In the first corridor the king stands before Ra-Horakhty and Osiris. At the end a ramp drops into the burial chamber: Nut across the vaulted ceiling, the king in his boat on the far wall, and a pit in the floor where the vanished sarcophagus stood.
story:
Ramesses IX ruled for nearly two decades while royal power and the economy drained away. His tomb was unfinished when he died and was completed in a hurry: the side rooms of the first corridor were never decorated, the four-pillared hall never finished. The burial chamber was painted fast, yet it glows with unusual yellows, deep blues and blacks: the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth on the walls, Nut overhead.

His reign is famous for crime. The mayor of Thebes, Paser, accused his rival on the west bank, Pawero, of failing to protect the royal tombs. The inquiry survives in the Abbott Papyrus, and the Amherst-Leopold Papyrus preserves the confession of a stonemason, Amenpanufer, who described breaking into the tomb of King Sobekemsaf, stripping the gold and setting fire to the coffins. Another papyrus records eight workmen arrested in year 17 for robbing the tomb of a queen, Isis.

In the end the thieves won. This tomb has stood open since antiquity, with Roman and Coptic graffiti, and the king's mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881. It is now at NMEC.
details: First corridor: the king offering to the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty and to Osiris.
Undecorated side rooms in the first corridor: the first sign of the rush after the king's death.
Burial chamber ceiling: Nut twice, back to back, in yellow on dark blue.
Far wall of the burial chamber: Ramesses in his sun boat, surrounded by gods.
The empty pit in the floor: the sarcophagus has vanished.
fun_fact: The great tomb-robbery trials began as a feud between two mayors, one on each bank of the river.
narration: Ramesses the Ninth, whose tomb this is, reigned for nearly two decades while Egypt slowly ran out of money and order. The tomb was not ready when he died, and the workmen finished it in a hurry. You can see the corners they cut: undecorated side rooms near the entrance and a pillared hall never completed. Yet the burial chamber is a delight, painted fast in strong yellow, deep blue and black. His reign is famous for a crime wave. The mayor of Thebes accused his rival, the mayor of the west bank, of letting thieves plunder the royal tombs, and the inquiry still survives on papyrus. One stonemason confessed to breaking into an old king's tomb, stripping the gold from the mummies and setting fire to the coffins. Eight workmen were arrested for robbing a queen's tomb. In the end the thieves won here too. This tomb has stood open since antiquity, and the king's mummy was found in 1881 in the priests' hiding place near Deir el-Bahari. In the burial chamber, look up at the sky goddess Nut stretched across the vaulted ceiling.

name: KV8: Merenptah
note: The 13th son and successor of Ramesses II (he outlived 12 brothers), of the 'Israel Stele'; a long steep tomb with the outer lid of his granite sarcophagus still in the corridor (they broke the door jambs to get the four nested sarcophagi in); the innermost one was reused by Psusennes I at Tanis (GEM/Tahrir); Book of Gates, the king as Osiris on the sarcophagus lid.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1213-1203 BC
summary: Ramesses II's 13th son finally became king, and his nested stone sarcophagi were so big the builders had to tear out the doorframes.
look: A long, steep descent: the burial chamber lies at the end of 160 metres of corridor. Near the entrance the reliefs are deep and fine; lower down, ancient floodwater has damaged the walls. Deep inside lies a huge granite sarcophagus lid with Merenptah carved as Osiris.
story:
Ramesses II reigned 66 years and outlived a dozen crown princes. His 13th son, Merenptah, finally took the throne as an old man and ruled about ten years. He is best known for his victory stela, which contains the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.

His tomb was built for four stone sarcophagi, one inside another. The outer one was so large that the builders demolished the doorjambs to get it in, then rebuilt them with inscribed sandstone blocks held by dovetail cramps; they also cut away pillars in the hall. Two of those pillars may have been stolen by Paneb, a notorious Deir el-Medina workman whose crimes were recorded in court.

About two centuries later, in the Third Intermediate Period, the outer sarcophagus was smashed to get at an inner one, which King Psusennes I reused for his own burial at Tanis in the Delta. Merenptah's mummy had been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb, where Victor Loret found it in 1898.

The walls carry the Amduat and the Book of Gates. Open since antiquity and low in the valley, the tomb has suffered from floods.
details: Start of the first corridor: Merenptah greeting the falcon-headed sun god Ra-Horakhty.
The doorways along the corridor: look for fitted sandstone blocks where the original jambs were knocked out.
The granite lid: Merenptah as Osiris, arms crossed, protected by the gods.
Lower walls: bare, scoured stone where floods stripped the plaster.
fun_fact: Merenptah outlived twelve older brothers to become king; two centuries after his death, another pharaoh borrowed his sarcophagus.
narration: Merenptah, whose tomb you are entering, was the 13th son of Ramesses the Second. His father reigned 66 years and outlived twelve of his older sons, so Merenptah came to the throne as an old man and ruled about ten years. He is famous for a victory stela that mentions Israel for the first time outside the Bible. The corridor runs steeply down for 160 metres, and it had a problem. Merenptah ordered four stone sarcophagi, one inside another, and the outer one was too big to fit. So the builders knocked out the door frames, moved it through, and rebuilt them with sandstone blocks. They also cut away pillars in the hall, and some Egyptologists suspect a notorious workman called Paneb carried off two of them. About two centuries later, priests smashed the outer sarcophagus to get at an inner one, and King Psusennes reused it for his own burial in the Delta. Merenptah's mummy was hidden elsewhere and is now in Cairo. As you go down, look for the great granite lid with the king carved as Osiris, arms crossed, ready for eternity.

name: KV14: Tausert and Setnakht, a tomb with two owners
note: One of the largest: begun for Queen Tausert (who ruled as pharaoh at the end of the 19th Dynasty after Seti II and Siptah), then taken over by Setnakht who plastered over her images and added a second burial chamber; you can see both sets of decoration and the two pillared halls; the empty sarcophagi; the story of the queen, Chancellor Bay and the boy king Siptah.
period: New Kingdom, late 19th to early 20th Dynasty, c. 1191-1186 BC
summary: A queen who ruled as pharaoh began this tomb; the man who replaced her painted himself over her figures and moved in.
look: One of the largest tombs in the valley, over 112 metres, in the southern part of the valley next to KV15. It runs straight through corridors and two burial chambers, one after the other: first Tausert's, then Setnakht's extension. Look on the walls and pillars for figures redone in ink where a queen once stood.
story:
Tausert was the great royal wife of Seti II. When he died the throne went to a sickly boy, Siptah, with Tausert and the chancellor Bay as the real power. Bay was executed in Siptah's fifth year, Siptah died young, and Tausert ruled alone as king, one of very few women to do so, after Sobekneferu and Hatshepsut.

Her tomb grew with her: begun for a queen, enlarged with a royal burial chamber when she became king. Seti II may even have been buried here first and moved later to the hastily finished KV15 next door.

Then Setnakht, founder of the 20th Dynasty, took over. We do not know how Tausert's reign ended, but he moved into her tomb. Her images were erased and replaced with his, and he cut further into the hill to add a second burial chamber, making this one of the largest royal tombs.

So you walk through two reigns stitched together. Tausert's mummy has never been securely identified: among the bodies hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb was an unknown woman lying in an upturned coffin lid inscribed for Setnakht, and some think she may be Tausert. The tomb was properly recorded only when Hartwig Altenmuller excavated it in 1983-87.
details: Pillars and walls: places where a woman's figure was erased and Setnakht painted over her in simple ink.
The first burial chamber with its pillars: Tausert's royal chamber.
The corridor continuing beyond it: Setnakht's extension to his own second burial chamber.
Scenes of Anubis, Isis and the four sons of Horus guarding the dead.
fun_fact: A tomb with two owners may have had three: Tausert's husband Seti II was perhaps buried here first and moved out.
narration: You are in a tomb with two owners, and you can still see the takeover. It was begun for Tausert, the wife of Seti the Second. After her husband died, a sickly boy, Siptah, became king, with Tausert and a powerful chancellor called Bay pulling the strings. Bay was executed, the boy died young, and Tausert ruled Egypt as king in her own right, one of very few women ever to do so. Her tomb grew with her ambitions into one of the largest in the valley. Then her reign ended, we do not know how, and a new king, Setnakht, founder of the next dynasty, moved in. He had her figures erased and painted himself on top, then dug on and added a second burial chamber beyond hers. Her own mummy has never been securely identified. So as you walk down, you are walking through two reigns stitched together. Look at the pillars for figures redone in simple ink: in at least one, the queen was erased and Setnakht painted where she had stood.

name: KV15: Seti II
note: Short. At the end of the wadi, a hurried tomb: fine raised relief at the start, then paint only, then outline sketches: watch the quality drop; unusual images of the king's funerary objects (the shrines, statues) painted on the walls; Carter used the entrance as his laboratory for Tut's objects in 1922-32.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1203-1197 BC
summary: A tomb that ran out of time: fine relief at the door, then paint, then hasty sketches, as Seti II's short reign ended.
look: At the head of a side wadi, at the foot of a sheer cliff beside KV14. Short corridors lead to a well room where the well was never dug, a pillared hall, and a corridor turned into a burial chamber. Only the sarcophagus lid remains.
story: Seti II reigned less than six years and lost Thebes for part of that time to a rival, Amenmesse. You can watch the clock run out: carved relief near the entrance, then painted plaster, then quick sketches. Seti's name was carved, erased, probably by Amenmesse's people, and carved again. The well room has unusual paintings of the king's funerary statues, standing on a panther or in a papyrus skiff, just like the gilded figures later found with Tutankhamun. Seti may first have been buried in KV14, then moved here; his mummy turned up in the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb. From 1922 Carter's colleagues Alfred Lucas and Arthur Mace used this tomb as their laboratory, cleaning and conserving Tutankhamun's treasures before they went to Cairo.
details: Near the entrance: crisp carved relief. Walk on and watch it give way to paint, then sketches.
Well room walls: the king's funerary statuettes, one standing on a panther's back.
The lid of Seti's sarcophagus, the only piece of his burial still in the tomb.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun's gilded statuette of a king on a panther was cleaned in this tomb, a few metres from a 3,200-year-old painting of the same kind of statue.
narration: Here is a tomb that ran out of time: the tomb of Seti the Second. Seti reigned less than six years. Walk in and watch the work get faster. Near the door the figures are carved in fine relief. Further in they are only painted, and in places only sketched. In the well room, where a shaft was planned but never dug, the painters showed the king's funeral statues, one standing on the back of a panther. Exactly that kind of gilded statue was later found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and in the 1920s Carter's team used this very tomb as their laboratory to clean his treasures. Look at the relief by the entrance, then compare it with the quick brushwork inside.

name: KV16: Ramesses I, small and brilliant
note: Founder of the 19th Dynasty, an old general who reigned barely two years; tiny tomb (one chamber) but painted on blue-grey background with vivid colours like Horemheb's: the king between Horus and Anubis, the Book of Gates; the red granite sarcophagus still in place; his mummy's odyssey: stolen c. 1860, a Niagara Falls museum for 130 years, returned in 2003, now in Luxor Museum (22 Oct).
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1292-1290 BC
summary: An old general's tiny tomb, painted in a rush and glowing with colour; his mummy spent over 130 years as a curiosity at Niagara Falls.
look: Only 29 metres long: two steep staircases and a sloping corridor lead straight down to a single burial chamber. The red granite sarcophagus, painted rather than carved, still stands in the middle. Around it the king meets the gods in bright colours on a blue-grey background, with scenes from the Book of Gates.
story:
Ramesses I was born Paramessu, into a military family from the Nile Delta. He rose to be vizier to Horemheb, the last king of the 18th Dynasty, who had no surviving children and chose him as heir. He reigned less than two years, but he founded a dynasty: his son was Seti I and his grandson Ramesses II.

The tomb shows the haste. There was only time for one room; the walls got a quick coat of plaster and paint, and the sarcophagus was painted instead of carved, with a number of mistakes in its texts. The result is one of the brightest rooms in the valley, close in style to Horemheb's tomb. Belzoni found it on 10 October 1817, six days before Seti I's.

His mummy had an odyssey. Taken from the Deir el-Bahari cache by the Abd el-Rassul family, it was sold to a Canadian doctor, James Douglas, and around 1860 ended up in the Niagara Falls Museum, displayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta bought it, and on 24 October 2003 it returned to Egypt. It is now in the Luxor Museum, which you visit on the 22nd.
details: The walls: figures on a blue-grey background, painted straight onto plaster in a hurry.
The king led by the gods: look for falcon-headed Horus and jackal-headed Anubis beside him.
The red granite sarcophagus: its figures and texts painted, not carved.
Book of Gates: the sun's boat towed through the night, in rows of small figures.
fun_fact: For over a century the founder of the Ramesside dynasty shared a museum at Niagara Falls with stuffed animals and the barrels of daredevils who had gone over the falls.
narration: This small, brilliant room is the tomb of Ramesses the First, founder of the dynasty of Seti and Ramesses the Great. He began life as Paramessu, an army officer from the Delta, and rose to be vizier for King Horemheb, who had no sons and named him heir. He reigned less than two years. So his tomb is tiny, just 29 metres, one room at the bottom of two staircases. The painters had to work fast, straight onto plaster, and the result is one of the brightest rooms in the valley, figures glowing against a blue-grey sky. Even the red granite sarcophagus is painted rather than carved, with a few spelling mistakes. His mummy had a stranger journey than the man. Stolen by tomb robbers in the 19th century, it was sold to a collector and spent more than 130 years in a museum at Niagara Falls. In 2003 it came home, and it now lies in the Luxor Museum, which you will visit tomorrow. Look at the wall where the king is led by the gods, and notice the confident, unhesitating lines.

name: KV34: Thutmose III, the cliff tomb with cartoon figures
note: High in a cleft at the valley's end, reached by steep metal stairs; the deep well shaft to foil robbers; the oval cartouche-shaped burial chamber with the earliest complete Amduat drawn in stick figures like a papyrus unrolled on the walls (741 deities listed), the king suckled by a tree-goddess (Isis as sycamore); the quartzite cartouche sarcophagus; the 'Napoleon of Egypt' and his 17 campaigns.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1425 BC
summary: Climb to a tomb hidden in a cleft of the cliff, where the gods of the night are drawn like stick figures on a giant papyrus unrolled around the walls.
look: High in a narrow cleft at the far end of the valley, reached by steep metal stairs, then a steep corridor that crosses a deep well shaft on a bridge. Beyond it are the antechamber, lined with rows of tiny gods, and the oval, cartouche-shaped burial chamber with the red quartzite sarcophagus. Expect heat and stooping.
story:
Thutmose III reigned 54 years, the first two decades alongside his aunt and stepmother Hatshepsut. Then he fought at least 16 campaigns, beginning with the victory at Megiddo in his 23rd year, which is why the American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

His tomb is cut high in the cliff of the furthest wadi, a deliberate hiding place. The corridor bends in a dog-leg and drops past a deep well, designed to stop robbers. It did not work: the tomb was plundered in antiquity and its location forgotten until Victor Loret found it in 1898.

The decoration is unlike almost anything else in the valley. On a yellowish background meant to look like aged papyrus, the Amduat is drawn in black and red outline, its deities as quick, almost naive stick figures, the text in the cursive hand of sacred books. The antechamber lists the 741 gods and demons of the Amduat. The burial chamber is shaped like a cartouche, the first of its kind. On a pillar, the king is suckled by Isis in the form of a tree. The red quartzite sarcophagus is cartouche-shaped too.

The king was not inside. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881 and is now at NMEC.
details: Antechamber walls: rows of tiny figures, a catalogue of the 741 deities of the Amduat.
Burial chamber walls: the Amduat in black and red on yellow, like a papyrus unrolled around the room.
A pillar in the burial chamber: a tree reaching out an arm and a breast to feed the king. The tree is Isis.
The red quartzite sarcophagus, shaped like a cartouche, still in place.
The ceiling: yellow stars on blue over the burial chamber.
fun_fact: Thutmose's own mother was a minor queen called Isis, so the tree goddess Isis nursing him on the pillar is a neat double meaning.
narration: You have climbed to the tomb of Thutmose the Third, the great conqueror of the 18th Dynasty. For his first 20 years his aunt Hatshepsut ruled beside him. Then he fought at least 16 campaigns, from Syria to Nubia, and an American Egyptologist later called him the Napoleon of Egypt. His tomb was hidden as well as possible: high in a cleft of the cliff, then down a steep corridor and across a deep well shaft meant to stop thieves. It failed. The tomb was robbed in antiquity, and his mummy turned up in the priests' hiding place at Deir el-Bahari. Now look at the walls. This is the Amduat, the book of what is in the underworld, drawn in black and red on a yellowish background, like a giant papyrus unrolled around the room. The hundreds of gods are quick, simple figures, almost cartoons. The burial chamber itself is shaped like a cartouche, the oval ring drawn around a royal name, so the king lies inside his own name. Find the pillar where a tree reaches out an arm and a breast to feed the king: that tree is the goddess Isis.

name: KV35: Amenhotep II and the second royal cache
note: Loret 1898 found the king still in his sarcophagus plus 9 other royal mummies hidden here by the priests (Thutmose IV, Amenhotep III, Merenptah, Seti II, Ramesses IV, V, VI...) and the 'Elder Lady' (Queen Tiye) and 'Younger Lady' (Tut's mother, DNA 2010); the Amduat in 'papyrus' style; the sporty king who boasted of rowing and archery; the pillared hall with the king before Osiris, Anubis, Hathor.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1400 BC
summary: Victor Loret found a king still in his sarcophagus here, and side rooms full of hidden royal mummies, including Tutankhamun's grandmother and mother.
look: A steep descent: stairs and corridors drop past a deep well shaft into a pillared hall and a large rectangular burial chamber, with an upper level of pillars and a lower crypt holding the cartouche-shaped sarcophagus. Only the burial chamber is decorated: the Amduat on the walls, and on the pillars the king before the gods.
story:
On 9 March 1898 the French Egyptologist Victor Loret entered this tomb and found something no one had seen in the valley: a king still in his own sarcophagus. Amenhotep II, son of Thutmose III, was a famous athlete; a stela he set up by the Sphinx boasts of his rowing and of arrows shot through copper targets.

Then Loret opened the side rooms. Priests of the Third Intermediate Period had hidden a second royal cache here, identified by labels on the wrappings: Thutmose IV, Amenhotep III, Merenptah, Seti II, Siptah, Ramesses IV, V and VI. In another room lay three unwrapped bodies side by side: an older woman, a younger woman and a boy. DNA studies published in 2010 identified the 'Elder Lady' as Queen Tiye, wife of Amenhotep III, and showed that the 'Younger Lady' was a daughter of Amenhotep III and Tiye and the mother of Tutankhamun. Her name is still unknown. Another unidentified woman lay in an upturned coffin lid inscribed for Setnakht.

The tomb has the classic early 18th Dynasty dog-leg plan. Its decoration is in the same papyrus style as Thutmose III's. The kings' mummies, and the Elder Lady, are now at NMEC, moved there in the Pharaohs' Golden Parade of 2021.
details: Burial chamber pillars: Amenhotep II face to face with Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.
The sarcophagus in the lower crypt: where Loret found the king still lying in 1898.
Burial chamber walls: the Amduat on yellow, drawn like a papyrus, as in Thutmose III's tomb.
The small side rooms off the burial chamber: in two of them the cached kings and the three unwrapped bodies were found.
fun_fact: The 'Younger Lady' was Tutankhamun's mother and, DNA suggests, also his father's sister. Royal family trees in Egypt could be very short.
narration: Amenhotep the Second, son of Thutmose the Third, was buried here, and he was a royal show-off: on a stela near the Sphinx he boasts of rowing better than his sailors and shooting arrows through copper targets. In March 1898 the French archaeologist Victor Loret came down here by candlelight and found something unique: a king still lying in his own sarcophagus. Then he opened the side rooms and found more kings. Around 3,000 years ago, priests had hidden other royal mummies here to save them from robbers: Thutmose the Fourth, Amenhotep the Third, Merenptah and several Ramesses among them. In another room lay three bodies side by side, an older woman, a younger woman and a boy. DNA tests published in 2010 showed that the older woman was Queen Tiye, Tutankhamun's grandmother, and that the younger one was Tutankhamun's mother. We still do not know her name. The kings are now in Cairo. In the burial chamber, look at the pillars, where the king stands face to face with Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.

name: KV43: Thutmose IV and Carter's first royal tomb
note: Short. Found by Carter in 1903 for Theodore Davis; the Dream Stele king (Giza, 12 Oct); well shaft and antechamber painted with the king before the gods on a yellow background; the burial chamber undecorated, enormous sarcophagus; the hieratic graffito of year 8 of Horemheb recording the 'renewal' (restoration) of the burial after a robbery: the earliest record of an official re-burial.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1390 BC
summary: Howard Carter's first royal tomb, found 19 years before Tutankhamun, with an ancient note recording that the king's burial was repaired after robbers.
look: A dog-leg tomb: corridors down to a deep well shaft, a pillared hall where the axis turns 90 degrees, then the burial chamber with a huge red stone sarcophagus. Only the well room and the antechamber are painted, with the king before the gods under ceilings of yellow stars on blue.
story: Howard Carter found this tomb in January 1903 while working for the American millionaire Theodore Davis. Thutmose IV is the king of the Dream Stele between the Sphinx's paws, which you saw at Giza on the 12th. Robbers had been here first, but they left a chariot body once covered in silver leaf, a leather archer's gauntlet, and in a side room the mummy of a young boy, probably Prince Amenemhat. The king himself had been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb. The red sarcophagus has Nephthys at the head and Isis at the feet. On the right-hand wall of the antechamber, an ink inscription of year 8 of Horemheb records that the treasurer Maya was ordered to renew the burial of Thutmose IV; his assistant Djehutymose added a line.
details: Right-hand wall of the antechamber: the ink note of year 8 of Horemheb about restoring the burial.
Well room, left wall: Thutmose before Osiris, Anubis and Hathor.
The red sarcophagus: Nephthys at the head end, Isis at the feet, texts filled in yellow.
fun_fact: The Dream Stele says a sleeping prince was promised the throne by the Sphinx if he cleared away its sand. This tomb is what he got for his trouble.
narration: Here lay Thutmose the Fourth, the prince who, according to the Dream Stele between the paws of the Sphinx, was promised the throne if he cleared away the sand. In January 1903 Howard Carter found it, nineteen years before Tutankhamun. Thieves had beaten him to it, but they left a chariot, an archer's leather glove and a huge red sarcophagus. Less than a century after the burial, the state stepped in. On the right-hand wall of the antechamber, a note in ink, dated to year 8 of King Horemheb, records that the treasurer Maya was ordered to restore this king's burial. Find that faint line of black writing: it is one of the earliest records of an official reburial.

name: KV47: Siptah, the boy king with the club foot
note: Short. Child king who died at about 16, mummy shows a deformed left foot (polio or club foot); Chancellor Bay (Syrian) and Queen Tausert as regents; fine Litany of Ra reliefs at the entrance with vulture ceilings, then unfinished; his names erased and recarved by his own court; the sarcophagus with the Book of the Earth.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1197-1191 BC
summary: The tomb of a teenage king with a deformed foot, a figurehead for a queen and a foreign chancellor, whose name was cut out and carved back in.
look: In the southern part of the valley, a long tomb whose first corridors are finely carved and painted with the Litany of Ra, vultures spreading their wings across the first ceiling and yellow stars on blue in the second. Further in it is largely unfinished. The pink granite sarcophagus, shaped like a cartouche, lies in the burial chamber.
story: Siptah came to the throne as a boy after Seti II died. His mummy shows a deformed left foot, perhaps from polio or a club foot, and he died young, perhaps in his mid-teens. Real power lay with Seti's widow, Queen Tausert, and the chancellor Bay until Bay was executed in Siptah's fifth year. The tomb tells the politics: Siptah's cartouches were cut out and later recarved throughout, and one view links the erasures to Tausert and the restorations to his supporters. The burial chamber was never finished, and a side passage was abandoned after the diggers broke into an earlier queen's tomb, KV32. Edward Ayrton found the entrance for Theodore Davis on 18 December 1905. The king's mummy had long since been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb.
details: First corridor ceiling: vultures with outstretched wings, guarding the way in.
Second corridor ceiling: yellow stars on dark blue.
Cartouches near the entrance: look for signs of recutting where Siptah's name was erased and restored.
The sarcophagus lid: the king as Osiris between Isis and Nephthys.
fun_fact: When the sarcophagus was cleared, all it held was a handful of bones from someone buried centuries after Siptah.
narration: A boy king with a deformed foot was buried here: Siptah. His mummy shows the left foot twisted, perhaps by polio, and he died young, maybe in his mid-teens. He was a king in name only. The real power lay with the old king's widow, Queen Tausert, and a chancellor called Bay, probably of Syrian origin, until Bay was executed. Even Siptah's name became a political football: his cartouches here were cut out and later carved back in. The beginning of the tomb is lovely, with the Litany of Ra on the walls and vultures spreading their wings across the ceiling. Then the work stops. Look up at those vultures in the first corridor, guarding the boy on his way in.

name: KV57: Horemheb, the unfinished masterpiece
note: The general who restored order after Amarna and erased Akhenaten, Tut and Ay; first royal tomb with the Book of Gates and the first with painted raised relief on blue-grey; the burial chamber left unfinished at every stage: red grid, black corrected outlines, carved, painted, letting you watch the artists work; the red granite sarcophagus with goddesses at the corners; his first tomb at Saqqara built as a general; often closed.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1319-1292 BC
summary: A burial chamber frozen mid-job: red grids, black corrections, carving and paint side by side show exactly how a royal tomb was made.
look: A jogged-axis tomb: stairs and corridors to a well shaft, a pillared hall, then steps down to the burial chamber with the red granite sarcophagus. Decoration starts at the well: painted raised relief on a blue-grey ground. In the burial chamber the walls stand at every stage of work, from red grid lines to finished paint. Often closed.
story:
Horemheb was a general who served Tutankhamun and Ay and then became king himself. He completed the return to the old order after Akhenaten's revolution, and later had his predecessors left off the official king lists. As a general he had already built a fine tomb at Saqqara; as king he started again here.

Edward Ayrton found the tomb for Theodore Davis in February 1908. It marks a turning point: the first royal tomb with painted raised relief instead of plain painting, the figures standing out from a blue-grey ground, and the first to put the Book of Gates in the burial chamber instead of the Amduat.

It was never finished, which is its gift to us. On the burial chamber walls you can follow every stage: a red grid laid down, figures sketched, corrected in black, then cut into relief, then painted. The red granite sarcophagus, shaped like a shrine, has a protective goddess at each corner.

Ayrton found the tomb robbed, with bones of several people. Some think Horemheb is among them. Graffiti from the end of the New Kingdom, one naming Herihor, suggest the priests checked on the burial.
details: Burial chamber walls: red grid squares and red sketches, with black corrections by a senior artist.
Next to them: the same kind of figures cut into relief, some painted, some bare stone.
Well room and antechamber: Horemheb offering to the gods, in raised relief on blue-grey.
The red granite sarcophagus: a goddess with outstretched wings at each corner.
fun_fact: Horemheb's first tomb, at Saqqara, was built while he was still a general. After he became king, a royal cobra was added to his brow on its reliefs.
narration: Horemheb, whose tomb this is, was the general who became king after Tutankhamun and Ay. He finished restoring the old gods after Akhenaten's revolution, and later had his predecessors left off the official lists of kings. As a general he had already built himself a fine tomb at Saqqara; as king he started again here. This tomb marks a change of style. It was the first royal tomb carved in raised relief and then painted, with bright figures standing out from a blue-grey background, and the first to put the Book of Gates in the burial chamber. But the best thing about it is that it was never finished. On the burial chamber walls, work stopped at every stage at once. In one place you see the red grid of squares the draughtsmen laid down. Next to it, figures sketched in red, then corrected in black by a senior hand. Then figures half cut into the stone, and finally some fully painted. It is a workshop frozen in time. Find a red grid and follow it along the wall until the figures become carved and coloured.

name: KV5: the sons of Ramesses II (not open, worth knowing)
note: Opposite KV62: the largest tomb in the valley, 130+ corridors and chambers mapped by Kent Weeks (Theban Mapping Project) from 1995, a family mausoleum for Ramesses II's sons (he had about 50 sons and 50 daughters); a 16-pillared hall, statues of Osiris in the corridors; flooded repeatedly, excavation continuing; not open to the public, the entrance is near the rest house.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1279-1213 BC
summary: Once used as a rubbish dump, it turned out to be the largest tomb in the valley: a family vault for the sons of Ramesses II.
look: You cannot go in. The entrance is a modest doorway low on the valley floor, opposite Ramesses II's own tomb, KV7, and not far from Tutankhamun's. Behind it, corridors run deep into the hill, with at least 130 rooms known so far.
story:
James Burton poked into this tomb in 1825, and in 1902 Howard Carter used its entrance as a dump for his spoil. It looked like a small, ruined, flood-filled tomb. Kent Weeks of the Theban Mapping Project began clearing it in 1987, and in 1995 he crawled through the debris of a pillared hall, 16 pillars strong, and found corridors leading on and on. It was the most dramatic find in the valley since Tutankhamun.

At least 130 rooms were known by 2006, laid out along long corridors, with a large statue of Osiris among the finds. Ramesses II reigned 66 years and fathered dozens of children; many died before him, and this seems to have been their family vault. Skull fragments of his eldest son, Amunherkhepeshef, were found and reconstructed. The other finds are humble but telling: thousands of potsherds, shabtis, beads, ostraca and glass vials.

Robbers emptied it in antiquity and flash floods packed it with debris. By 2006 only about 7 percent of the rooms had been cleared. The work is slow, careful and continuing, and the tomb is closed to visitors.
details: The entrance: a modest doorway low on the valley floor, easy to walk past.
Across the path: KV7, Ramesses II's own tomb. Father and sons lie a stone's throw apart.
The low level of the doorway: flood debris from the slopes above poured straight in.
The path you are on: Carter dumped his rubble here in 1902 without suspecting anything.
fun_fact: In 2006 Weeks's team reckoned only about 7 percent of the rooms had been cleared. Archaeology here runs on geological time.
narration: In front of you is the tomb known as K V 5, the tomb of the sons of Ramesses the Second. You cannot go in, but it is worth a minute. For most of two centuries nobody thought much of it. An explorer looked in in 1825, and in 1902 Howard Carter dumped his rubble at its door. Then, in 1995, the American Egyptologist Kent Weeks, who had been clearing it for years, crawled through the debris of a pillared hall and found corridors running on and on into the hill. It is now the largest tomb in the valley, with at least 130 rooms. Ramesses the Second reigned for 66 years and had dozens of children. Many of his sons died before him, and this seems to have been their family vault. Fragments of the skull of his eldest son were found inside, along with thousands of potsherds, beads and little funerary figures. Robbers emptied it long ago and floods packed it with rubble, so the clearing is slow and still going on. Turn around and look across the path: that is Ramesses' own tomb, so father and sons lie a stone's throw apart.

name: KV55: the Amarna cache and the mystery mummy
note: 1907, Davis/Ayrton: a jumble of objects from Amarna (Tiye's gilded shrine, canopic jars of Kiya, magic bricks of Akhenaten) and a desecrated coffin with the name cut out and the gold face torn off; the skeleton: a man 20-25 or 35-45? DNA 2010 says Tutankhamun's father, likely Akhenaten; still argued; the tomb is a bare chamber, closed; good lore stop near KV6.
period: New Kingdom, late 18th Dynasty, c. 1330 BC
summary: A small chamber held a coffin with its gold face ripped off and its names cut out; the bones inside may be Akhenaten, Tutankhamun's father.
look: A small, undecorated tomb, 27.6 metres long: 20 steps down, a corridor and a single chamber. It is closed, so this is a story stop. The entrance is cut into the bedrock of the valley floor, just below Ramesses IX's tomb, KV6.
story:
On 6 January 1907 Edward Ayrton, digging for Theodore Davis, uncovered a staircase here, and three days later they went in. The little chamber held a jumble from Akhenaten's court: panels of a gilded shrine made by Akhenaten for his mother, Queen Tiye; four alabaster canopic jars whose stoppers probably show Kiya, one of his wives; magic bricks naming Akhenaten; and a coffin, most likely made for Kiya, whose names had been cut out and whose gold face had been torn away. Davis announced he had found Queen Tiye. But the bones were a man's.

Who is he? Age estimates have swung for a century, from about 20 to 35-45 in CT scans published in 2010 and 2016. A DNA study published in 2010 found that this man was a son of Amenhotep III and the father of Tutankhamun, which fits Akhenaten. Others prefer the shadowy king Smenkhkare, an idea going back to 1931, and the genetic arguments continue.

Most Egyptologists think the burial was brought here from Amarna after the court abandoned the city, then partly dismantled later. The coffin was long displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
details: The entrance: cut into the bedrock of the valley floor, which was lower in Tutankhamun's day.
Twenty steps down to one undecorated chamber; nothing remains inside.
Look up to KV6 and across towards KV62: the Amarna family story lies within a few minutes' walk.
fun_fact: Davis published his find as The Tomb of Queen Tiyi. The real Tiye was found a few hundred metres away, in KV35, and the skeleton here was a man.
narration: Below Ramesses the Ninth's tomb is a small closed doorway, K V 55, and it hides one of the great mysteries of Egyptology. In January 1907 Edward Ayrton, digging for the American Theodore Davis, went down 20 steps into a single bare room. Inside was a jumble from Akhenaten's court: panels of a gilded shrine he made for his mother, Queen Tiye, canopic jars with a woman's face, magic bricks naming Akhenaten, and a beautiful coffin. Someone had cut the names off the coffin and torn away its gold face, as if to erase whoever lay inside. Davis announced that he had found Queen Tiye. But the bones were a man's. In 2010 a DNA study found that he was a son of Amenhotep the Third and the father of Tutankhamun, which points to Akhenaten himself, though some still prefer a shadowy king called Smenkhkare. So, possibly, the heretic king who tried to replace the gods was buried here without a name. Look at the entrance, cut into the valley floor itself, and imagine the priests carrying him down.

name: KV1: Ramesses VII
note: Short. First tomb by the entrance road, often empty of people: one corridor and a chamber with the Book of Caverns and Book of the Earth, the sarcophagus pit covered by a lid carved with the king between Isis and Nephthys; Greek and Coptic graffiti; good quick choice if the famous ones are crowded.
period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1136-1129 BC
summary: The first tomb by the entrance road and often empty of people: short, straight, with the king's grave sealed by an upside-down stone box.
look: A single straight corridor leads to the burial chamber and a small unfinished end room. In the chamber, the burial pit is covered by a stone box turned upside down, roughly cartouche-shaped. Nut stretches twice across the ceiling; Greek graffiti mark the corridor.
story: Ramesses VII died in his seventh year, and his workmen made do. They widened a corridor into a burial chamber and abandoned the room beyond. The decoration follows the tomb of Ramesses VI closely: the Book of Gates, the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth, with a double Nut on the burial chamber ceiling. Instead of a free-standing sarcophagus, the king lay in a pit in the floor under an upturned stone box, the last known sarcophagus in a royal tomb in the valley. The mummy is lost, though four cups with his name turned up in the Deir el-Bahari cache. Open since antiquity, the tomb carries 132 Greek and Roman graffiti, and Coptic monks later lived here.
details: The stone box over the burial pit: turned upside down, roughly cartouche-shaped.
Burial chamber ceiling: the sky goddess Nut twice, back to back.
Corridor walls: Greek and Roman names scratched by ancient tourists.
The unfinished end room: work stopped when the king died.
fun_fact: In 1743 the traveller Richard Pococke labelled this simply 'Tomb A': it has been first in line for visitors for 2,000 years.
narration: The first tomb you meet on the road in, and often the quietest, belongs to Ramesses the Seventh. He died in his seventh year, so his workmen made do. They widened a corridor into a burial chamber and abandoned the little room beyond. Instead of a standing sarcophagus, the king was laid in a pit in the floor, under an upside-down stone box. The walls copy the tomb of Ramesses the Sixth, with gods of the night and the earth, and the sky goddess Nut stretched twice across the ceiling. Greek and Roman tourists came here too and left 132 graffiti. Look for their scratched names in the corridor as you walk in.

name: KV7: Ramesses II's own tomb, ruined by floods
note: Short. The great king's tomb is one of the most damaged: low in the valley floor, filled 11 times by flash floods with debris that set like concrete; Christian Leblanc's team has been clearing it for 30 years; the mummy was moved by the priests to the DB320 cache, now at NMEC; not open.
period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1279-1213 BC
summary: The tomb of Egypt's most famous king is one of the most ruined in the valley, packed by floods with debris that set like concrete.
look: Closed. The entrance is low on the valley floor, opposite KV5 and near Merenptah's tomb, KV8. Inside, a corridor descends about 58 metres before the axis bends towards the burial chamber; most of the decoration is lost.
story: Ramesses II started this tomb before the end of his second year, and the work took 10 to 12 years. The builders cut it low in the valley floor. Flash floods have filled it again and again with debris that hardened like cement, destroying most of the decoration. Christian Leblanc's Franco-Egyptian mission has been clearing and conserving it since 1991. In a recess appears Nefertari's cartouche: the only queen shown in her husband's tomb in the Ramesside period. Ramesses' mummy was moved by priests to his father Seti I's tomb, then to the Deir el-Bahari cache; it is now at NMEC. Greek visitors scratched names in the first corridor, among them Echeboulos of Rhodes and a man from Cyprus.
details: The entrance, low on the valley floor: compare it with tombs cut into the cliffs higher up.
Across the path: KV5, the tomb of his sons.
A few steps away: KV8, the tomb of his son and successor Merenptah.
fun_fact: The great king's granite sarcophagus was reused around 1000 BC by a high priest of Amun, Menkheperre.
narration: In front of you, low on the valley floor, is the tomb of Ramesses the Second, Egypt's most famous king, and one of the most ruined tombs in the valley. The builders cut it too low. For three thousand years flash floods have poured in, filling it with mud and stones that set almost like cement. Most of the paintings are gone. A French team led by Christian Leblanc has been clearing it since 1991. The king himself left long ago: priests moved his mummy to his father's tomb and then to a hidden cache, and today he lies in Cairo. Even ancient Greek tourists came by, one of them from Rhodes. Notice how the entrance sits almost at the level of the path.

name: Deir el-Bahari: the bay of temples
note: The natural amphitheatre under the Qurn with three temples: Mentuhotep II (c. 2050 BC, the model), Hatshepsut (c. 1470 BC) and Thutmose III (ruins between them, found 1961); the Coptic 'Northern Monastery' that gave the name; the Beautiful Festival of the Valley when Amun crossed the river to visit; the 1997 attack memorial context handled lightly; the royal cache tomb DB320 in the cliff behind; the little train.
period: Middle and New Kingdom, c. 2050-1425 BC; Coptic monastery 6th-8th century AD
summary: A natural amphitheatre of cliffs under the Qurn, where three kings across six centuries built terraced temples facing Karnak.
look: Face the cliffs: Hatshepsut's three terraces are in the middle, the low ruins of Mentuhotep II's temple to the left, and the scant remains of Thutmose III's temple tucked between them, higher up. The bay of cliffs rises behind towards the Qurn. The royal cache tomb is in a hidden recess of the cliffs further south.
story:
The Arabic name, Deir el-Bahari, means 'the Northern Monastery', after the Coptic monastery of Saint Phoibammon that stood on Hatshepsut's upper terrace from the 6th to the 8th century AD; its monks painted over some reliefs. But the bay was holy long before.

Around 2050 BC Mentuhotep II, the Theban king who reunited Egypt, built his temple and tomb here, terraced against the cliff. About five centuries later Hatshepsut placed her temple right next to it, borrowing its terraces and outdoing them. Thutmose III then squeezed a third temple, Djeser-Akhet, between the two, higher up; the Polish-Egyptian mission found it in 1961-62 under rockfall.

Orientation is meaning here. Hatshepsut's temple points across the Nile to Karnak. Each year, in the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Amun's statue left Karnak in its sacred boat, crossed the river and visited the temples of the west bank, while Theban families feasted at the tombs of their dead.

In a hidden recess of the southern cliffs, priests of the 21st Dynasty hid the royal mummies in tomb DB320, the great cache found in 1881; another cache, Bab el-Gasus, held 153 reburied priests.

The excavators read like a roll call: Mariette, Naville from the 1890s, Herbert Winlock for the Metropolitan Museum in 1911-31, and the Polish mission from 1961. In November 1997 the temple was the scene of a terrorist attack in which more than 60 people died; today security is tight and the site is calm. A small electric train runs from the visitor centre towards the temple, welcome in the heat.
details: Left of Hatshepsut's temple: the low ruined terraces of Mentuhotep II's temple, five centuries older.
Between the two, higher up: the scant remains of Thutmose III's temple, found in 1961-62.
The cliff behind the temple: its vertical folds echo the rows of columns below.
Turn round on any terrace: the temple's axis points across the river to Karnak.
fun_fact: The name means 'Northern Monastery': for the villagers who named it, the memorable thing here was a Christian monastery, not a pharaoh's temple.
narration: In front of you is Deir el-Bahari, a great bay of golden cliffs under the peak of the Qurn, and one of the most sacred places on the west bank. The name is Arabic for the Northern Monastery, because Coptic monks once lived on the top terrace of the temple you see. But the story starts thousands of years before them. Around 2050 BC, King Mentuhotep the Second, who reunited Egypt, built a terraced temple and tomb against these cliffs. Look to the left of the big temple: those low ruins are his. Five centuries later Hatshepsut chose the spot next door, borrowed his idea of terraces, and outdid it. Then Thutmose the Third squeezed a third temple in between them, higher up, now just a scatter of stones. Why here? Turn around and look east. The temples point across the river to Karnak. Once a year, at the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, the statue of Amun left Karnak in his gilded boat and crossed the Nile to visit, while families picnicked at the tombs of their ancestors. And there is a secret in these cliffs: in a hidden shaft to the south, priests hid the mummies of Egypt's greatest kings, found only in 1881. Now look at the cliff behind the temple and notice how its vertical folds echo the rows of columns: the architect designed with the mountain.

name: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut (Djeser-Djeseru)
note: 'Holy of Holies': three terraces with colonnades against the cliff, designed by Senenmut, aligned with Karnak across the river and with the winter solstice sunrise; the garden with incense trees from Punt (stumps visible), the sphinx avenue, the Osiride statues of the queen as king on the upper terrace, the erasure of her images by Thutmose III 20 years after her death, the Polish-Egyptian restoration since 1961; the route: ramp, Punt and Birth colonnades, Hathor and Anubis chapels, upper court, Amun sanctuary cut into the rock.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1472-1458 BC
summary: A woman who ruled as king built Egypt's most modern-looking temple: three colonnaded terraces set against a cliff, called 'Holy of Holies'.
look: Face the cliff: a long ramp climbs through three terraces, each fronted by a colonnade. On the middle terrace the Punt reliefs are in the colonnade to the left of the ramp and the Divine Birth to the right; the Hathor chapel is at the far left end, the Anubis chapel at the far right. On top, a row of statues of the queen as Osiris fronts the upper court, with the sanctuary cut into the rock behind.
story:
Hatshepsut, daughter of Thutmose I and widow of Thutmose II, ruled first as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III and then, by about his seventh year, as king herself. She called this temple Djeser-djeseru, 'Holy of Holies', built it between her 7th and 20th years, and dedicated it to Amun as 'a garden for my father Amun'. Its architect may have been her steward Senenmut, or the high priest Hapuseneb.

The temple is 273.5 metres long. A causeway about a kilometre long, lined with more than 100 sandstone sphinxes, the oldest known sphinx avenue, led up from the valley temple. Persea trees and T-shaped pools stood on the lower terrace. The axis points across the Nile to Karnak, and around the winter solstice the rising sun shines along it into the sanctuary.

About 20 years after her death, late in Thutmose III's reign, her names and images were hacked out and her statues smashed. Akhenaten's men later erased Amun. Later kings restored, the Ptolemies added chapels for healing gods, and Christians built a monastery on top.

Much of what you see has been rebuilt. The Polish-Egyptian mission has worked here since 1961, reassembling blocks and statues; the upper terrace reopened in 2000, the solar court in 2015 and the Amun sanctuary in 2017.
details: In front of the lower terrace: ancient tree pits and a stump, said to be from the incense trees of Punt.
Middle terrace, left colonnade: the expedition to Punt.
Middle terrace, right colonnade: the divine birth of Hatshepsut.
Upper terrace: the queen as Osiris, arms crossed, wearing a king's false beard.
At the top, turn round: the temple's axis runs straight across the fields to Karnak.
fun_fact: Many of Hatshepsut's statues in museums were pieced together from fragments that Herbert Winlock dug out of dumps near the causeway, which is why New York's Metropolitan Museum has so many.
narration: Before you is the temple of Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled Egypt as king for about 20 years. She called it Djeser Djeseru, the Holy of Holies, and dedicated it to the god Amun as, in her words, a garden for my father. Its clean lines and colonnades look almost modern, and they are set right against the cliff, so that the mountain itself becomes the back wall. Hatshepsut was the daughter of one king and the widow of another. When her husband died, she ruled for her young stepson, Thutmose the Third, and then simply made herself king, with the titles, the crown and even the false beard. The temple, possibly designed by her steward Senenmut, makes her case in stone. Walk up the ramp to the middle terrace. On your left, her ships sail to the land of Punt for incense. On your right, the god Amun himself fathers her. Higher up, the queen stands as Osiris, arms crossed. About 20 years after her death, Thutmose the Third had her name and her face hacked out all over Egypt, here included, and her statues smashed. What you see has been patiently pieced back together by a Polish and Egyptian team working here since 1961. When you reach the top terrace, turn around: the temple's axis runs straight across the river to Karnak, the house of her father Amun.

name: The Punt reliefs: an expedition to the land of incense
note: South colonnade of the middle terrace: five ships sail to Punt (Eritrea/Somalia/Sudan coast, year 9), the stilt houses, the fat Queen Ati and her donkey ('the donkey that carried his wife'), the loading of myrrh trees in baskets, baboons, giraffes, leopard skins, electrum weighed; the fish of the Red Sea identified by species; the first recorded botanical expedition; where the originals of some blocks are (Cairo); how to read the direction of the scenes.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, expedition in year 9 of Hatshepsut, c. 1471 BC
summary: A travel report in stone: Hatshepsut's ships sail to the incense land of Punt, meet its king and queen, and bring home live myrrh trees.
look: Middle terrace, in the colonnade to the left (south) of the central ramp. The scenes cover the back wall in registers: Punt itself with its stilt houses, the ships under sail and being loaded, and the cargo presented to Amun and measured. Queen Ati's figure here is a cast; the original block is in Cairo.
story:
In year 9 of her reign, about 1471 BC, Hatshepsut sent five ships down the Red Sea to Punt, the land of incense, under the chancellor Nehsi. Egyptians had traded with Punt since at least the 5th Dynasty, but nobody recorded a voyage like this. Where was Punt? Most scholars place it on the African coast of the southern Red Sea, around Eritrea, Sudan, northern Ethiopia or Somalia. Studies of mummified baboons, whose isotopes and DNA match animals from Eritrea and its region, point the same way.

The reliefs read like a reporter's notebook. The Puntites live in round houses on stilts, reached by ladders, among palms and myrrh trees. Their king, Parahu, comes forward with his wife, Queen Ati, a strikingly large woman whom modern doctors have diagnosed in every way imaginable; nearby is a small donkey, captioned as the one that carries his wife. The Egyptians load myrrh trees in baskets, ebony, ivory, gold, animal skins and baboons. Under the ships swim fish drawn so accurately that Red Sea species can be identified.

Back home the haul is presented to Amun, the incense measured in heaps and the gold weighed. The texts say 31 live myrrh trees came back, to be planted in Amun's garden here, which is why this is often called the first recorded plant-collecting expedition.

The original Queen Ati block went to Cairo in the 19th century; what you see is a cast. You may find the original at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label.
details: The village of Punt: round houses on stilts with ladders, under palms and trees.
Queen Ati, large and heavy-set, walking behind her slim husband, King Parahu.
Myrrh trees with their root balls in baskets, carried on poles up to the ships.
Under the ships: Red Sea fish and a turtle, drawn precisely enough to name the species.
Baboons on board among the cargo, bound for Thebes.
fun_fact: Some of the frankincense was charred and ground into kohl eyeliner: the first recorded use of the resin that way.
narration: You are standing in front of the Punt colonnade, the record of Hatshepsut's great trading expedition. In her ninth year, around 1471 BC, five ships sailed down the Red Sea to Punt, the land of incense. Most scholars now place Punt on the African coast, around Eritrea, and studies of mummified baboons brought back from there point the same way. The carvers recorded the trip like reporters. Look for the people of Punt living in round houses on stilts, reached by ladders, under palm trees. Their king comes to meet the Egyptians, followed by his wife, Queen Ati, a very large woman, and a little donkey whose caption says it is the animal that carries her. The Egyptians load their ships with ebony, ivory, gold, animal skins and baboons. Most precious of all are the myrrh trees, dug up with their roots and carried aboard in baskets slung from poles. The texts say 31 live trees came home, to be planted in Amun's garden right here. Under the ships, the sea is full of fish, drawn so accurately that experts can name the Red Sea species. One warning: the Queen Ati you see is a cast, and the original block is in a Cairo museum. Now find the myrrh trees in their baskets, and follow them up the gangplank.

name: The Divine Birth colonnade: how a woman became king
note: North colonnade of the middle terrace: Amun disguised as Thutmose I visits Queen Ahmose, 'the palace was flooded with the god's fragrance', Khnum shapes the baby and her ka on his wheel, Heket the frog gives life, the pregnant queen led to the birth room, the child presented to the gods; the theological proof that Hatshepsut was Amun's daughter and legitimate king; compare Amenhotep III's copy at Luxor Temple (22 Oct); the faces hacked out.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1470 BC
summary: Hatshepsut's answer to anyone who doubted a woman could be king: a strip cartoon in stone showing the god Amun fathering her.
look: Middle terrace, in the colonnade to the right (north) of the central ramp. Along the back wall the story runs in scenes: Amun with Queen Ahmose, Khnum at his potter's wheel, the pregnant queen led to the birth, the baby presented to the gods. Wherever Hatshepsut appeared, her figure has been chiselled out, so look for the gaps.
story:
How do you make a woman into a legitimate king? You show that the god Amun is her father. Hatshepsut's artists did exactly that here, in the oldest known version of a story that later kings copied.

Amun takes the form of her father, Thutmose I, and visits Queen Ahmose. The text says she woke to the god's fragrance, the scent of Punt incense filling the palace. They sit face to face, and the conception is told with complete decorum. Amun then orders the ram-headed potter god Khnum to make the child, and Khnum shapes two small figures on his wheel: the baby and her ka, her life force. The frog goddess Heket holds out the sign of life. Khnum and Heket lead the visibly pregnant queen to the birth, and the newborn is presented to Amun, whose greeting begins 'Welcome my sweet daughter, my favourite'.

Notice that the children on the wheel are drawn as boys. Kingship had a male template, and Hatshepsut used it; elsewhere she wears a king's kilt and false beard.

About 20 years after her death her figures were chiselled away, so in places Khnum and the goddesses fuss over an empty space. The idea outlived the vandalism: Amenhotep III had the same story carved for his own birth at Luxor Temple, which you will see on the 22nd.
details: Khnum, ram-headed, at his potter's wheel shaping two small figures: the child and her ka.
Heket, the frog-headed goddess, holding out the ankh, the sign of life.
Amun and Queen Ahmose seated face to face: the divine conception, told with great discretion.
The queen, visibly pregnant, led by the hand towards the birth.
Chiselled gaps: wherever Hatshepsut appeared, her figure has been cut away.
fun_fact: The birth story was such good propaganda that Amenhotep III copied it a few generations later, with himself as the baby.
narration: Here, on the right side of the middle terrace, Hatshepsut explains why a woman could be king. Her answer: because the god Amun is my father. Follow the story along the wall. Amun takes the form of the king, Thutmose the First, and visits Queen Ahmose in the palace. The text says she woke to the god's perfume, the smell of incense from Punt. They sit face to face, everything told with perfect decorum. Then Amun gives orders to Khnum, the ram-headed potter god. Look for Khnum at his wheel, shaping two small figures: the baby and her ka, her life force. Beside him the frog goddess Heket holds out the sign of life. The pregnant queen is led to the birth, and the newborn is presented to Amun, who greets her as his sweet daughter. Notice that the children are drawn as boys: kingship had a male template, and Hatshepsut used it. Now look for the gaps. About 20 years after her death, her figure was cut out wherever it appeared, so in places you see gods fussing over nothing at all. The idea outlived the vandalism: Amenhotep the Third copied the same story for himself at Luxor Temple, which you will see tomorrow. Find Khnum at his potter's wheel, and count the two little figures in front of him.

name: Chapels of Hathor and Anubis, and the upper terrace
note: Hathor chapel (south): Hathor-head capitals, the cow licking the queen's hand and suckling her, the festival boats, Senenmut's hidden self-portrait behind a door; Anubis chapel (north): the best-preserved colour, 12 fluted 'proto-Doric' columns, the ceiling of stars; upper terrace: 24 Osiride colossi restored, the festival court, the solar altar court, the sanctuary of Amun cut into the cliff later used by Ptolemies for Imhotep and Amenhotep son of Hapu as a healing shrine.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1470 BC; Ptolemaic additions 3rd-2nd century BC
summary: Side chapels with the temple's best colour, Hathor's cow licking the queen's hand, a hidden portrait of her architect, and a sanctuary cut into the rock.
look: Hathor's chapel is at the far left (south) end of the middle terrace, behind columns topped with Hathor's face; Anubis's chapel is at the far right (north) end, with 12 fluted columns and bright paint. The ramp leads up to the upper terrace: the Osiride statues, the festival court, the solar court with its altar to the right, and the Amun sanctuary cut into the cliff straight ahead.
story:
Hathor, the cow goddess who protected the western mountain, had her own chapel here, and Hatshepsut presented herself as Hathor's favourite. The entrance columns carry Hathor capitals: a woman's face with cow's ears. Inside, the goddess as a cow licks the queen's hand and suckles her. Senenmut, the queen's steward and probable architect, had small figures of himself placed behind doors in the temple, hidden whenever the doors stood open; Hatshepsut evidently allowed it.

The Anubis chapel has some of the best-preserved colour in the temple: Anubis escorting the queen, offerings piled high, a ceiling of stars. Its 12 fluted columns are sometimes called proto-Doric, because they recall Greek columns a thousand years later.

On the upper terrace the queen stands as Osiris in a row of statues 5.2 metres tall, rebuilt from fragments. Behind is the festival court with 26 columns, the solar court with a great open-air altar to Ra, and, on the main axis, the rock-cut sanctuary of Amun. Under Ptolemy VIII it became a shrine to Imhotep and Amenhotep son of Hapu, two wise men turned healing gods, and to the Greek goddess Hygieia. The sick came here hoping for a cure.
details: Hathor chapel entrance: column capitals carved as Hathor's face with cow's ears.
Inside the Hathor chapel: the cow goddess licking the queen's hand.
Door recesses in the chapels and sanctuary: small kneeling figures of Senenmut, hidden when the doors were open.
Anubis chapel: fluted columns and a starry ceiling in blue and yellow.
Upper terrace: the Osiride statues of the queen, 5.2 metres tall, arms crossed.
fun_fact: Under the Ptolemies Greek-speaking pilgrims came here to be healed by Imhotep, whom they called Asklepios: a little Epidaurus inside a pharaoh's temple.
narration: These side chapels and the upper terrace hold the temple's best colour. At the far left end of the middle terrace is the chapel of Hathor, the cow goddess of love and of this western mountain. Her columns end in her face, with a woman's features and a cow's ears. Inside, Hathor as a cow licks the queen's hand and suckles her like a calf. Behind some of the temple's doors are small figures of Senenmut, the queen's steward and probably its architect, carved where nobody would see him while the door stood open. At the opposite end is the chapel of Anubis, with fluted columns that look almost Greek, a thousand years early, and paint that still looks fresh. On the upper terrace, the queen stands as Osiris in a row of giant statues. The sanctuary of Amun is cut into the cliff, and much later, under the Ptolemies, it became a healing shrine where the sick prayed to Imhotep, whom the Greeks called Asklepios. In the Anubis chapel, look up at the starry ceiling.

name: Senenmut: the queen's architect, and more?
note: Of humble birth, 'steward of Amun', tutor of princess Neferure (the block statues holding her), overseer of works for Djeser-Djeseru; 25 statues, two tombs (TT71 and the unfinished TT353 under the temple forecourt with the earliest astronomical ceiling); the graffito near the temple of a man and a figure in royal headdress making love, the gossip then and now; his disappearance before her death; his name erased too.
period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Hatshepsut, c. 1479-1458 BC
summary: A provincial boy who became the queen's steward, guardian of her daughter, probable builder of her temple, and the subject of 3,500 years of gossip.
look: There is no single Senenmut monument here: he is all over the site. His second tomb, TT353, runs under the temple forecourt and is closed; small figures of him hide in door recesses inside the temple. Elsewhere you will meet his block statues holding the princess Neferure.
story:
Born to Ramose and Hatnofer, literate provincial people from Armant, south of Thebes, he carried a name meaning 'brother of Mut'. He became steward of Hatshepsut while she was queen, then high steward when she became king, and steward of the king's daughter Neferure: some of his block statues show the princess's head peeping out of his cloak. He oversaw the twin obelisks at Karnak and is most often credited with designing this temple.

He prepared two tombs: TT71 among the nobles, and TT353, a 97-metre passage cut under the temple forecourt, whose ceiling is the earliest known astronomical ceiling in Egypt. His sarcophagus is quartzite, a stone normally reserved for kings; it was never finished and is now in New York.

Were they lovers? A crude graffito in an unfinished tomb used as a workmen's shelter shows a man with a figure in royal regalia in an explicit act, and gossip has run ever since. Christine Meyer and others note that he appears alone with his parents on his monuments and may never have married. In the later years of the reign he drops out of the record; his burial place is unknown, and his tombs were heavily vandalised, perhaps as part of the attack on Hatshepsut's memory.
details: Under the temple forecourt: his tomb TT353, 97 metres long, with the oldest star ceiling in Egypt; closed.
Door recesses in the chapels and sanctuary: look for a small kneeling figure of Senenmut.
Some of his hidden figures survived the purge; others were hacked out.
fun_fact: His sarcophagus was carved from quartzite, a stone normally reserved for kings, which tells you how high he had climbed. It was never used.
narration: Let me introduce Senenmut, the man most often credited with designing this temple. He was born to modest, literate parents in Armant, south of Thebes, and rose to become steward to Hatshepsut, first when she was queen and then when she was king. He also looked after her only daughter, Neferure; some of his statues show the little princess's head peeping out of his cloak. He prepared two tombs, one with the oldest known star ceiling in Egypt, cut deep under this temple's forecourt. And he dared to place small figures of himself behind doors in the temple, where the gods would see him and visitors would not. Were he and the queen lovers? A rude ancient sketch in a nearby workmen's shelter suggests that people gossiped, and they have not stopped. Some Egyptologists think he never married at all. Then, in her later years, he vanishes from the record, and his burial has never been found. Look into the door recesses as you walk through the chapels: you might catch him kneeling there.

name: Temple of Mentuhotep II: the original
note: South of Hatshepsut's: the 11th Dynasty reunifier's terraced temple-tomb, 500 years older, with a central massif (pyramid or mound?) and the tombs of six royal wives, the Bab el-Hosan cenotaph where Carter's horse stumbled and found the black statue (GEM/Tahrir); his tomb 150 m into the cliff; Hatshepsut copied the terraces; the 60 soldiers' mass grave of Mentuhotep's wars found by Winlock nearby.
period: Middle Kingdom, 11th Dynasty, c. 2050 BC
summary: The temple that gave Hatshepsut her idea: the king who reunited Egypt built terraces against this cliff five centuries before her.
look: Just to the left (south) of Hatshepsut's temple: low ruined terraces, stumps of octagonal columns, and a square platform where the central building stood. From the courtyard, a passage 150 metres long runs down into the rock to the king's burial chamber. Usually you view it from the edge.
story:
Mentuhotep II was a Theban king who fought his way to rule all Egypt, ending the division of the First Intermediate Period; around his 39th year he took the name 'He who unifies the two lands'. The Turin King List gives him 51 years. His temple, Akh-sut, 'transfigured are the places of Nebhepetre', was new in Egypt: terraces, a covered walkway of 140 octagonal columns around a central core, a pillared hall cut back towards the cliff, and a grove of 55 sycamores in the courtyard. Whether the core carried a small pyramid, as Naville thought, or a flat roof, as Dieter Arnold argued, is still debated.

Women of his household were buried in pits under the terrace, among them Kawit, Henhenet, Ashayet, Kemsit and Sadeh, and a five-year-old girl, Mayet.
